### PREFACE TO THE ENGLISH TRANSLATION.

---

THERE are many respects in which Paracelsus at the present day seems to be little more than a name. Even among self-proclaimed mystics, the knowledge concerning him—which is very meager and very indefinite—is knowledge that has been obtained secondhand, in most cases from Eliphas Levi. In his *Dogma and Ritual of High Magic*, and again in his *History of Magic*, Levi has delivered an intuitive judgment upon the German "Monarch of Arcana," expressed in epigrams in the best French style.<note>The cures of Paracelsus were miraculous, and he deserved to have the name of Aureolus Paracelsus added to his name of Philippus Theophrastus Bombast, along with the title of divine.—*Dogma of High Magic*, ch. 1. Paracelsus, that reformer in magic, who has surpassed all other initiates by his own practical success.—*Ibid.*, ch. 5. Paracelsus, the most sublime of the Christian magi.—*Ibid.*, ch. 16. Paracelsus was a man of inspiration and miracles, but he exhausted his life with his devouring activity, or rather, he rapidly wore out and destroyed its physical shell: for men like Paracelsus can both use and abuse life fearlessly; they know well that they can no more die than grow old in this world.—*Ritual of High Magic*, ch. 2. Paracelsus was naturally aggressive and combative; his familiar spirit, he said, was concealed in the hilt of his great sword, which he never set aside. His life was incessant warfare; he traveled, he argued, he wrote, he taught. He was more attentive to physical results than to moral victories; so he was the first of practical magicians and the last of wise adepts. His philosophy was entirely based on sagacity, and he himself called it *Philosophia Sagax*. He divined more than anyone without ever completely understanding anything. There is nothing to equal his intuitions unless it be the boldness of his commentaries. He was a man of daring experiences; he was intoxicated by his opinions and his talk; he even got drunk otherwise, if we are to believe his biographers. The writings which he has left behind him are precious for science, but they must be read with caution; he may be called the divine Paracelsus, if the term is understood in the sense of a diviner; he is an oracle, but not invariably a true master. He is great as a physician above all, for he had discovered the Universal Medicine; yet he could not save his own life, and he died while still young, worn out by his toil and excesses, leaving a name of fantastic and doubtful glory based on discoveries by which his contemporaries did not profit. He died without having uttered his last message, and he is one of those mysterious personages of whom one may affirm, as of Enoch and St. John: he is not dead, and he will revisit the earth before the last day.—*History of Magic*, Book V., ch. 5. His success was prodigious, and never has any physician approached Paracelsus in the multitude of his marvelous cures.—*Dogma of High Magic*, ch. 16.</note> But, wherever it is derived from, the knowledge is thin and ghost-like. Paracelsus is indeed cited as an authority in occult science, as a great alchemist, a great magician, and a great doctor; he is somehow supposed to be living evidence of the "wisdom of a plundered past," and to offer a unique instance of malice on the part of the enemies of Hermetic philosophy, because such persons have dared to pronounce him an impostor. Thus there is a very strong opinion concerning him, which occultists and mystics of all schools have derived from a kind of mystical tradition, and this represents one side of modern thought concerning him. It is not an altogether satisfactory side, because it is not obtained firsthand. In this respect, however, it may compare—without suffering by comparison—with the alternative opinion which

<summary>The author explains that modern knowledge of Paracelsus is often superficial and secondhand, frequently based on the epigrammatic but critical writings of Eliphas Levi. prevails among non-mystics, namely, that Paracelsus was a great charlatan, though at the same time it is true that he was a great physician, at least for the time in which he lived. This judgment—perhaps even less than the other—is not based on any solid knowledge concerning the man or his writings.<note>M. Louis Figuier, the French scientist, who might otherwise perhaps be regarded as showing more than Gallic precision, may be cited in this connection. Referring to the fact that Paracelsus emphasized an opinion common among alchemists—namely, that astrology and magic are secondary aids to the seeker of the Great Work—he goes on to claim that the writings of Paracelsus are filled with foolish invocations to the invisible world. In fact, there is not a single treatise included in the large Geneva folio, nor is there any other surviving work attributed to Paracelsus and known to the current editor, that contains any invocations at all. M. Louis Figuier later states, apparently based solely on his intuition as a Frenchman and a man of talent, that the sooty Swiss physician enjoys only a disputed authority among alchemists (which is only partially true); he adds that Paracelsus was a theoretical writer who did not personally work to achieve the *Magnum Opus*, which, so far as it is possible to judge, is not true at all.</note> At the same time, it is noticeable that even hearsay condemnations admit that Paracelsus performed notable cures. How it happens that the application of what would be called a confused theory in both medicine and physics enabled its inventor to amaze his era with what seemed like miracles of the healing art would be a conundrum for such criticism, if that criticism knew anything about it. It is not a conundrum for the mystics, because they would reply that Paracelsus was a true adept, that his Hermetic teachings require interpretation, and that the key to their meaning would reveal to those who possess it an abundant treasure of wisdom, for which the literal meaning is only a *strange* veil. Between these views, it is unnecessary to make a choice here. The intention is to enable those who are interested in either view to judge this matter for themselves by placing before them completely, for the first time in an English translation, the Hermetic writings of Paracelsus. It is also intended, by way of a brief introduction, to note a few facts regarding the life of the author, which may be useful at the beginning of an inquiry.

There are, however, many debatable points regarding the life of Paracelsus that hardly need to be mentioned here. What portion of his long name belonged to him by birth or baptism; to what countries he actually traveled during the constant wanderings that ended only with his death; under what circumstances he died and the precise manner of his death—all these are points about which there is considerable uncertainty, and they are not likely to be settled today. Theophrastus and Bombast seem to have been assumed names, to one of which an unfortunate and, in some respects, undeserved meaning has since been attached. The surname of Paracelsus was given to him by his father in alchemy, and it signified that he was greater than Celsus, the physician of ancient fame. It is believed that he had only a doubtful right to the title of Hohenheim. His alternative name of Eremite suggests a monastic state, but the reference is simply to his birthplace, Maria Einsiedeln, or Our Lady of the Hermits, a short distance from Zurich. He appears to have been baptized Philippus Aureolus, and in his writings he indifferently

<meta>This page continues the Preface to the English Translation, providing a biographical sketch of Paracelsus's early life, family background, and the educational influences that shaped his alchemical theories.</meta>

[Paracelsus] describes himself as a Helvetian and a German. He was born in the year 1493, according to the tradition that is most generally accepted, but other dates have been suggested, the earliest being 1490. According to one account, he was descended from the ancient and honorable family of Bombast, which had lived for many generations at the castle of Hohenheim, near Stuttgart, Württemberg, but this is most likely a fabrication. His father was a physician of reputation, who is said to have possessed a large collection of curious books, and has also been described as a grand master of the Teutonic order; however, the precise meaning attached to this pretentious title is uncertain and the source is suspicious. His mother is variously identified as the matron of a hospital and "superintendent of the university of Einsiedeln." Paracelsus is reputed to have been their only child, born one year after marriage, but it has also been hinted that his parents were not married, and that the great master of Hermetic medicine was an illegitimate son. He is also said to have been castrated in his childhood, but there is reason to suppose that this was merely a theoretical explanation to account for his beardless and somewhat feminine appearance, and for that hatred of women which seems to have been one of his social characteristics and can be traced indirectly, but with sufficient clarity, in his writings.* About 1502, the family moved to Carinthia, and there the father continued to practice medicine until his death in 1534. From him, Paracelsus is supposed to have received the first basics of his education, and he entered the University of Basel at the age of sixteen, where he applied himself to the study of alchemy, surgery, and medicine. He had previously received some introduction to the first of these sciences through the works of Isaac the Hollander, which are said to have sparked his ambition to cure diseases with medicine superior to the <term>materia</term> at that time in use. It was from the same source that he derived the central principle which is stated everywhere in his writings: namely, that salt, sulphur, and mercury are the three elementary constituents of all substances. This doctrine, however, by no means originated with the first alchemist of Holland, and Isaac himself was a follower of Geber, Morien, and Arnold.† The actual initiation of Paracelsus into the mysteries of alchemy is, however, supposed to have been achieved under the...

<margin>
* Paracelsus was so free from all romantic weaknesses that he even made his gender seem doubtful.—*Dogme de la Haute Magie*, ch. 11.
† Living at the same time as Basilius Valentinus were Isaac the Hollander and his son, who are supposed to have worked successfully. They were the first alchemists of Holland, and their operations were highly regarded by Paracelsus, Boyle, and Kunckel. In practical chemistry, they followed the traditions of Geber, and their alchemical experiments are the most plain and explicit in the entire range of Hermetic literature. They worked mainly with metals, describing the details of every process minutely. Their lives are almost unknown. . . . They are estimated to have lived in the fifteenth century, based on the fact that they do not cite any philosophers after that period. They speak of Geber, Dastin, Morien, and Arnold, but not of more modern authorities; on the other hand, their references to <term>aquafortis</term> and <term>aqua regia</term>, which were discovered in the fourteenth century, prevent us from assigning their work to an earlier era. The two Isaacs were particularly skilled in the manufacture of enamels and artificial gemstones. They taught that the <term>Grand Magisterium</term> could convert a million times its own weight into gold, and declared that any person taking a small portion of the <term>philosophical stone</term> weekly will be forever preserved in perfect health, and his life will be extended to the very last hour which God has assigned to him.—*Lives of Alchemistical Philosophers*.

instruction of the Abbot Trithemius,* who is regarded as an adept of a high order, and had previously been the instructor of the more celebrated, though less illustrious, Henry Cornelius Agrippa.† From this mysterious ecclesiastic—who at the present day, as far as he is remembered at all, is best known by his treatises on cryptic writing—he is supposed to have acquired "the <term>Kabbalah</term> of the spiritual, astral, and material worlds." About 1516, he is still found at Basel pursuing his researches in mineralogy, medicine, surgery, and chemistry, under the guidance of Sigismund Fugger, a wealthy physician of that city. Subsequently, having gotten into some trouble with the authorities, he fled and began his nomadic life, which an apparently inaccurate tradition represents as having begun at the age of twenty. Although his father was still alive, he appears to have been without any means of subsistence and supported himself, like many distressed students of that period, by psalm-singing, astrological predictions, chiromantic soothsaying, and, it is even said, by necromantic practices. He wandered through Germany, Hungary, Italy, France, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, and Russia. In the last-mentioned country, if it is true that he ever reached it, he is reported to have been made prisoner by the Tartars, to have been brought before "the Great Khan," to have become a favorite at the court of that potentate, and to have accompanied his son on an embassy from China to Constantinople. In spite of the instruction of Trithemius, he apparently had something to learn, and that was nothing less than "the supreme secret of alchemy," the "universal dissolvent," the <term>*Azoth*</term>, <term>*alcahest*</term>, or sophic fire. This was imparted to him by a generous Arabian, about whom no other particulars are available. It is easy to see that the greater part of this nomadic legend is purely fabulous, and so also, in all probability, is his subsequent journey to India and Egypt. It is not an unusual device to account for obscure periods in the lives of Hermetic philosophers by extensive Eastern travels. However this may be, Paracelsus ultimately returned to Europe and passed along the Danube into Italy, where he appears as an army surgeon and where his wonderful cures also began. He is said to have re-entered Germany in 1526, at the age of thirty-two, and if this is accepted, the date 1516, when he is supposed to have been at work with Sigismund Fugger, will be found approximately correct. It is to the period immediately following his return that most of his biographers assign his induction into a professorship of physics, medicine, and surgery at the university he entered

---

<note>* Trithemius was a monk of the Benedictine order who began life as a beggar child setting forth in search of knowledge. He was received into a convent at Trier, where he made astounding progress in his studies. Having exhausted the possibilities of his teachers, he went to Louvain, then to Heidelberg, and subsequently to Mainz. He became familiar with Oriental languages, pagan and Christian philosophy, astronomy, and alchemy. He was a theologian, a poet, an astronomer, and a necromancer. He took monastic vows in 1482, and in the following year, he became the abbot of a convent at Sponheim, which he quickly transformed into a sanctuary of art and the sciences. He was subsequently made superior of an abbey at Würzburg, and there it would appear he remained until his death in the year 1516. as a youth. This was a position of some importance, and it was offered to him at the request of Erasmus and Oecolampadius. “There, in his lectures, he taught internal medicine, denounced the outdated systems of Galen and other authorities, and began his instruction by burning the works of these masters in a brass pan with sulfur and nitre. He created countless enemies through his arrogance and his innovations, but the value of his mineral medicines was proven by the cures he performed.* These cures only increased the hatred of his persecutors, and Paracelsus, with characteristic defiance, invited the faculty to a lecture in which he promised to teach the greatest secret of medicine. He began by uncovering a dish that contained excrement. The doctors, indignant at the insult, departed hastily, with Paracelsus shouting after them: ‘If you will not hear the mysteries of putrefactive fermentation, you are unworthy of the name of physicians.’” It will be easily understood that the Hermetic doctor did not keep his professorship at Basel for long. He came into conflict with the municipal authorities, and for a second time he was forced to flee the place. He returned once more to a wandering lifestyle. In 1528, he proceeded to Colmar; in 1530, he is found at Nuremberg, in a dispute, as usual, with the medical faculty, by whom he was denounced as an impostor. However, the tables were turned on his opponents after his successful treatment of several severe cases of elephantiasis. For the ten years following this date, there are no certain records of his movements; he usually stayed at inns and other public places, still performing cures that were astonishing for the period, and, according to the accusations of his enemies, also drinking to excess.† The testimony of Oporinus on this point is very clear, though it has been indignantly rejected by some of his later defenders. In 1541, Paracelsus was invited by Archbishop Ernst to settle at Salzburg, and there, according to one account, he died on September 24 of the same year, but the manner of his death, like that of his birth, has been the subject of contradictory reports.‡ According to an alternative statement, it occurred on a bench by the kitchen fire in a Strasbourg inn. One writer suggests the event was accelerated by a fight with assassins in the pay of the orthodox medical faculty.

There can be no doubt that Paracelsus obtained a wide, though not altogether happy, reputation during the brief period of his turbulent life, and there is also no doubt that this was immeasurably increased after death.

* Paracelsus, who was the first to make zinc known, has earned an immense and deserved reputation by introducing into medicine the use of chemical compounds derived from metals. It is not at all inaccurate to claim that he founded a new school in both medicine and alchemy. The commentaries on his medical system grew into a body of literature that is formidable in its extent, at least; from the mystical physics of his alchemical teachings, the Rosicrucian doctrines developed in the early part of the following century. The works of Benedictus Figulus prove that he was idolized by his disciples. He was called the noble and beloved monarch, the German Hermes, the Philosopher Trismegistus, our dear teacher and King of Arts, Theophrastus of blessed memory and immortal fame. The collection of his authentic writings was gathered with devout care, and as a result of his fame, many fake treatises were eventually attributed to him.<note>Dear friends, we have especially to complain about the devilishly cunning way the works of Theophrastus have been suppressed until now; only a few of them (and those considered the very worst) have appeared in print. For although his books on Astronomy, Philosophy, Chemistry, Cabala, and Theology—numbering some thousand volumes—have been collected from all the countries where Theophrastus lived and traveled, this has only been done out of a greedy desire for riches. Because they have been traded and sold for large sums, they have become scattered among the courts of princes and nobles, while the rest of Christendom—for whose use and benefit Theophrastus wrote—has no access to them. His theological works in particular (because they destroy the godless and do not suit the people of this world—those who serve only their own appetites and are deceived by the devil) have been completely suppressed until now. . . . But on the Last Day, I, along with all true Sons of the Doctrine, will demand an account from those who have . . . shut Truth away in boxes, walls, and vaults, and behind locks and bolts. These precious and revered writings were ordained by God in our modern times, through Theophrastus, for the use and well-being of all Christendom. Regarding our dear, highly favored Monarch and Teacher, . . . we, for our part, will not suppress the story of his life or his well-deserved praise, . . . given to him by God, the angels, and the whole heavens, but will sincerely defend his honor and teaching until the very end of our lives. — Benedictus Figulus, *A Golden and Blessed Casket of Nature's Marvels.*</note> Students drawn to his doctrines traveled far to find like-minded people to compare observations and to unravel the mystery of his teachings. In the course of these inquiries, it became clear from the experience of his followers that his prescriptions in many cases were not to be understood literally, even when they seemed to be standard formulas dealing with the known materials of medicine. It is hardly necessary to add that in alchemical matters, the literal meaning of his teachings was found to need interpretation even more.

The very strange influence Paracelsus exerted for about two hundred years over certain areas of restless experimentation and speculation remains unwritten, and it would be interesting to trace it here, if it were possible within the limits of a preface. However, such an ambitious task is beyond those limits and should perhaps be more wisely left to others; it is primarily a part of the history of medicine and requires an expert in the medical literature and medical knowledge of the past. The following translations concern only the Hermetic writings of Paracelsus, excluding many extensive treatises on surgery and the causes and cures of disease. They include what Paracelsus himself would have included in a collection of his alchemical writings, which is far more than what is usually understood by that term. For Paracelsus, the field of alchemy was not limited to the transformation of metals. Broadly speaking, it was the development of hidden possibilities or virtues in any substance, whether by God, man, or

Nature. Thus, it included the philosophy of creation and dealt with the first matter as it developed into the universe through Divine Power. It also included the natural evolution that takes place around us, whether in the formation of metals within the earth or the formation of animals in the matrix. Finally, it included the development, through human skill and art, of whatever was capable of improvement among the products of Nature. Thus, the Hermetic and alchemical writings of Paracelsus have a wider scope than might at first be inferred from the title. The purpose of this translation is entirely unpretentious. It aims to provide, for the first time, a complete and faithful text of everything Paracelsus is known or supposed to have written on the subject of alchemy and Hermetic medicine. It does not attempt to distinguish between the works falsely attributed to him; regarding this question, there are no satisfactory standards of criticism, because those indicated by the old author of the *Onomastikon* are arbitrary and impractical. A careful reader will probably view the "Aurora of the Philosophers" with suspicion, at least in its present state, and he will possibly completely reject the treatise "Concerning the Spirits of the Planets." There is nothing else in these volumes, except the uncertain "Manual," which based on internal evidence is unlikely to be the work of Paracelsus. It is unnecessary to enter into the question raised by some of his biographers regarding his employment of scribes, who transcribed his dictations and may have misrepresented their master. The text adopted for translation is the Latin Geneva folio of 1658, in four volumes. The *bizarre* mixture of Latin and Old German in which Paracelsus originally wrote presents many difficulties that are unnecessary to struggle with, as the collected Latin edition appears to satisfactorily represent both the letter and the spirit of the originals.

It also seems desirable to state that a comparison of the medical and chemical knowledge possessed by Paracelsus with modern chemistry and medicine is outside the scope of this edition, as it is impossible within the limits of two volumes. There is no doubt that it would be an interesting and important task to establish the exact position of Paracelsus, not only regarding modern knowledge but also regarding the science that preceded him; it is hoped that such a work will eventually be performed. If students regard this translation as definitive, or at least as a satisfactory foundation for a complete understanding of the sage of Hohenheim, and if the support essential for such a long and costly undertaking is adequately provided, it is proposed that—after a reasonable interval—these two volumes of unannotated text will be followed by a third. This third volume will contain all the materials required to understand Paracelsus and will further trace, methodically and historically, the development of alchemical symbolism and the growth of chemical knowledge from the Byzantine period to the dawn of the Reformation. It is anticipated that this inquiry will establish for the first time the true objectives of Hermetic physics and the position that must be assigned to Paracelsus in relation to it. Only the less ambitious but essential preliminary to this inquiry has been attempted here; the simple provision of a text, as understandable as circumstances permit, has truly been no small task, nor should it be viewed as the work of just one person. The editor has accomplished his task with the collaboration of other specialists and is responsible only for certain portions of the actual translation, and for its general revision and comparison. The work, as it stands, consists of (*a*) the large body of literature, entire and unabridged, attributed to Paracelsus, and treating directly of alchemy and the transcendental doctrines and physics of the *Magnum Opus*; (*b*) the whole Paracelsian literature of the Great Elixir and the Universal Medicine; (*c*) as much of the Hermetic philosophy and cosmogony of Paracelsus as has been judged necessary to illustrate his alchemical teachings; (*d*) one important treatise illustrating the application by Paracelsus of metallic and mineral substances to the treatment of diseases; (*e*) an exhaustive collection of alchemical references scattered through the <term>chirurgical</term> <note>surgical</note> works of Paracelsus. Thus, the present edition is practically inclusive of everything except the exoteric medicine of Paracelsus, which is thought to be of inferior importance to the modern student.

# THE <term>CŒLUM PHILOSOPHORUM</term>,

### THE SCIENCE AND NATURE OF ALCHEMY, AND WHAT OPINION SHOULD BE FORMED OF IT.

->*Regulated by the Seven Rules or Fundamental Canons according to the seven commonly known metals; and containing a preface with certain treatises and appendices.*<-

### THE PREFACE
### OF THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS TO ALL ALCHEMISTS AND READERS OF THIS BOOK.

You who are skilled in alchemy, and as many others as promise yourselves great riches or chiefly desire to make gold and silver—which alchemy in different ways promises and teaches—equally, too, you who willingly undergo toil and hardships, and do not wish to be freed from them until you have attained your rewards and the fulfillment of the promises made to you: experience teaches this every day, that out of thousands of you, not even one accomplishes his desire. Is this a failure of nature or of art? I say no; rather, it is the fault of fate or the lack of skill of the operator.

Since, therefore, the characters of the signs, of the stars and planets of heaven, together with the other names, inverted words, recipes, materials, and instruments are thoroughly well known to those who are acquainted with this art, it would be completely unnecessary to return to these same subjects in the present book, although the use of such signs, names, and characters at the proper time is by no means without advantage.

But in this book, another way of treating alchemy will be observed, different from the previous method and derived by Seven Canons from the sevenfold series of the metals. This will not provide an opportunity for a pompous display of words; nevertheless, in the consideration of those Canons, everything that should be separated from alchemy will be treated at sufficient length. Moreover, many secrets of other things are contained here. From this also result certain marvelous speculations and new operations which frequently

<summary>Paracelsus introduces the Cœlum Philosophorum, addressing the common failures of alchemists and proposing a new approach to the art based on Seven Canons related to the seven metals.</summary>
<keywords>Paracelsus, alchemy, Seven Canons, gold, silver, Cœlum Philosophorum, Book of Vexations, metallurgical philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 23 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of the Cœlum Philosophorum, further explaining the necessity of the Seven Canons and the role of fire in the alchemical process.</meta>

differ from the writings and opinions of ancient practitioners and natural philosophers, but have been discovered and confirmed by full proof and experimentation.

Moreover, in this art, nothing is more true than this, though it is little known and gains little confidence. All the fault and cause of difficulty in alchemy—by which many people are reduced to poverty and others labor in vain—is wholly and solely due to the operator's lack of skill and the defect or excess of materials, whether in quantity or quality. From this, it follows that in the course of the operation, things are wasted or reduced to nothing. If the true process is found, the substance itself, while transmuting, approaches perfection more and more each day. The straight road is easy, but it is found by very few.

Sometimes it may happen that a speculative artist may, by his own eccentricity, think out some new method in alchemy for himself, whether the consequence is something or nothing. He needs to do nothing in order to reduce something to nothing and then bring something back out of nothing. Yet this proverb of the skeptical is not entirely false. Destruction perfects that which is good, for the good cannot appear because of what conceals it. The good is least good while it is thus concealed. The concealment must be removed so that the good may be able to appear freely in its own brightness. For example, the mountain, the sand, the earth, or the stone in which a metal has grown is such a concealment. Each one of the visible metals is a concealment of the other six metals.

By the element of fire, all that is imperfect is destroyed and taken away—for instance, the five metals: Mercury, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Saturn.<note>The three primary substances are proven only by fire, which manifests them as pure, naked, clean, and simple. In the absence of any ordeal by fire, no proof of a substance is possible. For fire tests everything, and when the impure matter is separated, the three pure substances are displayed.—*On the Origin of Diseases from the Three Primary Substances (Paramirum)*, Book I, ch. 1. Fire separates that which is constant or fixed from that which is fleeting or volatile.—*On Metallic Diseases*, Book II, Tract I. Fire is the father or active principle of separation.—“Third Fragment on Tartar,” from the *Medical Fragments.*</note> On the other hand, the perfect metals, Sol and Luna, are not consumed in that same fire. They remain in the fire; and at the same time, out of the other imperfect ones that are destroyed, they assume their own body and become visible to the eyes. How and by what method this occurs can be gathered from the Seven Canons. From these, one may learn the nature and properties of each metal, how it affects other metals, and its powers when mixed with them.

But this should be noted first of all: these Seven Canons cannot be perfectly understood by every casual reader at a first glance or a single reading. An inferior intelligence does not easily perceive occult and abstruse subjects. Each one of these Canons demands significant discussion. Many people, puffed up with pride, imagine they can easily comprehend all that this book contains. Thus, they dismiss its contents as useless and futile, thinking they have something far better of their own, and that they can therefore afford to despise what is included here.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that failures in alchemy are due to human error rather than the art itself, explaining that fire acts as a purifying agent that reveals perfect metals by destroying their concealments. He warns that the Seven Canons require deep study and cannot be understood through a superficial reading.</summary>

# THE CŒLUM PHILOSOPHORUM.

---

## PART I.
## THE SEVEN CANONS OF THE METALS.

---

### THE FIRST CANON.
#### Concerning the Nature and Properties of Mercury.*

ALL things are concealed in all. One among them all is the concealer of the rest—their physical vessel, external, visible, and movable. All liquefactions are manifested in that vessel. For the vessel is a living and physical spirit, and so all coagulations or solidifications enclosed in it, when prevented from flowing and surrounded, are not content with that state. No name can be found for this liquefaction by which it may be designated, and even less can one be found for its origin. And since no heat is so strong as to be equal to it, it should be compared to the fire of Gehenna. A liquefaction of this kind has no connection with others produced by the heat of natural fire, or solidified or coagulated by natural cold. These solidifications, because of their weakness, are unable to persist within Mercury, and therefore, for that reason, he completely scorns them. From this, one may gather that elementary powers, in their process of destruction, can add nothing to nor take away anything from celestial powers (which are called Quintessence or its elements), nor do they have any capacity for operating. Celestial and infernal powers do not obey the four elements, whether they be dry, moist, hot, or cold. None of them has the ability to act against a Quintessence; instead, each one contains within itself its own powers and means of action.<note>By the mediation of Vulcan, or fire, any metal can be generated from Mercury. At the same time, Mercury is imperfect as a metal; it is semi-generated and lacks coagulation, which is the goal of all metals. Up to the halfway point of their generation, all metals are Mercury. Gold, for example, is Mercury; but it loses the Mercurial nature through coagulation, and although the properties of Mercury are present in it, they are dead, for their vitality is destroyed by coagulation. — *On Metallic Diseases (De Morbis Metallicis)*, Book III, Treatise II, ch. 2. The essences and arcanas that are hidden in all the six metals are to be found in the substance of Mercury. — *Ibid.*, ch. 3. There are two kinds of Mercury: the fixed Mercury of earth and another kind which descends from the daily constellation. — *Ibid.*, Book I, Treatise II, ch. 4. Just as there is a red and white Sulphur of Marcasites, a yellow, red, and black Sulphur of Talc, a purple and black Sulphur of the Cachimiæ, a Sulphur of Cinnabar, and, in like manner, of marble, amethyst, etc., so is there a special Mercury of Copper, Plumbago, Zinc, Arsenic, etc. — *Ibid.* Mercury is not Quicksilver, for Mercury is dead, while Quicksilver is living. — *On Dropsy (De Hydropisi)*.</note>

---

<note>Nothing of true value is located in the body of a substance, but in its virtue. And this is the principle of the Quintessence, which reduces, for example, 20 lbs. into a single ounce, and that ounce far exceeds the entire 20 lbs. in potency. Hence, the less there is of physical body, the more the virtue increases in proportion. — *On the Origin of Invisible Diseases (De Origine Morborum Invisibilium)*, Book IV.</note>

## THE SECOND CANON.

### CONCERNING THE NATURE AND PROPERTIES OF JUPITER.

In that which is visible (that is to say, the body of Jupiter), the other six physical metals are spiritually hidden, though some are more deeply and firmly concealed than others. Jupiter contains no Quintessence in his composition but is made of the four elements. Because of this, his melting is brought about by the application of a moderate fire, and, similarly, he is solidified by moderate cold. He has an affinity with the melting processes of all other metals. For the more similar he is to another nature, the more easily he is joined to it. For the interaction of those closely related is easier and more natural than those that are distant. A distant body does not exert pressure on the other. Likewise, it is not feared, even if it is very powerful. This is why people do not strive for the higher orders of creation; they are far away, and people do not see their glory. Similarly, they do not greatly fear those of a lower order because they are distant, and no living person knows their condition or has experienced the suffering of their punishment. For this reason, an infernal spirit is considered to be nothing. More distant objects are valued less and occupy a lower status for that reason, since every object is improved or transformed according to the suitability of its position. This can be proved by various examples.

Therefore, the further Jupiter is found to be from Mars and Venus, and the closer it is to Sol and Luna, the more "gold-like" or "silver-like" qualities (if I may say so) it contains within its body. In this state, it is found to be greater, stronger, more visible, more tangible, more lovely, more acceptable, more distinguished, and more genuine than in some distant body. Furthermore, the more distant a thing is, the less it is valued in all the ways mentioned above, since what is present is always preferred over what is absent. Just as what is near is clear, what is distant is hidden. Therefore, as an Alchemist, you must seriously consider how you can push Jupiter away into the distant and hidden place occupied by Sol and Luna, and how, in turn, you can call Sol and Luna from their distant positions to the near place where Jupiter is physically located, so that Sol and Luna may also be physically present before your eyes. There are several practical recipes for the transformation of metals from imperfection to perfection. Mix one with the other. Then, separate the pure one from the rest. This is nothing other than the process of exchange, established by perfect alchemical work. Note that Jupiter contains much gold and quite a bit of silver. Apply Saturn and Luna to it, and the remaining Luna will be increased.<note>Tin, or Jupiter, is pure Mercury solidified with a small amount of Salt, but combined with a larger proportion of white Sulphur. It derives its colors—white, yellow, or red—from its Mercury. Its sublimation is also achieved by Mercury, and its breakdown by Salt, and it is refined and dissolved by these.—*Concerning the Element of Water*, Treatise III, Chapter 6.</note>

<summary>This page defines the alchemical nature of Jupiter (tin), explaining its elemental composition and its relationship to other metals. Paracelsus describes the process of transmutation as moving these metallic spirits between "near" and "remote" states to achieve perfection.</summary>

### THE THIRD CANON.
#### CONCERNING MARS AND HIS PROPERTIES.

The six hidden metals have expelled the seventh from among them and have made it physical, leaving it with little effectiveness and imposing upon it great hardness and weight. Since this is the case, they have shaken off all their own power of solidification and hardness, which they display in this other body. On the contrary, they have retained within themselves their color and fluidity, along with their nobility. It is very difficult and taxing for a prince or a king to be produced from an unfit and common man. But Mars acquires dominion with a strong and combative hand and seizes the position of king. He should, however, be on his guard against traps, so that he is not taken captive suddenly and unexpectedly. It must also be considered by what method Mars may be able to take the place of the king, and how Sol and Luna, with Saturn, may hold the place of Mars.*

### THE FOURTH CANON.
#### CONCERNING VENUS AND ITS PROPERTIES.

The other six metals have rendered Venus an external body by means of all their color and method of melting. To understand this, it may be necessary for us to show, through some examples, how a visible thing may be made hidden, and a hidden thing made physically visible by means of fire. Whatever is combustible can be naturally transformed by fire from one form into another—namely, into lime, soot, ashes, glass, colors, stones, and earth. This earth can again be reduced to many new metallic bodies. If a metal, too, is burnt or made brittle by old rust, it can again acquire malleability through the application of fire.†

### THE FIFTH CANON.
#### CONCERNING THE NATURE AND PROPERTIES OF SATURN.

Of his own nature, Saturn speaks thus: The other six have cast me out as their examiner. They have thrust me out from them and from a spiritual place. They have also added a corruptible body as a place to live, so that I may be what they neither are nor desire to become. My six brothers are spiritual, and because of that, it follows that as often as I am put in the fire, they penetrate my body and perish in the fire along with me. Sol and Luna

When there is more Salt than the composition of Sulphur requires, the metal can in no way be made, for it depends upon an equal weight of each. For fluidity comes from Mercury and solidification from Salt. Accordingly, if there is too much Salt, it becomes too hard.—*De Elemento Aquæ*, Lib. IV., Tract III., c. 4.</note>

### THE SIXTH CANON.
#### CONCERNING LUNA AND THE PROPERTIES THEREOF.

The endeavor to make <term>Saturn</term> or <term>Mars</term> out of <term>Luna</term> involves no lighter or easier work than to make <term>Luna</term>, with great gain, out of <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Mars</term>, <term>Venus</term>, or <term>Saturn</term>. It is not useful to transmute what is perfect into what is imperfect, but rather the latter into the former. Nevertheless, it is well to know what the material of <term>Luna</term> is, or from where it proceeds. Whoever is not able to consider or find this out will likewise be unable to make <term>Luna</term>. It will be asked, What is <term>Luna</term>? It is among the seven metals which are spiritually concealed, itself the seventh, external, corporeal, and material. For this seventh always contains the six metals spiritually hidden within itself. And the six spiritual metals do not exist without one external and material metal. So also no corporeal metal can have a place or essence without those six spiritual ones. The seven corporeal metals mix easily by means of liquefaction, but this mixture is not useful for making <term>Sol</term> or <term>Luna</term>. For in that mixture each metal remains in its own nature, either fixed in the fire or fleeing from it. For example, mix, in any way you can, <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Mars</term>, <term>Venus</term>, <term>Sol</term>, and <term>Luna</term>. It will not result from this that <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term> will so change the other five that, by the agency of <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>, these will become <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>. For though all be liquefied into a single mass, nevertheless each remains in its own nature, whatever it is. This is the judgment which must be passed on corporeal mixture. But concerning spiritual mixture and

Regarding the communion of the metals, it should be known that no separation or mortification is spiritual, because such spirits can never exist without bodies. Though the body should be taken away from them and mortified a hundred times in one hour, they would nevertheless always acquire another much more noble than the previous one. And this is the transposition of the metals from one death to another—that is to say, from a lesser degree into one greater and higher, namely, into <term>Luna</term>; and from a better into the best and most perfect, that is, into <term>Sol</term>, the brilliant and altogether royal metal. It is most true, then, as frequently said above, that the six metals always generate a seventh, or produce it from themselves, clear in its *esse*.

A question may arise: If it is true that <term>Luna</term> and every metal derives its origin and is generated from the other six, what then is its property and its nature? To this we reply: From <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Mars</term>, <term>Venus</term>, and <term>Sol</term>, nothing and no other metal than <term>Luna</term> could be made. The cause is that each metal has two good virtues of the other six, of which there are twelve in total. These are the spirit of <term>Luna</term>, which may thus be made known in a few words. <term>Luna</term> is composed of the six spiritual metals and their virtues, of which each possesses two. Altogether, therefore, twelve are thus placed in one corporeal metal, which are compared to the seven planets and the twelve celestial signs. <term>Luna</term> has from the planet <term>Mercury</term>, and from <term>Aquarius</term> and <term>Pisces</term>, its liquidity and bright white color. ☿, ♒, and ♓. So <term>Luna</term> has from <term>Jupiter</term>, with ♐ (<term>Sagittarius</term>) and <term>Taurus</term>, its white color and its great firmness in fire. ♃, ♐, ♉. <term>Luna</term> has from <term>Mars</term>, with <term>Cancer</term> and <term>Aries</term>, its hardness and its clear sound. ♂, ♋, and ♈. <term>Luna</term> has from <term>Venus</term>, with <term>Gemini</term> and <term>Libra</term>, its measure of coagulation and its malleability. ♀, ♊, and <term>Libra</term>. From <term>Saturn</term>, with <term>Virgo</term> and ♏ (<term>Scorpio</term>), its homogeneous body, along with gravity. ♄, ♍, and ♏. From <term>Sol</term>, with <term>Leo</term> and <term>Virgo</term>, its spotless purity and great constancy against the power of fire. ☉, ♌, and ♍. Such is the knowledge of the natural exaltation and of the course of the spirit and body of <term>Luna</term>, with its composite nature and wisdom briefly summarized.

Furthermore, it should be pointed out what kind of a body such metallic spirits acquire in their primitive generation by means of celestial influx. For the metal-digger, when he has crushed the stone—as contemptible as it is in appearance—liquefies it, corrupts it, and altogether mortifies it with fire. Then this metallic spirit, in such a process of mortification, receives a better and more noble body, not brittle but malleable. Then comes the <term>Alchemist</term>, who again corrupts, mortifies, and artificially prepares such a metallic body. Thus once more that spirit of the metal assumes a more noble and more perfect body, putting itself forward clearly into the light, unless it is <term>Sol</term> or <term>Luna</term>. Then at last the metallic spirit and body are perfectly united, are safe from the corruption of elementary fire, and are also incorruptible.

This is the most pure quality of <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Salt</term>, and <term>Sulphur</term>, most clear.</note>

### THE SEVENTH CANON.

### Concerning the Nature of Sol and Its Properties.

The seventh after the six spiritual metals is physically <term>Sol</term>, which in itself is nothing but pure fire. What in outward appearance is more beautiful, more brilliant, more clear and perceptible, or a heavier, colder, or more homogeneous body to behold? And it is easy to perceive the cause of this: namely, that it contains within itself the solidifications of the other six metals, from which it is formed externally into one most compact body. Its liquefaction proceeds from elementary fire, or is caused by the melting of <term>Mercury</term>, along with <term>Pisces</term> and <term>Aquarius</term>, which are concealed spiritually within it. The most obvious proof of this is that <term>Mercury</term> is easily mingled physically with the <term>Sun</term> as if in an embrace. But for <term>Sol</term>, once the heat is withdrawn and the cold sets in after liquefaction, to coagulate and become hard and solid, it requires the other five metals, whose nature it embraces within itself—<term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Mars</term>, <term>Venus</term>, and <term>Luna</term>. In these five metals, the cold dwellings with their governing powers are especially found. Hence it happens that <term>Sol</term> can only be liquefied with difficulty without the heat of fire, because of the cold previously mentioned. For <term>Mercury</term> cannot assist with its natural heat or liquefaction, nor defend itself against the cold of the five metals, because the heat of <term>Mercury</term> is not sufficient to keep <term>Sol</term> in a state of liquefaction. Therefore, <term>Sol</term> must obey the five metals rather than <term>Mercury</term> alone. <term>Mercury</term> itself has no function of its own except to always flow. Hence it happens that in the solidification of the other metals it can achieve nothing, since its nature is not to make anything hard or solid, but liquid. To make things fluid is the nature of heat and life, but cold has the nature of hardness, consolidation, and immobility, which is compared to death. For example, if the six cold metals—<term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Venus</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Mars</term>, <term>Venus</term>, <term>Luna</term>—are to be liquefied, they must be brought to that condition by the heat of fire. Snow or ice, which are cold, will not produce this effect, but rather will cause hardening. As soon as the metal liquefied by fire is removed from the heat, the cold, seizing it, makes it hard, solidified, and immovable of itself. But so that <term>Mercury</term> may remain fluid and alive continually, tell me, I pray you, whether this is achieved by heat or cold? Whoever answers that this is brought about by a cold and damp nature, and that it derives its life from cold—the proponent of this opinion, having no knowledge of Nature, is led astray by common ignorance. For the common man judges only falsely, and always holds firmly to his error. So then, let him who loves truth withdraw from such views. <term>Mercury</term>, in fact, does not live at all from cold, but from a warm and fiery nature.

---

These two essences, namely, the white and the purple, are separated by the <term>Archeus</term>; and out of the first, fixed and solidified, silver is formed, while from the purple, gold is generated, which is the most noble <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Salt</term>, and <term>Mercury</term>, separated from all other colors and consisting of purple alone. Its clay-like or yellow appearance is explained by the subtlety and clarity of the metal, because all the dull colors are removed. In Silver, the most prevalent colors are green and blue, which are respectively derived from the <term>Mercury</term> and the <term>Salt</term>, with the <term>Sulphur</term> contributing nothing to the coloring. On the other hand, in gold, the purple color is derived from <term>Salt</term>, the transparent redness from <term>Sulphur</term>, and the yellow from <term>Mercury</term>. — *Ibid.*, chapter 8.

Whatever lives is fire, because heat is life, but cold is the cause of death. The fire of <term>Sol</term> is pure in itself; it is not indeed alive, but hard, and it shows the color of sulfur in that yellow and red are mixed within it in due proportion. The five cold metals are <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Mars</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Venus</term>, and <term>Luna</term>, which assign their virtues to <term>Sol</term>: the body itself comes from cold; color from fire; solidity from dryness; weight from humidity; and sound from brightness. But the fact that gold is not burned in the element of terrestrial fire, nor even corrupted, is achieved by the firmness of <term>Sol</term>. For one fire cannot burn or even consume another; rather, if fire is added to fire, it increases and becomes more powerful in its operations. The celestial fire which flows to us on the earth from the Sun is not the same kind of fire as exists in heaven, nor is it like that which exists upon the earth; rather, that celestial fire here with us is cold and congealed, and it is the body of the Sun. Therefore, the Sun can in no way be overcome by our fire. It only happens that it is liquefied, like snow or ice, by that same celestial Sun. Fire, therefore, does not have the power to burn fire, because the Sun is fire, which, dissolved in heaven, is coagulated here with us.

Gold is in its Essence three-fold:
1. Celestial — and is — Dissolved
2. Elementary — and is — Fluid
3. Metallic — and is — Corporeal

## PART II.

### CERTAIN TREATISES AND APPENDICES ARISING OUT OF THE SEVEN CANONS.

---

#### God and Nature do Nothing in Vain.

The eternal disposition of all things, independent of time, without beginning or end, operates everywhere. It works essentially where there is otherwise no hope. It accomplishes that which is deemed impossible. What appears beyond belief emerges into truth in a wonderful fashion.

#### Note on <term>Mercurius Vivus</term> (Quicksilver).

Whatever colors things white has the nature of life, and the properties and power of light, which fundamentally produces life. Whatever, on the other hand, stains things black, or produces blackness, has a nature in common with death, the properties of darkness, and forces that produce death. The earth, with its coldness, is a coagulation and fixation of this kind of hardness. For the house is always dead; but he who inhabits the house lives. If you can discover the meaning of this illustration, you have succeeded.

#### Tested liquefying powder.
#### Burn fat verbena.*

Recipe.—Saltpeter, four ounces; a half-portion of sulfur; tartar, one ounce. Mix and liquefy.

#### WHAT IS TO BE THOUGHT CONCERNING THE CONGELATION OF MERCURY.

To mortify or congeal mercury, and afterwards seek to turn it into silver (<term>Luna</term>), and to sublimate it with great labor, is a waste of effort, since it involves a scattering of the gold (<term>Sol</term>) and silver (<term>Luna</term>) existing within it. There is another method, very different and much more concise, by which, with little waste of mercury and less expenditure of toil, it is transmuted into silver (<term>Luna</term>) without freezing. Anyone can learn this Art in Alchemy at their pleasure, since it is so simple and easy; and by it, in a short time, he could make any quantity of silver and

There is not, nor ever will be, any art so easy to find and practice, and so effective in itself. The method of making gold and silver by Alchemy is so prompt that there is no more need of books, or of elaborate instruction, than there would be if one wished to write about last year's snow.

### CONCERNING THE RECIPES OF ALCHEMY.

What, then, shall we say about the recipes of Alchemy, and about the diversity of its vessels and instruments? These are furnaces, glasses, jars, waters, oils, limes, sulfurs, salts, saltpeters, alums, vitriols, <term>chrysocollaæ</term> (gold-solder), copper-greens, <term>atraments</term> (vitriol or inks), <term>auri-pigments</term> (orpiment), <term>fel vitri</term> (glass gall), <term>ceruse</term> (white lead), red earth, <term>thucia</term> (tutty), wax, <term>lutum sapientiæ</term> (philosopher's clay), pounded glass, verdigris, soot, <term>testæ ovorum</term> (eggshells), crocus of Mars (iron oxide), soap, crystal, chalk, arsenic, antimony, <term>minium</term> (red lead), elixir, <term>lazurium</term> (lapis lazuli), gold-leaf, salt-nitre, sal ammoniac, calamine stone, magnesia, <term>bolus armenus</term> (Armenian bole), and many other things. Moreover, concerning preparations, putrefactions, digestions, probations, solutions, cementings, filtrations, reverberations, calcinations, graduations, rectifications, amalgamations, purgations, etc.—alchemical books are crammed with these. Then, again, concerning herbs, roots, seeds, woods, stones, animals, worms, bone dust, snail shells, other shells, and pitch. These and the like—of which some are very far-fetched in Alchemy—are mere encumbrances to the work; since even if gold and silver could be made by them, they rather hinder and delay than further one's purpose. But to say the truth, it is not from these that the Art of making gold and silver is to be learned. So, then, all these things should be passed by, because they have no effect on the five metals, so far as gold and silver are concerned. Someone may ask, "What, then, is this short and easy way, which involves no difficulty, and yet by which gold and silver can be made?" Our answer is, this has been fully and openly explained in the Seven Canons. It would be wasted labor if one sought to further instruct someone who does not understand those. It would be impossible to convince such a person that these matters could be so easily understood, but in a hidden (<term>occult</term>) rather than in an open sense.

THE ART IS THIS: After you have made "heaven," or the sphere of lead (<term>Saturn</term>), with its life to run over the earth, place on it all the planets—or such as you wish, one or more—so that the portion of silver (<term>Luna</term>) is the smallest. Let all run, until heaven, or Saturn, has entirely disappeared. Then all those planets will remain dead with their old corruptible bodies, having meanwhile obtained another new, perfect, and incorruptible body.

That body is the spirit of heaven. From it, these planets again receive a body and life, and live as before. Take this body from the life and the earth.

### HOW TO CONJURE THE CRYSTAL SO THAT ALL THINGS MAY BE SEEN IN IT.

To conjure is nothing other than to observe anything correctly, to know and to understand what it is. The crystal is a representation of the air. Whatever appears in the air, whether movable or immovable, the same appears also in the <term>speculum</term> <note>mirror</note> or crystal as a wave. For the air, the water, and the crystal, as far as vision is concerned, are one—like a mirror in which an inverted copy of an object is seen.

### CONCERNING THE HEAT OF MERCURY.

Those who think that <term>Mercury</term> is of a moist and cold nature are clearly in error, because it is by its nature extremely warm and moist, which is the cause of its being in a constant state of fluidity. If it were of a moist and cold nature, it would have the appearance of frozen water and be always hard and solid, so that it would be necessary to liquefy it by the heat of fire, as in the case of the other metals. But it does not require this, since it has liquidity and flow from its own naturally inborn heat, which keeps it in a state of perpetual fluidity and renders it "quick," <note>living or fluid</note> so that it can neither die, nor be coagulated, nor congealed. And this is well worth noting: that the spirits of the seven metals—or as many of them as have been mixed together—as soon as they come into the fire, contend with one another, especially Mercury, so that each may put forth its powers and virtues in the endeavor to gain mastery in the way of liquefying and transmuting. One seizes on the virtue, life, and form of another, and assigns some other nature and form to it. So then the spirits or vapors of the metals are stirred up by the heat to operate mutually one upon the other, and transmute from one virtue to another, until perfection and purity are attained.

But what else must be done to Mercury so that its moisture and heat may be taken away, and in their place such an extreme cold introduced as to congeal, consolidate, and altogether mortify the Mercury? Do what follows in the instructions below: Take pure Mercury closely shut up in a silver <term>pixis</term> <note>a small box or container</note>. Fill a jar with fragments of lead, in the midst of which place the <term>pixis</term>. Let it melt for twenty-four hours—that is, for a natural day. This takes away from Mercury its hidden heat, adds an external heat, and contributes the internal coldness of <term>Saturn</term> and <term>Luna</term> (which are both planets of a cold nature), by which the Mercury is compelled to congeal, consolidate, and harden.

Note also that the coldness (which Mercury needs in its consolidation and mortification) is not perceptible by the external senses, as the cold of snow or of ice is, but rather, externally, there is a certain amount of apparent heat. Just in the same way is it with the heat of Mercury, which is the cause of its fluidity. It is not an external heat, perceptible in the same way as one of our

### WHAT MATERIALS AND INSTRUMENTS ARE REQUIRED IN ALCHEMY.

There is need of nothing else but a furnace, bellows, tongs, hammers, cauldrons, jars, and cupels made from beechen ashes. Afterward, lay on <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Mars</term>, <term>Sol</term>, <term>Venus</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>Luna</term>. Let them operate finally until they reach <term>Saturn</term>.

### THE METHOD OF SEEKING MINERALS.

The hope of finding these in the earth and in stones is very uncertain, and the labor is great. However, since this is the primary way of obtaining them, it is in no way to be despised, but rather greatly commended. Such a desire or appetite should no more be done away with than the lawful inclination toward marriage in young people and those in the prime of life. Just as bees long for roses and other flowers for the purpose of making honey and wax, so too should men—aside from greed or their own self-aggrandizement—seek to extract metal from the earth. He who does not seek it is not likely to find it. God endows men not only with gold or silver, but also with poverty, squalor, and misery. He has given to some a unique knowledge of metals and minerals, through which they have obtained a shorter and easier method of creating gold and silver—by extracting them from their primitive bodies—rather than digging and smelting them as was commonly done. And this is the case not only with subterranean substances; through certain arts and knowledge, they have extracted them from the five general metals (that is, from metals smelted from minerals which are imperfect and called metals): namely, from <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Mars</term>, and <term>Venus</term>. From all of these, and from each of them separately, <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term> can be made, though more easily from some than from others. Note that <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term> can be made easily from <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, and <term>Jupiter</term>, but with difficulty from <term>Mars</term> and <term>Venus</term>. It is possible to make them, however, with the addition of <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>. Out of <term>Magnesium</term> and <term>Saturn</term> comes <term>Luna</term>, and out of <term>Jupiter</term> and <term>Cinnabar</term>, pure <term>Sol</term> arises. The skillful artist, however (how well I remember!), will be able through diligent consideration to prepare metals so that, guided by a true method of reasoning, he can advance the perfection of metallic transformation more than the courses of the twelve signs and the seven planets do. ### WHAT ALCHEMY IS.

Alchemy is nothing else but the set purpose, intention, and subtle endeavor to transmute the kinds of metals from one to another.<note>Alchemy is, so to speak, a kind of lower heaven, by which the sun is separated from the moon, day from night, medicine from poison, and what is useful from what is waste.—*De Colica.* Therefore learn Alchemy, which is otherwise called <term>Spagyria</term>. This teaches you to discern between the true and the false. It is such a Light of Nature that it is a mode of proof in all things, and walks in light. From this light of Nature we ought to know and speak, not from mere fantasy, from which nothing is born except the four humours and their compounds, increase, stagnation, and decrease, with other trifles of this kind. These proceed, not from the clear intellect, that full treasure-house of a good man, but rather are based on a fictitious and insecure foundation.—*Paramirum*, Book I., chapter 3.</note> According to this, each person, by his own mental grasp, can choose for himself a better way and Art, and therein find truth, for the man who follows a thing more intently does find the truth. It is highly necessary to have a correct estimation of stars and of stones, because the star is the informing spirit of all stones. For the <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term> of all the celestial stars are nothing but one stone in itself; and the terrestrial stone has come forth from the celestial stone. Through the same fire, coals, and ashes, and the same expulsions and purgations as that celestial stone, it has been separated and brought forth, clear and pure in its brightness. The whole ball of the earth is only something thrown off, solidified, mixed, corrupted, ground, and again coagulated, and gradually liquefied into one mass—into a stony work, which has its seat and its rest in the midst of the firmamental sphere.

Further, it is to be remarked that those precious stones which shall immediately be listed have the nearest place to the heavenly or sidereal ones in point of perfection, purity, beauty, brightness, virtue, power of withstanding fire, and incorruptibility, and they have been fixed with other stones in the earth.<note>When the occult dispenser of Nature in the prime principles—that is to say, the potency called <term>Ares</term>—has produced the gross and rough types of stones, and no further coarseness remains, a transparent and subtle substance remains, out of which the <term>Archeus</term> of Nature generates the precious stones or gems.—*De Elemento Aquæ*, Book IV., Treatise IV., chapter 10.</note>

They have, therefore, the greatest affinity with heavenly stones and with the stars, because their natures are derived from these. They are found by

Men in unrefined environments, and the common masses (whose tendency it is to hold mistaken views of things), believe that gems were produced in the same place where they are found, and that they were afterwards polished, carried around, and sold, and considered to be great wealth because of their colors, beauty, and other virtues. A brief description of them follows:—

*The Emerald.* This is a green, transparent stone. It is beneficial for the eyes and the memory. It protects chastity; and if this be violated by the one who carries it, the stone itself does not remain whole.*

*The Adamant.* A black crystal called Adamant or else Evax, because of the joy which it is effective at instilling in those who carry it. It is of a dark and transparent blackness, the color of iron. It is the hardest of all; but it is dissolved in the blood of a goat. Its size at its largest does not exceed that of a hazelnut.†

*The Magnet* Is an iron stone, and so attracts iron to itself.‡

*The Pearl.* The Pearl is not a stone, because it is produced in sea shells. It is of a white color. Seeing that it grows in living beings, in men or in fishes, it is not properly of a stony nature, but properly a corrupted (otherwise transmuted) nature occurring within a perfect work.§

*The Jacinth* Is a yellow, transparent stone. There is a flower of the same name which, according to the myths of the poets, is said to have been a man.||

*The Sapphire* Is a stone of a celestial color and a heavenly nature.¶

*The Ruby* Shines with an intensely red nature.**

*The Carbuncle.* A solar stone, shining by its own nature like the sun.††

*The Coral* Is a white or red stone, not transparent. It grows in the sea, out of the nature of the water and the air, into the form of wood or a shrub; it hardens in the air, and cannot be destroyed by fire.‡‡

*The Chalcedony* Is a stone made up of different colors, holding a middle place between opaque and transparent, also clouded and liver-colored. It is the lowest of all the precious stones.*

*The Topaz* Is a stone shining by night. It is found among rocks.†

As a pledge and firm foundation of this matter, note the following conclusion. If anyone intelligently and reasonably takes care to train himself in learning about metals—what they are and where they come from—he may know that our metals are nothing other than the best part and the spirit of common stones; that is, pitch, grease, fat, oil, and stone. But this is least pure, uncontaminated, and perfect as long as it remains hidden or mixed with the stones. It should, therefore, be sought and found in the stones, recognized in them, and extracted from them—that is, forcibly drawn out and liquefied. For then it is no longer a stone, but a refined and perfect metal, comparable to the stars of heaven, which are themselves, as it were, stones separated from those of the earth.

Whoever, therefore, studies minerals and metals must be equipped with such reason and intelligence that he shall not only consider those common and known metals which are found solely in the depths of the mountains. For there is often found at the very surface of the earth such a metal as is not met with at all, or not of equal quality, in the depths. And so every stone that comes into view—whether great or small, flint or simple rock—should be carefully investigated and weighed with a true balance, according to its nature and properties. Very often a common stone, cast aside and despised, is worth more than a cow. One must not always consider the place of digging from which this stone came; for here the influence of the sky prevails. Everywhere earth, dust, or sand is presented to us, which often contains much gold or silver; take note of this.

# THE BOOK CONCERNING THE TINCTURE OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.

## WRITTEN AGAINST THOSE SOPHISTS BORN SINCE THE FLOOD, IN THE AGE OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, THE SON OF GOD;

### By PH. THEOPHRASTUS BOMBAST, OF HOHENHEIM,

#### *Philosopher of the Monarchy, Prince of Spagyrists, Chief Astronomer, Surpassing Physician, and Trismegistus of Mechanical Arcana.*

---

### PREFACE.

SINCE you, O Sophist, everywhere abuse me with such foolish and deceptive words, on the ground that being born in unrefined Helvetia I can understand and know nothing; and also because, being a duly qualified physician, I still wander from one district to another; therefore I have proposed by means of this treatise to disclose to the ignorant and inexperienced: what good arts existed in the first age; what my art avails against you and yours against me; what should be thought of each, and how my descendants in this age of grace will imitate me. Look at Hermes, Archelaus, and others in the first age: see what Spagyrists and what philosophers then existed. By this they testify that their enemies, who are your patrons, O Sophist, at the present time are but mere empty forms and idols. Although this would not be attested by those who are falsely considered your authentic fathers and saints, yet the ancient Emerald Tablet shows more art and experience in philosophy, alchemy, magic, and the like, than could ever be taught by you and your crowd of followers. If you do not yet understand, from the facts mentioned above, what and how great these treasures are, tell me why no prince or king was ever able to subdue the Egyptians. Then tell me why the Emperor Diocletian ordered all the Spagyric books to be burned (so far as he could lay his hands upon them). Unless the contents of those books had been known, they would have been obliged to still bear his intolerable yoke—a yoke, O Sophist, which shall one day be put upon the neck of yourself and your colleagues.

From the middle of this age the Monarchy of all the arts has been at length derived and conferred on me, Theophrastus Paracelsus, Prince of Philosophy and of Medicine. For this purpose I have been chosen by God to

extinguish and blot out all the fantasies of elaborate and false works, of delusive and presumptuous words, whether they are the words of Aristotle, Galen, Avicenna, Mesva, or the dogmas of any among their followers. The practice, following the theory at the same time, will be proved by wonderful and incredible signs, so as to be accessible to craftsmen and common people; they will thoroughly understand how firm and immovable this Paracelsic Art is against the trifles of the Sophists—even though, meanwhile, that sophistical science has to have its incompetence propped up and fortified by papal and imperial privileges. Since I am esteemed by you as a begging and vagabond sophist, the Danube and the Rhine will answer that accusation, even if I remain silent. Those slanders of yours, falsely devised against me, have often displeased many courts and princes, many imperial cities, the knightly order, and the nobility. I have a treasure hidden in a certain city called Weinden, belonging to Forum Julii, at an inn—a treasure which neither you, Leo of Rome, nor you, Charles the German, could purchase with all your wealth. Although the signed star has been applied to the <term>arcanum</term> <note>secret mystery</note> of your names, it is known to none but the sons of the divine Spagyric Art. So then, you wormy and lousy Sophist, since you consider the monarch of <term>arcana</term> a mere ignorant, foolish, and wasteful quack, I have determined in my present treatise, in this middle age, to disclose the honorable course of procedure in these matters: the virtues and preparation of the celebrated Tincture of the Philosophers for the use and honor of all who love the truth, and so that all who despise the true arts may be reduced to poverty. By this <term>arcanum</term>, the last age shall be clearly illuminated and compensated for all its losses by the gift of grace and the reward of the spirit of truth, so that since the beginning of the world, no similar growth of intelligence and wisdom shall ever have been heard of. In the meantime, vice will not be able to suppress the good, nor will the resources of those wicked persons, many though they be, cause any loss to the upright.

# THE BOOK CONCERNING THE TINCTURE OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.

---

## CHAPTER I.

I, Philippus Theophrastus Paracelsus Bombast, say that, by Divine grace, many ways have been sought to reach the **Tincture of the Philosophers**, all of which finally arrived at the same goal and end. Hermes Trismegistus, the Egyptian, approached this task using his own method. Orus, the Greek, observed the same process. Hali, the Arabian, remained firm in his order. But Albertus Magnus, the German, also followed a lengthy process. Each of these advanced according to his own method; nevertheless, they all arrived at one and the same end: a long life, so greatly desired by the philosophers, as well as an honorable sustenance and the means of preserving that life in this Valley of Misery. Now at this time, I, Theophrastus Paracelsus Bombast, Monarch of the Arcana, am endowed by God with special gifts for this purpose, so that every seeker of this supreme philosophic work may be forced to imitate and follow me—whether he be Italian, Pole, Frenchman, German, or whoever he may be. Follow me, all you philosophers, astronomers, and spagyrists, no matter how lofty your names may be; I will reveal and open to you, Alchemists and Doctors—who are elevated by my most perfect labors—this corporeal regeneration. I will teach you the tincture, the arcanum,* the quintessence, wherein lie hidden the foundations of all mysteries and all works. For every person can and should believe another only in those matters that he has tested by fire. If anyone brings forward anything contrary to this method of experimentation in the Spagyric Art or in Medicine, there is no reason for you to believe him, since the true is separated from the false experimentally through the agency of fire. Indeed, the light of Nature is created so that the proof or trial of everything may appear through it, but only to those who walk in this light. With this light, using the best methods of demonstration, we will show that everyone before me who approached this difficult field with their own fantasies and clever speculations has, to their own loss, risked the danger of their own foolishness. On which account, from my standpoint, many rustics have been

---

<note>* The arcanum of a substance is not its virtue (*virtus*) but its essence (*vis*) and potency (*potentia*), and it is stronger than the virtue; nevertheless, an old error of doctors gave the name of "virtues" to these potential essences.—*Paramirum*, Book IV. Many things are stated elsewhere concerning the Quintessence, but what is described there is actually a separation or extraction of the pure from the impure, not a true quintessence, and it is more correctly called an Arcanum.—*Explicatio Totius Astronomia*.</note>

He emphasizes that true knowledge in the Spagyric Art must be proven through experimentation by fire and the "light of Nature."</summary>

First of all, then, one must learn—digestions, distillations, sublimations, reverberations, extractions, solutions, coagulations, fermentations, fixations—and every instrument which is required for this work must be mastered through experience, such as glass vessels, <term>cucurbites</term>, circulators, vessels of Hermes, earthen vessels, baths, blast-furnaces, reverberatories, and similar instruments, as well as marble, coals, and tongs.
