### CHAPTER II.

#### CONCERNING THE DEFINITION OF THE SUBJECT AND MATTER OF THE TINCTURE OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.

Before I come, then, to the process of the Tincture, it is necessary that I reveal the subject of it to you: for, up to the present time, this has always been kept in a specially occult way by the lovers of truth. So, then, the matter of the Tincture (when you understand me in a Spagyric sense) is a certain thing which, by the art of Vulcan,* passes out of three essences into one essence, or it may remain as it is. But, to give it its proper name according to the use of the ancients—though it is called by many the <term>Red Lion</term>—it is still known by few. This, by the aid of Nature and the skill of the Artist himself, can be transmuted into a <term>White Eagle</term>, so that out of one, two are produced; and beyond this, the brightness of gold does not shine as much for the Spagyrist as do these two when kept as one. Now, if you do not understand the use of the Cabalists and the ancient astronomers, you are not born by God for the Spagyric art, nor chosen by Nature for the work of Vulcan, nor created to open your mouth concerning Alchemical Arts. The matter of the Tincture, then, is a very great pearl and a most precious treasure, and the noblest thing next to the manifestation of the Most High and the consideration of men which can exist upon earth: This is the <term>Lili</term> of Alchemy and of Medicine, which the philosophers have so diligently sought after, but, through the failure of entire knowledge and complete preparation, they have not progressed to the perfect end of it. By means of their investigations and experiments, only the

---

<note>* The role of Vulcan is the separation of the good from the bad. So the Art of Vulcan, which is Alchemy, is like death, by which the eternal and the temporal are divided from one another. So also this art might be called the death of things.—*De Morbis Metallicis*, Book I, Tract III, c. 1. Vulcan is an astral and not a physical creator.—*De Caduco Matricis*, Part VI. The artist working in metals and other minerals transforms them into other colors, and in so doing his operation is like that of heaven itself. For just as the artist cooks by means of Vulcan, or the fiery element, so heaven performs the work of cooking through the Sun. The Sun, therefore, is the Vulcan of heaven accomplishing the cooking in the earth.—*De Icteritiis*. Vulcan is the creator and architect of all things, nor is his home in heaven only, that is, in the firmament, but equally in all the other elements.—*Lib. Meteorum*, c. 4. Where the three primary principles are missing, there also the fiery essence is absent. The Fiery Vulcan is nothing else but Sulphur, Salt Nitre, and Mercury.—*Ibid.*, c. 5.</note>

The initial stage of the Tincture has been given to us; but the true foundation, which my colleagues must imitate, has been left for me, so that no one should mingle their shadows with our good intentions. I, by right after my long experiences, correct the <term>Spagyrists</term>, and separate the false or the erroneous from the true, since, by long investigations, I have found reasons why I should be able justly to blame and to change various things. If, indeed, I had found out experiments of the ancients better than my own, I should scarcely have taken up such great labors as I have willingly undergone for the sake, the utility, and the advantage of all good Alchemists. Since, then, the subject of the Tincture has been sufficiently declared, so that it scarcely could or ought to be exceeded in fidelity between two brothers, I approach its preparation; and after I have laid down the experiences of the first age, I wish to add my own inventions, to which at last the Age of Grace will by-and-by give its adherence, whichever of the patriarchs, O Sophist, you, in the meantime, shall have made leaders.

### CHAPTER III.

#### CONCERNING THE PROCESS OF THE ANCIENTS FOR THE TINCTURE OF THE PHILOSOPHERS, AND A MORE CONCISE METHOD BY PARACELSUS.

The old <term>Spagyrists</term> putrefied <term>Lili</term> for a philosophical month, and afterwards distilled the moist spirits from it until at length the dry spirits were elevated. They again saturated the <term>caput mortuum</term> with moist spirits, and drew them off from it frequently by distillation until the dry spirits were all elevated. Then afterwards they united the moisture that had been drawn off and the dry spirits by means of a pelican, three or four times, until the whole <term>Lili</term> remained dry at the bottom. Although early experience provided this process before fixation, our ancestors nonetheless often attained a perfect realization of their wish by this method. They would, however, have had a shorter way of arriving at the treasure of the Red Lion if they had learned the agreement of Astronomy with Alchemy, as I have demonstrated it in the <term>Apocalypse of Hermes</term>.* But since every day (as Christ says for the consolation of the—

Hermes, Plato, Aristotle, and other philosophers, flourishing at different times, who have introduced the Arts, and more especially have explored the secrets of inferior Creation, all these have eagerly sought a means whereby man's body might be preserved from decay and become endowed with immortality. And just as the Heavens, with respect to the other elements, are held to be the <term>fifth substance</term> (for they are indestructible, stable, and suffer no foreign admixture), so also this One *Thing* (compared to the forces of our body) is an indestructible essence, drying up all the superfluities of our bodies, and has been philosophically called by the above-mentioned name. It is neither hot and dry like fire, nor cold and moist like water, nor warm and moist like air, nor dry and cold like earth. But it is a skillful, perfect balance of all the Elements, a right mingling of natural forces, a most particular union of spiritual virtues, an indissoluble uniting of body and soul. It is the purest and noblest substance of an indestructible body, which cannot be destroyed nor harmed by the Elements, and is produced by Art. It is the Last and the Highest Thing to be sought under the Heavens, a wondrous closing and finish of philosophical work, by which are discovered the dews of Heaven and the strongholds of Earth. What the mouth of man cannot utter is all found in this spirit. As <term>Morienus</term> says: “He who has this has all things, and wants no other aid. For in it are all temporal happiness, bodily health, and earthly fortune. It is the spirit of the <term>fifth substance</term>, a Fount of all Joys (beneath the rays of the moon), the Supporter of Heaven and Earth, the Mover of Sea and Wind, the Outpourer of Rain, upholding the strength of all things, an excellent spirit above Heavenly and other spirits, giving Health, Joy, Peace, Love; driving away Hatred and Sorrow, bringing in Joy, expelling all Evil, quickly healing all Diseases, destroying Poverty and misery, leading to all good things, preventing all evil words and thoughts, giving man his heart's desire, bringing to the pious earthly honor and long life, but to the wicked who misuse *it*, Eternal Punishment.” This is the <term>Spirit of Truth</term>, which the world cannot comprehend without the interposition of the <term>Holy Ghost</term>, or without the instruction of those who know it. The same is of a mysterious nature, wondrous strength, boundless power. The Saints, from the beginning of the world, have desired to behold its face. By <term>Avicenna</term> this Spirit is named the <term>Soul of the World</term>. For, as the Soul moves all the limbs of the body, so also does this Spirit move all bodies. And as the Soul is in all the limbs of the Body, so also is this Spirit in all elementary created things. It is sought by many and found by few. It is beheld from afar and found near; for it exists in every thing, in every place, and at all times. It has the powers of all creatures; its action is found in all elements, and the qualities of all things are therein, even in the highest perfection. By virtue of this essence did <term>Adam</term> and the Patriarchs preserve their health and live to an extreme age, some of them also flourishing in great riches. When the philosophers had discovered it, with great diligence and labor, they straightway concealed it under a strange tongue, and in parables, lest the same should become known to the unworthy, and the pearls be cast before swine. For if everyone knew it, all work and industry would cease; man would desire nothing but this one thing, people would live wickedly, and the world be ruined, seeing that they would provoke God by reason of their avarice and excess. For eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has the heart of man understood what Heaven has naturally incorporated with this Spirit. Therefore have I briefly enumerated some of the qualities of this Spirit, to the Honor of God, that the pious may reverently praise Him in His gifts (which gift of God shall afterwards come to them), and I will herewith show what powers and virtues it possesses in each thing, also its outward appearance, that it may be more readily recognized. In its first state, it appears as an impure earthly body, full of imperfections. It then has an earthly nature, healing all sickness and wounds in the bowels of man, producing good flesh and consuming <term>proud flesh</term>, expelling all stench, and healing generally, inwardly and outwardly. In this form it cures cold and hot fevers, and is a specific remedy against poisons, which it drives from the heart and lungs, healing them when injured or wounded, purifying the blood, and, taken three times a day, is of great comfort in all diseases. In its fifth and last nature, it appears in a glorified and illuminated form, without defects, shining like gold and silver, wherein it possesses all previous powers and virtues in a higher and more wondrous degree. It converts crystals into the most precious stones of all colors, equal to those from the mines, and does many other incredible wonders which may not be revealed to the unworthy. This essence also reveals all treasures in earth and sea, converts all metallic bodies into gold, and there is nothing like it under Heaven. This spirit is the secret, hidden from the beginning, yet granted by God to a few holy men for the revealing of these riches to His Glory—dwelling in fiery form in the air, and leading earth with itself to heaven, while from its body there flow whole rivers of living water. And although these writings may be regarded as false by the reader, yet to the initiated they are true and possible, when the hidden sense is properly understood. For God is wonderful in His works, and His wisdom is without end. This spirit in its fiery form is called a <term>Sandaraca</term>, in the aerial a <term>Kybrick</term>, in the watery an <term>Azoth</term>, in the earthly <term>Alcohoph</term> and <term>Aliocosoph</term>. For a refined spirit cannot appear except in a body suitable to its nature. That is the spirit which, when rising, illumines the Heavens, when setting incorporates the purity of Earth, and when brooding has embraced the Waters. This spirit is named Raphael, the Angel of God, the subtlest and purest, whom the others all obey as their King. This spiritual substance is neither heavenly nor hellish, but an airy, pure, and hearty body, midway between the highest and lowest, without reason, but fruitful in works, and the most select and beautiful of all other heavenly things. This work of God is far too deep for understanding, for it is the last, greatest, and highest secret of Nature. It is the Spirit of God, which in the Beginning filled the earth and brooded over the waters, which the world cannot grasp without the gracious interposition of the Holy Spirit and instruction from those who know it, which also the whole world desires for its virtue, and which cannot be prized enough. O desirable knowledge, lovely above all things beneath the circle of the Moon, by which Nature is strengthened, and heart and limbs are renewed, blooming youth is preserved, old age is driven away, weakness is destroyed, beauty in its perfection is preserved, and abundance is ensured in all things pleasing to men! O you spiritual substance, lovely above all things! O you wondrous power, strengthening all the world! O you invincible virtue, highest of all that is, although despised by the ignorant, yet held by the wise in great praise, honor, and glory, that—proceeding from humors—wakes the dead, expels diseases, and restores the voice of the dying! O you treasure of treasures, mystery of mysteries, called by Avicenna "an unspeakable substance," the purest and most perfect soul of the world, than which there is nothing more costly under Heaven, unfathomable in nature and power, wonderful in virtue and works, having no equal among creatures, possessing the virtues of all bodies under Heaven! For from it flow the water of life, the oil and honey of eternal healing, and thus has it nourished them with honey and water from the rock. Therefore, Morienus says: "He who has it, also has all things." Blessed are You, Lord God of our fathers, in that You have given the prophets this knowledge and understanding, that they have hidden these things (lest they should be discovered by the blind, and those drowned in worldly godlessness) by which the wise and the pious have praised You! For the discoverers of the mystery of this thing to the unworthy are breakers of the seal of Heavenly Revelation, thereby offending God's Majesty, and bringing upon themselves many misfortunes and the punishments of God. Therefore, I beg all Christians possessing this knowledge to communicate it to nobody, except it be to one living in Godliness, of well-proved virtue, and praising God, Who has given such a treasure to man. For many seek, but few find it. Hence the impure and those living in vice are unworthy of it. Therefore, this Art is to be shown to all God-fearing persons, because it cannot be bought with a price. I testify before God that I do not lie, although it may appear impossible to fools, that no one has hitherto explored Nature so deeply. The Almighty be praised for having created this Art and for revealing it to God-fearing men. Amen. And thus is fulfilled this precious and excellent work, called the revealing of the occult spirit, in which lie hidden the secrets and mysteries of the world. But this spirit is one genius, and a divine, wonderful, and lordly power. For it embraces the whole world, and overcomes the Elements and the <term>fifth Substance</term>. To our <term>Trismegistus Spagyrus</term>, Jesus Christ, be praise and glory immortal. Amen.

## CHAPTER V.
### CONCERNING THE CONCLUSION OF THE PROCESS OF THE ANCIENTS, MADE BY PARACELSUS.

Lastly, the ancient <term>Spagyrists</term> <note>alchemists</note>, having placed <term>Lili</term> in a pelican <note>a circulatory distilling vessel</note> and dried it, fixed it by means of a regulated increase of the fire. They continued this so long until, changing from blackness through all the colors, it became red as blood, and thereby assumed the condition of a salamander. Indeed, they proceeded rightly with such labor, and in the same way it is right and fitting that everyone who seeks this pearl should proceed. It will be very difficult for me to make this clearer to you unless you have learned in the School of the Alchemists to observe the degrees of the fire and also to change your vessels. For then at last you will see that soon after your <term>Lili</term> has become heated in the Philosophic Egg, it becomes—with wonderful appearances—blacker than a crow; afterward, in the course of time, whiter than a swan; and at last, passing through a yellow color, it turns out more red than

# CHAPTER VI.
## CONCERNING THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS BY THE PERFECTION OF MEDICINE.

If the <term>Tincture of the Philosophers</term> is to be used for transmutation, a pound of it must be projected onto a thousand pounds of melted <term>Sol</term> <note>gold</note>. Then, at length, a Medicine will have been prepared for transmuting the leprous moisture of the metals. This work is a wonderful one in the light of Nature—namely, that by the <term>Magistery</term>, or the operation of the <term>Spagyrist</term>, a metal which formerly existed should perish, and another be produced. This fact has made Aristotle himself, with his ill-founded philosophy, appear foolish. For truly, when the peasants in Hungary cast iron at the proper season into a certain fountain, commonly called <term>Zifferbrunnen</term>, it is consumed into rust; and when this is liquefied with a blast-fire, it soon exists as pure <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note> and never returns to iron again. Similarly, in the mountain commonly called <term>Kuttenberg</term>, they obtain a lixivium <note>a solution obtained by leaching</note> out of <term>marcasites</term> <note>iron pyrites</note>, in which iron is immediately turned into <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note> of a high grade, and more malleable than the other produced by Nature. These things, and more like them, are known to simple men rather

### CHAPTER VII.

#### CONCERNING THE RENOVATION OF MEN.

Some of the first and ancient philosophers of Egypt lived by means of this Tincture for a hundred and fifty years. The lives of many others have also been extended and prolonged for several centuries, as is very clearly shown in various histories, though it seems hardly credible to anyone. For its power is so remarkable that it extends the life of the body beyond what is naturally possible and maintains it so firmly in that state that it lives on in safety from all infirmities. And although, indeed, the body eventually reaches old age, it still appears as if it were established in its original youth.

So, then, the <term>Tincture of the Philosophers</term> is a Universal Medicine and consumes all diseases, by whatever name they are called, just like an invisible fire. The dose is very small, but its effect is most powerful. By means of it, I have cured leprosy, venereal disease, dropsy, epilepsy, colic, scabies, and similar afflictions; also lupus, cancer, ulcers, fistulas, and the entire range of internal diseases, more certainly than one could believe. Germany, France, Italy, Poland, Bohemia, etc., will provide the most abundant evidence of this fact.

Now, Sophist, look at Theophrastus Paracelsus. How can your Apollo, Machaon, and Hippocrates stand against me? This is the Catholicum <note>universal remedy</note> of the

# THE GRADATIONS OF METALS.

## PREFACE.

<margin>* The term "gradation" is used by Paracelsus in more than one sense; here, it refers to the process by which one substance is developed into another. Care must be taken to distinguish between this and the "grades" of metals, etc. For example, in gold there are said to be twenty-four grades; in silver, thirty-two grades of softness; in iron, forty-six grades of hardness; in lead, eighteen degrees of fluidity; twelve of malleability in copper; and in Mercury, eighty-three properties or branches. — *Chirurgia Minor*, Book III. Preface.</margin>

We now intend to speak concerning gradations,* and specifically those of a kind where a metal dissolved or digested in them can be promoted to the degree of gold (<term>Sol</term>) and transmuted. Many people endeavor to transmute the lesser metals into silver, and others of a mediocre nature into gold, though with some difference in their joining, so that in a cupel (<term>cineritium</term>), through the transmutation of graduation, the lesser metals may be brought to the perfection of the greater ones—a perfection that satisfies any suitable tests. We will, therefore, set down fourteen gradations in this place. Many others may be found, but we intentionally omit those and have collected only those established by experience and worth writing about. These we arrange into three categories: some are "strong waters," others are oils, and the rest are liquids. We arrange them in this order, as is clear from our method of treating them. That is to say, we put strong waters first, oils second, and liquids last.

### THE FIRST GRADATION.

<margin>† From the time of Basil Valentine, antimony played almost as important a role in the operations of Alchemy as it did in Medicine. It is described in various ways by Paracelsus. Sometimes the term is made to include all marcasites, <term>cachimiæ</term>, talcs, <term>ogerta</term>, etc.—*De Morbis Metallicis*, Tract III., c. 3. Again, antimony is a mucilage, or, so you may understand me better, <term>firnisium</term>.—*Ibid.*, c. 7. It transmutes <term>Saturn</term> (lead) into <term>Venus</term> (copper).—*De Aridura*. It receives its body from Mercury and is the crudest nature of Mercury after it has been purged out (that is, expelled from the prime principle). It retains all the powers and virtues of Mercury. Of all products coming forth from the three first principles, there is none that retains the virtue of Mercury more clearly than antimony. It is nothing but Mercury coagulated through the Spirit of Salt and Sulfur. But, at the same time, understand that it is derived from the coarse and rough, not from the subtle nature of the said Mercury.—*De Elemento Aquæ*, Tract V., c. 5.</margin>

Take two pounds each of vitriol, alum, and saltpeter; a quarter pound each of <term>flos aeris</term> (flower of copper), crocus of Mars (iron oxide), and hematite; a pound and a half of cinnabar; three-eighths of a pound of antimony;† and one-eighth of a pound of arsenic.

Let all be distilled with a very strong fire into a "strong water," which you should purify and clarify according to the standard method for such waters. Dissolve in it "cemented" silver (<term>Luna</term>), or an equal mixture of silver (<term>Luna</term>) and copper (<term>Venus</term>). Then, put it in digestion for a month. Afterward, remove the residue by fulmination, and in this way you will

Care should be taken that the aforementioned simples be prepared and separated, first of all, through purification, because any impurity hinders this work of transmutation very seriously.

### THE SECOND GRADATION.

In this second gradation it is worthwhile to note carefully another process, it being one which can be adopted with greater gain and subtlety, as follows: Take of saltpeter and of cinnabar each one pound. Let them be pounded together, and the water distilled from them; preserve this water. Do the same with an equal weight of antimony and arsenic. Mix together the three waters, and add of saltpeter, alum, and vitriol each one pound. Distill everything again, in the manner of <term>aquafortis</term>. Afterwards, pour this on its *caput mortuum* (the residue), which has been finely powdered. Distill it again to its ultimate spirit, and clarify it, just as any other <term>aquafortis</term>. In the case of all metals which have been dissolved in it, and have remained in digestion until perfect, its powers of operation are incredibly great. In very truth, there are latent in a composition with these ingredients all the forces of those metals which have in themselves a corporeal matter. For three of such distillations tinge so powerfully, by the force of the water, that scarcely any greater or more powerful means of working with strong waters could be found.

### THE THIRD GRADATION.

The third gradation, which is reckoned as the last among the strong waters, is to be understood and compounded as follows:—Take of cinnabar, arsenic, and antimony, each half a pound; of saltpeter two pounds; and of sulfur half a pound. Let these be pounded together, mixed, and distilled into a strong water with a very powerful fire. Afterwards, take two parts of this water; of common alum and <term>alumen plumosum</term> each a part and a half; of vitriol one part; and of verdigris and <term>crocus of Mars</term> each half a part. Let all these be distilled together into a strong water with a very violent fire. At length, for the whole of this water, take two parts of the *caput mortuum*; and of antimony, verdigris, cinnabar, and sulfur, half a part each. Distill these from their dregs by strongly driving them into a receiver. Afterwards, in this water, when it has been clarified, dissolve half a part with ten parts of flowers of brass and <term>crocus of Mars</term>, and let it be digested therein. You will afterwards find more of the residue transmuted to <term>Sol</term> <note>gold</note> than you would deem possible by the Art.

The following is the process adopted: Take one pound of Antimony and half a pound of sublimated Mercury. Let both be distilled together over a powerful fire by means of an alembic, and the redness will ascend as thick as blood. This tinges and graduates all <term>Luna</term> into <term>Sol</term>, and brings the latter, when pale, to the highest degree of permanent color.

### THE FIFTH GRADATION.

The fifth gradation, the oil of which is considered second in order, is made in the following manner: Take one pound of the Oil of the Philosophers, with which mix half a pound each of Calcined Alum and of Citrine Colcothar. Distill a second time, and afterwards rectify to purity and a constant color. Put in <term>Luna</term>, and let it remain in digestion. Reduce what remains, separate it in <term>aquafortis</term>, and, lastly, fulminate it by means of <term>Saturn</term>.

### THE SIXTH GRADATION.

The sixth gradation, third in order among the oils, is made in the following way: Take two pounds of Live Sulphur* and four pounds of Flax Oil (linseed oil). Let these be formed into a compound, and let this be distilled into an oil. To this, let the same quantity of Live Sulphur be added, and let it be treated just as it was for the compound. Let it be digested in horse-dung for a month, or if longer, so much the better. After this, let one-eighth of a pound of each of the following be added: Salt Nitre, Vitriol, Alum, <term>Flos Aeris</term>, <term>Crocus of Mars</term>, and Cinnabar. Distill whatever will ascend. Remove the liquids, keeping only the oils. Put these aside in a glass cucurbite, adding the ingredients as above, and the <term>Caput Mortuum</term> in powder. Distill again as before. Afterwards, pour it off again from the dregs, let it be putrefied a second time for a month, and further distilled. When the colors are gone or separated, keep the red, and rectify it as required. Lastly, let plates of <term>Luna</term> be digested at the proper time, and at length reduced by a process of fulmination.

<note>* Live Sulphur is that of which fragments or particles will cohere without being in a dissolved or fluid state.—*De Praeparationibus*, Book I, Treatise 2.</note>

### THE SEVENTH GRADATION.

Gradations which are produced by liquids are found in two different forms, namely, the tenacious and the watery. First, let us speak concerning the tenacious. Take one pound of Honey, and in it decoct one-quarter of a pound each of Vitriol and of Alum with an eighth of a pound of Iamen. Distill the water from these over a strong fire, and add to it one-eighth of a pound each of the <term>Caput Mortuum</term> from a human skull, and half a pound of Sulphur. Decoct into the form of a <term>hepar</term> and digest for a month; then distill and rectify with water until pure. Afterwards, add one-eighth of a pound each of Sal Ammoniac, <term>Flos Aeris</term>, <term>Crocus of Mars</term>, and Alum; a quarter of a pound of Vitriol, and two ounces each of fixed Antimony and fixed Red Arsenic. ### THE EIGHTH GRADATION.

The gradation by the second liquid is as follows:
Take a sufficient quantity of <term>aquafortis</term>. In one part of it, dissolve <term>Sol</term>; in another part, <term>Venus</term>; and in another part, <term>Mars</term>. Mix these solutions together, and afterwards distill the water from them. Pour this again onto its dregs, and once more distill and pour as before, until a thick liquid is produced from it. To this, add five parts of distilled and prepared honey. Let all be digested for a month, and afterwards separate the <term>phlegma</term>. Keep the liquid, and in it let metallic plates be digested for a month. Finally, let it be coagulated into a mass and into one distinct body. Let this be subjected to a process of fulmination and <term>quartation</term>. Fulminate a second time, and thus an excellent transmutation by means of liquid will be found.

### THE NINTH GRADATION.

By the third liquid, the ninth gradation is made in the following manner:
Take <term>aquafortis</term>, in which you dissolve <term>verdigris</term>, and let both be kept together in horse dung for the space of a month. Now distill the water from the dregs, pour it on again, and distill and pour it over several times until an oil is produced from it. Into that liquid put metallic filings, and in the course of its being digested, you will find a transmutation. Although the liquid may be small in quantity, it nevertheless graduates most effectively and affects the very largest amount of metal in proportion to its own quantity.

### THE TENTH GRADATION.

In the following manner, the fourth liquid is to be understood:
Take the best <term>aquafortis</term>, and in it dissolve as much steel as possible. Let these remain in digestion for a month, and from them a compound of one color will be formed. Let this compound also be distilled into a liquid, in which metallic filings must remain in digestion until the liquid is incorporated. Then let both be fulminated together—that is to say, the liquid and the metal—by means of <term>Saturn</term>. Then this transmutation will be found, which must be separated and prepared in the usual way.

### THE ELEVENTH GRADATION.

The eleventh gradation is made by the first aqueous liquid according to the formula subjoined:
Take four pounds of the most highly purified saltpeter, and repurge this from its <term>phlegma</term> by combustion. Add two pounds of duly prepared common salt. Mix these together, and distill with an <term>alembic</term> six or nine times, until the salts altogether pass over through the alembic into the receiver

### TWELFTH GRADATION.

By means of the second aqueous liquid, the twelfth gradation is produced in the following manner:
Take three pounds of the most highly corrected *<term>Vinum Ardens</term>*; one pound of the water of saltpeter; half a pound of the water of common salt; and three-quarters of a pound each of <term>vitriol</term>, <term>Alumen Plumosum</term>, and <term>Alumen Aochi</term>. ### THE THIRTEENTH GRADATION.

By the third aqueous liquid, the thirteenth gradation is produced in the following manner:
Take one pound of <term>Isteris of Blood</term>. Distill it thirteen times from its dregs, and place in it two ounces each of <term>Flos Aeris</term> and of sulphur. Let them be dissolved in horse dung for a month. Afterwards, put in <term>Calx Lunae</term>, so that the color and substance may be consumed. Afterwards, let them be coagulated and fulminated in <term>Saturn</term>. Know that in this liquid, common <term>mercury</term>, as well as the mercury of metals, is coagulated according to the conditions of Transmutation.

### THE FOURTEENTH GRADATION.

The fourth liquid in this place is the Water of Mercury, which is made for the fourteenth gradation as follows below:
Take one pound of <term>mercury</term> sublimated twenty times with <term>sal ammoniac</term>, and one ounce each of the <term>Flowers of Venus</term>, <term>Mars</term>, sulphur, and <term>antimony</term>. Grind and mix all together, and then let them be resolved into a water. This water requires no other labor whatever. Metals projected into it, digested for a short time, and afterwards fulminated, are graduated in a wonderful manner.

# THE TREASURE OF TREASURES FOR ALCHEMISTS.

## BY PHILIPPUS THEOPHRASTUS BOMBAST, PARACELSUS THE GREAT

---

NATURE produces a mineral in the depths of the earth. There are two kinds of it, which are found in many districts of Europe. The best which has been offered to me, and which has also been proven genuine in experimentation, is externally in the form of the greater world, and is found in the eastern part of the sphere of the Sun. The other, in the Southern Star, is now in its first flowering. The depths of the earth push this forth through its surface. It is found red in its first solidification, and in it lie hidden all the flowers and colors of minerals. Much has been written about it by the philosophers, for it is of a cold and moist nature, and corresponds with the element of water.

So far as it relates to the knowledge of it and experimentation with it, all the philosophers before me—though they have aimed at it with their arrows—have missed the mark significantly. They believed that <term>Mercury</term> and <term>Sulphur</term> were the mother of all metals, never even dreaming of mentioning a third; and yet, when the water is separated from it by <term>Spagyric Art</term>, the truth is plainly revealed, though it was unknown to Galen or to Avicenna. But if, for the sake of our excellent physicians, we had to describe only the name, the composition, the dissolution, and solidification—as Nature proceeds with all growing things from the beginning of the world—a whole year would scarcely be enough for me; and in order to explain these things, not even the hides of many cows <note>This refers to the vast amount of parchment that would be required.</note> would be sufficient.

Now, I assert that in this mineral three principles are found, which are <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Sulphur</term>, and the <term>Mineral Water</term> which has served to solidify it naturally. <term>Spagyric science</term> is able to extract this last from its proper juice when it is not yet fully matured, in the middle of the autumn, just like a pear from a tree. The tree potentially contains the pear. If the Celestial Stars and Nature agree, the tree first of all puts forth shoots in the month of March; then it pushes out buds, and when these open the flower appears, and so on in due order, until in autumn the pear grows ripe. It is the same with minerals. These are born, in like manner, in the depths of the earth. Let the Alchemists who are seeking the Treasure of Treasures carefully note this. I will show them the way, its beginning, its middle, and its end. In the

### CONCERNING THE SULPHUR OF CINNABAR.

Take mineral Cinnabar and prepare it in the following manner. Cook it with rain water in a stone vessel for three hours. Then purify it carefully, and dissolve it in Aqua Regis, which is composed of equal parts of vitriol, nitre, and sal ammoniac. Another formula is vitriol, saltpeter, alum, and common salt.

Distill this in an alembic. Pour it on again, and separate the pure from the impure carefully in this way. Let it putrefy for a month in horse-dung; then separate the elements in the following manner. If it puts forth its sign,<gloss>The *Sign* is nothing other than the mark left by an operation. Thus, the sign is the achievement itself.—*De Colica*.</gloss> commence the distillation by means of an alembic with a fire of the first degree. The water and the air will ascend; the fire and the earth will remain at the bottom. Afterwards join them again, and gradually treat with the ashes. So the water and the air will again ascend first, and afterwards the element of fire, which expert artists recognize. The earth will remain in the bottom of the vessel. Collect this there. It is what many seek after and few find.

Prepare this dead earth in the reverberatory according to the rules of Art, and afterwards apply a fire of the first degree for five days and nights. When these have elapsed, you must apply the second degree for the same number of days and nights, and proceed according to Art with the material enclosed. At length, you will find a volatile salt, like a thin alkali, containing in itself the Astrum of fire and earth.<gloss>The earth also has its Astrum, its course, and its order, just as much as the Firmament, but peculiar to the element. So also there is an Astrum in the water, even as in the earth, and in like manner with air and fire. Consequently, the upper Astrum has the Astra of the elements as its medium and operates through them by an irresistible attraction. Through this operation of the superior and inferior Astra, all things are fertilized and led on to their end.—*Explicatio Totius Astronomiae*. Without the Astra the elements cannot flourish. . . . In the Astrum of the earth all the celestial operations thrive. The Astrum itself is hidden, the bodies are manifest. . . . The motion of the earth is brought about by the Astrum of the earth. . . . There are four Astra in man (corresponding to those of the four elements), for he is the lesser world.—*De Caducis*, Part II.</gloss> Mix this with the two elements that have been preserved—the water and the earth. Again place it on the ashes for eight days and eight nights, and you will find that which has been neglected by many Artists. Separate this according to your experience, and according to the rules of the Spagyric Art, and you will have a white earth, from which its color has been extracted. Join the element of fire and salt to the alkalized earth. Digest in a pelican to extract the essence. Then a new earth will be deposited; set this aside.

### CONCERNING THE GREEN LION.

Take the vitriol of Venus,† carefully prepared according to the rules of the Spagyric Art, and add to it the elements of water and air which you have reserved. Go on, and do not despair of the work. Rectify it until you find the true, clear Green Lion, which you will recognize by its great weight. You will see that it is heavy and large. ### CONCERNING THE
# TRANSMUTATIONS OF METALS AND OF CEMENTS.
### By THEOPHRASTUS.

---

Just as we have given instructions concerning other transmutations, we will also fulfill our task with reference to cements in the same way. We will mention six cements, which will include all types of cements; we shall deal with these individually in serial order according to the recipes and methods of operation. This consideration must be made general in all respects, so that all cements may be reduced to a single method of fixation and coloring. These two conditions should not be separated; instead, they should always persist and remain together in one <term>cineration</term>, <term>coloration</term>, and <term>quartation</term>, just as the properties of true gold are established.

<margin>* From everything that has come down to us concerning the labors and investigations of the ancient philosophers, we see how tireless was their search for the best method of preserving and lengthening life. But because they themselves lacked perfect instruction in the preparation of medicines, they did not hesitate to turn to the Alchemists; thus, through the combined labors of both parties, a genuine science of pharmacy eventually arose, which was then marvelously spread and increased by various chemical experiments devoted to medicine. But what they call the <term>Tincture</term> excelled everything else. Yet, at the same time, it had fallen into some discredit because of the gold-makers, who thought it was mainly useful for the transmutation of metals. Having compounded the Tincture—by which they transmuted the colors of metals and purged away their dross—the ancient philosophers, as might be expected, next began to think of using it for medical purposes. Seeing that the flowers of the metals were endowed with greater virtues than the metals themselves, they attempted to use these for the benefit of the physician. Accordingly, whether by the kind disposition of Heaven or through the fertility of their minds, those Tinctures were discovered and improved. Their efficacy is proven by ancient manuscripts, which have been suppressed by the crowd of false doctors; however, we do not hesitate to publish them.— *Chirurgia Magna*, Tract III., c. 1.</margin>

This book on cements does not state how inferior metals are to be transmuted into others, such as lead into copper, or iron into copper, etc. But it teaches at least this: how metals may be cemented into the primary metal, gold—that is, *Sol*. For cements with other recipes cannot perfectly fulfill their operation for transmuting into other metals; but in these alone, there is a complete and rapid work of transmutation into *Sol*, which masters all the other metals—not, indeed, by <term>quartation</term>, but by coloring and <term>tincture</term>.* And notice should be taken of which bodies provide their own harmony as if belonging to the same species. For there are some bodies that are receptive and others that are not. Some must first of all be reduced

...to their flowers; with others, this is not necessary. In the same way, some species color according to the red <term>Sol</term> [gold], others according to the clayey <term>Sol</term>; some in flux, and some in a partial cement. Likewise, diligent attention should be paid to the fire, as it is the medium in which the secret of all cements primarily lies hidden, and from which they gain their operational power. Fire contains within itself the entirety of Alchemy through its innate power to tint, graduate, and fix—qualities that are, as it were, born with it and impressed upon it.* Every practitioner who prepares cements must also attend carefully to the method of the process; for the method is of even greater importance than the prescription or recipe.

So, then, let us proceed to the series of the six cements, which serve as the standards by which all cements are regulated. Among these, the first is the Royal Cement. Paying little attention to the methods of the ancients, we will follow experience as our guide, and we will omit those prescriptions that experience proves to be useless. Thus:—

Take half a pound each of Flower of Brass, Antimony, Brick Tiles, and Common Salt. Having ground all these into a very fine powder and mixed them together, let them be soaked in wine and then dried. Repeat this process twenty-four times. With this powder, let plates of <term>Luna</term> [silver] be cemented in a moderate fire for four hours. Then, finally, take the <term>Regulus</term>, hammered into plates and in its raw state from the previous process, and cement it with the same materials and an equal degree of fire, repeating the operation four or five times. Afterward, having purified it again with cinders or ashes, reduce it once more to <term>Luna</term>. The instruments, such as the melting vessels and so forth, must be thoroughly sealed with lute and stopped up. And although the process we describe here is somewhat lengthy, you must understand that we make it so because experience teaches us that there is no benefit in short fire-based processes. Indeed, since the duration and intensity of the fire provide the primary fixation for the Royal Cement, it would actually be far better if the substances mentioned were left for four days in the same kind of cement.

Note also that the flowers of brass should be extracted from copper using vitriol. For when obtained in this way, it contains a certain natural fixation, for many reasons.

Similarly, the tiles should be taken from a good house; for the roof has the power to fix the vapors that exist in <term>Luna</term>, which would otherwise all fly away and escape.

<note>* Fire tests everything; what is impure it removes, and it brings about the manifestation of pure substances.—*Paramirum*, Book I, ch. 1. Fire separates the fixed from the fleeting.—*De Morbis Metallicis*, Book II, Tract I, ch. 1. Whatever pertains to separation belongs to the science of Alchemy. It teaches how to extract, coagulate, and separate every substance in its own specific vessel.—*De Morbis Tartareis*, ch. 16. Whatever man does, the planets do also, but in an alchemical sense and process. Accordingly, as the Alchemist seeks saltpeter in nitre, mercury in dung, and sulfur in fire, so he also seeks the firmament, which is the invisible Vulcan. When he has collected these substances and united them, a detonation follows, the kind of which is called a thunderbolt in heaven, but the Alchemist calls it a *Bombard*. For he has the power of producing thunder, as in magic, which is the philosophy of Alchemy. There are foolish people who confuse it with (what is now understood as) Necromancy, yet there is a sense in which it is properly so named, and in which Nigromancy is its true name from its earliest origin, being derived from the word for blackness, because its initiates walk about as black as charcoal burners. All those who serve Vulcan are Nigromantics.—*De Colica*, see under *Paralysis*.</note>

# The Transmutations of Metals and Cements.

Salt corrects and fixes leprous <term>Luna</term> [silver], cleansing it of its blackness. These four details should exist and be put into practice together; however, it is the fire that must be especially observed and noted. To this cement, no other metal is applied; and after it is purified, it discloses and exhibits gold. Therefore, this cement should be considered sufficient for one purpose.

### CONCERNING THE SECOND CEMENT.

The cement which we wish to place in the second position is only for <term>Sol</term> [gold], and regarding it, there are four objectives which must be considered. The first is that <term>Sol</term> is sometimes found in this cement to be defective in the fourth or middle part, because it is not "fixed," or not brought to its proper degree without its deficiencies, as we described in our treatise on Gradations. For this reason, it has to be cemented so that it may be able to retain its own volatile body, which otherwise sometimes flies off during cementation, or in the process of incineration, or else in <term>aqua fortis</term>.

The second objective is that a good deal of <term>Sol</term> is found which is defective in color, and it is necessary that one should know how to bring it to its perfection of coloring without a reduction of its bulk, and so that the colors may remain in the test specimens.

The third is that this white, imperfect color of <term>Sol</term>, having the appearance of <term>Luna</term>, may be cemented so that it may retain the color acquired from the process in every specimen.

The fourth concerns the weight, in which the <term>Sol</term> is sometimes defective, so that it is esteemed as somewhat common. This weight must be entirely restored to it, when it proves its higher quality by its color; a higher grade of <term>Sol</term> exists for many reasons. For the weight deceives no true artist, as the probe may also be deceptive for many reasons.

By means of cement, gold can be perfected in these four particulars so that afterward no defect shall be found in it, nor any volatile or unfixed condition. Let the preparation of this cement be as follows:—<term>Antimony</term> and <term>Flower of Brass</term>, half a pound of each; of coagulated <term>mercury</term>, one-fourth of a pound; let all be mixed together and soaked with red oil of antimony until the whole is reddened. Afterward, cement the gold (in very thin plates or grains) with it, liquefied by fire for twenty-four hours without the heat being allowed to decrease, in a fusing vessel closely fastened. When this time has elapsed, take out the <term>Regulus</term> not acted upon by the crude antimony. Let it be liquefied with the addition of copper-green <note>verdigris</note> or <term>borax</term>, and afterward pour it into a mold. In this way, you will have the very best and most abundant cement for rendering <term>Sol</term> free from defects and at its highest degree, fixed and permanent in all cements, incinerations, and <term>quartations</term>.

So far we have set down the two fixations or cementations for <term>Luna</term> and <term>Sol</term>, which ought to be adopted when these metals are to be multiplied. But

Others, too, have to be cemented and afterwards placed in a coloring cement. This third cement is adapted for perfecting the other metals and making them fit in themselves for the tincture of the other cements. For where a metal has not been prepared and smeared over for this tincture, it is not able to take it, or only to a very slight degree, and by a dangerous process.

Quicksilver,* which is included under this cement, is not among the number of the metals, but only among metallic materials and malleable bodies. The cement is to be made thus: Antimony, one pound; Saltpetre, one pound; common Salt and Salt of Tartar, half a pound each. Having mixed all these together, put them in a dish, placed layer by layer with plates or filings of the metals. Let them be closely shut up and cemented for twelve hours with a very powerful fire, which had originally been a gentle one for only the first two hours. When this time has elapsed, let all that remains be extracted—that is to say, the loppa (refuse) along with the Regulus. This must be noted, that all cementings of this kind do not show the Regulus, but some of them only the loppas. These should be afterwards treated with <term>Saturn</term>, according to the ordinary method, and <term>Saturn</term> of the same kind burned in the vessel; then the metal will be found fixed upon it. And here mark the difference of the separation by means of the jar, the cupella, or the cineritium. The metal enters into the cineritium or the cupella, but in the other case it remains on the jar. Metal of this kind, which remains on the surface of the jar, you will cement a second or a third time, as above, so that it may turn out more fixed and remain on the cineritium. When this has been done, it is fixed for receiving the tincture, which is given to it by cementation.

With regard to this cement, it should be remarked that two or three metals can be blended together in one mixture and one body, which will be better than before. The following is the method. Take filings of <term>Mars</term>, <term>Venus</term>, and <term>Jupiter</term>, or <term>Saturn</term>. Let them stand in a fire of liquefaction for twelve hours. *Addition.* The cement will be more useful if, besides the above, there be taken of Antimony and Salt each one pound; filings of <term>Mars</term>, <term>Venus</term>, and <term>Saturn</term>, half a pound each. Treat them as mentioned before.

### THE FOURTH CEMENT.

The fourth cement is that which is composed of minerals containing within them a perfect metal and losing it by means of liquefaction. Here it should be noted that metals cannot be better fixed than when they are crude. They vanish altogether in the process of liquefaction. Transmutation of this kind takes place in minerals and metals before liquefaction, so that the metals may be fixed in their own nature, or may be transmuted into some other metal. Therefore we will here include two cements under one. The former is

When this is done, a transmutation of the <term>cineritium</term> will be found in the vat. For a transmutation of this kind, you can even add a mixture of metals, taking into account, however, the special aptitude existing in them, by which one can be more easily transmuted than another.

### THE FIFTH CEMENT.

This fifth cement concerns only volatile bodies, such as common <term>Mercury</term>, and metals like <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Venus</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Mars</term>, etc. It must be noted that the "corporal" <term>Mercuries</term> derived from metals differ from common <term>Mercury</term> in their tincture, since they require more tincture from the tested metals than the common variety does. Similarly, it should be understood that both types of <term>Mercury</term>—the corporal and the common—should first of all be coagulated so that they are able to resist the cement and recover their physical substance, along with their tincture and coloring, just as the best metals should.

The coagulation of <term>Mercury</term>* is as follows: Take <term>Aquafortis</term>, weakened by a solution of <term>Luna</term> to such a degree that it no longer has any corrosive force or sharpness for dissolving. Into this, put either of the <term>Mercuries</term> mentioned before; let the liquid be warmed a little and afterward stirred into a thick mass. Then the <term>Mercury</term> will coagulate and harden into the form of—

### THE SIXTH CEMENT.

It now remains to be said in what way "part with part" comes to be cemented so that it receives more of the tincture, and receives it sooner than by other similar operations of the artists, because <term>Sol</term> <note>Gold</note> is fixed and graduated by the cement. It should be understood, too, that these should be cemented and both raised to the highest degree, prepared, refined, and re-purified; afterward, they should be melted at the same time and formed into plates of equal weight, then layered in a tightly closed crucible with the following powder: Cinnabar, Flower of Brass, and Bloodstone, half a dram each; Sal Ammoniac, Calamine, Sulphur, Common Salt, Vitriol, Alum, and Crocus of Mars, two ounces each.

After having been well ground and mixed into one body, let them be exposed to a gentle fire, then soaked with urine, and finally use it for the aforementioned layering. Let them be placed in the fire for six hours to melt: then renew and melt for another six hours. Do the same a third time for twelve hours, and a fourth time for twenty-four hours. Lastly, melt by a "lightning" of <term>Saturn</term> <note>Refining with lead</note>. In this way, you have transmutation. If, however, you have selected other metals, such as <term>Venus</term> <note>Copper</note> or <term>Mars</term> <note>Iron</note>, add more of the powder and more heat, so that they may be able to mix and be brought to a state of transmutation.

The patriarch Jacob painted, as it were, the sheep with various colors; and this was done by magic. For in the theology of the Chaldeans, Hebrews, Persians, and Egyptians, they held these arts to be the highest philosophy, to be learned by their chief nobles and priests. So it was in the time of Moses, when both the priests and also the physicians were chosen from among the Magi—the priests for the judgment of what related to health, especially in the knowledge of leprosy. Moses, likewise, was instructed in the Egyptian schools at the expense and care of Pharaoh's daughter, so that he excelled in all the wisdom and learning of that people. So too was it with Daniel, who in his youth absorbed the learning of the Chaldeans, so that he became a cabalist. Witness his divine predictions and his exposition of those words, "Mene, Mene, Tecelphares." These words can be understood by the prophetic and cabalistic art. This cabalistic art was perfectly familiar to, and in constant use by, Moses and the prophets. The prophet Elijah <note>Elias</note> foretold many things by his cabalistic numbers. So did the Wise Men of old learn to know God rightly by this natural and mystical art. They lived by His laws and walked in His statutes with great firmness. It is also evident in the Book of Samuel that the Berelists <note>Likely referring to those who practiced scrying or divination using beryl stones</note> did not follow the devil's side, but became, by Divine permission, partakers of visions and true apparitions, of which we shall treat more at length in the *Book of Supercelestial Things*.* This gift is granted by the Lord God to those priests who walk in the Divine precepts. It was a custom among the Persians never to admit anyone as king unless he was a Wise Man, pre-eminent in reality as well as in name. This is clear from the common name of their kings, for they were called Wise Men. Such were those Wise Men and Persian Magi who came from the East to seek out the Lord Jesus and are called natural priests. The Egyptians, also, having obtained this magic and philosophy from the Chaldeans and Persians, desired that their priests should learn the same wisdom; and they became so fruitful and successful in it that all the neighboring countries admired them. For this reason, Hermes was so truly named Trismegistus because he was a king, a priest, a prophet, a magician, and a scholar <note>sophist</note> of natural things. Such another was Zoroaster.

Since, however, the theological study of the law of Moses did not satisfy them, they trusted to their own peculiar genius and fell away from the right foundation of those natural secrets and arts. This is evident from their fabulous conceptions and from their errors respecting the doctrine of Moses. It was the custom of the Egyptians to put forward the traditions of that surpassing wisdom only in enigmatic figures and abstruse histories and terms. They then attempted to elaborate a certain kind of philosophy which descended from them to the Latins. These in their turn, being educated in this, adorned it with their own doctrines, and by these the philosophy was spread over Europe. Many academies were founded for the propagation of their dogmas and rules so that the young might be instructed; and this system flourishes among the Germans and other nations right down to the present day.

## CHAPTER III.

### WHAT WAS TAUGHT IN THE SCHOOLS OF THE EGYPTIANS.

The Chaldeans, Persians, and Egyptians all had the same knowledge of the secrets of Nature, and also the same religion. It was only the names that differed. The Chaldeans and Persians called their doctrine Sophia and Magic <note>Above all things, it is necessary to have a right understanding of the nature of celestial magic. Finally, there is the magus of perdition. — *Philosophia Sagax*, Book II, ch. 6.</note>; and the Egyptians, because of the sacrifice, called their wisdom priestcraft. ### CHAPTER IV.
#### WHAT MAGI THE CHALDEANS, PERSIANS, AND EGYPTIANS WERE.

Many persons have endeavored to investigate and make use of the secret magic of these wise men; but it has not yet been accomplished. Many even of our own age exalt Trithemius, others Bacon and Agrippa, for magic and the cabala*—two things apparently quite distinct—not knowing why they do so. Magic, indeed, is an art and faculty whereby the elementary bodies, their fruits, properties, virtues, and hidden operations are comprehended. But the cabala, by a subtle understanding of the Scriptures, seems to trace out the way to God for men, to show them how they may act with Him, and prophesy from Him; for the cabala is full of divine mysteries, even as Magic is full of natural secrets. It teaches of and foretells from the nature of things to come as well as of things present, since its operation consists in knowing the inner constitution of all creatures, of celestial as well as terrestrial bodies: what is latent within them; what are their occult virtues; for what they were originally designed, and with what properties they are endowed. These and the like subjects are the bonds wherewith celestial things are bound up with things of the earth, as may sometimes be seen in their operation even with the bodily eyes. Such a conjunction of celestial influences, whereby the heavenly virtues acted upon inferior bodies, was formerly called by the Magi a Gamahea,†

---

This art, formerly called cabalistic, was in the beginning named caballa, and afterwards caballia. It is a species of magic. It was also, but falsely, called Gabanala, by one whose knowledge of the subject was profound. It was of an unknown ethnic origin, and it passed subsequently to the Chaldeans and Hebrews, by both of whom it was corrupted.—*Philosophia Sagax*, Book I., under the heading *Probatio in Scientiam Nectromanticam*.

It is possible, magically, for a person to project his influence into these stones and some other substances.—*Ibid.*, chapter 13. There was also an artificial Gamaheus invented and prepared by the Magi, and this seems to have been more powerful.—*De Carduo Angelico*.

The devil attempted with all his force and effort to darken this light; nor was he entirely frustrated in his hopes, for he deprived all Greece of it, and, in its place, introduced among that people human speculations and plain blasphemies against God and against His Son. ### CHAPTER V.

#### CONCERNING THE CHIEF AND SUPREME ESSENCE OF THINGS.

The <term>Magi</term> in their wisdom asserted that all creatures might be brought to one unified substance, which they affirm may, through purifications and purgations, attain to so high a degree of subtlety, such divine nature and occult property, as to work wonderful results. For they considered that by returning to the earth, and by a supreme magical separation, a certain perfect substance would come forth, which is at length, through many diligent and prolonged preparations, exalted and raised up above the range of vegetable substances into mineral, above mineral into metallic, and above perfect metallic substances into a perpetual and divine <term>Quintessence</term>,<note>Man was regarded by Paracelsus as being, in a special manner, the true Quintessence. He extracted the essence out of the four elements into one mass; He also extracted the</note> including in itself the

Whoever obtained this Stone overshadowed it with various puzzling figures, deceptive resemblances, comparisons, and fictitious titles, so that its matter might remain hidden. Very little or no knowledge of it, therefore, can be gained from them.

# CHAPTER VI.

## CONCERNING THE DIFFERENT ERRORS AS TO ITS DISCOVERY AND KNOWLEDGE.

The philosophers have assigned highly hidden names to this matter of the Stone, based on mere similarities. Arnold, observing this, says in his *Rosary* that the greatest difficulty is to find out the material of this Stone; for they have called it vegetable, animal, and mineral, but not according to the literal sense. This is well known to such wise men as have had experience with divine secrets and the miracles of this same Stone. For example, Raymond Lully’s *Lunaria* may be cited. This produces flowers of wonderful virtues familiar to the philosophers themselves; but it was not the intention of those philosophers that you should think they meant any projection upon metals, or that any such preparations should be made; rather, the hidden mind of the philosophers had another intention. In like manner, they called their matter by the name of *Martagon*, to which they applied a hidden alchemical operation; yet, despite that name, it denotes nothing more than a hidden similarity. Moreover, no small error has arisen regarding the liquid of vegetables, with which a good many have sought to solidify Mercury,* and afterwards to convert it with fixing waters into Luna, since they supposed that he who could solidify it in this way without the aid of metals would succeed in becoming the chief master. Now, although the liquids of some vegetables do effect this, yet the result is due merely to the resin, fat, and earthy sulphur with which they abound. This attracts the moisture to itself

The mass was extracted, and therein the firmament and the elements were condensed. What was extracted from the four in this manner constituted a fifth. The Quintessence is the nucleus and the place of the essences and properties of all things in the universal world. ### CHAPTER VII.

->CONCERNING THE ERRORS OF THOSE WHO SEEK THE STONE IN VEGETABLES.<-

Some alchemists have pressed the juice out of celandine, boiled it until thick, and placed it in the sun so that it might coagulate into a hard mass. They then pounded this into a fine black powder, intended to turn Mercury into <term>Sol</term> <note>Gold</note> through projection. This they also found to be in vain. Others mixed <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> with this powder; others used the <term>Colcothar</term> of Vitriol, believing they would achieve their desired result this way. Through their solutions, they turned it into a yellow water, so that the Sal Ammoniac would allow the tincture to enter the substance of the Mercury. Yet again, nothing was accomplished. There are some again who, instead of the substances mentioned above, take the juices of <term>persicaria</term>, <term>bufonaria</term>, <term>dracunculus</term>, the leaves of willow, <term>tithymal</term>, <term>cataputia</term>, <term>flammula</term>, and the like. They seal them in a glass vessel with Mercury for several days, keeping them in warm ashes. Consequently, the Mercury is turned into ashes, but deceptively and without any useful result. These people were misled by the empty rumors of the common folk, who claim that whoever is able to coagulate Mercury without using metals possesses the entire <term>Magistery</term>, as we have stated before. Many have also artificially extracted salts, oils, and sulphurs from vegetables, but entirely in vain. From such salts, oils, and sulphurs, no coagulation of Mercury, perfect projection, or tincture can be produced. However, when the philosophers compare their matter to a certain golden tree with seven branches, they mean that this matter contains all seven metals within its "seed," and that they lie hidden there. For this reason, they called their matter "vegetable," because, like natural trees, they also produce various flowers in their season. Similarly, the matter of the <term>Stone</term> shows most beautiful colors during the production of its "flowers." The comparison is also appropriate because a certain substance rises out of the philosophical earth like a thicket of branches and sprouts, or like a sponge growing on the ground. Therefore, they say that the fruit of their tree reaches toward heaven. Thus, they propose that the entire process...

## CHAPTER VIII.

### CONCERNING THOSE WHO HAVE SOUGHT THE STONE IN ANIMALS.

Using names based only on resemblances, they have also called this matter *Lac Virginis* and the "Blessed Blood of Rosy Color," which, nevertheless, is appropriate only for the prophets and sons of God. Consequently, the sophists* concluded that this philosophical matter was found in the blood of animals or humans. Sometimes, too, because animals are nourished by vegetables, others have sought it in hair, in the salt of urine, and in <term>rebis</term> <note>Excrement or waste matter</note>; others sought it in hens' eggs, milk, and the powder of eggshells, believing they would be able to fix Mercury with all of these. Some have extracted salt from foul-smelling urine, assuming that to be the matter of the Stone. Some persons, again, have considered the small stones found in <term>rebis</term> to be the matter. Others have soaked the membranes of eggs in a sharp lye, with which they also mixed calcined eggshells as white as snow. To these they attributed the secret of fixation for the transmutation of Mercury. Others, comparing the egg white to silver and the yolk to gold, have chosen it for their matter, mixing with it common salt, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, and burnt tartar. They sealed these in a glass vessel and purified them in a *Balneum Maris* <note>A water bath</note> until the white matter became as red as blood. This, again, they distilled into a most offensive liquid, which was utterly useless for the purpose they had in view. Others have purified the white and yolk of eggs, from which a <term>basilisk</term> <note>A mythical creature; here used to describe a failed or monstrous chemical result</note> has been generated. They burned this to a deep red powder and sought to tinge with it, as they learned from the treatise of Cardinal Gilbert. Many, again, have soaked the galls of oxen mixed with common salt and distilled this into a liquid, with which they moistened the cementing powders, supposing that, by means of this Mastery, they would tinge their metals. They called this by the name of "a part with a part," and from it came—absolutely nothing. Others have attempted to transmute <term>tutia</term> <note>Zinc oxide</note> by the addition of dragon's blood and other substances, and also to change copper and <term>electrum</term> <note>An alloy of gold and silver</note> into gold. Others, according to the "Venetian Art," as they call it, take twenty lizard-like animals, more or less, shut them up in a vessel, and drive them mad with hunger so that they devour one another until only one survives. This survivor is then fed with filings of copper or of electrum. They suppose that this animal, simply through the digestion of its stomach, will bring about the desired transmutation. Finally, they burn this animal into a red powder, which they thought must be gold; but they were deceived. Others, again, having burned the fish called <term>truitas</term> <note>Trouts</note>, have sometimes, upon melting them, found some gold in them; but there is no other reason for it than this: those fish in rivers sometimes—

The matter of the philosophers is not to be sought in animals; this I announce to all. ### CHAPTER IX.

#### CONCERNING THOSE WHO HAVE SOUGHT THE STONE IN MINERALS.

To this are added the many ignorant men who suppose the stone to be threefold and to be hidden in a triple genus—namely, vegetable, animal, and mineral. It is for this reason that they have sought for it in minerals. Now, this is far from the opinion of the philosophers. They affirm that their stone is uniformly vegetable, animal, and mineral. Now, note here that Nature has distributed its mineral sperm into various kinds, such as: sulphurs, salts, boraxes, nitres, ammoniacs, alums, arsenics, atraments, vitriols, tutias, hematites, orpiments, realgars, magnesias, cinnabar, antimony, talc, cachymia, marcasites, etc. In all these, Nature has not yet attained our matter, although in some of the named species it displays itself in a wonderful aspect, and although Nature has reached some perfection by means of prepared minerals. Truly, long experience and practice with fire show many and various permutations in the matter of minerals, not only from one color to another, but from one essence to another, and from imperfection to perfection. And although Nature has reached some perfection through prepared minerals, yet philosophers will not accept that the matter of the philosophic stone proceeds from any of these minerals, even though they say their stone is universal. Hence, the sophists take the opportunity to persecute Mercury himself with various torments, such as sublimations, coagulations, mercurial waters, *aqua fortis*, and the like. All these erroneous ways should be avoided,

It is true that I have seen Mercury, through this Art and by such fixations, transformed into a metallic body resembling and counterfeiting good silver in every way; however, when put to the test, it proved to be false.

### CHAPTER X.

#### CONCERNING THOSE WHO HAVE SOUGHT THE STONE AND ALSO PARTICULARS IN MINERALS.

Some deceivers have tried to extract a fixed oil from Mercury that has been sublimated seven times and dissolved just as often using aquafortis. In this way, they attempt to bring imperfect metals to perfection, but they have been forced to abandon their useless efforts. Some have purified vitriol seven times through calcination, solution, and coagulation, adding two parts of sal ammoniac and using sublimation so that it might be resolved into a white liquid. To this, they added a third part of quicksilver so that it might be coagulated by water. Afterward, they sublimated the Mercury several times from the vitriol and sal ammoniac until it became a stone. They claimed that this stone—being created from the vitriol—was the Red Sulfur of the philosophers, through which, by means of solutions and coagulations, they made some progress toward attaining the Stone; but in projection, it all came to nothing. Others have coagulated Mercury with alum water into a hard mass like alum itself, and they have fruitlessly attempted to fix this with fixative waters. These deceivers propose many ways to fix Mercury, but to no purpose, for nothing perfect or stable can be obtained from them. It is therefore useless to add minerals to it through deceptive processes, since through all of them, it is stirred up to greater malice and rendered

### CHAPTER XI.

#### CONCERNING THE TRUE AND PERFECT SPECIAL SECRET <note>ARCANUM</note> OF ARSENIC FOR THE WHITE TINCTURE.

Some people have written that arsenic is composed of Mercury and Sulfur, others of earth and water; but most writers say that it is of the nature of Sulfur. But, however that may be, its nature is such that it transmutes red copper into white. It may also be brought to such a perfect state of preparation as to be able to transform <note>tinge</note>. But this is not done in the way pointed out by such evil sophists as Geber in “The Sum of Perfection,” Albertus Magnus, Aristotle the chemist in “The Book of the Perfect Magistery,” Rhasis and Polydorus; for those writers, however many they may be, are either themselves in error, or else they write falsely out of sheer envy, and put forth recipes while not ignorant of the truth. Arsenic contains within itself three natural spirits. The first is volatile, combustible, corrosive, and penetrates all metals. This spirit whitens Copper <note>Venus</note> and after some days renders it spongy. But this technique relates only to those who practice the caustic art. The second spirit is crystalline and sweet. The third is a transforming <note>tingeing</note> spirit separated from the others mentioned before. True philosophers seek for these three natural properties in arsenic with a view to the perfect projection of the wise men.\* But those barbers who practice surgery seek after that sweet and crystalline nature separated from the transforming spirit for use in the cure of wounds, swellings <note>buboes</note>,

### CHAPTER XII.

#### GENERAL INSTRUCTION CONCERNING THE ARCANUM OF VITRIOL AND THE RED TINCTURE TO BE EXTRACTED FROM IT.*

Vitriol is a very noble mineral among the rest, and was always held in the highest estimation by philosophers because the Most High God has adorned it with wonderful gifts. They have veiled its secret <note>arcanum</note> in enigmatical figures like the following: “You shall go to the inner parts of the earth, and by rectification you shall find the hidden stone, a true medicine.” By the earth, they understood the Vitriol itself; and by the inner parts of the earth, its sweetness and redness, because in the hidden part of the Vitriol lies concealed a subtle, noble, and most fragrant juice, and a pure oil. The method of its production is not to be approached by roasting <note>calcination</note> or by distillation. For it must not be deprived on any account of its green color. If it were, it would at the same time lose its secret <note>arcanum</note> and its power. Indeed, it should be observed at this point that minerals, and also vegetables and other similar things which show greenness on the outside, contain within themselves an oil as red as blood, which is their secret <note>arcanum</note>. Hence it is clear that the distillations of the druggists are useless, vain, foolish, and of no value, because these people do not know how to extract the blood-like redness from vegetables. Nature herself is wise, and turns all the waters of vegetables to a lemon color, and after that into an oil which is very red, like blood. The reason why this is so slowly accomplished arises from the too great haste of the ignorant operators who distil it, which causes the greenness to be consumed. They have not learned to strengthen Nature with their own powers, which is the method by which that noble green

\* The secret <note>arcanum</note> of vitriol is the oil of vitriol. It works like this: after the wateriness <note>aquosity</note> has been removed from vitriol through boiling <note>coction</note>, the spirit is drawn out by the application of greater heat. The vitriol then comes over pure in the form of water. This water is combined with the dregs <note>caput mortuum</note> left by the process, and on separating it again in a water bath <note>balneum maris</note>, the watery <note>phlegmatic</note> part passes off, and the oil—or the secret <note>arcanum</note> of vitriol—remains at the bottom of the vessel. — *Ibid.*
