# CHAPTER XIII.

## SPECIAL INSTRUCTION CONCERNING THE PROCESS OF VITRIOL FOR THE RED TINCTURE.

<margin>
* As long as the greenness of vitriol remains within it, it is of a soft quality and substance. But if it is cooked through heat so that it is deprived of its moisture, it is thereby changed into a hard stone from which even fire can be struck. When the moisture is evaporated from vitriol, the sulfur which it contains predominates over the salt, and the vitriol turns red.—*De Pestilitate*, Tract I.
</margin>

<margin>
† The diagnosis of vitriol is concerned with it both in medicine and alchemy. In medicine, it is a paramount remedy. In alchemy, it has many additional purposes. The art of medicine and alchemy consists in the preparation of vitriol, for it is worthless in its crude state. It is like wood, out of which it is possible to carve anything. Three kinds of oil are extracted from vitriol—a red oil, by distillation in a retort after an alchemical method, and this is the most acidic of all substances and also has a corrosive quality—also a green and a white oil, distilled from crude vitriol by descension.—*De Vitriolo*. Nor let it be regarded as absurd that we assign such great virtues to vitriol, for therein resides, secret and hidden, a certain peculiar golden force, not corporeal but spiritual; this excellent and admirable virtue exists in greater potency and certainty therein than it does in gold. When this golden spirit of vitriol is volatilized and separated from its impurities, so that the essence alone remains, it is like potable gold.—*De Morbis Amentium, Methodus II., c. 1.*
</margin>

Vitriol contains within itself many muddy and viscous imperfections. Therefore, its greenness* must be often extracted with water and rectified until it sheds all the impurities of earth. When all these rectifications are finished, take care above all that the matter shall not be exposed to the sun, for this turns its greenness pale and at the same time absorbs the secret <note>arcanum</note>. Let it be kept covered up in a warm stove so that no dust may defile it. Afterwards, let it be digested in a closed glass vessel for the space of several months, or until different colors and deep redness show themselves. Still, you must not suppose that by this process the redness is sufficiently fixed. It must, in addition, be cleansed from the interior and accidental defilements of the earth in the following manner: it must be rectified with vinegar <note>acetum</note> until the earthy defilement is altogether removed and the dregs are taken away. This is now the true and best rectification of its tincture, from which the blessed oil is to be extracted. From this tincture, which is carefully enclosed in a glass vessel with an alembic afterwards placed on it and sealed <note>luted</note> so that no spirit may escape, the spirit of this oil must be extracted by distillation over a mild and slow fire. This oil is much pleasanter and sweeter than any aromatic balsam of the druggists, being entirely free from all acridity.† There will settle in the bottom of the cucurbite some very white earth, shining and glittering like snow. Keep this and protect it from all dust. This same earth is altogether separated from its redness.

Thereupon follows the greatest secret <note>arcanum</note>, that is to say, the Supercelestial Marriage of the Soul, consummately prepared and washed by the blood of the

## CHAPTER XIV.

### CONCERNING THE SECRETS AND ARCANA OF ANTIMONY, FOR THE RED TINCTURE, WITH A VIEW TO TRANSMUTATION.

Antimony is the true bath of gold. Philosophers call it the examiner and the stilanx <note>likely referring to a balance or touchstone</note>. Poets say that in this bath Vulcan washed Phoebus, and purified him from all dirt and imperfection. It is produced from the purest and noblest Mercury and Sulphur, under the genus of vitriol, in metallic form and brightness. Some philosophers call it the White Lead of the Wise Men, or simply the Lead. Take, therefore, of Antimony, the very best of its kind, as much as you will. Dissolve this in its own <term>aquafortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note>, and throw it into cold water, adding a little of the <term>crocus of Mars</term> <note>iron oxide</note>, so that it may sink to the bottom of the vessel as a sediment, for otherwise it does not throw off its dregs. After it has been dissolved in this way it will have acquired supreme beauty. Let it be placed in a glass vessel, closely fastened on all sides with a very thick lute <note>a clay or cement seal</note>, or else in a stone bocia <note>a glass or ceramic vessel</note>, and mix with it some calcined <term>tutia</term> <note>zinc oxide</note>, sublimated to the perfect degree of fire. It must be carefully guarded from liquefying, because with too great heat it breaks the glass. From one pound of this Antimony a sublimation is made, perfected for a space of two days. Place this sublimated substance in a phial so that it may touch the water with its third part, in a luted vessel, so that the spirit may not escape. Let it be suspended over the <term>tripod of arcana</term>, and let the work be pushed forward at first with a slow fire equal to the sun's heat at midsummer. Then at length on the tenth day let it be gradually increased. For with too great heat the glass vessels are broken, and sometimes even the furnace goes to pieces. While the vapor is ascending different colors appear. Let the fire be moderated until a red matter is seen. Afterwards dissolve it in very sharp <term>Acetum</term> <note>distilled vinegar</note>, and throw away the dregs. Let the <term>Acetum</term> be abstracted and let it be again dissolved in common distilled water,

Let these two oils in combination be shut up together in a phial after the manner described, hung on a tripod for a philosophical month, and warmed with a very gentle fire; although, if the fire is regulated in due proportion, this operation is concluded and brought to perfection in thirty-one days. By this, <term>Mercury</term> and any other imperfect metals acquire the perfection of gold.

## CHAPTER XV.

### CONCERNING THE PROJECTION TO BE MADE BY THE MYSTERY AND ARCANUM OF ANTIMONY.

No precise weight can be assigned in this work of <term>projection</term> <note>the process of transmuting base metals into gold</note>, though the <term>tincture</term> itself may be extracted from a certain subject in a defined proportion and with fitting appliances. For instance, that <term>Medicine</term> colors <note>tinges</note> sometimes thirty, forty, occasionally even sixty, eighty, or a hundred parts of the imperfect metal. So, then, the whole business hinges chiefly on the purification of the <term>Medicine</term> and the industry of the operator, and, next, on the greater or lesser cleanliness and purity of the imperfect body taken in hand. For instance, one <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note> is more pure than another; and hence it happens that no one fixed weight can be specified in <term>projection</term>. This alone is worth noting: if the operator happens to have taken too much of the <term>tincture</term>, he can correct this mistake by adding more of the imperfect metal. But if there is too much of the subject, so that the powers of the <term>tincture</term> are weakened, this error is easily remedied by a <term>cineritium</term> <note>a cupellation process using ashes</note>, or by <term>cementations</term>, or by <term>ablutions</term> <note>washings</note>.

---

* <term>Antimony</term> can be made into a paste with the water of vitriol, and then purified by <term>sal ammoniac</term>, and in this manner a thick purple or reddish liquor may be obtained from it. This is oil of antimony, and it has many virtues. —*Great Surgery* <note>Chirurgia Magna</note>, Book V. Take three pounds of antimony and as much <term>sal gemmæ</term> <note>rock salt</note>. Distil them together in a retort for three natural days, and so you will have a red oil, which has incredible healing power in cases of otherwise incurable wounds. —*Minor Surgery* <note>Chirurgia Minor</note>, Tract II., c. 11.

->ANIMATION IS PRODUCED IN THE FOLLOWING WAY.<-

In this way, it is purged and purified from its dense greenness and from its own impure <term>Sulphur</term>. You will have to be on your guard against calcinations made with common sulfur. But if a projection of a red stone is to be made, with a view to a red transmutation, it must first fall on gold, afterwards on silver, or on some other metal thoroughly purified, as we have directed above. From this arises the most perfect gold.

### CHAPTER XVI.

### CONCERNING THE UNIVERSAL MATTER OF THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE.

After the mortification of vegetables, they are transmuted into a mineral nature by the combination of two minerals, such as <term>Sulphur</term> and <term>Salt</term>, so that at length they themselves become perfect minerals. So it is that in the mineral burrows and caves of the earth, vegetables are found which, over a long succession of time and by the continuous heat of sulfur, shed their vegetable nature and assume that of the mineral. This happens, for the most part, where the appropriate nourishment is taken away from vegetables of this kind, so that they are afterwards compelled to derive their nourishment from the sulfur and salts of the earth, until what was before vegetable passes over into a perfect mineral. From this mineral state, too, sometimes a perfect metallic essence arises, and this happens by the progression from one degree into another.

But let us return to the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term>. The matter of this, as certain writers have mentioned, is above all else difficult to discover and

The most certain method and rule for discovering this, as well as other subjects—what they contain or are capable of achieving—is a careful examination of the root and seed through which they become known to us. For this, a consideration of principles is absolutely necessary before anything else, as is an understanding of the way Nature proceeds from imperfection to the state of perfection. Now, regarding this consideration, it is helpful to have it thoroughly understood from the beginning that all things created by Nature consist of three primary elements—namely, natural <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Sulphur</term>, and <term>Salt</term>—in combination, so that in some substances they are volatile, while in others they are fixed. 

Whenever physical <term>Salt</term> is mixed with spiritual <term>Mercury</term> and animated <term>Sulphur</term> into one body, Nature begins to work within those subterranean places that serve as her vessels, using a separating fire. Through this, the thick and impure <term>Sulphur</term> is separated from the pure, the earth is divided from the <term>Salt</term>, and the clouds from the <term>Mercury</term>, while the purer parts are preserved; these Nature welds together again into a pure geogamic <note>Earth-born</note> body. The <term>Magi</term> regard this operation as a mixture and conjunction formed by the uniting of three constituents: body, soul, and spirit. When this union is completed, a pure <term>Mercury</term> results from it. Now, if this <term>Mercury</term>, while flowing down through subterranean passages and veins, meets with a chaotic <term>Sulphur</term>, it is coagulated by it according to the condition of that <term>Sulphur</term>. However, it remains volatile, so that it is hardly transformed into a metal even in a hundred years. 

This led to the common idea that <term>Mercury</term> and <term>Sulphur</term> are the matter of metals, as is indeed reported by miners. However, it is not common mercury and common sulfur that are the matter of metals; rather, the <term>Mercury</term> and the <term>Sulphur</term> of the philosophers are incorporated and innate within perfect metals and their forms, so that they never flee from the fire, nor are they corrupted by the force of the elements. It is true that by the dissolution of this natural mixture, our <term>Mercury</term> is subdued, as all the philosophers say. In this sense, our <term>Mercury</term> is drawn from perfect bodies and from the forces of the earthly planets. This is what <term>Hermes</term> asserts in the following terms: "The Sun and the Moon are the roots of this Art." The Son of <term>Hamuel</term> says that the <term>Stone of the philosophers</term> is coagulated water—namely, in <term>Sol</term> <note>gold</note> and <term>Luna</term> <note>silver</note>. 

From this, it is clearer than the sun that the material of the <term>Stone</term> is nothing other than <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>. This is confirmed by the fact that like produces like. We know that there are only two Stones: the white and the red. There are also two matters of the Stone—<term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>—joined together in a proper marriage, both natural and artificial. Now, just as we see that a man or a woman cannot generate without the seed of both, in the same way, our man, <term>Sol</term>, and his wife, <term>Luna</term>, cannot conceive or produce anything through generation without the seed and sperm of both. Therefore, the philosophers concluded that a third thing was necessary—namely, the animated seed of both the man and the woman—without which they judged that their entire work was fruitless and in vain. Such a sperm is <term>Mercury</term>,

Thus the philosophers have said that this same *Mercury* is composed of body, spirit, and soul, and that it has assumed the nature and property of all elements. Therefore, with their most powerful genius and intellect, they asserted their Stone to be a living being. They even called it their *Adam*, who carries his own invisible *Eve* hidden in his body, from that moment in which they were united by the power of the Supreme God, the Maker of all creatures. For this reason it may be said that the *Mercury* of the Philosophers is none other than their most abstruse, compounded *Mercury*, and not the common *Mercury*. So then they have wisely said to the sages that there is in *Mercury* whatever wise men seek. *Almadir*, the philosopher, says: "*We extract our Mercury from one perfect body and two perfect natural conditions incorporated together, which indeed puts forth externally its perfection, whereby it is able to resist the fire, so that its internal imperfection may be protected by the external perfections.*" By this passage of the wise philosopher is understood the Adamic matter, the <term>limbus</term> of the <term>microcosm</term>, and the homogeneous, unique matter of the philosophers. The sayings of these men, which we have before mentioned, are simply golden, and always to be held in the highest esteem, because they contain nothing superfluous or without force. In summary, then, the matter of the *Philosopher's Stone* is none other than a fiery and perfect *Mercury* extracted by *Nature* and *Art*; that is, the artificially prepared and true hermaphrodite *Adam*, and the microcosm. That wisest of the philosophers, *Mercurius*, making the same statement, called the *Stone an orphan*. Our *Mercury*, therefore, is the same which contains in itself all the perfections, force, and virtues of the *Sun*, which also runs through all the streets and houses of all the planets, and in its own rebirth has acquired the force of things above and things below; to the marriage of which it is to be compared, as is clear from the whiteness and the redness combined in it.

sophic Stone. Moreover, it should be remarked that those common preparations of Geber, Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, Rupescissa, Polydorus, and such men, are nothing more than some particular solutions, sublimations, and calcinations, having no reference to our universal substance, which needs only the most secret fire of the philosophers. Let the fire and Azoth therefore suffice for you. From the fact that the philosophers mention certain preparations, such as putrefaction, distillation, sublimation, calcination, coagulation, dealbation, rubification, ceration, fixation, and the like, you should understand that in their universal substance, Nature herself fulfills all the operations in the matter spoken of, and not the operator, only in a philosophical vessel, and with a similar fire, but not common fire. The white and the red spring from one root without any intermediary. It is dissolved by itself, it copulates by itself, grows white, grows red, is made crocus-colored and black by itself, marries itself and conceives in itself. It is therefore to be decocted, to be baked, to be fused; it ascends, and it descends. All these operations are a single operation and produced by the fire alone. Still, some philosophers, nevertheless, have, by a highly graduated essence of wine, dissolved the body of Sol, and rendered it volatile, so that it should ascend through an alembic, thinking that this is the true volatile matter of the philosophers, though it is not so. And although it is no contemptible arcanum to reduce this perfect metallic body into a volatile, spiritual substance, yet they are wrong in their separation of the elements. This process of the monks, such as Lully, Richard of England, Rupescissa, and the rest, is erroneous. By this process they thought that they were going to separate gold in this fashion into a subtle, spiritual, and elementary power, each by itself, and afterward by circulation and rectification to combine them again in one—but in vain. For although one element may, in a certain sense, be separated from another, yet, nevertheless, every element separated in this way can again be separated into another element, but these elements cannot afterward by circulation in a pelican, or by distillation, be again brought back into one; but they always remain a certain volatile matter, and *aurum potabile*, as they themselves call it. The reason why they could not achieve their intention is that Nature refuses to be in this way dragged asunder and separated by man's disjunctions, as by earthly glasses and instruments. She alone knows her own operations and the weights of the elements, the separations, rectifications, and copulations of which she brings about without the aid of any operator or manual artifice, provided only the matter is contained in the secret fire and in its proper occult vessel. The separation of the elements, therefore, is impossible for man. It may appear to take place, but it is not true, whatever may be said by Raymond Lully, and of that famous English golden work which he is falsely supposed to have accomplished. Nature herself has within herself the proper separator, who again joins together what he has put asunder, without the aid of man. She knows best the proportion of every element, which man does not know, however mis-

Leading writers romanticize in their frivolous and false recipes about this volatile gold.

This is the opinion of the philosophers: that when they have put their matter into the more secret fire, and when it is cherished on every side with a moderated philosophical heat, it begins to undergo corruption and turns black. This operation they term putrefaction, and they call the blackness by the name of the **Crow's Head**. Its ascent and descent they term distillation, ascension, and descension. The drying they call coagulation; and the whitening they call calcination; while, because it becomes fluid and soft in the heat, they make mention of ceration. When it ceases to ascend and remains liquid at the bottom, they say fixation is present.

In this manner, the terms of philosophical operations are to be understood, and not otherwise.

---

### CHAPTER XVIII.

#### CONCERNING INSTRUMENTS AND THE PHILOSOPHIC VESSEL.

False philosophers have misunderstood the occult and secret philosophical vessel, and even worse is what is said by Aristoteles the Alchemist (not the famous Greek Academic philosopher), who claims that the matter is to be decocted in a triple vessel. Worst of all is what is said by another, namely, that the matter in its first separation and first degree requires a metallic vessel; in its second degree of coagulation and whitening of its earth, a glass vessel; and in the third degree, for fixation, an earthen vessel. Nevertheless, by this, the philosophers mean only one vessel throughout all the operations until the perfection of the red stone. Since, then, our matter is our root for the white and the red, our vessel must necessarily be fashioned so that the matter in it may be governed by the heavenly bodies. For invisible celestial influences and the impressions of the stars are necessary for the work at the very first stage. Otherwise, it would be impossible for the Oriental, Chaldean, and Egyptian stone to be realized. By this, Anaxagoras knew the powers of the entire firmament and foretold that a great stone would descend from heaven to earth, which actually happened after his death. To the Cabalists, our vessel is perfectly well known, because it must be made according to a truly geometrical proportion and measure, and from a definite quadrature of the circle, so that the spirit and the soul of our matter, separated from their body, may be able to raise this vessel with themselves in proportion to the altitude of heaven. If the vessel is wider, narrower, higher, or lower than is fitting, and than the dominating operating spirit and soul desire, the heat of our secret philosophical fire (which is, indeed, very severe) will violently excite the matter and urge it on to excessive operation, so that the vessel is shivered into a thousand pieces, with imminent danger to the body and even the life of the operator. On the other hand, if it is of greater capacity than is required in due proportion for the heat to have an effect on the matter, the

work will be wasted and thrown away. So, then, our philosophical vessel must be made with the greatest care. What the material of the vessel should be is understood only by those who, in the first solution of our fixed and perfected matter, have brought that matter to its own primal quintessence. Enough has been said on this point.

The operator must also very accurately note what the matter sends forth and rejects from itself during its first solution.

The method of describing the form of the vessel is difficult. It should be such as Nature requires, and it must be sought out and investigated from every possible source so that, from the height of the philosophical heaven elevated above the philosophical earth, it may be able to operate on the fruit of its own earthly body. It should have this form, too, in order that the separation and purification of the elements may be accomplished when the fire drives one from the other, and so that each may have the power to occupy the place to which it adheres. It must also be formed so that the sun and the other planets may exercise their operations around the elemental earth while their course in their circuit is neither hindered nor agitated with too swift a motion. In all these particulars which have been mentioned, it must have a proper proportion of roundness and of height.

The instruments for the first purification of mineral bodies are fusing-vessels, bellows, tongs, capels, cupels, tests, cementatory vessels, cineritiums <note>Vessels or hearths used for refining metals with ashes.</note>, cucurbites, bocias <note>A type of glass flask or vial.</note> for *aquafortis* and *aqua regia*, and also the appliances which are required for projection at the climax of the work.

### CHAPTER XIX.
#### CONCERNING THE SECRET FIRE OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.

This is a well-known wise saying of the philosophers: “Let fire and Azoc <note>A term for Azoth, the universal solvent or the mercury of the philosophers.</note> suffice you.” Fire alone is the whole work and the entire art. Moreover, those who build their fire and keep their vessel in that heat are in error. In vain, some have attempted it with the heat of horse dung. By the coal fire, without a medium, they have sublimated their matter, but they have not dissolved it. Others have obtained their heat from lamps, asserting that this is the secret fire of the philosophers for making their Stone. Some have placed it in a bath—first of all in heaps of ants’ eggs; others in juniper ashes. Some have sought the fire in quicklime, in tartar, vitriol, nitre, and so on. Others, again, have sought it in boiling water. Thomas Aquinas speaks falsely of this fire, saying that God and the angels cannot do without this fire, but use it daily. What blasphemy is this! Is it not a manifest lie that God is not able to do without the elemental heat of boiling water? All the heats produced by those means which have been mentioned are utterly useless for our work. Take care not to be misled by Arnold de Villa Nova, who has written on the subject of the coal fire, for in this matter he will deceive you.

Almadir says that the invisible rays of our fire of themselves suffice.

Another person cites, as an illustration, that heavenly heat, through its reflections, tends toward the coagulation and perfection of Mercury, just as through its continual motion it tends toward the generation of metals. Again, this same authority says, “Make a vaporous, digesting fire, as if for cooking; it should be continuous but not volatile or boiling; enclosed and shut off from the air; not burning, but altering and penetrating. Now, in truth, I have mentioned every mode of fire and of exciting heat. If you are a true philosopher, you will understand.” This is what he says.

Salmanazar remarks: “Ours is a corrosive fire, which brings over our vessel an air like a cloud, in which cloud the rays of this fire are hidden. If this dew of chaos and this moisture of the cloud fail, a mistake has been committed.” Again, Almadir says that unless the fire has warmed our sun with its moisture, by the excrement of the mountain and with a moderate ascent, we shall not be partakers of either the Red or the White Stone.

All these matters show quite openly to us the occult fire of the wise men. Finally, this is the substance of our fire: it must be kindled by the quiet spirit of sensible fire, which drives the heated chaos upward, as it were, from the opposite quarter and above our philosophical matter. This heat, glowing above our vessel, must urge it toward the motion of a perfect generation, temperately but continuously, without intermission.

## CHAPTER XX.

### CONCERNING THE FERMENT OF THE PHILOSOPHERS, AND THE WEIGHT.

Philosophers have labored greatly in the art of ferments and fermentations, which seems more important than all others. Regarding this, some have made a vow to God and to the philosophers that they would never divulge its <term>arcanum</term> <note>A profound secret or mystery.</note> through metaphors or parables.

Nevertheless, Hermes—the father of all philosophers—most clearly discloses the secret of ferments in the “*Book of the Seven Treatises*,” saying that they consist only of their own paste. Further, he says that the ferment whitens the mixture, hinders combustion, completely slows the flow of the tincture, consoles bodies, and amplifies unions. He also says that this is the key and the end of the work, concluding that the ferment is nothing but paste—just as the ferment of the sun is nothing but sun, and that of the moon is nothing but moon. Others affirm that the ferment is the soul, and if this is not rightly prepared from the <term>magistery</term> <note>The mastery or the process of creating the philosopher's stone.</note>, it accomplishes nothing. Some zealots of this Art seek the Art in common sulphur, arsenic, <term>tutia</term> <note>Zinc oxide.</note>, <term>auripigment</term> <note>Orpiment; arsenic trisulfide.</note>, vitriol, etc., but in vain; for the substance being sought is the same as that from which it must be extracted. It should be noted, therefore, that fermentations of this kind do not succeed according to the wishes of these zealots in the way they desire but, as is clear from what has been said above, simply through natural processes.

But, to finally come to the matter of weight, this must be noted in two ways.

The first is natural, the second artificial. The natural attains its result in the earth by Nature and harmony. Of this, Arnold says: If more or less earth than Nature requires is added, the soul is suffocated, and no result is perceived, nor any fixation. It is the same with the water. If more or less of this is used, it will bring a corresponding loss. An excess makes the matter unduly moist, and a deficiency makes it too dry and too hard. If too much air is present, it is too strongly impressed on the <term>tincture</term>; if there is too little, the body will turn out pale. In the same way, if the fire is too strong, the matter is burnt up; if it is too weak, it does not have the power to dry, nor to dissolve or heat the other elements. In these things, elemental heat consists.

Artificial weight is quite hidden. It is comprised of the magical art of <term>ponderations</term>. Between the spirit, soul, and body, say the philosophers, weight consists of Sulphur as the director of the work; for the soul strongly desires Sulphur and necessarily adheres to it by reason of its weight.

You can understand it this way: Our matter is united to a red fixed Sulphur, to which a third part of the governance has been entrusted, even to the final degree, so that it may perfect the operation of the Stone to infinity, may remain there together with its fire, and may consist of a weight equal to the matter itself, in and through everything, without any variation. Therefore, after the matter has been prepared and mixed in its proportionate weight, it should be tightly closed with its seal in the vessel of the philosophers and committed to the secret fire. In this, the Philosophic Sun will rise and surge up, and will illuminate all things that have been looking for his light, expecting it with the highest hope.

In these few words, we will conclude the <term>arcanum</term> of the Stone—a secret which is in no way incomplete or defective—for which we give God undying thanks. Now we have opened our treasure to you, which cannot be bought by the riches of the entire world.

### PROLOGUE.

HAVING first of all invoked the name of the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior, we will enter upon this work; in which we shall not only teach how to change any inferior metal into better, such as iron into copper, copper into silver, and silver into gold, but also how to heal all infirmities which seem impossible to pretentious and presumptuous physicians; and—what is even more—how to preserve men to a long, healthy, and perfect age. This Art was bestowed by the Lord our God, the supreme Creator, engraved, as if in a book, in the body of the metals from the beginning of Creation for this end: that we might diligently learn from them. When, therefore, any man desires to become thoroughly and perfectly acquainted with this Art from its true foundation, it will be necessary that he should learn it from its Master, that is, from God, who created all things; who also alone knows what nature and properties He has placed in every creature. He, therefore, is able to teach everyone certainly and perfectly; and from Him we can be taught absolutely what He means when He says, “Of Me you shall learn all things.” For nothing in Heaven or on earth is found so hidden that He who created all things does not see through its properties, and know and perceive all. We will therefore take Him to be our Master, Operator, and Leader into this most true Art. Him alone will we imitate, and through Him learn and attain to the knowledge of that Nature which He Himself has, with His own finger, produced and written on the bodies of these metals. Hence it will come to pass that the Most High Lord God will bless all His creatures in us, and will sanctify all our ways, so that in this work we may be able to bring our beginning to its desired end, and to attain the deepest joy and charity in our hearts.

But if anyone shall follow their own mere private opinion, they will not only greatly deceive themselves, but also all others who shall cast in their lot with them, and will bring them to great trouble. For man is assuredly born in ignorance, so that he cannot know or understand anything of himself, but only that which he receives from God, and understands from Nature. He who learns

Nothing from these resembles the heathen teachers and philosophers, who follow the subtleties and crafts of their own inventions and opinions. Such teachers are Aristotle, Hippocrates, Avicenna, Galen, and the rest, who based all their arts simply upon their own opinions. Even if, at any time, they learned anything from Nature, they destroyed it again with their own fantasies, dreams, and inventions, before they reached the final conclusion. By means of these men, then, and their followers, nothing perfect can be discovered.

This is what has moved and incited us to write a special book concerning Alchemy, basing it not on men, but on Nature herself, and upon those virtues and powers which God, with His own finger, has impressed upon metals. The initiator of this impression was <term>Mercurius Trismegistus</term>. He is not without good cause called the father of all wise men, and of all who followed this Art with love and earnest desire. He teaches and proves that God is the only author, cause, and origin of all creatures in this Art.* But he does not attribute the power and virtue of God to creatures or to visible things, as did the heathens mentioned above, and others like them.

Seeing, then, that all art must be learned from the Trinity—that is, from God the Father, God the Son, Jesus Christ, and God the Holy Ghost, three distinct persons, but one God—we will also divide this, our <term>alchemical</term> work, into three short treatises. In the first of these, we will set down what the Art itself embraces, and the property and nature of every metal. Secondly, by what method a man may work and bring similar powers and forces of metals to a successful result; and, thirdly, what <term>tinctures</term> are to be produced from the <term>Sun</term> and from the <term>Moon</term>.

# CHAPTER I.

->CONCERNING SIMPLE FIRE.<-

In the first place, it is necessary to state clearly what this Art comprises, what its subject is, and what its peculiarities are.

First and foremost, the principal subject of this Art is fire, which always exists in one and the same property and mode of operation, nor can it receive its life from anything else.* It possesses, therefore, a state and power, common to all fires that lie hidden in secret, of giving life, just as the sun is appointed by God and heats all things in the world—whether hidden, apparent, or manifest—such as the spheres of Mars, Saturn, Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, and the Moon, which can only shine as they borrow their light from the Sun and are in themselves dead. When, however, they are lit up, as said above, they live and work according to their special properties. But the sun receives light from no source other than God Himself, who rules it, so that in the sun God Himself is burning and shining. It is just the same with this Art.† The fire in the furnace may be compared to the sun. It heats the furnace and the vessels, just as the sun heats the vast universe. For just as nothing can be produced in the world without the sun, so also in this Art nothing can be produced without this simple fire. No operation can be completed without it. It is the <term>Great Arcanum</term> of Art,‡ embracing all things which are comprised within it, nor can it be contained by anything else. It exists by itself and needs nothing; but all others that stand in need of this can enjoy its benefits and have life from it. Therefore, first of all, we have undertaken to make this clear.

# CHAPTER II.

->CONCERNING THE MULTIPLICITY OF FIRE FROM WHICH SPRING THE VARIETIES OF METALS.<-

Having first written concerning the simple fire which lives and subsists by itself, it now remains to speak of a manifold spirit or fire which is the cause of variety or diversity of creatures, so that not one can be found exactly like

Therefore, fire cannot be an element, but it can be, and is, a visible and sensible death. The other death is invisible and is seen by no man.—*Lib. Meteorum*, chapter 1.</note>

another and identical in every part. This may be seen in the case of <term>metals</term> where no one has another exactly like itself. The <term>Sun</term> produces gold; the <term>Moon</term> another and widely different metal, namely, silver; <term>Mars</term>, another, namely, iron; <term>Jupiter</term>, tin; <term>Venus</term>, copper; and <term>Saturn</term> yet another, namely, lead; so that all these are unlike. In the same way does it hold good with men and other creatures, and the cause of this diversity is the manifoldness of fire. For example, the *<term>Venter Equinus</term>* produces one kind of creature through the moderate heat generated by its corruption; the *<term>Balneum Maris</term>* produces another; ashes another; sand, in like manner, another; the flame of fire another; coals another, and so on. This variety of creatures is not produced by the first simple fire, but from the regimen of the <term>elements</term>, which varies, not from the sun, but from the courses of the seven <term>planets</term>. And this is the reason why the universe contains no likeness amongst its individuals. For as the heat is changed every hour and minute, so all other things vary. For this transmutation takes place in the <term>elements</term>, on the bodies of which it is impressed by this fire. Where there is no great mixture of the <term>elements</term>, <term>Sol</term> is produced; where it is a little more dense, <term>Luna</term>; where still more so, <term>Venus</term>; and thus according to the diversity of mixtures are produced different <term>metals</term>, so that no metal appears in its mineral form exactly like another. It should be known, therefore, that this variety of metal is caused by the mixture of the <term>elements</term>, because the spirits of these <term>elements</term> are found to be diverse and without likeness: whereas, if they were born of simple fire they would be so much alike that one could not be distinguished from another. But the manifold fire intervening, variety of form is introduced among creatures. Hence it may be easily gathered why so many and such varied forms of <term>metals</term> are found, and why no one is like another.

### CHAPTER III.
### CONCERNING THE SPIRIT OR TINCTURE OF SOL.

Let us now come to the spirits of the <term>planets</term>, or of the <term>metals</term>. The spirit or <term>tincture</term> of <term>Sol</term> took its beginning from a pure, subtle, and perfect fire,

---

<note>That fire, then, is manifold which is varied according to the diversity of the subject into which it flows, and by means of which it is afterwards kindled in other subjects—such as the fire of ashes, sand, the bath, filings, etc.—which has a mediated heat flowing from an immediate source into the subject-matter of the instrument, and from there into the matter underlying the Art. In that manifold fire there is a difference of position. This is because nothing in the nature of things can be seen which is in all respects like any other thing, even though both come under the same species, or even though both may be members of the same individual. One metal produces gold from that which generates silver; another brings forth the metal of <term>Saturn</term>, of <term>Venus</term>, or of <term>Mars</term>. Each one of these is varied according to the difference of the place where it originated and was created. No two men, no two members of the same body, no two leaves of the same tree, are found exactly alike: and so it is for the rest. Dissimilarity proceeds not from the first fire of created things, but from the differing rule over the <term>elements</term> by means of the <term>planets</term>, and not by the sun. Every moment, by this disposition of things, the heat in the <term>elements</term> varies, and at the same time the form of decomposed things varies from their compounds, though not from the simples. Where the mixture of the <term>elements</term> is not so great, <term>Sol</term> is generated; where it is a little greater and less pure, <term>Luna</term> is generated; from that which is still more imperfect, <term>Venus</term>; and so of the rest, according to the mixture of the <term>elements</term>. The mineral of each metal is not like another, nor do their spirits in all respects agree with one another. If they were generated from the simple fire alone, without the intervention of the manifold, no distinction of forms could occur either in metals or in any other created things. Why there are in use no more than seven <term>metals</term>, of which six are solid and the seventh fluid and thin, is explained in adept philosophy but not in <term>Alchemy</term>.—*<term>De Transmutationibus Metallorum</term>*, c. 3. for which reason it far surpasses all the other spirits and tinctures of the metals. It remains constant and fixed in the fire; it does not flee from it, nor is it consumed by it, but rather through its influence it becomes clearer, purer, and more beautiful. Nothing either hot or cold can injure it, nor can any other accident, as they can injure the other spirits or tinctures of metals, and for this reason: that the body which it once assumes it defends from all accidents and diseases, and enables it to sustain the fire without injury. This body does not have such power and virtue in itself, but derives it from the spirit alone which is shut up within it. For we know with regard to the body of Mercury that it cannot sustain or endure the fire, but flees from it; but when it is in Sol, it does not fly off but remains fixed and constant; this affords a most certain proof that it receives such constancy from the spirit or tincture of Sol.* If, therefore, this spirit can be in Mercury, anyone can infer that it would have some similar effect in the bodies of men when it is received into them. In our *Chirurgia Magna* we have said concerning the tincture of Sol that it will not only restore and preserve from weaknesses one who uses it, but also conserve him for a long and healthy life.† In like manner, the strength and virtue of other metals may be known from true experience, not from the wisdom of men and of the world, which is foolishness with God and with His truth; and all who build and rest their hope on that wisdom are miserably deceived.

# CHAPTER IV.

## CONCERNING THE SPIRIT AND TINCTURE OF LUNA.

After having spoken with sufficient clarity concerning the tincture of Sol, it remains to present something about the tincture of Luna and of the White Tincture which, in like manner, is produced from the perfect spirit, though it be less perfect than the spirit of Sol; but, nevertheless, it excels in purity and subtlety all the other tinctures of the metals which follow it in order. This, indeed, is well known to all who handle Luna, even the unlearned. It does not

---

<note>* It is well understood that the body of Sol is Mercury, which cannot at all stand the fire, but flees from it.—*De Transmutationibus Metallorum*, chapter 10.</note>

<note>† In the collection of treatises to which reference is here made, there is the following process for the manufacture of a tincture of gold:—Let the body first be deprived of its metallic and malleable nature; that is to say, let it be corrupted; then let the residue be cleansed with sweet water, and the color extracted by means of spirit of wine, when the desired tincture will remain at the bottom. To compose the Spirit of Wine: Take one <term>sextarius</term> (about a pint) of generous wine; let it be poured into a circulatory vessel of appropriate size, that is, of such capacity that the wine can be shaken within it. Then place in a cucurbite, and extract the spirit with a slow fire. As soon as it has passed over (which you will know by the usual signs), stop increasing the fire, for the residue is a simple sublimate. Pour the spirit of wine upon the above-mentioned powder (which should be like <term>alcohol</term> [fine powder]) to the height of a palm, enclose it in a glass, and keep it for a month in a warm bath to digest, at which point the color will be separated and mixed with the spirit. A white powder will remain at the bottom. Having separated all these things, melt the powder, and it will be separated into a metallic water. Evaporate the spirits according to the art, and the desired spirit will remain at the bottom. Perform its gradation in a retort of the proper size. This is done most conveniently by elevation, which is highly thinning. —*Chirurgia Magna*, Part II., Tract III., chapter 2.</note>

### CHAPTER VI.
#### CONCERNING THE SPIRIT OF MARS.

Speaking of the Spirit of <term>Mars</term>, this comes from a denser and more combustible mixture of the elements than was the case with the others that preceded it. But <term>Mars</term> is endowed with greater hardness than the other metals, so it does not melt in the fire as they do. True, it is damaged by water and air more than they are, so much so that it is completely destroyed by these influences; it is also burnt in the fire, as experience proves. So, then, its spirit is less perfect than that of any of those mentioned above. But in hardness and dryness, it exceeds all metals, whether ranked above or below it. For it not only makes the perfect metals, <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>, resistant to the hammer, but even those which rank below it, such as <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, and the like.§ Since, then, it produces this effect on metals, it is a sign that it has the same effect on the human body—that is, it produces a struggle. Especially when it is taken for a disease for which it is not suited, it contorts the limbs with great pain. But when it is used and applied to wounds that do not exceed its degree, it possesses powerful cleansing qualities. Thus, this spirit is endowed with no less power and potency than those mentioned above, regarding those things for which it was appointed by God and by Nature.

### CHAPTER VIII.
### CONCERNING THE SPIRIT OF SATURN.

The spirit of <term>Saturn</term> is solid and formed from a dry, dark, and cold mixture of elements. As a result, among all others, it has the least power to remain and survive in the fire. However, when <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term> must be tested and purified, <term>Saturn</term> is added to them, and this has the effect of thoroughly cleansing them. Nevertheless, it is of such a nature that it takes away their malleability.<note>It leaves them broken and decomposed after washing. — *Ibid.*</note> It has the same painful effect on men as <term>Jupiter</term> and <term>Mars</term>. Being mixed with cold, it cannot act gently.<note>It distorts the limbs with more severe pains than even tin and iron; but since this spirit is solidified with a much more intense cold than others, it does not act as violently. — *Ibid.*</note> It has the greatest powers and virtues for curing fistulas, cancer, and similar ulcers which fall under its own degree and nature. It drives the same kind of diseases from man as it expels impurities from <term>Luna</term>. But if it does not leave the body entirely at the same time, it brings more harm than good. Consequently, whoever would use it must know what diseases it cures, what it should be taken for, and what effects Nature has assigned to it. If this is well considered, it can do no harm.

### CHAPTER IX.

The spirit of <term>Mercury</term>, which is only subordinate to the spirits mentioned above, has no fixed or certain form in itself. Because of this, it accepts every metal, just as wax receives all impressions, of whatever form. So this thick elemental spirit may be compared to the other spirits of the metals. For if it receives the spirit of <term>Sol</term> into itself, <term>Sol</term> will be produced from it; if <term>Luna</term>, then <term>Luna</term>; and it does the same with the other metals. It agrees with them and adopts their properties for itself. For this reason, so far as relates to its

# THE SECOND TREATISE.

---

## CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHER'S MERCURY, AND THE MEDIUM OF TINCTURES.

In the first treatise, we have written concerning the spirits of the metals, their tinctures, etc., making clear their properties and natures, and what each separate metal generates. In this second treatise, we will treat the medium of tinctures, that is, the <term>Philosophers' Mercury</term>, by which the tinctures and fermentations of the metals are made; in seven chapters, as follows:

### CHAPTER I.

### FROM WHAT TINCTURES AND LEAVENS ARE MADE.

Whoever wishes to have a tincture of the metals must take <term>Philosophers' Mercury</term> and project it toward its own end; that is, into the quick mercury from which it proceeded.<note>Nonetheless, the tincture of mercury is a supreme secret.—*De Ulcerum Curatione*, chapter 10.</note> From this, it will follow that the <term>Philosophers' Mercury</term> will be dissolved in the quick mercury and shall receive its strength, so that the <term>Philosophers' Mercury</term> shall kill the quick mercury and render it fixed in the fire like itself. For there is as much agreement between these two mercuries as there is between a man and his wife. They are both produced from the coarse spirits of metals, except that the body of <term>Sol</term> remains fixed in the fire, while the quick mercury is not fixed. One, however, is assigned to the other as grain or seed is to the earth, which we will illustrate by an example: If anyone has sown barley, he will gather barley; if corn, corn, etc. It is no different in this Art. If anyone sows <term>Sol</term>, he will gather gold, while from <term>Luna</term> he will collect silver, and so it goes with the other metals. In this way, we say here that tinctures are produced from the metals—that is, from the <term>Philosophers' Mercury</term> and not from common quick mercury. But this produces the seed which it had previously conceived.<note>The dead wife of the metal is like an uncultivated field or soil; if it is macerated or revived by the philosophic plow (the wife remaining fixed and incorruptible during the process), it is united to the aforementioned physical spirit by the degrees of fire, into its own nature and substance, and this occurs with the dead body of the metal. Now, this cannot be done with the coarse spirit of mercury. And although the mercury or quicksilver of <term>Sol</term> exists and is fixed, nevertheless common mercury, not yet fixed, never attains resurrection. For the resurrection of the metals is an immortal regeneration and the medium by which tinctures of this kind are advanced to their generation. For this reason, therefore, it cannot be united to dead bodies to bring about their fixation, but only to extracted spirits—specifically the physical ones mentioned above, which are subject to the metals just as common mercury is to all metallic spirits. The coarse spirit of mercury can no more generate this tincture in its substance than a concubine can bring forth legitimate offspring. The coarse spirit of mercury must be judged in the same way, until the metallic and physical spirit is produced by means of natural matter. Without this medium, it will be impossible for anything good or perfect to be accomplished in tinctures of this kind. Moreover, if the fire is too intense, it cannot generate; if too weak, the same result follows.—*De Transmutationibus Metallorum*, chapter 10.</note>

It explains that this mercury must be united with common mercury to achieve fixation and "resurrection," comparing the process to sowing seeds in the earth.</summary>

### CHAPTER II.
#### CONCERNING THE CONJUNCTION OF THE MAN WITH THE WOMAN.

In order that the <term>Philosophers' Mercury</term> and the <term>quick mercury</term> may be joined, and this latter united with the fixed, it must necessarily be known how much of it must be taken, since more or less than the proper quantity may hinder or altogether destroy the whole operation. For by excess the seed is suffocated, so that it cannot live until it is fixed by the <term>Philosophers' Mercury</term>. But by deficiency, since the body cannot be altogether dissolved, it is also destroyed so that it is able to produce no fruit. Therefore, it should be clearly determined how much of the one and the other ought to be taken, if, indeed, the artificer wishes to bring this work to its legitimate end. Let the recipe be as follows, namely: Take one part to two, or three to four, and you will not err, but will arrive at the desired end.

### CHAPTER III.
#### CONCERNING THE FORM OF THE GLASS INSTRUMENTS.

When the matter has been rightly joined, it is necessary that you should have properly-proportioned glass vessels, neither larger nor smaller than is right. If they are too large, the woman—that is, the <term>phlegm</term>—is dispersed, which results in the seed being unable to be born; where they are too small, the <term>germ</term> is suffocated so that it cannot come to fruit, just as when seed is sown under a tree or among thorns, it cannot germinate but perishes without fruit. Therefore, significant errors may arise through the vessels; and once this has occurred, it cannot be corrected again in the same operation, nor can it arrive at a satisfactory conclusion. Therefore, note what follows: namely, that you take three ounces and a half and four pounds; thus, having proceeded rightly, you will save the matter from being dispersed and prevent the <term>phlegm</term>, or the <term>germination</term>, from being impeded.

### CHAPTER IV.
#### CONCERNING THE PROPERTIES OF FIRE.

After you have placed the matter in the proper vessels, you will nurture it with natural heat, so that the outside heat shall not exceed the inside. For if the heat is excessive, no conjunction will take place, because by the intense heat the matter is dispersed and burnt, so that no advantage arises from it. On this account, the middle region of the air has been arranged by Nature between heaven and earth; otherwise, the sun and the stars would burn up all the creatures on the earth, so that nothing could be produced from it. Take care, therefore, that between the matter and the fire you interpose an airy space of this kind, or a certain distance. In this way, the heat will not easily be able to do injury in any way, nor to disperse, and still less to burn. For if the heat is insufficient, neither will the spirit remain active, performing no work upon

In the same way, in the great world, the seed cast into the earth is dead and cannot grow by itself unless it is vitalized by the heat of the sun. Therefore, first of all, it is necessary to build the fire for this work in the correct proportion, neither too large nor too small; otherwise, this work will never be carried to its desired and perfect end.

### CHAPTER V.

#### CONCERNING THE SIGNS WHICH APPEAR IN THE UNION OF CONJUNCTION.

When the regulation of the fire is moderated, the matter gradually turns black. Afterward, when the dryness begins to act upon the moisture, various flowers of different colors appear simultaneously in the glass, just as they appear in the <term>peacock's tail</term>, and such as no one has ever seen before. Sometimes, too, the glass looks as though it were entirely covered with gold. When this is observed, it is a certain sign that the male seed is acting upon the female seed, ruling it and fixing it. That is, the <term>fixed Mercury</term> acts on the quick <term>mercury</term> and begins to embrace it. Afterward, when the moisture has dissipated during the drying process, those colors disappear, and the matter at length begins to turn white, continuing to do so until it reaches the highest degree of whiteness. First of all, care should be taken not to hasten the matter unduly, according to the opinion of those who think that such a process is in all respects like what is observed in the growth of corn or in the production of a human being—the latter process taking nine months, the former ten or twelve. <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term> do not ripen so soon, nor are they born as quickly as a child from its mother's womb or grain from the womb of the earth. The higher and more perfect anything is or should be in its nature, the longer the time necessary for its production. For it should be known that everything born quickly perishes quickly. Both herbs and men provide proof of this. In proportion as they are quickly produced or born, their lives are short. It is not so with <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>; they have a more perfect nature than men, from which it follows that they offer a long life to men and protect them from many incidental diseases.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### CONCERNING THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE PERFECT <term>TINCTURE</term>.

In the preceding chapter, we stated how the matter itself is refined. In this one, we will make clear how it may be recognized when it is perfect. Do this: When the <term>White Stone of Luna</term> appears in its whiteness, remove a small piece from it with forceps and place it, glowing, over the fire on a copper plate. If the stone emits smoke, it is not yet perfect; therefore, it must be left longer in <term>decoction</term> until it reaches the grade of a perfect stone. But if it emits no smoke, you may believe it to be perfect. Proceed in the same way with the <term>Red Stone of Sol</term> in its proper stage of development.

### CHAPTER VII.

### CONCERNING THE AUGMENTATION OR THE MULTIPLYING OF TINCTURES.

When you wish to augment or multiply the tincture you have found, combine it again with common mercury. Proceed in all ways as before, and it will tinge a hundred times more than it did previously. You can repeat this as often as you wish, so that you have as much of the material as you desire. The longer it remains in the fire, the more highly refined it becomes, so that one part of it will transmute an infinite number of parts of quick mercury into the best <term>Luna</term> and the most perfect <term>Sol</term>. Thus you have the entire process from beginning to end. With these few words, we will conclude this second treatise and now begin the third.

# THE THIRD TREATISE.

---

### CHAPTER I.
### CONCERNING THE BUILDING OF THE FURNACE AND THE FIRE.

In the second treatise, we described the method by which the tinctures or fermentations should be produced. In this third one, we will explain how the tinctures of <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term> are made. We shall clarify this at sufficient length, as well as the manner in which <term>Sol</term>, along with the other planets, should be produced—namely, with the furnace and fire.

<term>Mercurius Hermes Trismegistus</term> says that he who perfects this art creates a new world. For in the same way as God created the heaven and the earth, the furnace with its fire must be constructed and regulated, in the following manner: First, let a furnace be built at a height of six palms (measured with the fingers and thumb extended), but in breadth only one palm; round and smooth inside, so that the coals do not stick to it. At the bottom, let a small mound be raised, sloping on all sides toward the edge. Leave holes open underneath, four fingers wide, and to each hole let its own furnace be applied with a copper cauldron containing water. Then take the best and most long-lasting coals, and break them into lumps the size of a walnut. Fill the long furnace with these, which must then be closed so they do not burn out. Afterward, add coals below, right up to the holes. If the fire is too great, put a cover before it; if it is too small, let the coals be stirred with an iron rod so they may meet the air and the heat may be increased. In this way, you will be able to regulate the fire according to the true requirements of its nature, so that it is neither excessive nor insufficient, but adapted to the movement of the matter. This is compared to the firmament. And there is another firmament in this place—namely, the matter contained in the glass. After these things follows the form of the world. The furnace, then, is to be placed like the sun in the great world, which provides light, life, and heat to the entire furnace itself and to all the instruments and other things it contains.

## CHAPTER III.
### CONCERNING THE COPULATION OF THE MAN WITH THE WOMAN, ETC.

When you have placed the husband and the wife in the matrimonial bed, so that he may act upon her and impregnate her, and so that the seed of the woman may be coagulated into a mass by the seed of the man—without which she can bear no fruit—it is necessary that the man should perform his operation on the woman.

## CHAPTER IV.
### CONCERNING THE PHILOSOPHIC COITION OF THE HUSBAND WITH HIS WIFE.

As soon as you see the woman take on a black color, know for certain that she has conceived and become pregnant; and when the seed of the man embraces the seed of the woman, this is the first sign and the key of this entire work and Art. Therefore, maintain a continuous natural heat, and this blackness will appear and disappear by being consumed, as one worm eats another and continues consuming until not one is left.

## CHAPTER V.

As soon as the blackness appears and is manifest, it may be known that the woman has become impregnated. But when the peacock’s tail begins to appear—that is, when many and various colors are seen in the glass—it is a sign that the <term>Philosophers' Mercury</term> is acting on the common mercury and extending its wings until it has conquered. Therefore, when the dry acts upon the moist, these colors appear.

# CHAPTER VI.
## CONCERNING THE BUD APPEARING IN THE GLASS.

When you have seen the different colors, it is necessary that you persevere in the work by constantly continuing the fire until the <term>peacock's tail</term> is quite consumed, while the matter of <term>Luna</term> becomes white and glittering as snow, and the vessel reaches its degree of perfection. Then at length, you may break off a morsel of the <term>regulus</term> and place it on a heated copper plate. If it remains firm and fixed there and tints it, then it is a <term>fermentation</term> brought to the highest perfection of <term>Luna</term>. That King has strength and power not only for transmuting metals but also for healing all infirmities. He is a King worthy to be praised and adorned with many virtues and such great power that he transmutes <term>Venus</term>, <term>Mars</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, and <term>Mercury</term> into <term>Luna</term>, which will stand all tests. He also frees the bodies of men from an infinite number of diseases, such as fevers, the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, leprosy, the gallic disease <note>syphilis</note>, and many mineral ailments which no herbs or roots, or anything of that kind, can remove. Whoever uses this medicine constantly prepares for himself a stable, long, and healthy life.

# CHAPTER VII.
## CONCERNING THE RED COLOUR.

After the King has assumed his perfect whiteness, the fire must be continued perseveringly until the whiteness takes a yellow tint, this being the color which succeeds the white; for so long as any heat acts on the white and dry matter, the longer such action lasts, the more it is tinted with yellow and saffron color, until it arrives at redness, like the color of a ruby. Then at last the <term>fermentation</term> is prepared for gold, and the Oriental King is born, sitting on his throne and powerful above all the princes of this world.

# CHAPTER VIII.
## CONCERNING INCREASE AND MULTIPLICATION.

The multiplying of this <term>fermentation</term> should be noted, which is performed in the following manner. Let it be dissolved in its own moisture and afterwards subjected to the regimen of fire as before. It will act on its own humidity more quickly than it previously did and will transmute into its own substance, just as a little leaven seems to transmute a large quantity of flour into leaven. Therefore, it is an unspeakable treasure on the earth, of which the universe has no equal, as Augurellus witnesses.

## CONCLUSION.

This secret was accounted by the ancient Fathers who possessed it as among the most occult, lest it should get into the hands of wicked men, who by its aid would be able more abundantly to fulfill their own wickedness and crimes. We, therefore, ask you, whoever has attained to this gift of God, that, imitating

# THE ECONOMY OF MINERALS.*
## ELSEWHERE CALLED THE GENEALOGY OF MINERALS.

---

### PREFACE TO THE READER.

ALTHOUGH order seems to demand that we should have treated the generation of minerals and metals before speaking of their transmutations, still, since theory cannot be more clearly taught than by its practice, I have thought it best for those who study this art to begin from the very beginning. For, above all else, <term>Alchemy</term> is a subject which is not comprised of mere words, but only of elaborate facts; just as is the case with the rest of those arts where familiarity is gained more by putting them into practice than by any mere demonstrations. It is true that these demonstrations do a very great deal for those who are somewhat advanced rather than for initiates. For these, it is best that from the very first they should have a finger in the pie (as the saying goes), and gradually learn from the very mistakes they make. Nobody ever acquired even the easiest art without making such blunders; and certainly no one will be able to follow <term>Alchemy</term> without making mistakes before he arrives at the truth. No one, again, will ever enter the true path as long as he holds back from the goal through fear of making a false step, or fails to correct his own errors by imitating the course of Nature. It will not be so easy to learn if we fail to compare alchemical with natural methods. So, then, it was thought well to let artificial <term>Alchemy</term> precede the natural, so that we may recall those who are venturing forth in this art to the genealogy of minerals, as if to a safe anchorage. It seemed opportune, nay, even necessary, to provide some such anchorage for this purpose for those who are studying <term>Alchemy</term>.

### CHAPTER I.
### CONCERNING THE GENERATION OF MINERALS.

I therefore determined first of all to lay before you the ultimate matter of minerals; from this, you will easily understand the primal matter from which they derive their origin. We may bring forward an example from medicine, where a disease has to be studied from its outcome and not just its origin. There is no knowledge of the origin because it was introduced in secret, and he who observes it is virtually blind. Now, a thing cannot be better judged than by learning for what purpose God created it; otherwise, it will often happen that the true use of God's creation turns into its abuse. Therefore, whoever undertakes any work with anything ought to thoroughly understand that with which he works, so that he may accomplish his task in the order prescribed by God. For this reason, God wills that everything He has created should be possessed by one who knows how to use it; and every man ought to apply himself to that pursuit to which he feels called by his own conscience, and not to learn some other fanciful thing suggested by the devil.

Thus water becomes the mother of those things which are developed in her, as if in her matrix; that is to say, Mineral Fire, Salt, and Mercury are formed into metals, stones, and all mineral substances, although the offspring is quite unlike the mother. In this way the Most High has created all things with their own nature: the birds of the air for one purpose, which is different from that of the fish in the sea. And so it is with the rest. Everything is to be committed to His divine will, Who makes everything as it is, and wills that what He makes shall be eternal. Just as water is not like its metallic offspring, nor the son like the mother, in the same way the earth itself is, as it were, wood and yet not wood, because it comes from that same source. In the same way, stone and iron are produced from water, which, however, becomes such water as never before existed: and the earth, too, becomes something which in itself it is not.

In a word, whatever is to pass into its ultimate matter must become something different from what its origin was—varied and diverse, though from one mother. Thus God willed to be One in all—that is, to be the one primal and ultimate matter of all things. He is such a wonderful and original architect of all things as has never existed before, nor will another ever exist. As, then, you have now heard so far concerning the mother of the minerals, we will in the following sections teach you more fully. The ancients have falsely written that this mother is the earth; but they have never been able to prove it.

## CHAPTER II.
### CONCERNING THE ULTIMATE AND PRIMAL MATTER OF MINERALS.

The first principle with God was the ultimate matter which He Himself made to be the primal matter, just as a fruit which produces another fruit. It has seed; and this seed ranks as primal matter. Likewise, out of the ultimate matter of minerals the primal element was made; that is, it was made into seed, which seed is the element of water. This resolves it, so that it becomes water. It has been entrusted to it by Nature, or so arranged, that it should produce the ultimate matter, and this is contained in water. Nature, therefore, takes under its own power and separation whatever there is in water; and whatever relates to a metal it puts on one side by itself for each particular metal. So also for gems, stones, the magnet, and other things of that kind, each separately and according to its own kind. For as God has appointed to the wheat its proper time for harvest, and the autumn for fruits, and to other things like these in their elements, so for the element of water He has

That is to say, where Nature ends, there the Art of man begins, for Nature’s ultimate matter is man’s primal matter. By such a wonderful method has God created water as the first matter of Nature—so soft and weak a substance, yet from it as a fruit come the most solid metals, stones, etc.; the very hardest from the very softest. God has created wonderful offspring from that mother, as also appears in men; if they are observed even within their mother, each will be found unique in his intellect and his properties, not according to his body, but according to his own state of constitution.

### CHAPTER III.
#### CONCERNING THE FIELD, THE ROOTS, AND THE TREES OF MINERALS.

The Most High created the element of water to be, as it were, a field in which the roots of mineral trees, springing forth from their seeds, should be fixed; from there, the trunk and the branches should be pushed forth over the earth. He separated it, therefore, from the other three elements, so that it should exist by itself as a free body—neither in the air, nor in the earth, nor in heaven—but placed on the lower globe to be on the earth and to have its center where it was established. It was created in such an admirable order that it should support man upon it just like the earth, so that man, carried in a ship, might speed over the water and take possession of it. What is even more marvelous is that although it surrounds our globe in every direction, the water does not fall away beyond its own boundaries, even though the part at our antipodes seems to hang downwards, just as our part seems to them. Yet each remains spread out as a flat surface on its own sphere, wherever you look at it, as if one were to imagine some pit which, descending perpendicularly to the abyss, should find no bottom and not be supported by the earth. It is even more wonderful than the egg in its shell, provided with everything it requires. The generations of minerals, then, are pushed out from the element of water into the earth, just as all fruits are pushed forward from the element of earth into the air, so that nothing but the root remains in the earth. Exactly so, all metals, salt, gems, stones, talc, marcasites, sulfurs, and every similar substance pass from their mother, the water, to another mother, namely, the earth, in which the growth of their trees is completed, while their roots remain fixed in the water. For just as those things which grow from roots in the earth are finished in the air, in the same way, those which derive their origin from the water are completely finished by Nature in the earth, so that they reach, as the others did, their ultimate matter.

<meta>This page continues the critique of ancient scientific theories regarding the origins of minerals, transitioning from the elemental nature of water to the metaphor of the "mineral tree" and how metals mature like fruit.</meta>

The ancients, led astray by this opinion, because they saw that metals were found in the earth, were so little advanced that they did not see their error when, on the subject of minerals, they wrote that out of the earth grew nothing but wood, leaves, flowers, fruits, and herbs, and that everything else was produced from water. No less mythical was the saying of that man who asserted that all things which were produced on the earth had their origin from the air, because they are in the air and are perfected there, though he saw their roots in the earth. Because he did not see the roots of minerals with his bodily eyes, he would even imagine that they are fixed in the earth. Such is the physical science of the Greeks, deduced only from what is seen, recognizing nothing hidden by mental experiment. It is just a fiction of lazy men who presume to chatter about natural science from eyesight alone; and who do not experiment so as to observe those hidden things which underlie the things which are manifest, the one over against the other.

### CHAPTER IV.
#### CONCERNING THE FRUITS AND THE HARVEST OF MINERALS.

Just as all the fruits of the earth have their harvest and autumn on the earth and in the air, according to the predestined time in their generation, so the fruits of the water, that is to say, minerals, are gathered at their own time of maturity. When the mineral root first germinates, they rise to their own trunk and tree, that is, into the body from which minerals or metals are subsequently produced; just as a nut or a cherry is not immediately produced from the earth, but first of all a tree grows, from which at length the fruit is generated. In like manner, Nature puts forth a mineral tree, that is, an aqueous body, in the element of water. This tree is produced in the earth so far as it fills the pores thereof, just in the same way as the earth itself fills the air. From this are eventually produced fruits according to the nature and property of its species, at the extremities of its branches, just as occurs in trees which we see on the surface of the earth. We must seek, then, first of all, for the aqueous tree, and by-and-by for its fruits, by a method not inaptly borrowed from agriculture, and in the following manner. Some of the visible trees produce their fruits covered up; for instance, chestnuts under a prickly bark, walnuts under one that is green and bitter, under that a wooden covering, and under this again a bitter membrane, and then at last the kernel. So it happens in minerals, the kernels of which, that is to say, the metals, are separated just like those others by barks. Other trees produce their fruits naked, such as plums, cherries, pears, apples, grapes, etc., where there is no such separation as that just described. So also some aqueous trees produce their gold, silver, corals, and other metals of that kind, free and naked, according to the condition and nature of the water. As we know by the rind what fruit lies concealed within it, and as the spirit is known by its body, just so, in the case of minerals, the spirit of the metal is recognized, though hidden,

Although, then, gold may be within a mineral body, that body is nevertheless of no significance; it must be separated from the gold as something impure, while the gold itself is pure. There are, therefore, two bodies in a mineral: one is the fruit—the pure body of gold—within which its spirit is inseparably combined. In this way, fruits are first introduced from the element into the tree, like the spirit into an impure body, and with that body finally into the earth as something noble and pure. The same thing is seen in man, who has been given two bodies: one corrupt, but the other incorruptible, which will be eternally united with him, since it is the image of God; by possessing this especially, man differs from all other creatures.

### CHAPTER V.
#### CONCERNING THE DEATH OF THE ELEMENTS, ESPECIALLY OF WATER.

Elements die as men die, on account of the corruption within them. Just as water, in its death, as it were, consumes and devours its own fruit, so the earth does its own fruits. Whatever is born from it returns to it again, is swallowed up and lost, just as past time is swallowed up by yesterday’s days and nights, the light or darkness of which we shall never see again. It is no heavier today than yesterday, not even by a single grain, and after a thousand years it will still be of the same weight. As it gives forth, so, in the same degree, it consumes. The death of water, however, occurs in its own proper element—in that great boundary and center of water, the sea—where rivers and whatever else flows into it die and are consumed like wood in a fire. Rivers, indeed, are not the element of water, but the fruit of that element, which is the sea; from this they derive their origin, and in this they receive both their life and their death.

#### CONCERNING THE DEATH OF THE TREE OF MINERALS.

After Nature has planted the mineral root of a tree in the center of its matrix—whether to produce a metal, a stone, a gem, salt, alum, vitriol, a saline or sweet, cold or hot spring, a coral, or a marcasite—and after it has pushed the trunk out toward the earth, this trunk spreads out into different branches,

There is no fire that can purge it from its stains in such a way as to make it fit for heaven. It does not allow for purging or glorification.
