The branches of the various trees of the same kind are extended over the entire sphere of the earth, just as the veins in the human body are extended into various limbs far apart from each other. But the fruits put forth by the extremities of the twigs, by the nature of the ultimate matter, soon fall to the earth. There is a momentary coagulation of them, and then at length, when all its fruit is shed, this tree dies and is utterly consumed by dryness, leaving its offspring in the earth. Afterwards, according to its natural state, a new tree appears. So, then, the first matter of minerals consists of water; and it comprises only Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury. These minerals are that element's spirit and soul, containing in themselves all minerals, metals, gems, salts, and other things of that kind, like different seeds in a bag. When these are poured into water, Nature then directs every seed to its peculiar and final fruit, incessantly organizing them according to their species and genera. These and similar things proceed from that true physical science and those fountains of sound philosophy from which, through meditative contemplation of the works of God, arises the most intimate knowledge of the Supreme Creator and of His virtues. To the minds and mental sight of true philosophers, no less than to their physical eyes, the clear light appears. To them the hidden becomes manifest. But that Greek Satan has sown weeds and his own false seed in the philosophical field of true wisdom—namely, Aristotle, Albertus, Avicenna, Rhazes, and that kind of men, enemies of the light of God and of Nature, who have perverted the whole of physical science since the time they changed the name of Sophia into Philosophy.*

We have previously said that the primal matter exists in its mother as if in a bag, and that it is composed of three ingredients meeting as one.

But there are as many varieties of Mercury, Salt, and Sulphur as there are different fruits among minerals. For a different Sulphur is found in lead, iron, and gold; in sapphire and other gems; in stones, marcasites, and salts; likewise, a different Salt is found in metals, salts, and so on. The same is true for Mercury: one kind exists in gems, another in metals. Furthermore, regarding their composition, different individuals are found within the same species. Gold is sometimes found where one specimen is heavier or more deeply colored than another, and so it is with the rest. Moreover, there are as many types of Sulphur of gold, Salts of gold, and variations of Mercury of gold—and for all others—as there are greater and lesser degrees of quality. Nevertheless, everything among them that receives its unique character from its subject is always included within the universality of one and the same Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury, which are mysteriously contained in universal Nature.

In this regard, Nature may be compared through a parable to a painter who, from a few colors, paints an infinite number of pictures, no two exactly alike. The only difference is that Nature produces living pictures, while the artist only imitates them. He represents the same things to the eye, but they are dead things. Now, all natural colors proceed from the Salt of Nature, in which they exist along with the balsam of things and coagulation. Sulphur reveals the substance of bodies and their structure; Mercury shows their virtues and <term>arcana</term> <note>secret healing properties or mysteries</note>. God alone assigns life to all, so that from each one should be produced that which He, from all eternity, predestined to be produced from it, just as He determined and willed that all things should be.

Therefore, whoever wishes to understand the physical bodies of natural things should learn from natural Sulphur what he must first understand well, while seeking natural colors as a foundation from Salt. But if he wishes to know the virtues of things, he must scrutinize the <term>arcana</term> belonging to the Mercury of the specific thing whose virtues he wishes to learn. Nature, being one and the same, embraces and separates all these matters at once; at the same time, she distributes, removes, or completely erases colors from them. 

I ask you to consider this tiny grain of seed, black or brown in color, from which grows a vast tree that produces such wonderful greenness in its leaves, such variegated colors in its flowers, and flavors in its fruits of such infinite variety. See this repeated by Nature in all her products, and you will find her so marvelous and so rich in her mysteries that you will have enough to last you your entire life in this book of Nature, without ever needing to refer to paper books. If God, then, shows Himself so powerful and wise to our discernment in Nature, how much more gloriously will He reveal Himself to our minds through His Holy Spirit, if only we seek Him? This is the way of safety that leads from below to above. This is what it means to walk in the ways of the Lord: to be occupied in admiring His works and to carry out His will, as far as it is within us, or as it should and can be in us.

This has been my Academy—not Athens, Paris, or Toulouse. After I had read many deceitful books by supposedly wise men, I turned to this one alone, from which I learned all that I write, and which I also know to be true. Still, I confess there are many more things that I do not know, but which will emerge in...

## CHAPTER VIII.
### CONCERNING THE NATURAL DISPENSER OF MINERALS AND HIS MINISTERS.

In the processing of minerals by men to prepare and adapt them for use, not just one man but many in succession are required, and each of these has his own special gift and duty. Who benefits from a metal being dug from the depths of the earth, unless it is its separator, preparer, or melter? What use is he, again, without the blacksmith? He, too, is of no use without a buyer, nor is the buyer of use unless there is someone who knows how to adapt those metals for use. Nature does not need all of these; nonetheless, she needs her own people. Among these is, first of all, <term>Archeus</term>, the dispenser of minerals, who has ministers under him.* He himself, the minister of Nature, has the following subordinates: the first, who provides the physical matter on which the operation acts—namely, the mineral Sulphur—is of this or that condition and nature; a second, who creates the properties and virtues and operates on the pre-existing matter, such as Mercury; a third, who, through compaction and coagulation, unites all the individual parts into one body—that is to say, Salt, which is the stabilizer of the work. When all these are brought together into one and enclosed in an <term>athanor</term>, <term>Archeus</term> matures them by heat, exactly like a seed in the earth; and not only so, but they are cooked together with one another in the following manner: The Sulphur submits its body to the other two so that they may do with it what they will and lead it to the end for which it is destined. Mercury is added with its virtuous properties, and this is matured by the other two. When all such processes of maturation are completed, then, finally, the salt begins to operate on the other matters associated with it and on itself. By first condensing, then congealing, and lastly coagulating, it strengthens the work for its autumn and harvest, so that nothing is missing except a harvester and a blacksmith.

Briefly, then, we have gone through the entire genealogy of minerals. It remains for us to hear specifically, yet concisely, the power and virtue of each in Alchemy and in Medicine respectively, so far as it is necessary to learn these for the mentioned fields. I would advise my readers to set aside for a while the mere dreams and opinions of others who romanticize these things, until they see that those writers are only philosophers on paper, not in Nature, having been taught by men like themselves and with the same amount of

## CHAPTER IX.
### CONCERNING THE VIRTUES AND PROPERTIES OF SALTS IN ALCHEMY AND IN MEDICINE.

God, in His goodness and greatness, willed that man should be led by Nature to such a state of necessity as to be unable to live naturally without natural Salt. Hence its necessity in all foods. Salt is the balsam of Nature, which drives away the corruption of the warm Sulphur with the moist Mercury; man is naturally composed of these two ingredients. Now, since it is necessary that these primary constituents should be nourished with something like themselves, it follows as a matter of course that man must use fiery foods for the sustenance of his internal Sulphur; moist foods for nourishing the Mercury; and salted foods for keeping the Salt in a capacity for building up the body. Its power for conservation is chiefly seen in the fact that it keeps dead flesh from decay for a very long time; from this, it is easy to guess that it will preserve living flesh even more effectively. Coming, at length, to its kinds, there are three which are considered especially useful for human life. The first of these is Sea Salt, the second is Spring Salt, and the third is Mineral Salt. Spring Salt is most conducive to health; in the second place is Mineral Salt; and, lastly, Sea Salt. This last and the first are boiled down by Art, while the other is prepared only by Nature. This Mineral Salt and the Sea Salt are not included under the nature of <term>muria</term> (brine), but that which is boiled down is first of all turned into brine before it is separated from the water into crystallized salt. There are, therefore, two types of Salt to be presented by us: one from brine, and the other from wholly refined salt. But first, consideration should be given to that condition which is common to every Salt. Where Salt has not been used with foods, there is no correction; and if the stomach receives those foods, it is unable to digest them. There is in Salt an expulsive force, acting through the excrement or through the urine, and unless these are kept in their regular course and motion, all the vital faculties are weakened in their efforts—

### CHAPTER X.
#### CONCERNING MURIA.

I just now mentioned two kinds of Salt: <term>Muria</term> <note>brine or saltwater</note> and dry Salt. First of all, <term>Muria</term> has the greatest power of drying up all excess moisture. It does more in one hour than dry Salt could effect in a month. Although dry salt may be reduced to <term>Muria</term>, it does not have the same power as the natural kind in curing moist gout, dropsy, moist tumors of the <term>tibia</term> <note>the shinbone</note>, and other tumors as well; in a word, it is for consuming all unnatural diseased liquids. Its heat should be so tempered that a patient could sit in it as in a bath without injury. The proof of perfection in <term>Muria</term> is that an egg shall float on its surface when thrown into it. It should be noticed that a bath of this kind is only adapted for stout people. People who are of a thin build should not use it, as it dries them out too much. If after one or two baths the tumors return, it would be best to live for a time in those places where the <term>Muriæ</term> and Salt are processed by boiling.

# CHAPTER XII.

## CONCERNING SALT NITRE.

There is also another kind of salt which is called nitre.<note>Nitre forms in the pens and stables where cattle urinate. It shows itself very clearly in the form of cones or of clumps, provided it be thoroughly separated from the excess nutritional salt not yet digested by the animal decoction.

### CHAPTER XIII.
->CONCERNING THE ILL EFFECTS OF NUTRIMENTAL SALT.<-

All salt used with food that has not been digested by the stomach—and which, upon being expelled, has passed down into the intestine—will generate colic and suffering in the bowels that are very difficult to cure unless it makes a thorough transit. Its corrosive nature sometimes causes it to perforate the intestines, as is shown by anatomy. If, however, it remains unexpelled in the stomach, belching and heartburn arise, along with many other stomach ailments. It sometimes happens, too, that the undigested salt hardens in the <term>mesaraic veins</term>, forming a granular deposit from which many severe and little-understood diseases proceed, not only in this particular part of the body but in others as well, especially the urinary organs. Enough has been said on the different species of salts, their benefits, and their faults. We now pass on to that salt which is more mineral in its character and is named <term>vitriol</term>. It excels all others in its utility, both in alchemy and in medicine.

### CHAPTER XV.

### CONCERNING THE TYPES OF VITRIOL AND THE TESTS OF IT.

The types of Vitriol are as varied as the mines or sources from which it is extracted. The tests of its greater or lesser excellence vary in equal proportion. First, if it tints an iron plate the color of copper, the more deeply it does so, the better it is considered. But this is the highest of all kinds. Secondly, when it is taken internally in a raw form it drives out intestinal worms better than any other medicine, and the more effectively it does this the better it is—

---

<note>
man. I say this concerning transmutation in order to make you understand how that envious philosopher, Aristotle, in his philosophy, has no sure foundation, but is simply foolish. I will lay before you, in due course, the recipe itself, so that in all parts of the German nation you may know how to make copper out of iron. From this power of transmutation we can easily gather that many other transmutations are possible, though they are at present unknown to us. It cannot be denied that many arts are still hidden, and that these are not revealed by God because we are not worthy of knowing them. Of course the change of iron into copper is not of the same importance as the change of iron into gold. God manifests the lesser, but the greater is kept hidden until the time of knowledge and of Elias who is to come. For these arts are not without their Elias. The following is the recipe for transmutation: Take raspings or filings of iron, without any other metal, such as copper, tin, etc., one pound; add quicksilver, half a pound. Put both into an iron pan or pot; pour over them one measure of <term>acetum</term> and a quarter of a pound of vitriol, with one ounce and a half of <term>sal ammoniac</term>. Let these be boiled together and constantly well stirred with wood. If the <term>acetum</term> is used up, pour in some more and add fresh vitriol. By this boiling the iron is transmuted into copper. If the copper is made it all passes away to the quicksilver. Having continued the boiling for ten or twelve hours, then separate as much of the quicksilver as is left from the iron, and wash it carefully so that it may be quite clean. Place the quicksilver in a bag made of soft leather or cotton and squeeze it out. Then you will see an amalgam left. Let that amalgam be consumed by heat, and you will find pure and good copper. Of this copper take half an ounce and the same quantity of silver. Let them be melted together, and the silver will immediately rise to the sixteenth degree. And this is the method of proving that such copper is made from iron. It is not, however, true that the grades are fixed. But whoever can work well with <term>regale</term> will be abundantly rewarded. Everything in this operation depends on skill in working. This is where most operators fail. By the above-mentioned process you can always make copper out of iron. I mention this to confirm the transmutation of one body into another. The nature of vitriol is such that if its <term>colcothar</term> is calcined it is at once, even with slight melting, turned into copper. A remarkable copper-like nature is in it, and there is also an equally remarkable vitriolic nature in copper. If the copper is dissolved in <term>aqua fortis</term> and granulated, all the copper becomes vitriol. There is no more copper left. So, also, copper is made out of vitriol, and no more vitriol [remains].
</note>

...considered to be a medicine. A third test is when it transmutes iron into copper. The more perfectly and rapidly it does this, the better it should be valued in both fields, for there is the greatest affinity between these two metals. Nor is this remarkable when, by means of borax water, mercury is made in a similar way from lead. There are other kinds of <term>cachimiæ</term> which convert metals; and besides these, there is a spring in Hungary—or rather a torrent—which originates from vitriol; indeed, its whole substance is vitriol, and any iron thrown into it is at once consumed and turned to rust, while this rust is immediately reduced to the best and most permanent copper by means of fire and bellows. A fourth test is when its red <term>colcothar</term>, subjected to a strong fire, produces copper on its own. This is comparatively weak in medicine, but of great excellence in alchemy. We must not fail to speak of its colors. That which is entirely cerulean is not as strong in medicine as that which, under the same color, has red and yellow spots mixed together. That which is of a pale sky-blue color should be selected before all others for the preparation of the green and the white oil. That which inclines toward a red or dark yellow color is best for preparing the red oil. The final test is when, with gallnuts, it makes a very black and dark ink. This should be chosen in preference to all others. The species, therefore, are categorized according to these tests.

## CHAPTER XVI.

### CONCERNING THE VIRTUES OF VITRIOL, CRUDE OR CALCINED, IN MEDICINE.

For the most severe pains in the stomach and discomforts arising from the excessive use of food or drink, administer crude vitriol to the extent of six <term>cometz</term> or three drops—that is, three grains. To weak patients, it should be administered in wine or in water; to stronger ones, in distilled wine. It purges

<note>
...remains, unless it is reconverted into vitriol by a sufficient quantity of <term>aqua fortis</term>. This kind of kinship between vitriol and copper is remarkable. Whatever is of the nature of copper gives good vitriol. Thus, <term>verdigris</term> gives good and highly concentrated blue vitriol. Although for us to discuss these matters at any length would perhaps be ridiculous, still none can deny that there is a latent tincture in vitriol which is of much higher excellence than most people imagine. Happy is he who understands this matter! Note other facts about the oil of vitriol. If the oil of mercury and this oil of vitriol are joined and thus coagulated according to their own special process, a sapphire of marvelous nature and condition is produced. It is not, indeed, the sapphire stone, but like it, with a wonderful tinge, concerning which I have much more to say. Hence it is evident that stupendous secrets lie hidden in Nature and in the different creations of Nature or of God; and it would be much more to our credit if we looked into these and investigated them, instead of indulging in revelry and debauchery. At present, the prize is given to debauchery, until one-third part of mankind, or of the population of the world, shall be killed, another shall be finished off by disease, and only the remaining third shall be saved and survive. In the present condition of depravity, the world cannot last or the arts flourish. It must be that the present condition and order of things go to destruction and be altogether eliminated; otherwise, no good thing can be achieved. Then at last the Golden Age will flourish: that is, then at last man will use his intelligence and live as a man, not as a beast; nor will he act like a pig, or live in caves and dens of the earth. Since, then, I have so far communicated to you these facts about vitriol with every good intention, I now pray you all that when you see those unlucky and unhappy creatures suffering from critical disease, for the sake of your own conscience, for God’s glory, and for the love of your neighbor, you will seriously reflect and not despise or lightly value the gifts implanted by God in vitriol. Let love constrain you, so that by night and by day you may be occupied in this work, and none be found taking his ease, but all ready to do anything for his neighbor’s good. Will this not move you lawyers? Listen to what Christ says: “Woe unto you, lawyers!” This saying is not outdated. Nor should you theologians place a stumbling block in the way—you who think so much more of your profits and your salaries than about your sick folk. These are they who pass by on the road to Jericho. Be like the Good Samaritan and follow the example of his virtue. Then God will so enlarge your gifts that in helping the sick you shall suffer no lack. All that you need shall be given to you. You only sell this treasure!

...out every ailment from the roots, driving it up and down. In secret medicine (<term>arcana</term>), it is called Vitriol Grillus, or Grilla. Neither hellebore, nor colocynth, nor <term>digridion</term> purge as strongly or cure as perfectly as this, nor do they have the same ability to expel worms. For curing the "falling sickness" (<note>epilepsy</note>), purgation by vitriol is the best of all methods. These properties come from its twofold nature—that is to say, its acidity and its saltiness. For this reason, it is a much nobler medicine than others. Its <term>colcothar</term>, or what they call its red *Caput Mortuum* (<note>dead head or residue</note>), should not be taken internally, except as an aid to surgical treatment for putrid ulcers of the first degree of severity; however, its oil may be taken for those of the second or third degree. Its medicinal virtues are described in other medical books, such as the treatise titled *De Naturalibus Rebus*. Sometimes medical topics tempt one to stray from one's intended purpose. Let us see, then, what vitriol does in alchemy beyond the transmutation of iron into copper, which we described earlier, providing the formula at the beginning. Although it is not such a difficult task to transmute iron into gold, God wills that the lesser operations be performed first, and that the greater ones remain hidden (<term>occult</term>) until the "Elias of the Art" (<note>a prophesied master of alchemy</note>) arrives. All arts have one person specifically assigned to them, as is understood in other disciplines. 

Now, take one pound of iron filings, without any other metal mixed in, and half a pound of mercury. Over these, pour one measure of the strongest <term>acetum</term> (<note>vinegar</note>), with a quarter pound of vitriol. Add an ounce and a half of <term>sal armoniac</term>. Boil everything together and stir constantly with a wooden spoon. As the vinegar evaporates, pour on fresh vinegar and more vitriol. After twelve hours, let the main part of the iron that has been transmuted be entirely separated with mercury from the part of the iron that has not been transmuted. When the mercury has been squeezed out through leather, a paste of amalgam will remain; when this is reduced by fire, it reveals the purest copper. Half an ounce of this is immediately mixed with an equal part of silver—six degrees being held back, though not fixed, but ready to be fixed in *regale* (<note>a refining process</note>)—so that the industrious artist may obtain a moderate profit for food and clothing. 

Vitriol is also made from Venus (<note>copper</note>), dissolved by means of <term>aquafortis</term> (<note>nitric acid</note>) and granulated. This does not return to copper again. Similarly, copper is made from the <term>colcothar</term> of vitriol (as we mentioned above among the tests), which is not turned back into vitriol on its own except by a special water. Verdigris, likewise, shows a spagyric (<note>alchemical</note>) vitriol of the highest degree. In vitriol, such a great and powerful tincture (<note>transformative essence</note>) is hidden that an inexperienced person would hardly believe it, though one who understands its secrets (<term>arcana</term>) certainly will. Whenever oil of vitriol is mixed with oil of mercury and both are coagulated together, they change into a stone of wonderful color and quality, very similar to a sapphire.

Having dealt with the salts, let us now pass on to sulphur.

# The Economy of Minerals.

## CHAPTER XVII.

### CONCERNING THE THREEFOLD SULPHUR OF MINERALS.

Sulphur should properly be called the resin of the earth, and within it are hidden countless virtues available in both fields of study, though its crude form is useful in neither. Its <term>arcanum</term> alone, when cleansed of impurities, operates in a wonderful way, having been washed to that whiteness seen in snow by means of the Isopic art. It has as many different virtues as it has varieties of sources; for every metal or mineral contains sulphur within itself. As we said above—using the analogy of chestnuts and other nuts—that minerals were likewise enclosed in their rinds, and that the chief excellence lay concealed in their nucleus, which is sustained and nourished by the external coverings; so regarding sulphurs, it must be understood that it is the interior one which excels the others, and is <term>spagyrically</term> termed "embryonated" because of its specific origin, being the sulphur of gold, stone, etc. The external sulphur, in which the embryonated lies concealed, is our mineral. There is also a third kind, extracted from the nuclei of minerals or of metals, which cannot have a better name in the art than “animated” and “<term>spagyric</term>.” It is of universal application in both fields. 

For better understanding: the first sulphur, which we have said is a resin of the earth—acting as the mother and the father of other sulphurs—we name "universal." The second kind is where it assumes a metallic or mineral appearance, but is now "embryonated." The third, which is purified from these and exists <term>spagyrically</term> pure from all waste, is "animated sulphur." 

There are two conditions of this embryonated sulphur which are worthy of notice. One, passing from the fixed stage, is made volatile; the other is a pure and living fire which destroys a log of wood or a disease with equal ease. The extraction of the embryonated sulphur is brought about either by sublimation or by descent. But sometimes it is not found naturally mixed with other ingredients; being unable, through its great subtlety, to withstand the heat of the fire in preparations of this kind, it has to be extracted from its minerals by means of <term>aqua-fortis</term> and afterwards coagulated. This, when set aside according to its true correspondence, contains a golden nature within itself. For this reason, it is to be sought before all others in alchemy, because it easily allows for fixation; indeed, it fixes the gold in cements and in other metals where it is not yet mature or volatile. 

However, gold is sought from it in vain unless it already existed there by Nature. It contains no silver, but only gold—some containing more than others—as in the embryonated sulphur of Venus (<note>copper</note>), of red talc, or of gold or iron marcasite; these rarely lack gold. Now, whoever wishes to turn their hand to these things, let them first of all remember and carefully note to separate sulphur of this kind from gold with the greatest activity and skill, so that nothing perishes with the gold. I could say more than this, but I must be silent. If it were not diametrically opposed to the will of God, it would be the easiest thing possible to make everyone equally rich by a very

If this is placed in it, it turns black and sheds the <term>calx</term> of <term>Sol</term>, though it is not fixed until it has arrived at its complete stage of perfection.

It is almost the most difficult of all alchemical operations regarding its preparation. This oil excels only in tints. For greater virtues, it is not to be trusted as much for its effects, because it contains only a tincture of color, not of medicinal virtue.

The Sulphur of <term>Luna</term>, too, exalts its own body to such a degree that <term>Venus</term>, when mixed with an equal weight of this <term>Luna</term>, is mistaken for the Lydian stone. The Sulphur of <term>Venus</term> fixes copper so that it will withstand the test of lightning, but it does not provide color. ## CHAPTER XVIII.
### CONCERNING ARSENIC USED FOR ALCHEMY.<note>In this case, also, the Geneva folio offers considerable variations from the text as it stands above. CONCERNING THE ALCHEMICAL VIRTUES IN ARSENIC.—Our ancestors invented and promoted a specific name, which is electrum. Electrum is a metal derived from another metal, yet different from the metal from which it descends. For example: Copper turns into a white metal. When its redness is removed, it is called electrum. Similarly, from copper, by means of cadmia, brass is made, and this is called red electrum. Certain ignorant alchemists and artists reckoned these different kinds of electrum as silver, and sometimes used them in place of gold; they neither understood nor believed anything else except that this was silver, and that silver could therefore be produced from copper. Forgetting the name of electrum, they mistook it for silver or for gold, and did not stop their investigations as long as a house or a courtyard remained to them. I point this out so that error may be avoided, and that proper consideration may be given to the questions: What is electrum? What is gold? and What is silver? In this way, no rash measures will be taken. Now, I will present a certain medicine to you. Take the metal arsenic, prepared in a metallic way; combine it with Venus in the usual manner, and you will find a large quantity of electrum in the copper. No one should incur great expense for this substance, because it costs a good deal to make electrum. Therefore, it is better to leave copper as copper in its own form. Its electrum is in no way better, but rather more common. By dissolving it in graduated water, it leaves a powder. It is not that silver is produced, but electrum; it is rendered so subtle that nothing whatever remains, but it vanishes, and because it is not fixed, it is consumed. Thus, not only in copper, but also in iron, tin, steel, etc., a residue is left; but nothing of a permanent character is present, and in this way many are deceived. Eventually, matters reached a crisis where electrum lost its name and was called silver, which began the destruction, exile, misery, and disappointed hopes of the alchemists. There are many recipes of this kind which it is not necessary to recount. They are well known to the artists who follow me in this chapter, and who have also weighed their own errors in seeking it in vain elsewhere. There is a great deal of temptation for younger students to abandon the methods of their elders; when the pupil wishes to be more learned than the master, he no longer remains on the right path but judges things for himself, prepared to stand by his own opinion. All that comes of it is that he labors in vain, thus atoning for his fault and incurring grievous loss. The ancients called this substance electrum, and that is its proper name. The moderns call it silver—its improper name. Our forefathers avoided all loss because they knew what they were doing; the rising generation does not know, and so they incur loss. It has been a constant custom in alchemy that</note>

It seems right to connect Arsenic generically with Sulphurs rather than with Mercuries, and to treat it immediately after Sulphurs. Some old chemists, or rather sophists, working at chemistry while consumed by greed—that is, by a desire for gold and a kind of yellow dropsy—when they saw the white Tincture of Venus in arsenic, and the red tincture in the calamine stone, believed that the true secret of the stone was contained in these. They thought the white and red electrum were silver and gold until they discovered the contrary through testing and learned that they had been engaged in a futile work. Not content with that, they stubbornly continued in order to achieve fixation, persevering until they had neither house nor property left. They had performed a transmutation upon themselves rather than upon the metals! And is it any wonder? They approached this work without judgment and possessed no knowledge of minerals and metals, just as so many who embark upon the Art today do. From the time the name of electrum given by the ancients was forgotten, the ruin of those practitioners immediately followed.

Therefore it is necessary that everyone in these things should be farsighted. He who has not full knowledge and comprehension of all names does nothing, and the heads, however full of brains, do not get at the foundation of the matter. Now, if an operator is skilled in separating gold from arsenic, whether by a cement or by some method of projection, or by another process, so that he can reduce that gold to some metal, such as silver, copper, or lead, without doubt he will find it to be gold, and of excellent quality too. To follow this up so that a tincture shall be produced, or it shall issue forth from a tincture, is nothing; but the gold is in the arsenic, and the whole matter lies in depurgation, separation, and kindred processes, according to how much experience anyone has therein. Arsenic, especially, which comes from gold-bearing districts, or from gold, is rarely without gold. The only point of importance is that the separation shall be properly made. I know nothing more of arsenic and its species beyond what I have put forward; at least, nothing which it is lawful and expedient to make known, whether with reference to medicine or to alchemical operations. Whoever has prudence ought to be sufficiently skillful for this purpose. If he has it not, let him altogether abstain. No faculty can subdue itself; but failure must ensue if due order and a genuine mode of procedure have not been preserved. You should follow the guidance of your own judgment. The man who follows no other guide is not in a state of subservience to any.

### CHAPTER XIX.
### CONCERNING QUICKSILVER.

Having dealt with salts and sulphurs, we come to <term>Quicksilver</term>. This cannot be properly termed a metal, but rather a metallic water; but it is called a metal for this reason: because, by means of Alchemy, it is brought to a solid substance and into a metallic color, sometimes being fixed and sometimes not fixed. It can only be known as the chief material of Alchemists, who are able from it to make gold, silver, copper, etc., which will stand the test. So, too, perhaps tin, lead, and even iron. It is of a wonderful nature, inscrutable except after great labor. In a word, it shows itself to be the first material of Alchemists in metallic degrees, and the chief <term>arcanum</term> in medicine. It is a water which wets nothing it touches, an animal without feet, and the heaviest of all metals. It consists of <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Salt</term>, and <term>Mercury</term>. It discloses the first and last matter in the liquefactions of the metals, especially those which liquefy by heat without fire, and in others by flux.

### CHAPTER XX.
### CONCERNING CACHIMIÆ AND IMPERFECT BODIES.

There is another kind of mineral bodies which is not saline, nor is it a metal, but metallic; such are <term>marcasites</term>,* <term>chiseta</term> red and white, perfect and imperfect <term>antimoniacs</term>, <term>arsenicals</term>, <term>auripigments</term>, various <term>talcics</term>, <term>cobleta</term>, <term>granata</term>, gem-like bodies, etc. I say these are metallic bodies since they have chiefly the first metallic matter and derive their origin from the first three metallic bodies, to which they fly, as it were, and are incorporated with them as metals—for instance, gold, silver, copper, iron, etc. But since a metallic enemy is incorporated together with them, they can only be separated

---

<note>Marcasites are to be found in all categories, whether you consider color, brilliance, form, or any other property. For they are nothing else than the superfluity of metals—that is, matter abundant in metals, being something which metals are unable to bear or contain within them, or convert into their own form. First of all, when the salts are separated from <term>Ares</term> (the occult dispenser of Nature), a separation of metals follows. Out of these, firstly, marcasite is produced, which is unfit to become a metal, and yet it resides in that matter so that at first, out of <term>Ares</term>, that matter of the metals grows. And it is the first matter, consisting of three things: the spirit of salt, the spirit of mercury, and the spirit of sulphur, but in such a manner that these three are one. Of these all metals and minerals consist. These things being so ordered, <term>Archeus</term> (the occult virtue of Nature) institutes the first operation of metals, so as to produce them and distinguish them into their forms and natures. But before he deals with the metals themselves, he ejects the superfluity which abounds in salt, mercury, and sulphur, and purges the three, after which the superfluity emerges along a simple line into its own <term>yliadum</term> (chaos), and is at first divided into two categories, <term>marcasites</term> and <term>cachimiæ</term>. Here it is coagulated into a mineral, consisting of salt, sulphur, and mercury. Yellow marcasite obtains its color from the predominance of sulphur; the white from the predominance of mercury. For sulphur and <term>cachimiæ</term> acquire their color from salt, for this is derived from the spirit of salt, just as weight is derived from mercury in all three. But if the separation is properly effected, each of the minerals—that is to say mercury, sulphur, and salt—settles in its own place. Of these three all minerals consist.—*Regarding the Element of Water, Treatise III, chapter 1.*</note>

An imperfect metal is made from <term>cobleta</term>. This can be liquefied and passes into a state of flux; it is blacker in color than lead and iron, but has no brightness or metallic glitter. It barely allows for hammering, so that scarcely anything can be made from it. Its ultimate matter has not yet been discovered, nor has the process of its separation. There is no doubt it is a mixed breed of male and female, as is the case with iron and steel, but these cannot be perfectly joined until some method of separation is discovered. There is another similar body called <term>zinchinum</term>; not the one commonly known by that name, but a peculiar kind in which various metals are found to be adulterated, being liquefiable in nature but not malleable. It differs much in color from the others, the last of which has not yet been found. In its preparation, it is almost as wonderful as <term>Mercury</term> itself. It avoids mixing with anything else and remains a unique glass, much to be admired among minerals. Metallic grains are also found in torrents and are called <term>granates</term> because of their outer form. They can be liquefied and can withstand the hammer, but they are still not capable of being made into any tool. The properties of these bodies cannot be known unless they are revealed by alchemy. Many contain adulterated metals, such as silver and gold, which flow to them as they usually do to copper and lead. They consist of a certain dense kind of <term>Sulphur</term>. Some granates of another kind are as clear as crystal, and there is gold and silver in them.*

# The Economy of Minerals.

[Lead is] above all others fusible. By corruption, it is easily reduced to its spirit, to white or yellow <term>cerussa</term>, to <term>minium</term>, and lastly, to glass, like the rest. Tin is made up of white fixed <term>Sulphur</term> and fixed <term>Salt</term>, but of <term>Mercury</term> that is not fixed. Because it is fixed in its body, but not in its Mercury, it easily loses its metallic fusion, as the spirit passes away by the fire; and when this is absent, it is no longer a metal but a vanishing body. Iron and steel are not made of liquefiable Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury, unlike tin and lead. Iron is coagulated into the hardest metal of all, and it marries itself: that is, two metals are found in one, steel the male and iron the female. These can be separated from one another, each for its own special use. Gold is generated from the very purest Sulphur, perfectly sublimated by Nature, purged of all its dregs and false admixtures, and raised to such a transparency that no metal can physically ascend higher. This Sulphur is one part of the primal element, and if Alchemists could possess this as something easily discoverable in its tree and root, they would have good cause to rejoice; for it is the true Sulphur of the philosophers from which gold is made, not that other "gold" from which iron, copper, etc., are made. This is its universal test. Its Mercury, too, is by Nature perfectly separated from all earthly and accidental excess, transmuted separately into its mercurial part and into extreme clarity; this <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> is the second part of the primal matter of gold, from which gold is generated. Lastly, Salt is the third part of the primal essence of gold and of the tree from which gold is to be produced, just as roses come from rose-seeds—gold which is brought to its supreme crystalline brightness and purified from all the sharpness, harshness, bitterness, darkness, and vitriolic nature of Salt, so that nothing of this kind belongs to it now that it delights in its clarity and transparency.

When these three meet together as one, the gold is boiled down into a mass, though not always of the same condition or quality. Nature exhibits thirty-two grains of gold, and in the work of Art, these become twenty-four grains at the highest level of perfection. The reason for this is that the gold is nourished in its tree like a cow in its pastures, or an epicurean in his kitchen and restaurant. As soon as one of these leaves his feeding place, he grows thin, and so it is with gold; it is diminished by eight degrees. And as some of these feeding places are occasionally inferior, it happens that the quality of the gold is worsened or diminished as well; so that Nature’s sum total of twenty-six is reduced in Art to ten. The accidents, or rather the influences, of the stars or of the elements sometimes hinder the generation of gold, so that it becomes coarser and less manageable in its nature. But it is especially the inequality in the weights of the three primals that has an effect. Too large a portion of Salt renders it too pale. With too much Mercury, it grows yellow, and with a too plentiful supply of Sulphur, it is rendered red. In Nature, just as much as in the work of man, errors occur because of these hindrances; but these can be removed by means of <term>antimony</term>, <term>cements</term>, and <term>quartations</term>. In Sulphur, nothing should be looked for but a body; in Salt, stability; but

In <term>Mercury</term> exists all virtue, property, essence, and medicine, which do not exist anywhere else as they do there; but rather as in a dead body from which the spirit has departed, in which, however, we try to keep some of the elementary powers—as, for instance, the remains of the fire of wine in <term>Acetum</term>, though these are corrosive rather than nourishing or strengthening. Natural objects clearly show that they are composed of the four elements; but beyond that, the matter is hidden. They are made up only of the three we have spoken about, which possess a magnet common to them all. This, during the boiling of the preparation, attracts the trinity of essence to itself. The ancient philosophers called this state *esse* (being), because the trinity acquires a condition of unity in which the natural motion rests and settles the degree. But that magnetic virtue should rightly be called a fourth *esse* (not an element), since it attracts the medicine to the <term>Mercury</term> in which it is found. In the ultimate separation, however, the <term>Mercury</term> loses most of its weight. All these matters being thus arranged by Nature, the gold grows into a tree, spreading forth first from the root by the trunk to its branches and twigs, on which flowers are produced (as we see on the earth); and when these fade, the fruit is not always found at the ends of the twigs, but sometimes a hundred paces farther away in the tree, occasionally in its very center, or some distance toward the surface of the earth. It will sometimes happen that nothing but <term>Mercury</term> is produced, when by its excess it has suppressed the other ingredients. If, however, the <term>Salts</term> predominate, their corrosive nature, like so many worms, consumes the flowers of the tree. By the predominance of <term>Sulphur</term>, everything is burned up, just as on earth by the too great heat of the sun. Copper is produced by brown <term>Sulphur</term>, red <term>Salt</term>, and yellow <term>Mercury</term> boiled into a metal. This contains within itself its masculine element—that is, the <term>scoria</term> (dross); and if it be again reduced to a metal after separation, it returns to masculine copper, which can no longer be corrupted; and the female will produce no <term>scoria</term> at all. In hammering (<term>malleation</term>) and melting (<term>fusion</term>), they differ from each other only as steel and iron, and can be separated in the same way, so that two different metals are produced from them. Silver is composed of white <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Salt</term>, and <term>Mercury</term>, naturally prepared and stabilized to the highest degree of purity and transparency—next after gold—in ashes, not in antimony, or in <term>royal cement</term>, or in <term>quartation</term>. The difference in stabilization between gold and silver can easily be understood by considering that gold is masculine and has the male virtues very strongly fixed, while silver, as the female, has them more weakly. They are of one and the same primal matter, and differ as to color and stabilization in no other way than as the male and the female. The metals, then, are seven in number, exclusive of <term>Mercury</term>: namely gold, silver, tin, lead, iron, steel, and copper. The last contains within itself the male and female when both are joined for use and are not separated by Nature, as steel and iron are; so that they are held as one, and since they possess the same malleability and power of being worked, they are not commonly separated, except when this is done chemically for purposes of the <term>Art</term>. ### Conclusion.

An appropriate treatise on the natural generation of metals was absolutely necessary so that it might be understood what is meant by the regeneration of metals brought about through Alchemical Art. The opinion of all those who philosophize on this Art is that the artist in this profession ought to imitate Nature exactly in all things. Therefore, it was necessary to explain and to understand how Nature works in the innermost parts of the earth, and what instruments she employs. Whoever has not understood it in this way will be unlikely to reach that knowledge through their own unaided efforts. Let him who investigates this difficult and obscure matter be not so much a disciple of Art as a disciple of Nature.

If anyone denies that there is great efficacy in the composition of metals as far as it relates to supernatural affairs, we will answer him and present so many proofs that will support our own opinion and force him to agree with it. For if the seven metals were, in just and proper order, compounded, mixed together, and united in the fire, you must certainly believe that all the virtues of the seven metals were joined and linked together in one body. It has been seen fit to call this body electrum. Moreover, its efficacy, power, and operations show themselves to be much greater, even supernaturally so, than those that exist in a hidden form grafted by Nature onto metals in their raw condition. In those solid and raw metals are only those powers with which God and Nature herself have endowed them. Gold, indeed, is the noblest of all, the most precious and primary metal, if we consider it correctly; and we are not prepared to deny that leprosy, in all its forms, can be removed from the human body by it. Nor are we unaware that external ulcers and wounds are cured by copper and mercury. The other metals, too, each have their own excellences, and these are by no means to be despised; but we will pass over these for the moment, since you will hear of them when we come to treat the Life of the Metals.<note>As far as the *Archidoxis Magicæ* are concerned, this promise is not fulfilled. If we were to pass over its praises in silence, we should consider that we were doing it an injury; but since its operation and mighty power surpass belief, we deem it necessary to pronounce a eulogy on its virtues and efficacy. We will defer for the moment any mention of the crude and solid metals, since they admit no comparison with our <term>electrum</term>. If any vessel used for food or drink is made of this material and diligently watched, it will be impossible for any poison or drug to be placed in it, because in our <term>electrum</term> there is so much sympathy toward man through the force, efficacy, and influence of the planets and the stars of Olympus that, out of very pity and as if in distress, as soon as it is taken in hand, it betrays the poison by breaking out into a sweat and producing spots. For this reason, our ancestors used to have their drinking cups, dishes, and other utensils made of this material. There still remain in our age many necklaces and ornaments, such as rings, bracelets, remarkable coins, seals, figures, bells, and shekels made out of this, which were hidden in the earth long ago. When they were dug up, nobody—or very few—understood them, and in their ignorance, they gilded them over or coated them with silver. It is simply a mark of the ignorance of our age that it cares nothing for such objects as these. But God would not have such a mystery of Nature and such a great treasure of His own hidden any longer; instead, what had been hidden by the more than Cimmerian darkness of the sophists should now, after a long season, come to light again. We do not claim to exhaust the virtues of our <term>electrum</term>. The ribald genius of the sophists would be hurt; the crowd of fools would be offended and would receive what we said with idiotic laughter. Over and over again we have been on our guard against scandalizing this impious crowd; so to avoid such a result, it will be safest to pass over these matters in silence. However, we cannot altogether leave unnoticed certain stupendous effects of our <term>electrum</term>; since they came under our own eyes, we shall be able to speak more freely concerning them, without any suspicion that we are romancing or making up a story. We have seen rings, for instance, which removed all fear of paralysis or spasms from those who wore them on their fingers. These people, too, never suffered from apoplexy or epilepsy. If an epileptic patient puts such a ring on the third finger, even if he is so overcome by the violence of the paroxysm as to be prostrated on the ground, he regains consciousness and gets up.

Something should also be added here that we do not report from others, for we have seen it with our own eyes and know it by experience. If the aforementioned ring is worn on the third finger by a man in whom any ailment is latent and growing, so that it would presently break forth in an eruption, the ring would immediately give an indication by bursting out in a sweat; as if seized with a sudden sympathy, it would produce spots and become degraded in appearance, as we shall show more fully in our book entitled “Sympathy.”

Lastly, since I would not pass over or omit any word in favor of <term>electrum</term>, it is a protection and an antidote against evil spirits. There is latent in it an operation and a conjunction of planetary influence which makes us more easily believe that the old <term>Magi</term> in <term>Persia</term> and <term>Chaldæa</term> attempted and accomplished much by its aid. If we sought to list all the cases specifically, we would indeed enter upon a marvelous chronicle. However, so as not to give any occasion for offense or allow people to use this as an excuse, it will suffice to have touched on the subject in a few words. The <term>Sophists</term>, who are my deadliest enemies, would not hesitate to proclaim me an <term>Arch-Necromancer</term>. But I cannot refrain from telling of a miracle which I saw in Spain when I was at the house of a certain <term>necromancer</term>. He had a bell weighing, perhaps, two pounds, and by a stroke of this bell he used to summon, and to bring, too, visions of many different specters and spirits. In the interior of the bell he had engraved certain words and characters, and as soon as the sound and ringing were heard, spirits appeared in any form he desired. Moreover, the stroke of this bell was so powerful that he produced in the midst many visions of spirits, of men, and even of cattle, whatever he wished, and then drove them away again. I saw many instances of this, but what I particularly noticed was that when he was going to do anything new, he renewed and changed the characters and the names. I did not, however, get so far as to persuade this man to impart to me the secret and mystery of the names and characters. At length I began to speculate more thoroughly about this circumstance; and there came into my mind—ideas which we will pass over in silence here. There was more in that bell than one can put into words; and of this be very sure, that the material of which it was composed was this <term>electrum</term> of ours. You will therefore have no difficulty in believing that <term>Virgil's bell</term> (<term>Nola</term>) was of such a kind as this. At its stroke all the adulterers and adulteresses in the king's palace were so excited and alarmed that suddenly, as if struck with lightning, they rushed over the bridge into the river. Do not think this story a mere fable: the thing really happened. Nor be so dense as to hesitate as to whether such properties can exist. For if, as you know to be the case, a visible man can call another visible man to him by a word, and force him to do what he wants—when a mere word, without the aid of arms, can effect so much, much more can it be that an <term>invisible man</term> can do this, since he commands both the visible and the invisible man, not by the aid of a word, but by the direction of his thought. The inferior always obeys the superior, and stands to him in the light of a subject. So, then, you will easily come around to our opinion if you conclude that the interior or <term>invisible man</term> is a kind of <term>constellation</term> or <term>firmament</term>. For he remains latent in the senses and thoughts of the exterior, visible man, and discloses or reveals himself only by imagination. # The Composition of Metals.

The same thing occurs with metals: namely, that things may be so influenced by celestial impressions as to make the operation and virtue which Nature originally determined really arise from the favorable aspect of the higher stars, and thus reveal itself, as is shown in other books of the *Archidoxis Magica*. I will add an illustration, if you wish. Let anyone create an amalgam of gold and mercury, making a conjunction of *Sol* and Mercury, but with a preponderance of *Sol*. Let him mix and blend them, and soon, with little effort, the two metals will become fixed. With these, if you choose, you can make a tincture on *Mercurius vivus*. That, in turn, can afterwards be increased and augmented with more *Mercurius vivus* under the same constellation. This is, indeed, a great <term>arcanum</term> of Nature. There will be a similar composition and union of gold or silver with mercury even without this conjunction. For if gold is placed above mercury so that the white fume of the mercury touches and penetrates the body of the gold, the gold will be rendered fragile and will melt with the greatest ease, like wax. The process is the same with silver.

This is the <term>Magnesia of the Philosophers</term>, in the discovery of which Thomas Aquinas, Rupescissa, and their disciples, though they worked hard, were unsuccessful. And let no one think it an easy matter to blend *Mercurius vivus* in the fire with harder metals and those that are slower to dissolve—such as silver,

---

* Moreover, it is entirely certain, and proven by experience, that the changes of time have a singular force and operation, and this is especially the case when certain metals are melted and crafted together. Furthermore, no one can prove that the metals are devoid of life. Their oils, sulfurs, salts, and quintessences—which are the best preservatives—have enormous power in nourishing and sustaining human life, and in this they entirely surpass the strength of all other medicinal simples, as is indeed the case with all our remedies. If they were devoid of life, how could they awaken a fresh and vital strength in the diseased and half-dead limbs and bodies of men, and restore them from the very start? . . . I therefore boldly assert that metals and stones, equally with roots, herbs, and fruits, have a life of their own, though with this distinction: that metals are prepared and crafted according to time. The efficacy of time is well-known, but we will speak only of those things which are difficult and not easily grasped by the senses, but indeed are almost contrary to their evidence. Furthermore, even signs, characters, and letters have their own virtues and powers. Now, if the nature and property of the metal, the influence and operation of the heavens and the planetary spheres, the meaning and formation of the characters, signs, and letters, along with the observation of the times, days, and hours, all harmonize and agree, why should not a sign or seal created in this manner have its own force and operation? And why, then, should not a particular medicine, applied at the right season, benefit the head, another the vision, or a third the veins? Especially in the case of those who dislike taking other remedies into the body. Yet none of these results are possible without the aid of the Father of Medicine Himself, Jesus Christ, the one and true Physician. Objectors may say that words or characters have no force, since they are mere signs or figures, and that at least none can compare in efficacy with the cross. But how is it that the serpent in Switzerland (Helvetia), Allgäu (Algovia), or Swabia (Suavia) understands the Greek phrase *Osy, Osya, Osy*, even though Greek is not so common in those countries that venomous reptiles could learn it? How is it that the moment they hear the words, they pull in their tails, stop up their ears, and, contrary to their nature, lie motionless without harming any man? . . . By this it is shown that characters, words, and signs have a hidden and latent force, not in the least opposed to Nature, nor having anything to do with superstition. It is found that these words have the same effect when they are written on paper and not spoken. Likewise, let it not be considered incredible that a man should be cured by medicine even when he does not take it internally, but carries it suspended like a seal from his neck. That there is a certain force even in dead things, I prove by the example of the kingfisher; for if you remove its skin after it is dead and hang it up, you will see that, although it is dry, it will annually shed its old feathers and produce fresh ones of the same color.—*Archidoxis Magica*, Book I. For it is certain that within the very signs of the planets themselves—if they are harmonized and carried about in the required manner according to a favorable hour and time regarding their course—there reside great force and virtue. For no one can deny that the higher stars and the influences of heaven have very great weight in transient and mortal affairs. If the higher stars and planets are able to control, rule, and sway the animal man according to their will—even though he is made in the image of God and endowed with life and reason—how much more should they rule an inferior thing, such as metals, stones, and images? Upon these they impress themselves or occupy them with all their virtue and efficacy, as an influence, as though they were substantially present just as they are in the firmament. It is possible for man himself to bring these into a certain medium in which they may effectively operate, whether this medium is a metal, a stone, or an image. But this is most important of all: to know that the seven planets have no greater force than that which they possess in their proper metals.—*Ibid.*, Book VII.

The same is the case with common mercury, which with its fume penetrates all other metals and, as it were, breaks through them, calcines them, and disposes them to its own nature. Nothing affects metals in the fire except what is of extreme cold and unable to bear the intensity of the fire. Such a metal is arsenic, which, being liquefied, ascends as a spirit from metals while they are in a state of flux.

Moreover, do not lose sight of the fact that Mercury is a metallic spirit, and that every spirit is more powerful than a body. So it is with Mercury in reference to the other metals. Just as it is easy for a spirit to penetrate walls, so it is not difficult for Mercury to penetrate metals.

How many are the wonderful operations and effects of Mercury on the metals! We cannot detail them all. But shall we send you away empty-handed to some other source? # The Composition of Metals.

In this way, you will prepare the Mercury of gold, of silver, of copper, of iron, of tin, and of lead. Although Arnold, Aristotle, and other philosophers boast about this in their books, I am well assured that it was never actually prepared or seen by them. It will now be for you to keep this great secret and mystery of Nature, and to take care that it does not fall into the hands of my adversaries; since it would be an indignity for them to come to know it. A pearl or a precious stone will not please a goose, because the goose does not know its price and value. It would infinitely prefer a turnip. We may rightly say the same of the sophists. It is no injustice to conceal secret mysteries from them. Let us not seem to cast pearls before swine or give what is holy to dogs, since God sternly forbids us to do so.

But let us proceed to the practical work of our electrum, as we promised at the outset. We would have it prepared, compounded, and joined according to the revolution of the heavens and the conjunctions of the planets. We will proceed in this way. First, you must diligently observe the conjunction of Saturn and Mercury; and, before this occurs, have ready the tools you require. These are: fire, a cauldron, lead cut into tiny pieces, and *Mercurius vivus* <note>Quicksilver or liquid mercury</note>. Take care that nothing is lacking which the work at hand requires, or for lack of which the process may be hindered or delayed. Then, when the conjunction is just about to take place, let the lead be melted in the fire. Let it not be too hot once it has fused, lest the Mercury which you pour in escape or, if the heat is too great, evaporate into smoke. Let this be done at the very moment of conjunction. Suddenly take the cauldron with the liquid lead from the fire; pour in the Mercury, and afterwards let them both be solidified.

Then there will be need for attention when the conjunction of Jupiter with Mercury or Saturn is about to take place, so that you are not ignorant of the time or let it pass by. Let everything you will want be ready at hand, as I previously advised you. You must take care, before the actual moment of conjunction, to melt fine English tin in one vessel, and in the other, the lead with Mercury. At the moment of conjunction, remove the metals from the fire, reducing the heat a little, and pour all into one crucible. When they have solidified into one body, you will have three metals that are softer and more easily melted over the fire. When they are united, do not let it escape your notice that these are to be dissolved and joined in the very first place. Then notice when there is a conjunction of any of the other four planets—*Sol* <note>Gold</note>, *Luna* <note>Silver</note>, *Venus* <note>Copper</note>, or *Mars* <note>Iron</note>—with one of the other three former ones: Saturn, Mercury, or Jupiter. Have all instruments and materials ready. Let them be dissolved individually first; then, when liquefied, pour them into one vessel at the very point of conjunction, and keep them. In a similar way, proceed with other metals which are to be joined and combined with the former ones, until you have reduced and united all seven according to the proper conjunctions of the planets. In this way, you will have prepared our electrum, about which enough has now been said.

# CONCERNING THE NATURE OF THINGS.

---

## BOOK THE FIRST.

### CONCERNING THE GENERATION OF NATURAL THINGS.

THE generation of all natural things is twofold*: one which takes place by Nature without Art, the other which is brought about by Art—that is to say, by Alchemy—though, generally, it might be said that all things are generated from the earth by the help of putrefaction. For putrefaction is the highest stage and the first step toward generation. But putrefaction originates from a moist heat. For a constant moist heat produces putrefaction and transmutes all natural things from their first form and essence—as well as their force and efficacy—into something else. For just as putrefaction in the bowels transmutes and reduces all foods into dung, so also, outside the belly, putrefaction in glass transmutes all things from one form to another, from one essence to another, from one color to another, from one odor to another, from one virtue to another, from one force to another, from one set of properties to another, and, in a word, from one quality to another. For it is known and proved by daily experience that many good things which are healthful and medicinal become, after their putrefaction, bad, unwholesome, and mere poison. So, on the other hand, many things are bad, unwholesome, poisonous, and hurtful which, after their putrefaction, become good, lose all their evil effects, and make excellent medicines. For putrefaction brings about great effects, as we see in the holy gospel where Christ says, “Unless a grain of wheat is cast into a field and putrefies, it cannot bear fruit a hundredfold.” Thus it may be known that many things are multiplied by putrefaction so that they produce excellent fruit. For putrefaction is the change and death of all things, and the destruction of the first essence of all natural objects, from which there issues forth for us regeneration and a new birth ten thousand times better than before.

Since, then, putrefaction is the first step and beginning of generation, it is in the highest degree necessary that we should thoroughly

* There is another aspect in which generation is also twofold; for example, that of wood and other things takes place naturally out of seed. But the worms which destroy wood are the product of a monstrous sperm. Hence there are two generations: natural and monstrous. Every sperm in living things has within it another sperm which is monstrous and can promote its likeness. There is also a monstrous sperm in all minerals.—*Paragraphorum* Lib. II., Par. IV.

We have also said that what is moist and warm constitutes the first grade and the beginning of putrefaction, which procreates all things as a hen procreates her eggs. Therefore, by and in putrefaction, everything becomes mucilaginous phlegm and living matter, whatever it eventually turns out to be. You see an example in eggs, in which there is mucilaginous moisture, which by continuous heat putrefies and is quickened into the living chicken—not only by the heat which comes from the hen, but by any similar heat. For by such a degree of heat, eggs can be brought to maturity in glass and by the heat of ashes, so that they become living birds. Any man, too, can bring the egg to maturity under his own arm and procreate the chicken as well as the hen. And here something more is to be noticed: If the living bird is burned to dust and ashes in a sealed cucurbite with the third degree of fire, and then, still shut up, is putrefied with the highest degree of putrefaction in a <term>venter equinus</term> <note>literally "horse's belly," referring to the moist heat of a horse-manure heap used in alchemy</note> so as to become a mucilaginous phlegm, then that phlegm can again be brought to maturity, and so be renovated and restored. This is to revive the dead by regeneration and clarification, which is indeed a great and profound miracle of Nature. By this process, all birds can be killed and again made to live, to be renovated and restored. This is the very greatest and highest miracle and mystery of God, which God has disclosed to mortal man. For you must know that in this way, men can be generated without a natural father and mother; that is to say, not in the natural way from the woman, but by the art and industry of a skilled <term>Spagyrist</term> <note>an alchemist who practices the art of separating and recombining natural substances</note> a man can be born and grow, as will hereafter be described.

It is also possible in Nature that men should be born from animals, and this result has natural causes, but still it cannot be produced without heresy and impiety. If a man has connection with an animal, and that animal, like a woman, receives the seed of the man with appetite and lust into its womb and shuts it up there, then the seed necessarily putrefies, and, through the continuous heat of the body, a man—and not an animal—is born from it. For always, whatever seed is sown, such fruit is produced from it. If this were not so, it would be against the light of Nature and contrary to philosophy. Whatever the seed is, such is the herb which springs from it. From the seed of an onion an onion springs up, not a rose, a nut, or a lettuce. So, too, from corn comes corn; from barley, barley; from oats, oats. Thus it is, too, with all other fruits which have seeds and are sown.

In like manner, it is possible, and not contrary to Nature, that from a woman and a man an irrational animal should be born. Neither on this account should the same judgment be passed on a woman as on a man—that is, she should not on this account be deemed heretical, as if she had acted contrary to Nature; but the result must be assigned to imagination. A woman is so active that, in conceiving seed into her body, she can transform the fetus in different ways; since her interior stars are so strongly directed toward the fetus that they produce an impression and influence. Therefore, an infant in the mother's womb is, during its formation, as much in the hand and under the will of the mother as clay is in the hand of the potter, who forms and makes from it what he likes and whatever pleases him. So the pregnant mother forms the fruit in her own body according to her imagination, and according to how her stars are. Thus, it often happens that from the seed of a man, cattle or other horrible monsters are begotten, as the imagination of the mother was strongly directed toward the embryo.*

But as you have already heard that many and various things are generated and brought to life out of putrefaction, you should also know that from different herbs, by a process of putrefaction, animals are produced, as those who have experience in such matters are aware. Here, too, you should learn that such animals as are produced in and by putrefaction all contain some poison and are venomous; but one contains far more and more potent venom than another, and one is in one form, another in another, as you see in the case of serpents, toads, frogs, basilisks, spiders, bees, ants, and many worms, such as canker-worms, locusts, and other creatures, all of which are produced out of putrefaction. For many monsters are produced among animals. There are those monsters, too, which are not produced by putrefaction, but are made by art in the glass, as has been said, since they often appear in very wonderful forms and horrible aspects; frequently, for instance, with many heads, many feet, or many tails, and of diverse colors; sometimes worms with fishes' tails or birds' wings, and other unusual shapes, the like of which one had never before seen. It is not, therefore, only animals which have no parents, or are born from parents unlike themselves, that are called monsters, but also those which are produced in other ways. Thus you see with regard to the basilisk, which is a monster above all others, and which none is more to be dreaded, since a man can be killed by the very sight and appearance of it; for it possesses a poison more virulent than all others, with which nothing else in the world can be compared. By her breath, too, as well as by her look, she affects many objects, rendering them corrupted and weak, and also by her touch. For the basilisk is produced and grows from the primary impurity of a woman, namely, from menstrual blood. So, too, from the blood of semen; if it is placed in a glass receptacle and allowed to putrefy in horse dung, a basilisk is produced from that putrefaction. But who would be so bold and daring as to wish to produce it, or even to take it and kill it at once, unless he had first clothed and protected himself with mirrors? I would persuade no one to do so and wish to advise everyone to be cautious. 

But, to go on with our treatise about monsters, know that monstrous growths among animals—which are produced by methods other than propagation from their own kind—rarely live long, especially near or among other animals. This is because, by their engrafted nature and by divine arrangement, all monsters are hateful to animals duly conceived in their own likeness. So, too, monstrous human growths seldom live long. The more wonderful and worthy of regard they are, the sooner death comes upon them; so much so that hardly any of them live past the third day in the presence of human beings, unless they are at once carried into a secret place and segregated from all people. 

It should be known, indeed, that God abhors monsters of this kind. They displease Him, and none of them can be saved because they do not bear the likeness of God. One can only speculate that they are shaped by the Devil and born for the service of the Devil rather than of God; since no good work was ever derived from any monster, but, on the contrary, only evil and sin, and all kinds of diabolical craft. For as the executioner marks his sons when he cuts off their ears, gouges out their eyes, brands their cheeks, or cuts off their fingers, hands, or head, so the Devil also marks his own sons through the imagination of the mother, which they derive from her evil desires, lusts, and thoughts during conception. All men, therefore, should be avoided who have more or fewer than the usual number of any limb, or have any limb duplicated. # The Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Paracelsus.

But we must by no means forget the generation of <term>homunculi</term>. For there is some truth in this matter, although for a long time it was held in a most occult manner and with secrecy, while there was no little doubt and questioning among some of the old Philosophers whether it was possible for Nature and Art to beget a man without the female body and the natural womb. I answer to this that this is in no way opposed to <term>Spagyric Art</term> and to Nature; indeed, it is perfectly possible. In order to accomplish it, you must proceed as follows: Let the semen of a man putrefy by itself in a sealed <term>cucurbite</term> with the highest putrefaction of the *<term>venter equinus</term>* [horse dung] for forty days, or until it begins at last to live, move, and be agitated, which can easily be seen. After this time, it will be in some degree like a human being, but, nevertheless, transparent and without a body. If now, after this, it is every day nourished and fed cautiously and prudently with the <term>arcanum</term> of human blood, and kept for forty weeks in the perpetual and equal heat of a *<term>venter equinus</term>*, it becomes, from then on, a true and living infant, having all the members of a child that is born from a woman, but much smaller. This we call a <term>homunculus</term>; and it should be afterwards educated with the greatest care and zeal, until it grows up and begins to display intelligence. Now, this is one of the greatest secrets which God has revealed to mortal and fallible man. It is a miracle and marvel of God, an <term>arcanum</term> above all <term>arcana</term>, and deserves to be kept secret until the last
