sperm of fish of unlike species coming together contrary to the genuine order of Nature. Thus, monsters are sometimes found in the sea exhibiting the form of man, which yet have not been generated *<term>ex sodomia</term>* [from sodomy] by men, but arise by the conjunction of different fish. . . . Even among men, monsters are sometimes found that remind us partly of a human being and partly of an animal. This is a repellent subject, but it requires to be fully explained so that the first birth may be correctly understood. The same also takes place in the sea. There is, for example, the <term>syren</term> [siren], of which the upper parts are those of a woman and the lower those of a fish. This does not form part of the original creation, but is a hybrid offspring from the union of two fish of the same kind, but of different forms. Other marine animals are also found, which, without corresponding exactly to man, yet resemble him more than any other animal. However, like the rest of the beasts, they lack a mind or soul. They have the same relationship to man as the ape does and are nothing but the apes of the sea. Whenever they unite, marine monsters of this kind are produced. Another such monstrous generation is the <term>monachus</term>, or monk-like fish. But there are many genera of fish and many modes of generation which do not always result from the sperm familiar or customary to them, but happen in various other ways. For example, certain monsters are drowned in the sea and are devoured by the fish. Now, if a sperm, constituted in "exaltation," were to perish by immersion and, having been consumed by a fish, were "exalted" again within it, a certain operation would undoubtedly follow from the nature of the fish and the sperm; from this it may be gathered that the majority of marine animals which recall the human form are produced in this manner. Yet, having the nature of a fish, they live in the waters and rejoice in them. The marine dog, the marine spider, and the marine man are of this class. If they are generated in any other way, it must be attributed to <term>sodomia</term>. But there may be a third cause, namely, when <term>spermatica</term> of this kind undergo digestion, and by reason of this conjunction a birth takes place. . . . Monsters are likewise generated in the air, from the droppings of the stars from above. For a sperm falls from the stars. The winds also in their courses bring many strange things from other regions to which they are indigenous. The sperm of spiders, toads, and other creatures floating in the air are broken down, and hence other living things are produced. In this way, grasshoppers and other monsters are begotten, their generation being from only one and not from two parents. Such births are more venomous and impure than other worms. Therefore, houses ought to be scrupulously cleaned, or else so constructed as not to favor the accumulation of much filth. For the air is effective against seeds dispersed in this manner. The earth is, however, the most fruitful matrix of monstrous growths. There, the animals of both land and sea congregate. The <term>basilisk</term> is generated from the sperm of a toad and a cock. The sperm of the cock uniting with that of the hen produces an egg. But if the cock emits his sperm without the hen doing likewise, the egg will be imperfect, and something will be generated unnaturally. There is another kind of <term>basilisk</term>, produced by the union, *<term>sedemiliter</term>* [in a similar way], of a cock and a toad. After the same manner, lizards unite with geckoes, and the copulation produces a peculiar worm, partaking of the nature of each, and known as a dragon. The asp is another instance of this unnatural generation. . . . From all that has been set down, we may learn that whoever lives for his body alone is a <term>basilisk</term>, a dragon, and an asp—not, indeed, generated as such yet, but meanwhile moving alive until he dies. You can now understand the abominable manner in which unnatural monsters are generated. For if a man lives in sperm, his very sperms turn into worms and remain worms, and in the day of the resurrection they shall be buried in the deepest parts of the earth, over which those who have risen shall walk. —*<term>De Animalibus natis ex Sodomia</term>*.

Here, too, it would be necessary to speak about the generation of metals, but since we have written sufficiently about these in our book *On the Generation of Metals*, we will treat the matter very briefly here; and only in a short space point out what we omitted there. Know, then, that all seven metals are born from a threefold matter—namely, Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt—but with distinct and peculiar colorings. In this way, Hermes truly said that all seven metals were made and compounded of three substances, and in like manner also tinctures and the Philosophers' Stone. These three substances he names Spirit, Soul, and Body. But he did not point out how this was to be understood, or what he meant by it, though possibly he might also have known the three principles, but he makes no mention of them. I do not, therefore, say that he was in error, but that he was silent. Now, in order that these three distinct substances—namely, spirit, soul, and body—may be rightly understood, it should be known that they signify nothing else than the three principles, Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt, from which all seven metals are generated. For Mercury is the spirit, Sulphur is the soul, and Salt is the body. The metal between the spirit and the body, of which Hermes speaks, is the soul, which indeed is Sulphur. It unites those two opposites, the body and the spirit, and changes them into one essence. But it must not be understood that from just any Mercury, any Sulphur, and any Salt, these seven metals can be generated, or likewise the Tincture or the Philosophers' Stone by the art and industry of the Alchemist in the fire; but all these seven metals must be generated in the mountains by the <term>Archeus</term> of the earth.<note>Elsewhere Paracelsus states that giants are born from sylphs, and dwarfs from pygmies. An alchemist will more easily transmute metals than generate or create them. Nevertheless, living Mercury is the mother of all the seven metals, and deserves to be called the Mother of Metals. For it is an open metal and, as it were, contains in itself all the colors which it yields from itself in the fire; and so also, in a hidden manner, it contains in itself all metals which it does not release without fire. But the regeneration and renewal of metals takes place like this: just as a man can return to the womb of his mother—that is, to the earth from which the first man sprang—and thus can be born again at the last day, so also all metals can return to quick mercury, can become Mercury, and be regenerated and purified by fire, if they remain for forty weeks in perpetual heat, like a child in its mother's womb. Now, however, they are born not as common metals, but as metals which tinge: for if, as has been said, *Luna* is regenerated, it will afterwards tinge all metals into *Luna*. So gold tinges other metals into *Sol*, and it must be understood in the same way for all other metals. Now, when Hermes said that the soul was the only medium which joins the spirit to the body, he had a proper understanding of the truth. And since Sulphur is that soul, and, like fire, it hastens and prepares all things, it can also link together the spirit and the body, incorporate and unite them, so that a most noble body shall be produced. Yet it is not common combustible sulphur which is to be considered the soul of metals; instead, that soul is another combustible and corruptible body. It cannot, therefore, be burnt with any fire, since it is itself entirely fire; and, in truth, it is nothing but the Quintessence of Sulphur, which is extracted by the spirit of wine from Reverberated Sulphur, and is ruby-colored and clear as the ruby itself. This is indeed a mighty and excellent <term>arcanum</term> for transmuting white metals, and for coagulating quick mercury into fixed and approved gold. Hold this in high regard as a treasure for making you rich; and you should be satisfied with this secret alone in the transmutation of metals. Concerning the generation of minerals and semi-metals, no more needs to be known than what we stated at the beginning concerning the metals—namely, that they are produced, in the same way, from those three principles: Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt. However, they are not made from these principles in their perfection, as the metals are, but from more imperfect and weaker Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt, yet still with their distinct colors.

# CONCERNING THE NATURE OF THINGS.

---

## BOOK II.

---

### CONCERNING THE GROWTH OF NATURAL THINGS.

It is clear enough, and well known to everyone, that all natural things grow and mature through warmth and moisture, as is plainly demonstrated by rain followed by sunshine. No one can deny that the earth is rendered fruitful by rain, and all must confess that every kind of fruit is ripened by the sun. Since, then, by Divine institution, this is possible for Nature, who will deny or refuse to believe that man possesses this same power through a prudent and skillful pursuit of the <term>Alchemical Art</term>, so that he may render the fruitless fruitful, the unripe ripe, and make all things increase and grow? The Scripture says that God subjected all created things to man and handed them over to him as if they were his own property, so that he might use them for his necessity; that he might have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and everything on the earth without exception. Therefore, man ought to rejoice because God has illuminated and endowed him, so that all God’s creatures are compelled to obey him and be subject to him—especially all the earth, together with all things which are born, live, and move in and upon it.

Since, then, we see with our eyes and are taught by daily experience that the more often and more plentifully the rain moistens the earth, and the sun dries it again with its heat and glow, the sooner the fruits of the earth emerge and ripen—while all fruits increase and grow, whatever the time of year—let no one wonder that the alchemist, too, by manifold <term>imbibitions</term> and <term>distillations</term>, can produce the same effect. For what is rain but the <term>imbibition</term> of the earth? What are the heat and glow of the sun other than the sun’s process of <term>distillation</term>, which again extracts the humidity? Therefore, I say that it is possible by such <term>co-optation</term> in the middle of winter to produce green herbs, flowers, and fruits from seed and root by means of earth and water.

Now, if this takes place with herbs and flowers, it will take place in many other similar things too—as, for instance, in all minerals, the imperfect metals of which can be ripened with mineral water by the industry and art of the skilled alchemist. So, too, can all <term>marchasites</term>, granites, zincs, arsenics, talcs, <term>cachimiæ</term>, bismuths, antimonies, etc.—all of which carry with them immature <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>—be so ripened as to

<summary>Paracelsus explains that growth in nature is driven by warmth and moisture, and asserts that alchemists can replicate these natural processes to ripen minerals and plants. He emphasizes man's God-given dominion over nature as the justification for using alchemy to perfect "unripe" or "fruitless" materials.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, maturation, growth, distillation, imbibition, minerals, Sol, Luna, dominion over nature</keywords>

...be made equal to the richest veins of gold and silver, only by such integration. In the same way, the Elixir and Tinctures of metals are matured and perfected.

Since, therefore, humidity and warmth mature all things and make them grow, let no one wonder that, after a long time, the beard, hair, and nails grow on a criminal on the gallows; nor should this be taken as a sign of innocence, as the ignorant interpret it. It is only natural and proceeds from natural causes. As long as there is moisture in the body, the nails, beard, and hair grow; and, what is more, in the case of a man buried in the earth itself, nails, beard, and hair grow up to the second year, or until the time of the body’s decay.

It should also be known that many substances grow and increase perpetually in size, weight, and power, both in water and on land, remaining good and effective in both—such as, for example, metals, <term>marchasites</term>, <term>cachymiae</term>, talcs, granites, antimony, bismuths, gems, pearls, corals, and all stones and clays. In the same way, it can be arranged that <term>Sol</term> shall grow and increase in weight and in body, if only it is buried in land facing east and is constantly fertilized with fresh human urine and pigeons' dung.

It is also possible for gold to be so acted upon by the industry and art of the skilled alchemist that it will grow in a <term>cucurbite</term> with many wonderful branches and leaves; this experiment is very pleasant to behold and full of marvels. The process is as follows: Let gold be calcined by means of <term>aqua regis</term> so that it becomes a chalky lime. Place this in a <term>cucurbite</term>, pouring in good and fresh <term>aqua regis</term> and water of gradation so that it covers the gold by the width of four fingers. Extract it again with the third degree of fire until nothing more rises. Again pour distilled water over it, and once more extract it by distillation as before. Do this until you see the <term>Sol</term> rise in the glass and grow in the form of a tree with many branches and leaves. Thus, there is produced from <term>Sol</term> a wonderful and beautiful shrub which alchemists call the Golden Herb, or the Philosophers' Tree. The process is the same with the other metals, except that the calcination may be different, and some other <term>aqua fortis</term> may have to be used. This I leave to your experience. If you are practiced in Alchemy, you will do what is right in these details.

Know also that any flint may be taken out of river water, placed in a <term>cucurbite</term>, and sprinkled with its own running water until the <term>cucurbite</term> is full. This may again be extracted by distillation, as long as a single drop rises, until the stone is dry. Let the <term>cucurbite</term> be filled again with this water, and once more extracted. Repeat this until the <term>cucurbite</term> is filled with this stone. In this way, by means of Alchemy, in a few days you will see that a very large stone can be made, such as the <term>Archeus</term> of the waters could scarcely make in many years. If you afterwards break the <term>cucurbite</term> on a stone, you will have a flint in the shape of the <term>cucurbite</term>, just as though it had been poured into the glass. Although this may be of no profit to you, still it is a very wonderful thing.

## BOOK III.

### CONCERNING THE PRESERVATION OF NATURAL THINGS.

In order for a thing to be preserved and protected from injury, it is necessary first of all that its enemy be known, so that the thing may be shielded from it, and so that it may not be harmed or corrupted in its substance, virtue, or power, or suffer loss in any other way. A great deal depends, then, on this: that the enemy of all natural things should be recognized; for who can guard himself against loss and misfortune if he is ignorant of his enemy? Surely, no one. It is therefore necessary that such an enemy be known. There are many enemies, and it is just as necessary to know the bad as the good. Who, in fact, can know the good without a knowledge of evil? No one. No one who has never been sick knows how great a treasure health is. Who knows what joy is if they were never sad or sorrowful? And who rightly knows what God is if they know nothing about the devil? Therefore, since God has made known to us the enemy of our soul—that is, the devil—He also points out to us the enemy of our life—that is, death—which is the enemy of our body, of our health, the enemy of medicine, and of all natural things. He has made known this enemy to us and also how and by what means we must escape him. For just as there is no disease for which a medicine has not been created and discovered to cure and drive it away, there is always one thing set against another—one water against another, one stone against another, one mineral against another, one poison against another, one metal against another—and the same in many other matters, all of which it is not necessary to recount here.

But it should be known how, and by what means, each individual thing is preserved and protected from loss: for instance, many things have to be kept for a long time in the earth. All roots, especially, remain fruitful and uncorrupted in the earth for a long while. In the same way, herbs, flowers, and all fruits stay green and undecayed in water. Many other fruits, and especially apples, can also be preserved in water and protected from all decay until new apples are produced.

So also flesh and blood, which very soon putrefy and become rancid, can be kept in cold spring water; and not only that, but by the constant addition of fresh spring water, they can be transmuted into a <term>quintessence</term>,

In the preservation of metals, the first thing to learn is what their enemies are, so that they may be better protected from loss. The principal enemies of metals, then, are all strong waters; all <term>aquae regiae</term>, all corrosives and salts show their hostility by the fact that they destroy all metals, calcine them, corrupt them, and reduce them to nothing. From gold, it takes away the pleasant yellowness and golden tint, turns it black, and makes it as unattractive as possible.

<term>Antimony</term> shows its hostility in this: it spoils all metals with which it is liquefied in the fire and with which it is mixed; it deprives and robs them; moreover, like sulfur, it robs metals of their genuine color and replaces it with another.

<term>Quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note>, on the other hand, exerts a hostile force upon the metals with which it is joined, in that it invades and dissolves them so that it creates an amalgam from them. Moreover, its smoke, which we call the soot of <term>Mercury</term>, makes all metals brittle and fragile; it calcines them and whitens all red and gold-colored metals. For oil and water are two contraries, and neither can mingle with the other. Just as the oil does not allow the waters to mix, so, on the other hand, the water prevents the oils from blending.

All timbers can be preserved, as in buildings or bridges, so that they shall never decay, whether they are in water, under water, or out of the water; in the ground, under the ground, or out of the ground; whether exposed to rain or wind, air, snow, or ice, in summer or winter; and moreover, preventing them from decaying or worms breeding in them when felled. They corrupt these things if they handle them or have anything to do with them, if they look at them, or breathe on them. The wine is changed and becomes thick; beer and <term>hydromel</term> turn sour; vinegar is weakened and loses its acidity; and milk also becomes sour and clotted.

The preservative for <term>hydromel</term> is <term>oil of sugar</term>, which must be used in the same way as the <term>oil of garyophyllon</term> or the <term>benedicta</term>.

The preservative of vinegar is <term>oil of ginger</term>, and for milk, the <term>expressed oil of almonds</term>. These two must be used as described above.

The preservative of cheese is the herb <term>hypericon</term> or <term>perforata</term>, which protects all cheeses from worms. If it is placed against the cheese and touches it, no worms are produced in it; and if some have already been produced, they die and fall out of the cheese.

Honey has no special preservative, except that it must be protected from its enemy. Its chief enemy is bread. If even a very small quantity of bread made from flour is put in or falls into it, all the honey is turned into ants and perishes entirely.

## BOOK IV.

### CONCERNING THE LIFE OF NATURAL THINGS.

No one can deny that the air gives life to all corporeal and substantial things which are born and generated from the earth. But as to what and of what kind the life of each particular thing is, it should be known that the life of things is nothing other than a spiritual essence, an invisible and intangible thing, a spirit and a spiritual thing.<note>Life is a veil or covering which encloses three principles—<term>sulphur</term>, <term>salt</term>, and <term>mercury</term>.—*Paramirum*, Book I. The life of the body is fire.—*De Ente Astrorum*, chapter 6. There is a twofold life in man: there is the life of the soul, which comes from the nature of God; but I speak here as a physician, and not as a theologian. There is also a life of the animal kind, which is of air and fire, and the same is housed in the body, which is earth and water. So is man endowed with an animal and a <term>sidereal life</term>.—*De Pestilitate*, Tract I. In another sense the life of man is said to be threefold—<term>necrocomic</term>, <term>cagastric</term>, and <term>salnitric</term>. But this has reference to the animal life only—*Liber Azoth*. That which sustains the body is the life, but the life itself is from God, and not from man. This life consists in four things—humors, temperaments, natural species, and gifts or virtues.—*De Generatione Hominis*.</note> On this account, there is nothing corporeal that does not have a spirit and life hidden within itself, which, as just now said, is nothing other than a spiritual thing. But not only does that live which moves and acts, such as men, animals, worms in the earth, birds under the sky, and fishes in the sea, but also all corporeal and substantial things. For here we should know that God, at the beginning of the creation of all things, created no body whatever without its own spirit, which the body contains in a hidden manner within itself. For what is the body without the spirit? Absolutely nothing. So it is that the spirit holds concealed within itself the virtue and power of the thing, and not the body. For in the body is death, and the body is subject to death, and in the body nothing but death must be expected. For the body can be destroyed and corrupted in various ways, but not the spirit: for it always remains a living spirit and is bound up with life. It also keeps its own body alive, but upon the removal of the body from it, it leaves the body separate and dead, and returns to its own place from which it had come—that is to say, into <term>chaos</term>, and into the air of the higher and lower firmament. Hence it is evident that there are different kinds of spirits, just as there are different kinds of bodies. There are celestial and infernal spirits, human and metallic, the spirits of salts, gems, and <term>marcasites</term>, arsenical spirits, spirits of drinkable liquids, of roots, of liquids, of flesh, blood, bones, etc. Therefore you may know that the spirit is in very truth the life and balsam

The life, then, of all men is nothing other than a certain astral balsam,<note>The flesh and blood of man are preserved and sustained by a certain balsam. Now, this balsam is the body of salt. The life of metals is a latent fatness which they have received from sulphur. This is shown from their fluidity, because everything which passes into a fluid state in the fire does so on account of its hidden fatness. Unless this were so, no metal could be reduced to a fluid state, as we see in the case of iron and steel, which have the least sulphur and fatness of all the metals; for this reason, they are of a drier nature than all the rest of them.

The life of mercury is nothing but inner heat and outer coldness. That is to say, within it gives heat, but without it causes cold; and in this respect it is aptly compared to a garment of skins, which, like mercury, causes both heat and cold. For if a garment of this kind is worn by a man, it warms him and protects him from the cold; but if he wears the hairless part against his naked body, it causes cold and defends him from excessive heat. So it happened that in very ancient times, and it is even the custom still, that these coats of skin are worn both in summer and in winter, as much against the heat as against the cold; in summer the hairless part is turned inward, and the hairy part outward, but in the cold winter season the hairy part is turned inward and the hairless part outward. As it is with the garment of skins, so it is with mercury.

The life of sulphur is a combustible, ill-smelling fatness. While it flames and sends forth its evil odor, it may be said to live.

The life of all salts is nothing else but a spirit of <term>aqua fortis</term>: for when the water is removed from them, that which remains at the bottom is called dead earth.

The life of gems and corals is mere color, which can be taken from them by spirits of wine. The life of pearls is their brightness, which they lose in their calcination. The life of the magnet is the spirit of iron, which can be extracted and taken away by rectified *vinum ardens* itself, or by spirit of wine.

The life of flints is a mucilaginous matter. The life of <term>marcasites</term>, <term>cachymiæ</term>, talc, cobalt, zinc, granites, <term>zwitter</term>, <term>vismat</term> (raw tin), is a metallic spirit of antimony, which has the power to tint. Of arsenicals, <term>auripigment</term>, orpiment, realgar, and similar matters, the life is a mineral coagulated poison.

# Concerning the Nature of Things.

The life of vile substances—that is to say, the dung of men and animals—is their strong and foul smell. When this is lost, they are dead.

The life of aromatic substances—namely musk, ambergris, civet, and whatever emits a strong, sweet, and pleasant odor—is nothing but that pleasing odor itself. If they lose this, they are dead and useless.

The life of sweet things, such as sugar, honey, manna, *Cassia fistula*, and the like, is a subtle sweetness with the power to impart its quality; for if that sweetness is taken away by distillation or sublimation, the things are dead, tasteless, and no longer of any value.

The life of resins, such as amber, turpentine, and gum, is a sticky, glittering oiliness. They all provide excellent varnish; when they no longer provide this and lose their glitter, they are dead.

The life of herbs, roots, apples, and other fruits of this kind is nothing other than the liquid of the earth, which they naturally lose if they are deprived of water and earth.

The life of wood is a certain resin. Any wood that is deprived of resin is no longer able to flourish.

The life of bones is the liquid of <term>mumia</term>. The life of flesh and blood is none other than the spirit of salt, which preserves them from foul odors and decay; it departs naturally as the water is separated from them.

But regarding the life of the elements, this must be known. The life of water is its flowing. When it is thickened by the cold of the heavens and congealed into ice, then it is dead, and all power of doing harm is taken from it, since no one can any longer be drowned in it.

So, too, the life of fire is air, for the air makes the fire blaze more strongly and with greater intensity. A certain amount of air comes from all fire, enough to extinguish a candle or to lift a light feather, as is obvious to the eyes. All living fire, therefore, if it is shut up or deprived of the power to release its air, must be suffocated.

The air lives of itself and gives life to all other things. The earth, however, is dead in itself; but its own element is its invisible and hidden life.

It concludes by describing the vital principles of the four elements, identifying air as the primary life-giver and the source of fire's intensity.</summary>

## BOOK V.

### CONCERNING THE DEATH OF NATURAL THINGS.

The death of all natural things is nothing other than an alteration and removal of their powers and virtues, an overthrow of their potential for evil or for good, an overpowering and erasing of their former nature, and the generation of a new and different nature.* For it should be known that many things which were good in life and had their own virtues, retain little or none of that virtue when they are dead, but appear altogether insipid and powerless. So, on the other hand, many things in their life are evil, but in death, or after they have been <term>mortified</term>, they display a manifold power and efficacy and do much good. We could recount many examples of this, but that is altogether foreign to our purpose. Yet, in order that you may see that I do not write from my personal opinion, no matter how likely it seems, but from my experience, it is well that I should provide one example with which I will quiet and silence the sophists who say that nothing can be gained from dead things, nor should anything be sought or found in them. The cause of this assertion is that they value as nothing the preparations of the alchemists, by which many great secrets of this kind are discovered. For look at <term>Mercury</term>, raw sulphur, and raw antimony; as they are brought from the mines—that is, while they are still "living"—how small is their virtue, and how slowly and poorly do they exercise their influence. Indeed, they bring more evil than good, and are more of a poison than a medicine. But if, by the diligence of a skilled alchemist, they are broken down into their primary substance and carefully prepared (that is, if the Mercury is coagulated, precipitated, sublimated, resolved, and turned into oil; the sulphur is sublimated, calcined, reverberated, and turned into oil; and, in like manner, <term>Venus</term> <note>Alchemical term for copper</note> is sublimated, calcined, reverberated, and turned into oil), you see what usefulness, what power and virtue, and what rapid efficiency they provide and display, so that no one can fully speak or write of it. For their manifold virtues are not easily investigated, nor can any one search them all out. Every alchemist, therefore, and every faithful—

# CONCERNING THE NATURE OF THINGS.

A physician ought to seek into these three things during his whole life, and even up to his death should play with them and find his pastime in them. Most assuredly, they will nobly compensate him for all his labor, study, and expense.

But let us come to particulars, and specifically describe the death and <term>mortification</term> of each natural thing—what its death is, and in what way it is mortified. First of all, then, with regard to the death of man, it should be understood that, beyond a doubt, it is nothing else but the end of his day's work, the taking away of his air, the vanishing of his <term>balsam</term>, the extinction of his natural light, and the entire separation of the three substances—body, soul, and spirit—and the return to his mother's womb. For since the natural, earth-born man comes from the earth, the earth, too, will be his mother, into which he must return and therein lose his earth-born natural flesh, so that at the last day he may be regenerated in a new, heavenly, and purified flesh, as Christ said to Nicodemus when he came to Him by night. For, as we said, these words apply to <term>regeneration</term>.

But the death or <term>mortification</term> of the metals is the removal of their bodily structure and of the sulfurous fatness which can be removed from them in many ways, such as by <term>calcination</term>, <term>reverberation</term>, <term>resolution</term>, <term>cementation</term>, and <term>sublimation</term>. But the <term>calcination</term> of metals is not of a single kind only. For one is produced by salt, one by mercury, one by strong waters, and one by the *<term>fuligo mercurii</term>* and quick mercury. <term>Calcination</term> by salt is when the metal is formed into very thin plates, and then stratified and cemented with salt. <term>Calcination</term> by sulfur is when the metal is formed into plates, then stratified and reverberated with sulfur. <term>Calcination</term> by strong waters is when the metal is granulated, dissolved in <term>aqua fortis</term>, and precipitated within it. <term>Calcination</term> by the *<term>fuligo mercurii</term>* is brought about thus: Let the metal be formed into plates; let the mercury be put into an earthen vessel, narrow at the top but broad below, and afterwards set on a moderate coal fire, which should be blown a little until the mercury begins to smoke and a white cloud issues from the mouth of the vessel. Then let the plated metal be placed on the orifice of the vessel. Thus the common mercury penetrates the metal and renders it as brittle as a lump of coal. <term>Calcination</term> by quick mercury is when the metal is cleft into small particles, made into plates, or granulated, and formed into an <term>amalgam</term> with mercury. Afterwards, let the mercury be pressed out through a skin, and the metal will remain within the skin in the form of lime or sand. But beyond these mortifications of the metals, and the destructions and whitenings of their life, you must know that there are many other mortifications of the metals. For beyond the fact that all rusting of iron and steel is a death, there are others which are to be esteemed as more important. For instance, it should be known that all <term>vitriol</term>, or even burnt brass, is mortified copper; all precipitated, sublimated, or calcined <term>cinnabar</term> is mortified mercury; all white lead, red lead, or yellow lead are mortified lead; all <term>lazurius</term> is mortified silver. So, also, all <term>Sol</term>, from which its tincture, quintessence, resin, crocus, or sulfur has been withdrawn, is dead.

But now let us go on to explain to you the means by which the <term>mortification</term> of metals is brought about. First of all, regarding iron, it should be known that it can be mortified and reduced to a <term>crocus</term> in the following way: Form very thin plates of steel, heat them until they are red hot, and then quench them in vinegar made from wine. Continue doing this until you see that the vinegar has become very red. When you have enough of this red vinegar, pour it all out and distill the moisture of the vinegar from it. Coagulate the residue into a dry powder. This is the most excellent <term>Crocus of Mars</term>. There is, however, another way of making the <term>Crocus of Mars</term> which in some ways surpasses the former method and is performed with much less expense and labor, as follows: Layer very thin plates of steel with equal quantities of sulfur and tartar. Afterward, <term>reverberate</term> them. This produces the most beautiful <term>crocus</term>, which should then be removed from the plates.

In the same way, you should be informed that if any plate of iron or steel is smeared with <term>aqua fortis</term>, it also produces a beautiful <term>crocus</term>. The same result occurs with oil of vitriol, salt water, alum water, water of <term>sal ammoniac</term>, water of salt nitre, and sublimated mercury—all of which mortify iron and reduce it to a <term>crocus</term>. However, none of these methods are to be compared with the two mentioned above, for these latter ones can only be used in Alchemy and not in medicine; therefore, use the first two methods by preference and avoid the rest.

The <term>mortification</term> of copper, to reduce it to <term>vitriol</term>, <term>verdigris</term>, or burnt brass, can also be accomplished in various ways. There are various processes for this metal as well, but some are better and more useful than others. Therefore, it will be good to take note of the best and most useful methods and say nothing about the others. The best, easiest, and most reliable method of reducing copper to <term>vitriol</term> is as follows: Let plates of copper be smeared with salt water or saltpeter water, and hung or exposed in the air until the plates begin to turn green. Wash off this greenness with clear spring water and dry the plates with a rag; smear the plates again with the salt water or saltpeter water and proceed as before, repeating the process until the water becomes quite green or sends a great deal of <term>vitriol</term> to the surface. Then remove the water by tilting the vessel or drawing it off, and you will have an excellent medicinal <term>vitriol</term>. For Alchemy, there is no more beautiful, noble, or better <term>vitriol</term> than that which is made by <term>aqua fortis</term>, <term>aqua regia</term>, or water of <term>sal ammoniac</term>. Proceed in this way: Let plates of copper be smeared with one of the aforementioned waters, and as soon as the greenness has been extracted and the plates have been dried, let the greenness be taken off with a hare's foot or by some other means as you wish, just as white lead is scraped off leaden plates. Let them be smeared again as before, until the plates are entirely consumed. From this is produced a very beautiful <term>vitriol</term>, such as you cannot fail to admire.

Water of saltpeter is made in this way: Purify the saltpeter, liquefy it, and then pulverize it.

To make <term>verdigris</term> from copper, there are several ways not necessary to recount here. We will therefore describe only two, with a twofold method of preparation: one for medicine and the other for <term>Alchemy</term>. The <term>verdigris</term> used in medicine allows for the following process: Take plates of copper and smear them with this compound: Take equal quantities of honey and vinegar, with enough salt to make the three together the consistency of a thick paste. Mix thoroughly, and afterward put them in a <term>reverberatory</term> furnace, or in a potter's furnace, for the same amount of time the potter bakes his vessels, and you will see a black substance adhering to the plates. Do not let this circumstance cause you any anxiety or delay you at all; for if you suspend or expose those plates in the open air, in a few days the substance will turn green and will become excellent <term>verdigris</term>, which may be called the "balsam of copper" and is highly esteemed by all physicians. And this need not cause surprise, because the <term>verdigris</term> first becomes green in the air, and because the air has the power of transmuting a black color into such a beautiful green. For here it should be known that, as daily experience in <term>Alchemy</term> proves, every "dead earth" or *<term>caput mortuum</term>*, as soon as it comes out of the fire and into the air, immediately acquires another color and loses the color it had assumed in the fire. The changes of these colors are very diverse. Depending on the material, such are the colors produced, though for the most part, they derive from the blackness of dead earth. You who are skilled in <term>Alchemy</term> see that every dead earth, flux of powder, or <term>aqua fortis</term> comes black from the fire, and the more ingredients there are in it, the more varied are the colors displayed in the air. Sometimes they only appear red, as <term>vitriol</term> makes them; sometimes only yellow, white, green, or cerulean; sometimes mingled, as in the rainbow or the peacock's tail. All these colors display themselves after "death" and as a consequence of death. For in the death of all natural things, new colors appear, and they are changed from their first color into another, each according to its own nature and properties. Moreover, we will say about <term>verdigris</term> that which we dedicate to <term>Alchemy</term>. The process of its preparation is as follows: Form very thin plates of copper, which you should layer on a large tile with equal portions of sulfur and tartar, pounded and mixed. <term>Reverberate</term> for twenty-four hours with a strong fire, taking care that the copper plates do not melt. Then take them out, break the tile, and expose the plates to the air with the matter that adheres to them for a few days; the matter on the plates will be converted into the most beautiful <term>verdigris</term>, which—in all strong waters, in waters of gradations, in cements, and in the coloring of gold—tinges gold and silver with a deep color.

The mortification of lead, in order to reduce it to white lead, is twofold: one for Medicine, the other for <term>Alchemy</term>. The preparation of <term>cerussa</term> for Medicine is as follows: Suspend plates of lead in an unglazed vessel over strong vinegar made from wine, ensuring the vessel is well closed so that no spirits may escape. Place the vessel in warm ashes or, in winter, behind the fire. Then, after ten or fourteen days, you will find the very best <term>cerussa</term> adhering to the plates. Scrape this off with a hare's foot, and replace the plate over the vinegar until you have enough <term>cerussa</term>. The other preparation of <term>cerussa</term> for <term>Alchemy</term> is like the former, except that a quantity of the best <term>sal ammoniac</term> must be dissolved in the vinegar. In this way, you will have a very beautiful <term>cerussa</term>, most subtle for purging tin or lead, or for removing whiteness from copper. But if we wish to make red lead out of the lead, it must first be calcined to ashes, and afterward burned from the side in a glazed jar, stirring it continually with an iron wire until it turns red. This <term>minium</term> is at once the best and the most valuable, and should be used in Medicine as well as in <term>Alchemy</term>. The other kind, which dealers sell in the shops, is of no use. It is made up only of the ashes which remain in the liquefaction of lead ore, and the potters buy it for glazing vessels. Such <term>minium</term> is useful only for paintings, but neither for Medicine nor for <term>Alchemy</term>.

In order to reduce lead to a yellow color, a process is required that is not altogether unlike the preparation of <term>minium</term>. Here, too, the lead must be calcined with salt and reduced to ashes. Afterward, it must be stirred continually with iron in one of the wide dishes used by those who test minerals, over a moderate coal fire, with a careful watch kept lest the heat should be too great or the stirring neglected. Otherwise, it would melt and produce yellow glass. In this way, you will have excellent yellow lead.

The mortification of silver so that <term>lazurium</term>, or some similar substance, may be produced from it, is brought about as follows: Let <term>Luna</term> be made into plates, mixed with <term>Mercury</term>, and suspended in a glazed jar over the best vinegar in which <term>auratæ</term> have been previously boiled. Afterward, dissolve it in <term>sal ammoniac</term> and <term>calcined tartar</term>. In all other particulars, proceed as directed in the case of <term>cerussa</term>. Then, after fourteen days, you will have the most precious and beautiful <term>lazurium</term> adhering to the silver plates, which you will wipe off with a hare's foot.

We do not consider it necessary here to repeat the method of mortifying gold so that it may be reduced to its <term>arcana</term>, as, for instance, to <term>tincture</term>, <term>quintessence</term>, <term>resin</term>, <term>crocus</term>, <term>vitriol</term>, and <term>sulphur</term>. These preparations are manifold, and for the most part we have already given such secrets in other books, such as the extraction of the Tincture of Sol, the Quintessence of Sol, the Mercury of Sol, Sol Potabilis, and the resin of Sol, and the Crocus of Sol. These have been given in the *Archidoxa* and elsewhere. But the secrets omitted there we will impart here. These concern the vitriol of Sol* and the sulphur of Sol, which are by no means the least among such secrets, and, indeed, ought to delight every physician. In order to extract vitriol from Sol, proceed thus: Take two or three marks of pure gold, which you should form into plates and suspend above boys’ urine, mixed with grape-berries, in a wide glass <term>cucurbite</term> closely sealed at the top. Bury this in a glowing heap of grape-berries, as they are taken from the wine-press, and let it stand there for two or three weeks. Then open it, and you will find a most subtle color, which is vitriol of Sol, adhering to the plates of Sol. Remove this with a hare’s foot, as you have been told in the case of the other metals—the crocus of Mars from the plates of iron, the vitriol of Venus and verdigris from the plates of copper, the <term>cerussa</term> from the plates of Saturn, the <term>lazurium</term> from the plates of Luna—all these being comprised under one process, but not with the same preparation. When, therefore, you have enough of this vitriol of Sol, boil it well in distilled rain water, stirring it continually with some sort of spatula. Then the sulphur of gold rises up to the surface like grease, which you should remove with a spoon. Also proceed this way with other vitriol. After the sulphur is taken away, evaporate that rain water to perfect dryness, and the vitriol of Sol will remain at the bottom. This you can easily dissolve on marble in a damp place. In these two arcana, that is to say, the vitriol of gold and the sulphur of gold, a diaphoretic virtue is latent. However, we will not describe those virtues here, because we have sufficiently indicated them in the book on *Metallic Diseases* and elsewhere.

The mortification of sulphur consists in taking away its combustible and fetid fatness, and reducing it to a fixed substance. This is accomplished in the following way: Take common yellow sulphur, reduced to a fine powder, and abstract from it the very acrid <term>aqua fortis</term> by a threefold distillation. Afterwards sweeten the sulphur which remains at the bottom, and is of a black color, with sweet water, repeating the process of distillation continually until nothing but sweet water proceeds from it and there is no more smell of sulphur. Reverberate this sulphur in a closed <term>reverberatory</term>, as in the case of antimony. Then it will become, at first white, afterwards yellow, and thirdly, red.

as cinnabar. When you have it in that form you ought to rejoice; for it is the beginning of wealth for you. This reverberated sulfur tints any silver very deeply so as to turn it into most precious gold, and it tints the human body into its most perfect condition of health. Such great virtue is found in this reverberated and fixed sulfur.

The mortification of all salts, and whatever is of a salty nature, is the removal and distillation of their watery and oily part, and additionally the spirit of salt; for if these are taken away, they are called afterwards dead earth, or *<term>caput mortuum</term>*.

The mortification of gems and corals is that they shall be calcined, sublimated, and dissolved into a liquid, like crystal. The mortification of pearls is that they be calcined and dissolved in sharp vinegar in the form of milk.

The mortification of the magnet is that it be smeared with oil of mercury or touched by common mercury. Afterwards, it attracts no iron.

The mortification of flints and stones is calcination.

The mortification of <term>marcasites</term>, <term>cachymiæ</term>, talc, cobalt, zinc, granites, <term>zwitter</term>, bismuth, and antimony, is sublimation—that is, their being sublimated with salt and vitriol. Then their life, which is the metallic spirit, ascends with the spirit of salt. Let whatever remains at the bottom of the sublimatory be washed, so that the salt may be removed from it, and you will have dead earth in which there is no virtue.

The mortification of arsenicals, <term>auripigment</term>, orpiment, <term>realgar</term>, etc., occurs when they are made fluid with salt nitre, are turned to oil or liquid on marble, and fixed.

The mortification of undulous things is a coagulation of the air.

The mortification of aromatic substances is the removal of their pleasant odor.

The mortification of sweet things is that they shall be sublimated with corrosives and distilled.

The mortification of <term>carabæ</term>, resins, turpentine, and gum is their being reduced to oil or varnish.

The mortification of herbs, roots, and the like is that their oil and water shall be distilled from them, the liquid squeezed out in a press, and afterwards the alkali extracted.

The mortification of woods is their being turned into charcoal or ashes.

The mortification of bones is their calcination.

The mortification of flesh and blood is the removal of the spirit of salt.

The mortification of water is produced by fire; for the heat of fire dries up and consumes all water. So the mortification of fire is by water; for the water extinguishes the fire and takes away from it its force and effectiveness.

Thus you are sufficiently informed, in few words, how death is latent in all natural things: how they are mortified and reduced to another form and nature, as also what virtues flow from them. Whatever else is necessary to say we will set down in our book concerning the <term>Resuscitation of Natural Things</term>.

### CONCERNING THE NATURE OF THINGS.

---

## BOOK THE SIXTH.

### CONCERNING THE RESUSCITATION OF NATURAL THINGS.

The resuscitation and reduction of natural things is not the least important aspect of the nature of things, but a profound and great secret, more divine and angelic than human and natural. I would, however, like to be understood on this point with the greatest discrimination, and in no other way than according to my fixed opinion, as Nature daily and clearly points out and experience proves; so that I may not be exposed to the lies and misrepresentations of my enemies, the quack doctors (by whom I am constantly ill-judged), as if I myself pretended to usurp some divine power, or to attribute to Nature that which she never claims. Therefore, at this point, the most careful observation is necessary, since death is twofold: that is to say, violent or spontaneous. From the one, a thing can be resuscitated, but not from the other. Do not, then, believe the sophists when they tell you that a thing once dead or mortified cannot be resuscitated, and when they make light of resuscitation and restoration; for their mistake is great. It is indeed true that whatever perishes by its own natural death, or whatever mortifies by Nature according to its own predestination, God alone can resuscitate, or it must be done by His divine command. Thus, whatever Nature consumes, man cannot restore. But whatever man destroys, man can restore, and break again once it is restored. Beyond this, man by his condition has no power, and if anyone strove to do more, he would be arrogating to himself the power of God, and yet would labor in vain and be confounded, unless God were with him, or he had such faith that he could move mountains. To such a man, this and still greater things would be possible, since Scripture says—for Christ Himself has said—"If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, and say to this mountain, 'Depart and place yourself yonder,' it would do so and place itself there; and all things shall be possible, and nothing impossible, to you."

But let us return to our proposition. What is the difference between dying and being mortified, and from which of these conditions is resuscitation possible? The matter is to be understood thus: whatever dies by its own nature has its end according to predestination, and as the pleasure and

<summary>The author introduces the concept of resuscitating natural things, distinguishing between natural death, which only God can reverse, and "mortification" or destruction caused by man, which man has the power to restore. He warns against the ignorance of "quack doctors" and emphasizes the role of faith and the limits of human power in relation to divine authority.</summary>
<keywords>resuscitation, natural things, mortification, spontaneous death, violent death, predestination, alchemy, quack doctors, faith</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the distinction between natural death—which is predestined and irreversible—and "mortification," which is a violent or artificial death from which a substance can be resuscitated or repurposed.</meta>

<page-num>147</page-num>
<header>Concerning the Nature of Things.</header>

the dispensation of God arranges. But this also happens from various diseases and accidents, and from these there is no resuscitation, nor is there any preservative which can be used against predestination and the related end of life. But what is mortified can be resuscitated and revived, as may be proved by many arguments which we will set down at the end of this book. So, then, there is the greatest difference between dying and mortifying, nor should it be thought that these are only two names for one thing. In very deed these differ as widely as possible. Examine the case of a man who has died by a natural and predestined death. What further good or use is there in him? None. Let him be cast to the worms. But the case is not the same with a man who has been slain with a sword or has died some violent death. His entire body is useful and good, and can be fashioned into the most valuable <term>mumia</term>. For though the spirit of life has gone forth from such a body, the balsam still remains, in which life is latent; this balsam also, indeed, preserves other human bodies. So, too, in the instance of metals you see that when a metal has a tendency to die it begins to be affected with rust, and that which has been so affected is dead; and when the whole of the metal is consumed with rust the whole is dead, and such rust can never be brought back to be a metal, but is mere ashes and no metal. It is dead, and death is in itself: nor does it any longer have the balsam of life, but has perished in itself.

The calx and the ashes of metals also are twofold, and there is the greatest difference between these two. For the one can be revived and brought back to be a metal, but not so the other. One is volatile, the other is fixed. One is dead, the other is mortified. The ash is volatile and cannot be brought back to be a metal, but only to glass or <term>scoriæ</term>. But the calx of metals is fixed and can be brought back again into its own metal. If you would understand the difference and its cause, know that in the ash there is less fatness and more dryness than in the calx, and it is this which allows the <term>fluxion</term>. The calx is fatter and moister than the ash, and still retains its resin and its fluxion; more especially does it retain the salt which, by its own special nature, is capable of flux, and also makes all metals pass into flux, thereby reducing them. Hence it follows that the ashes of metals cannot be brought back into metals. The salt must be extracted; then they are perfectly volatile. This is the chief point, and must be very carefully noted, since no little depends upon it. Among sham physicians a vast error is prevalent. In place of <term>Sol Potabilis</term>, the <term>Quintessence of gold</term>, the <term>Tincture of gold</term>, and so on, they have passed off to men a leprous <term>Calx of Sol</term>, not considering the difference or the evils resulting from it. For two notable and necessary facts must here be observed, namely, that either calcined or pulverized Sol, when given to men, is gathered into one mass in the bowels, or passes out *per anum* with the dung, and so is vainly and uselessly taken; or else by the great internal heat of the body it is reduced, so that it encrusts and clogs the bowels, from which result many and various diseases, and at last even death.

And as with Sol (the Sun or Gold), so also in the case of other metals, you should take no metallic arcanum or medicine into the body unless it has first been rendered volatile, so that it cannot be brought back to its metallic condition. Therefore, the first step and beginning of preparing <term>Aurum Potabile</term> (Potable Gold) is this; afterwards, such a volatile substance can be dissolved by spirit of wine, so that both ascend together, becoming volatile and inseparable. Just as you prepare gold, in the same way you prepare potable Luna (the Moon or Silver), Venus (Copper), Mars (Iron), Jupiter (Tin), Saturn (Lead), and Mercury.

But to return to our proposal, and to prove by illustrations and by adequate reasons that mortified things are not dead and forced to remain in death, but can be brought back, resuscitated, and vitalized by man, according to natural guidance and rule. You see this in the case of lions, who are all born dead, and are first vitalized by the loud roar of their parents, just as a sleeping person is awakened by a shout. So the lions are stirred up; not that they are sleeping in the same way—for one who sleeps a natural sleep would necessarily wake—but this is not the case with lions. Unless they were stirred up with this noise they would remain dead, and life would never be found in them. Hence it is understood that they acquire their life and are vitalized by that noise. You see the same thing in all animals, except those which are produced from decay, like flies, which, if they are drowned in water so that no life could be seen in them, and were so left, would continue dead, and never would revive of themselves. But if they are sprinkled with salt and placed in the warm sun, or behind a heated furnace, they recover their former life, and this is their resuscitation. If this were not done they would remain dead. So you see in the case of the serpent. If it is cut in pieces, and these pieces are put in a cucurbit, and decayed in a *venter equinus* <note>Literally "horse's belly"; a term for the gentle, steady heat produced by fermenting horse manure.</note>, the whole serpent will revive in the glass in the form of small worms or the spawn of fishes. Now, if these little worms are—as they ought to be—brought out by decay and nourished, more than a hundred serpents will be produced from the one, any single serpent being as big as the original one. This can be accomplished by decay alone. And just as with the serpent, so many animals can be resuscitated, recalled, and restored. By this process, with the aid of necromancy, Hermes and Virgil attempted to renew and resuscitate themselves after death, and to be born again as infants, but the experiment did not turn out according to their intention and it was unsuccessful.

Let us, however, move past these examples, and come to the practical method of resuscitation and restoration. It is advisable to begin with metals, because metallic bodies more frequently resemble human bodies. Know, then, that the resuscitation and renewal of metals are twofold: one brings back calcined metals by a process of reduction to their original metallic body; the other reduces metals to their first matter. The former is a reduction to *argentum vivum* (quicksilver), and such, too, is the latter process. Calcine a metal by means

Put this calx and a sufficient quantity of quicksilver into a sublimatory vessel, and let them stand for some time until the two are solidified into one amalgam. Then, by means of sublimation, raise the Mercury from the calx. Once raised, grind it again with the metallic calx and sublimate as before. Repeat this until the metallic calx melts over a candle like wax or ice, and the process is then complete. Let this metal be placed in digestion for as long as may be required, and the whole will be changed into *living Mercury* (*Mercurius vivus*), which is its original matter. This is called the Philosophers' Mercury of Metals. Many alchemists have sought it, but few have found it. In this way, *living Mercury* is now prepared from all metals—namely, the Mercury of Gold, Silver, Copper, Iron, Tin, and Lead.

The resuscitation or restoration of calcined Mercury is achieved by distillation in retorts. For only *living Mercury* rises into the cold water, while the ashes of Lead, Copper, or sulfur are left behind. However, the resuscitation and restoration of sublimed Mercury is brought about in hot water. It is necessary, though, that it should first be very finely ground, so that the boiling water may separate from it the spirit of salt and of vitriol, which it carries up with itself during the process of sublimation; the *living Mercury* then gathers together at the bottom of the water. Now, if such *living Mercury* is sublimated again with fresh salt and vitriol, and resuscitated once more in boiling water—and if this is repeated seven or nine times—it will be impossible to purify and renew it more effectively. Keep this as a great secret in Alchemy and Medicine, and rejoice over it greatly; for in this way all impurity, darkness, and poisonous nature are removed from Mercury. The resuscitation, restoration, and renewal of Mercury cannot be accomplished without sublimation; for unless it is sublimated after calcination, it will never be revived. Therefore, sublimate it, and afterward reduce it as you would any other sublimated substance.

The resuscitation of cinnabar, lapis lazuli (*lazurium*), mosaic gold (*aurum musicum*), or precipitated gold, so that they may be revived into *living Mercury*, is performed as follows: Take any one of these substances, grind it very fine in a marble mortar, and make it into a paste with egg whites and soap (<term>smegma</term>). Then make pills the size of a nut and place them in a strong earthenware cucurbit. At its opening, place an iron plate that has several small holes, and let it be fastened with lute (sealant). Distill by descent over a strong fire so that it may fall into cold water, and again you will have *living Mercury*.

The resuscitation and restoration of wood is difficult and demanding; it is indeed possible, but not to be accomplished without exceptional skill and diligence. The method of its revival is as follows: Take wood which has first of all been charcoal, then ash, and place it in a cucurbit with the resin, liquid, and oil of its own type of tree, using an equal weight of each. Let them be mixed and melted over a gentle fire. Then a mucilaginous matter will be produced, and so you will have the three principles together from which all things are born and generated: namely, moisture (<term>phlegma</term>), fat, and ash. Now, when you have these three principles together, place them in a *venter equinus* <note>Latin: "horse's belly," referring to a warm, fermenting heap of manure used for gentle, steady heat</note>, and let them putrefy for the time required by each respectively. If afterwards that matter is buried, or poured into a rich soil, you will see it begin to revive, and a tree or a little log will be produced from it, which, indeed, is in its nature much higher than the original one.

This is truly wood, and is called resuscitated, renewed, and restored wood. It was wood from the beginning, but it was mortified, destroyed, and reduced to coals, to ashes—to nothingness; and yet from that nothingness it is made into something and is reborn. Truly, in the light of Nature, this is a great mystery: that a thing which had altogether lost its form, and had been reduced to nothingness, recovers that form and becomes something from nothing—something which afterwards is much nobler in its virtue and its efficacy than it had been at first.

But, in order that we may speak generally concerning the resuscitation and restoration of natural things, this should be understood as the principal foundation—that to each thing may be again returned that which had been taken from it and separated during mortification. It is difficult to explain this specifically here; so we will conclude this book, and in the following book make these things clearer with regard to the transmutations of natural things.

# BOOK VII.

## CONCERNING THE TRANSMUTATION OF NATURAL OBJECTS.

If we are to write concerning the transmutation of all natural objects, it is right and necessary that, first and before all else, we should point out what transmutation is; secondly, what the successive steps toward it are; and thirdly, by what means and in what manner it is brought about. Transmutation, then, occurs when an object loses its own form and is so changed that it bears no resemblance to its previous shape, but assumes another appearance, another essence, another color, another virtue, another nature, or a different set of properties: as when a metal becomes glass or stone; when stone or wood becomes coal; when clay becomes stone and slate; hide becomes glue; rags become paper; and many such things. All these are transmutations of natural objects. After this, it is most necessary to know the steps of transmutation and how many there are. There are no more than seven. For although some people count a greater number, in truth there are only seven principal steps; the others which might be included among the steps are contained within these seven. They are the following:

->CALCINATION, SUBLIMATION, SOLUTION, PUTREFACTION, DISTILLATION, COAGULATION, TINCTURE.<-

If anyone climbs that ladder, they will arrive at such a wonderful place that they will see and experience many secrets in the transmutation of natural objects.

The first step, then, is Calcination, under which are included Reverberation and Cementation. Among these three, there is little difference regarding Calcination. Here, therefore, Calcination is the primary step, for through Reverberation and Cementation many physical objects are calcined and reduced to ashes, especially metals. However, what is calcined is not necessarily reverberated or cemented. Through Calcination, all metals, minerals, stones, glasses, and all physical objects become carbon and ashes; and this is done in an open fire, strong and exposed to the air. By means of this all

<term>Sublimation</term>* is the second step, also very important for the transmutation of many natural objects. Under this are included <term>Exaltation</term>, <term>Elevation</term>, and <term>Fixation</term>†; and it is not altogether unlike <term>Distillation</term>. For, just as from all phlegmatic and watery objects, water ascends in distillation and is separated from its body, so, in the process of Sublimation, in dry substances such as minerals, the spiritual is raised from the physical, refined, and the pure separated from the impure. For in Sublimation many excellent virtues and wonderful qualities are found in minerals, and many things are fixed and become permanent, so that they remain in the fire in the following way: Let the body which is sublimated be ground again and mixed with its own dregs. Let it be sublimated again as before, and let this be repeated until it sublimates no longer, but all remains at the bottom and is fixed. Thus it will afterward become a stone and an oil whenever and as often as you wish. For if, after cooling it, you put it in the air or in a glass vessel, it is there immediately resolved into an oil. If you put it in the fire once more, it is again coagulated into a stone, which possesses great and wonderful powers. But consider this a great secret and mystery of Nature, and do not disclose it to sophists. Moreover, as in Sublimation many corrosives become sweet by the conjunction of the two natures, so, on the other hand, many sweet substances become sour or bitter; while many bitter things are made sweet as sugar. Here it should be remarked, too, that every metal which is brought to a state of Sublimation by means of <term>sal ammoniac</term> may afterward be dissolved into an oil in the cold or in the air, and, conversely, may be coagulated to a stone in the fire. This is one of the greatest and most complete transmutations in all natural objects, namely, to transmute a metal into a stone.

The third step is <term>Solution</term>, under which term are comprised <term>Dissolution</term> and <term>Resolution</term>. This step frequently follows Sublimation and Distillation, as, for instance, when you dissolve the matter which remains at the bottom. Solution, however, is twofold: one by cold, another by heat; one out of the fire, the other in the fire. The cold process of Solution dissolves all salts, corrosives, and calcined bodies. Whatever salt and corrosive quality there may be, it resolves into an oil, a liquid, or water; and this takes place in a damp and cold chamber, or otherwise in the air alone, in marble or glass. For everything that is dissolved in the cold contains the sharp spirit of salt, which it often acquires and assumes in Sublimation or Distillation. And everything which is dissolved in the cold or in the air is again, by the heat of fire, changed

But solution by heat dissolves all fatty and sulfurous bodies; and whatever the heat of fire dissolves, cold coagulates into a mass, and whatever the heat coagulates, the air and the cold dissolve again. This should also be known: whatever the air or the cold chamber dissolves is of great dryness and holds a corrosive fire concealed within itself. So, whatever is dissolved in fire and by its heat has sweetness and cold within it, but not fire. In this way, and no other, is Solution to be understood.

Putrefaction* is the fourth step, under which Digestion† and Circulation are comprised. Now, Putrefaction is a very important step that might deservedly stand first, except that would be contrary to the proper order and to the mystery concealed here, which is known to very few. For these steps should follow one another in turn, as has been said, like the links of a chain or the rungs of a ladder. For if one of the links of the chain were taken away, the chain would be broken and the captive would escape. And so, too, if one of the rungs of the ladder were removed from the middle and put in the highest or the lowest place, the ladder too would be broken, and many would fall headlong from it and endanger their lives. Understand, then, that these steps follow one another in a proper order; otherwise, the whole work of our mystery would be perverted, and all our toil and effort frustrated and rendered void. Putrefaction is of such great efficacy that it blots out the old nature and transmutes everything into a new nature, bearing new fruit. All living things die in it, all dead things decay, and then all these dead things regain life. Putrefaction takes away the harshness from all corrosive spirits of salt, makes them soft and sweet, transmutes their colors, separates the pure from the impure, and places the pure higher and the impure lower, each by itself.

Distillation is the fifth step in the transmutation of all natural objects. Under it are included Ascension, Lavation, Imbibition, Cohobation, and Fixation. By Distillation, all waters, liquids, and oils are refined; the oil is extracted from all fatty substances, the water from all liquids, and in all phlegmatic substances, the oil and the water are separated.

Moreover, many things in Distillation are fixed by Cohobation, especially if the substances to be fixed contain water within them, as vitriol does. When this is fixed, it is called <term>colcotar</term>. Alum, if it is fixed with its own water, is

The process of <term>Cohobation</term> is when a *caput mortuum* is frequently soaked with its own water, and this is again drawn off by means of Distillation. Moreover, in Distillation many bitter, sharp, and acrid things become very sweet, like honey, sugar, or manna; and, on the other hand, many sweet things, such as honey, sugar, or manna, become sharp, like oil of vitriol or vinegar, or bitter, like gall or gentian, or corrosive. Many foul things lose their excessive stench in distillation, since it passes out into the water. Many aromatic things lose their pleasant odor. And just as Sublimation alters things in their quality and nature, so does Distillation.

Coagulation is the sixth step. There is, however, a twofold process of Coagulation: one by cold, and another by heat; that is, one by the air, and another by the fire. Each of these, again, is twofold, so that there are really four processes of Coagulation: two by cold, and two by fire. The Coagulations by fire are fixed; the others by cold are not fixed. One, indeed, is produced only by common air, or without fire. Another is produced by the upper firmament of winter stars, which coagulate all waters into snow and ice. The Coagulation by fire is produced by the artificial and graduated fire of the alchemist, and is fixed and permanent. For whatever such a fire coagulates becomes permanent. Another Coagulation is produced by the volcanic and mineral fire in mountains, which, indeed, the *Archeus* of the earth rules and regulates in much the same way as the alchemist; and whatever is coagulated by such a fire is also fixed and constant, though originally its matter was slimy; it is coagulated by the *Archeus* of the earth and by the work of Nature into metals, stones, flints, and other bodies. But it should also be known that fire coagulates no water or moisture, but only the liquids and juices of all natural things. For this reason no phlegm can be coagulated, unless it was originally a corporeal matter, to which, indeed, it can be restored again by the industry of an experienced alchemist. So every slimy matter or spermatic <term>lentor</term> can, by the heat of fire, be coagulated into a body and physical material, but cannot again be resolved

<term>Tincture</term> is the seventh and last step, which concludes the work of our mystery regarding <term>transmutation</term>. It makes all imperfect things perfect, transmutes them into their noblest essence and highest state of health, and changes them to another color. *Tincture, therefore, is the noblest substance with which bodies—both metallic and human—are tinted, transformed into a better and far more noble essence, and into their supreme health and purity.* For a <term>Tincture</term> colors all things according to its own nature and its own color. But there are many and various Tinctures, and not only for metallic and human bodies; since everything that penetrates another matter, or tints it with another color or essence so that it is no longer like what it was before, may be called a Tincture. Thus, there are many kinds of tinctures—namely, of metals, minerals, human bodies, waters, liquids, oils, salts, and all fatty substances—in a word, of all things which, with or without fire, can be brought or reduced to a state of flow. For if the tincture is to work, it is necessary that the body or material which is to be tinted should be open and in a liquid state; for unless this were so, the tincture could not operate. It would be just as if one were to throw saffron, or some other color, into frozen water or ice; it would not tint the ice as quickly with its color as if one were to put it into liquid water. And although it might tint the ice, it would at the same time melt it back into water. Therefore, metals also, which we wish to tint, must be liquefied by fire and freed from their solid state. And here it should be known that the more intensely they are liquefied, the more rapidly the tincture runs through them, just as <term>fermentation</term> penetrates the whole mass and imparts acidity to it. The better it is covered up, and the warmer the mass is kept, the more perfectly it ferments, and the better bread it produces; for fermentation is a Tincture of the dough and of the bread.

<note>All created things proceed from a solid, and afterward this solid must pass into a liquid. From a liquid, then, all produced things proceed, whether these are liquids or solids possessing a defined shape. Furthermore, the solid can never be so perfectly liquefied that it does not strive to return to its solidity. For example: salt, when it is dissolved in water, seeks to revert to its original state. It is the same with all other substances. Moreover, no solid is so completely dissolved that it will not eventually return to its original shape by means of the nature it retains. Understand that any solid proceeds from one of the three principles—<term>sulphur</term>, <term>mercury</term>, and <term>salt</term>—whichever it may be. <term>Sulphur</term> is never liquefied so completely as not to leave some solidity adhering to it. This is also the case with <term>salt</term> and <term>mercury</term>. Great attention must be paid to this solidification and dissolution. One frequently prevails over the other. . . . Understand, therefore, regarding things in general, that they proceed from three principles; but that from which they proceed is a solid—for example, seed, earth, all fruits, and all growing things. Nothing exists which is not a solid. But this is not the solidification mentioned here; rather, it is above it and existed before it. For fruits were produced from that liquid and were again solidified. The result is that a certain kind of generation takes place here; if it is not followed again by a second digestion—as in the digestion which followed the first dissolution into fruits—that which finally remains becomes the principle of <term>tartar</term>.—*Another Fragment on Tartar*.</note>

<note>The animals themselves have an innate knowledge, both good and bad. Nonetheless, man also has his tinctured knowledge, which is bad and good, being influenced by the stars regarding his earthly nature and condition. In consequence of this nature, a most supreme and exhaustive investigation of philosophy is permissible. The right and proper understanding of the animal condition of human nature is contained in an understanding of the tincture of the animal man. Man has two tinctures: one regarding his inferior being from the stars, and the other, supernatural, from God.—*On the Plague*, Treatise I.</note>
