<meta>This page continues the discussion of the final step of the alchemical process, Tincture, expanding on the preparation of tinctures from dregs and their application to both metals and the human body.</meta>

It should also be noted that some dregs are of a more stable substance than their liquid, and are also of a sharper and more penetrating nature. This is seen in the case of *vinum ardens* (burning wine), which is made from the dregs of wine, and in the case of *cerevisia ardens* (burning beer), which is distilled from the dregs of beer. Just as *vinum ardens* burns, and as sulfur is ignited, so too, if another vinegar were distilled from the dregs of *acetum* in the same way that *vinum ardens* is commonly distilled, a vinegar of such a fiery and sharp nature would be produced that it would consume all metals, stones, and other substances, just like <term>aquafortis</term>.

Furthermore, a tincture must be of a stable nature, capable of melting, and fireproof, so that if a little of it is thrown on a red-hot plate of metal, it will immediately flow like wax without any smoke. It will penetrate the metal as oil penetrates paper, or water a sponge, and tint all metals white and red—that is, in the case of <term>Luna</term> (silver) and <term>Sol</term> (gold).* These are the Tinctures of the metals, which must first of all be reduced to <term>alcohol</term> <note>In this context, alcohol refers to an incredibly fine, impalpable powder produced by calcination.</note> by the step of <term>Calcination</term>. Afterward, by the second step of <term>Sublimation</term>, their own easy and gentle flow must be produced; finally, by the steps of <term>Putrefaction</term> and <term>Distillation</term>, the Tincture is evolved—stable, fireproof, and of unchanging color.

But the Tinctures of human bodies—by which those bodies may be tinted into their highest state of health, and all diseases may be expelled, so that their lost powers and colors may be restored and the bodies themselves invigorated and renewed—are these: Gold, pearls, antimony, sulfur, vitriol, and the like. We provide the preparations for these in many other books, so it does not seem necessary for us to repeat them here.

Concerning Tinctures, nothing more needs to be written, seeing that every extracted color may be called a Tincture; indeed, these tint things with a permanent color that do not enter the fire, or keep their colors fixed within the fire. All these things are in the hand and power of the dyer or the painter, who prepares them according to his own pleasure.†

It is especially necessary in this book to know the degrees of fire, which can be graduated and intensified in many ways. Each degree has its own peculiar operation, and no one degree gives the same result as another, as every skillful alchemist finds from his daily experience and the practice of his art. One is the live flaming fire which reverberates and calcines all bodies.

---

* I call the tincture of gold the color of the body itself, which, if separated from the body so that a white body remains, will be a perfect work. For color and body are two different things, and for this reason they allow for separation; that is to say, the pure (the color) is separated from the impure (the body). Unless this is done, all the labor will turn out useless. When, accordingly, this separation is accomplished, we must immediately hasten to the clarification of the color, and to the highest grade of exaltation. But the grade to which the tincture can be exalted is five times double—that is, five times into five times twenty-four—for it cannot become more sublimated.—*Chirurgia Magna*, Part II., Tract III., c. 2.

† Tinctures operate approximately as follows: Just as you see fire completely consume firewood and similar bodies which, unlike gold, etc., have no human form, so we must believe that tinctures operate. Thus, as antimony purges away all the dross of gold, perfects it, and raises it to the highest grade by cementation, in like manner it becomes manifest that the tinctures themselves have obtained a nature similar to cement, inasmuch as they perform operations completely similar to those of cement and of fire. The ancient artists exhausted themselves trying to join tinctures with fire, for they anticipated a medicine in their almost sacred conjunction, but all in vain.—*Ibid.*, c. 8.

# Concerning the Nature of Things.

Another is the fire of the candle and lamp, which fixes all volatile bodies. Another is the coal fire, which cements, colors, and purges metals from their <term>scoriae</term> <note>dross or slag</note>, graduates more highly <term>Sol</term> <note>gold</note> and <term>Luna</term> <note>silver</note>, takes the whiteness from <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note>, and, in a word, renovates all the metals. Another is the fire of an ignited iron plate, on which the tinctures of metals are tested, which also is useful for other purposes. In another way, <term>scobs</term> <note>filings or shavings</note> (that is, alkali) of iron produces heat; in another way, sand; in another, ashes; in another, the <term>balneum maris</term> <note>a water bath</note>, by which many distillations, sublimations, and coagulations are produced. In yet another way operates the <term>balneum roris</term> <note>a vapor bath</note>, in which many solutions of physical things take place. Otherwise, again, acts the <term>venter equinus</term> <note>literally "horse's belly," a source of gentle heat from a bed of fermenting dung</note>, in which the principal putrefactions and digestions take place; and in another way operates the invisible fire, by which we understand the rays of the sun. This is also shown by a mirror, or steel plate, or crystal, and displays its operation and effect—a fire about which the ancients wrote scarcely anything. By this fire, indeed, the three principles in any physical substance can be separated on a table. This fire is of such wonderful power that by means of it metals are liquefied, and all fat and fluid things—indeed, all combustible things—can be reduced to coal and ashes on a table, even without fire.

Since, then, I have placed before you and disclosed the steps of the Alchemical Art and the degrees of alchemical fire, I will, moreover, point out to you and describe generally the various transmutations of natural objects. First of all, one should speak of the metals; secondly, of stones; thirdly, of various objects according to their kind. The transmutation of metals, then, is the great secret in Nature, and can only be produced with difficulty on account of many hindrances and obstacles. Yet it is not contrary to Nature or the will of God, as many falsely say. But in order to transmute the five lower and baser metals—<term>Venus</term>, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>tin</note>, <term>Saturn</term> <note>lead</note>, <term>Mars</term> <note>iron</note>, and <term>Mercury</term> <note>quicksilver</note>—into the two perfect metals, <term>Sol</term> and <term>Luna</term>, you must have the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term>. But since we have already, in the seven steps, sufficiently unveiled and described the secrets of the Tinctures, it is not necessary to labor further about this, but rather rest satisfied with what we have written in other books on the Transmutations of Metals.

But there are further transmutations of imperfect and impure metals, as, for instance, of <term>Mars</term> into <term>Venus</term>. This may be effected in different ways: Firstly, if iron filings are heated in water of vitriol; or, secondly, if iron plates are cemented with calcined vitriol; thirdly, if glowing iron plates are extinguished with oil of vitriol. In these three ways, iron is transmuted into the best, natural, and heavy copper, which, indeed, flows very well and has its own weight as well as any native copper. Iron filings can also be reduced and transmuted as if into lead, so that it becomes entirely soft, like native lead, but it does not flow easily. Therefore proceed thus: Take some iron filings and the same quantity of the best liquefying powder. Mix them; place them on a <term>tigillum</term> <note>a crucible</note> in a blast furnace; make a strong fire, not so much as to melt the iron, but let it stand as if in a cement for a whole hour. Afterwards increase the

But in order to transmute <term>Venus</term> <note>copper</note> into <term>Saturn</term> <note>lead</note> proceed thus: First of all, sublimate copper, and reduce it by fixed arsenic to a white substance, as white as <term>Luna</term> <note>silver</note>. Then granulate it. Of this, and of good reduced powder, take the same quantity; first cement them, and, lastly, pour into the <term>regulus</term>, when you will have the true leaden <term>regulus</term>.

On the other hand, it is very easy to turn lead into copper, nor is any great skill required. This is the process: Calcine plates of lead in <term>vitriol</term> <note>sulfate minerals</note>, or stratify with the <term>crocus of Venus</term> <note>copper oxide</note>, cement, and, lastly, liquefy. Then you will see as much native lead as you please transmuted into good, heavy, and ductile copper.

If, now, such copper, or any other copper, be made into plates and stratified with <term>tutia</term> <note>zinc oxide</note> and <term>calamine</term> <note>zinc ore</note>, cemented, and if, lastly, it be cast, it is changed into a splendid amber or red color, like gold.

If you wish to change <term>Saturn</term> <note>lead</note> into <term>Jupiter</term> <note>tin</note>, take plates of <term>Saturn</term>, and stratify with <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>, cement, and, lastly, cast, as above. So all its blackness and darkness are taken away from the lead, and it becomes in whiteness like the best English tin.

As you have now heard in brief a summary of some transmutations of metals, so, moreover, know concerning the transmutations of <term>gems</term>, which, indeed, are various and by no means alike. For you see how great a <term>transmutation</term> of <term>gems</term> lies hidden in oil of sulphur. Any crystal can be tinged and transmuted in it, and in course of time graduated with distinct colors so as to become like a grained <term>jacinth</term> <note>zircon</note> or ruby.

Understand in like manner concerning the <term>magnet</term>. It can be transmuted into ten times its power and virtue in the following way: Take a <term>magnet</term>, and heat it in the coals to such a degree that it may be at a high temperature, but still not red hot. Extinguish this immediately in the oil of the <term>crocus of Mars</term> <note>iron oxide</note>, which is made of the best Carinthian steel, so that it may imbibe as much as it can take. Thus you will make a <term>magnet</term> so powerful that with it you can pull out the nails from a wall, and do other wonderful things which a common <term>magnet</term> could never accomplish.

Moreover, in the transmutations of <term>gems</term>, it must be known that the world is situated in the two grades of <term>tincture</term> and <term>coagulation</term>. For as the white of an egg can be tinged with saffron, and afterwards coagulated into a beautiful yellow amber; with the dye of a pine into black amber; with verdigris into green amber, like the cyanean or Turkish stone <note>turquoise</note>; with green juice into the likeness of an emerald; with <term>lazuleum</term> <note>lapis lazuli</note> into a cerulean amber like sapphire; with Brazilian wood into a red amber like the grained <term>jacinth</term> or ruby; with a purple color like amethyst; or with <term>ceruse</term> <note>white lead</note> made to resemble alabaster—so all other liquids, and especially metals and minerals, can be tinged with fixed colors, afterwards coagulated, and transmuted into <term>gems</term>.

-># Concerning the Nature of Things.<-

Similarly, pearls can also be made to look entirely like true ones in appearance, so that by means of their brightness and beauty they can scarcely be distinguished from genuine ones. Proceed thus: Purify the white of eggs as much as possible with a sponge. Into this, put and mix some fair white talc, or pearl shell, or <term>Mercury</term> <note>quicksilver</note> coagulated with <term>Jupiter</term> <note>tin</note> and reduced to <term>alcohol</term> <note>a fine metal powder</note>. At the same time, pound it very fine on marble so that it becomes a thick amalgam, which must be dried in the sun or behind a warm furnace until it becomes like cheese or <term>hepar</term> <note>a liver-colored substance, likely a sulfur compound</note>. Lastly, from this mass make as many pearls as you wish, and fix them on hog bristles. Having thus bored them, dry them as you did the amber, and you have prepared them. If they do not shine sufficiently, anoint them externally with the white of an egg and dry them again. Thus they will become most beautiful pearls, like true ones in form, though not in virtue.

Almost in the same way, corals are made by those who wish to deceive people, just as with the pearls just spoken of. Proceed thus: Pound <term>cinnabar</term> <note>mercury sulfide</note> with white of eggs in a marble mortar for an hour. Afterwards, dry it like potter's earth. Then form from it pills or small branches, as you will; lastly, dry them thoroughly, and anoint them externally, as you did the pearls, with white of egg. Dry them again, and thus they will become like native coral in appearance, but not in virtue.

It should also be known that the white of eggs by itself can be coagulated into a very fine varnish, into which coagulation <term>Luna</term> <note>silver</note> or <term>Sol</term> <note>gold</note> may be put.

There are many other and various transmutations, of which I will tell you briefly—and in passing—those which I know and have experimented on. First, learn that any wood, if at a particular time it is put in the water of the salt of a gem, is converted into stone in a manner calculated to cause wonder. So, too, stones are transmuted into coals by <term>Ætnean fire</term> <note>intense volcanic heat</note>, and these are called stone coal.

In the same way, glue is made from hides, paper from linen rags, and silk is produced out of linen with a very sharp <term>lixivium</term> <note>a lye or alkaline solution</note> made from lime and the ashes of woad. If the downy parts are taken from feathers and dressed with this <term>lixivium</term>, they can be spun and woven like cotton. Any oil or spermatic mucilage can be coagulated into varnish; any liquid into gum. All these are transmutations of natural objects: of which we have now said enough, and therefore write our end.

-># CONCERNING THE NATURE OF THINGS.<-

## BOOK THE EIGHTH.

### CONCERNING THE SEPARATIONS OF NATURAL THINGS.

In the creation of the world, the first separation began with the four elements, when the first matter of the world was one chaos. From that chaos God built the Greater World, separated into four distinct elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth. Fire was the warm part, Air only the cold, Water the moist, and, lastly, Earth was but the dry part of the Greater World.

<margin>* Separation is grounded in heat, as in a faculty of digestion, from which, sometimes in one way and sometimes in another, the ultimate matter is formed. — *Method of Dispensing* (*Modus Pharmacandi*), Tract III. The function of the <term>Archeus</term> <note>the internal alchemist or vital force within the body</note> is the sequestration of the pure from the impure. — *On Tartaric Diseases* (*De Morbis Tartareis*), Chapter 5. For unless there is separation in the greater world, there can be no metal, and unless there is separation in the smaller world—that is, in the <term>microcosmos</term> <note>man</note>, which is man—there can be neither health nor disease, but an equal and perpetual disposition of all things. — *Great Surgery* (*Chirurgia Magna*), Part III., Book 2.</margin>

Now, so that you may learn our method in this Eighth Book as briefly as possible, you must know that we do not propose to treat here concerning the Separation of the Elements in all natural things, since we have fully and perfectly taught concerning these <term>arcana</term> <note>secrets or mysteries</note> in our *Archidoxa* on the Separations of the Elements. But here we touch only on the separation of natural things, where some one thing is singly, and by itself, materially and substantially separated and segregated, even when two, three, four, or more have been mingled in one body, and yet only a single matter is touched and seen. And here it frequently happens that corporeal matter of this kind can be known by nobody, nor be designated by an express name, until the process of separation is initiated. Then sometimes from a single matter two, three, four, five, or more proceed, as is made evident by daily experience in Alchemy. By way of example for you, there is <term>electrum</term> <note>in this context, likely a complex alloy or the "primal" metallic state</note>, which by itself is not a metal, but still conceals all the metals in one metal and body. If this, by alchemical art, be anatomized and separated, all the seven metals proceed from it—and these pure and unmixed—namely gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, iron, quicksilver, etc.

But in order to understand what separation is, you should know that it is nothing else but the segregation of one thing from another, whether two, three, four, or more have been mixed: I mean the segregation of the three principles, such as <term>mercury</term>, <term>sulphur</term>, and <term>salt</term>, and the extraction of the pure from the impure, or of the pure and noble spirit and <term>quintessence</term> from the dense and

There are many and various modes of separation, not all of which are known to us; but those among the soluble natural elements that we have investigated shall be set down here and described according to their species.

The first separation of which we speak should begin with man, since he is the <term>Microcosm</term>—the lesser world—and for his sake the <term>Macrocosm</term>—the greater world—was founded, so that he might be its separator. But the separation of the <term>Microcosm</term> begins with death.* For in death, the two bodies of man separate from each other—that is to say, the Celestial and the <term>Terrestrial</term>, the <term>Sacramental</term> and the <term>Elemental</term>. One of these soars on high, like an eagle; the other sinks down to the earth, like lead.†

The elemental body decays and is consumed. It becomes a putrid corpse, which, when buried in the earth, never again comes forth or appears. But the Sacramental body—that is, the <term>sidereal</term> and celestial body—does not decay, is not buried, and occupies no place. This body appears to men and is seen even after death. From this we get specters, visions, and supernatural apparitions. Based on these, the <term>Cabalistic Art</term> was elaborated by the ancient <term>Magi</term>, which is discussed at greater length in the books on the <term>Cabala</term>.‡

After this separation has occurred through the death of the man, the three substances separate from one another—that is to say, the body, the soul, and the spirit—each wending its way to its own place, as if to an ark from

from which it first came: the body to the earth, as the first matter of the elements; the soul to the first matter of the sacraments; and, lastly, the spirit to the first matter of the aerial chaos.

What has now been said concerning the separation of the Microcosm should also be understood of the greater world, which the mighty ocean has separated into three parts, so that the universal world is thus divided into three portions: Europe, Asia, and Africa. This separation is a sort of prefiguration of the three principles, because they, too, can be separated from every terrestrial and elemental thing. These principles are Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt. Of these three the world is built up and composed.

From this, the separation of the metals from their mountains should be known—that is to say, the separation of metals and minerals. By the separation which is established in these, many things come forth from one matter. You see that from minerals come forth metal, dross, glass, sand, pyrites, marcasite, granite, cobalt, talc, cachimia, zinc, bismuth, antimony, litharge, sulphur, vitriol, verdigris, chrysocolla, caeruleum or lazulum, orpiment, arsenic, realgar, cinnabar, fireclay, spar, gypsum, tripoli, red earth, and other similar things; and then of each one of these, the waters, the oils, the resins, the calx or ash, the Mercury, Sulphur, Salt, etc.

Vegetables, in their separation, yield waters, oils, juices, resins, gums, electuaries, powders, ashes, Mercury, Sulphur, Salt, etc.

Animals, in their separation, yield water, blood, flesh, fat, bones, skin, body, hair, Mercury, Sulphur, Salt, etc.

Whoever, therefore, boasts to be a separator of such natural things needs long experience and perfect knowledge of all natural objects. Besides this, he must be a skilled and practiced alchemist, to know what is or is not

<note>The matter is briefly as follows: Earth, water, air, and fire have their origin from three things, which, however, are not to be regarded as having been created before them, for they are and have been fire, air, water, and earth. The three have all proceeded from one mother. This mother was water. When the whole world was formed, the Spirit of God moved over the waters, for by the word *Fiat* water was first created, and from it all other creatures, animate and inanimate. These three are truly called sulphur, mercury, and salt. These, therefore, are the true principles, the true matter, out of which all animals and man himself are formed. Thus, for perfect generation in all things, three seasons are required—spring, summer, and autumn. This is especially the case in man himself. Now, sulphur, mercury, and salt recognize two rulers. Salt has the Moon and is thereby governed. It is also a subject of water, in which it is dissolved and liquefied. It belongs to autumn and winter. But the Sun is king and lord of sulphur, which is hot, fiery, and dissolved in fire. Now, the Sun is the ruler of spring and summer. But all things are nothing else except sulphur, mercury, and salt, which, further, are the most certain mark of every true physician. Salt is the body of autumn and winter, and sulphur is that of spring and summer. Salt gives form and color to all creatures; sulphur gives body, growth, and digestion. These two are father and mother, from which mediating stars all creatures are produced. But mercury needs daily nourishment and also continual increase from sulphur and salt. Know also that God has put much sulphur and salt into earth and water, and every creature, animate and inanimate, in water and earth, has its proper sulphur and salt, from which they receive nourishment and flavor. Salt gives flavor and form, sulphur gives odor and the power of decay. The Sun and Moon work diligently to generate these three things abundantly and also to mature them. The Sun and Moon are the parents of all creatures, while sulphur and salt are the seed. The seed is brought by the parents, and the fetus, which is mercury, is born. The manner of the birth of everything has its analogies in the great world. When the death of winter has passed, all things that are capable of receiving life are set in motion by the pleasantness of May, and all creatures are moved with singular delight, even as a pregnant woman who desires to give birth. Now, every individual being has assigned to it its own May for its conception and birth, its respective autumn, and its peculiar harvest. So are there various springs, summers, and autumns, according to the infinite varieties of creatures. The doctrine of the three primary principles recurs continually in the writings of Paracelsus and is elsewhere treated at length in the text of this translation. At the same time, the obscurity involving the subject seems to warrant the citation of passages such as the above, not exactly to clarify the question, but to exhibit the primeval mystery of Paracelsian philosophy with all its available variations.</note>

He details how metals, minerals, vegetables, and animals can be refined into these basic components through the skill of a practiced alchemist.</summary>

combustible, what is fixed and what is volatile, what does or does not melt, and what substance is heavier than another. He must also have investigated in every object its natural color, odor, acidity, harshness, pungency, bitterness, sweetness, its degree, constitution, and quality.

Moreover, it is necessary to know the stages of separation, which consist of distillation, resolution, putrefaction, extraction, calcination, reverberation, sublimation, reduction, coagulation, pulverization, and washing. By distillation, water and oil are separated from all physical substances. By resolution, metals are separated from minerals, and one metal from another, salt and fatness from other things, and the light is separated from the heavy. By putrefaction, the fat is separated from the lean, the pure from the impure, and the decayed from the undecayed. By extraction, the pure is separated from the impure, the spirit and the quintessence from their body, and the pearl from its dense shell. By calcination, watery moisture, fatness, natural color, odor, and whatever is otherwise combustible are separated. By reverberation, color, odor, inflammability, all moisture and wateriness, fat, and in a word, whatever there is in the substance which is meltable or unstable is separated, and so on. By sublimation, the fixed and the volatile are separated from each other, as are the spiritual and the physical, the pure from the impure, the Sulphur from the Salt, the Mercury from the Salt, and the rest. By reduction, the meltable is separated from the solid, the metal from its mineral ore, one metal from another, metal from ash, and the fat from that which is not fat. By coagulation, moisture is separated from mere humidity, and water from earth. By pulverization, dust and sand, ashes and lime, and the mineral from the animal and vegetable substance are separated from one another. All powders which are of unequal weight are separated by the process of winnowing, just as the chaff is separated from the corn. By washing or cleansing, ashes and sand are separated, as are the mineral from its metal, the heavy from the lighter substance, the vegetable and animal portion from the mineral, Sulphur from Mercury and Salt, and Salt from Mercury.

But now, setting aside mere theory, let us approach the practical work of separation and address specific details. It must be noted that the separation of metals is rightly the first task of all. For this reason, therefore, we will treat that first.

### CONCERNING THE SEPARATION OF METALS FROM THEIR MINERALS.

The separation of metals from their mineral ores can be performed in many ways—for instance, by boiling or refining, or by melting with certain liquefying powders such as alkali salt, litharge, *sal fluxum* <gloss>flux salt</gloss>, *fel vitri* <gloss>glass gall</gloss>, ash, *sal gemmæ* <gloss>rock salt</gloss>, saltpeter, etc. Put them into a vessel or dish and let them melt in a furnace. Then the metal will sink to the bottom of the vessel as a <term>regulus</term> <note>a mass of impure metal</note>, but the mineral matter will float on the surface and turn to ash. You must then process this metallic regulus in a furnace by means of a reverberatory, until all the pure metal is liberated without any dirt or ash. In

In this way, the metal is thoroughly digested and, so to speak, refined or purged of all its dirt and <term>scoria</term> <note>slag or dross</note>. Mineral ores of this kind will sometimes contain more than one metal, as is very often the case: for example, copper and silver, copper and gold, lead and silver, tin and silver, etc., may be found in a single mineral ore. The sign of this circumstance will be apparent if the <term>metallic regulus</term> <note>the metallic mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</note>, after being treated in the <term>reverberatory</term> <note>a furnace that reflects heat onto the material</note>, is resolved in a small vat in the proper fashion and manner. All the imperfect metals in it are separated—such as copper, iron, tin, and lead—and so they pass away in smoke along with the lead (of which twice as much as the <term>regulus</term> should be added), and then only fine silver and gold remain in the vat. A similar result is attained, too, if the <term>metallic rex</term> <note>literally "king," referring to the refined metallic state or core</note> is liquefied and poured upon the lumps. By that method of fusion, the intermixed metals are separated. That which is best and weightiest always sinks to the bottom, while the lighter rises above.

Two or three metals in a mixture can also be separated in acrid and strong water <note>acid, such as aqua fortis or nitric acid</note>, and one can be extracted from the other, expanded, and resolved. But if both metals are resolved together, one of them in that resolution—as sand or <term>calx</term> <note>a powdery metallic oxide</note>—can be reverberated and depressed <note>precipitated</note> with salt according to the usual method, and so separated.

Besides this, metals can also be separated by <term>fluxion</term> <note>the process of melting or flowing</note> according to the following process. Bring the metals to a state of flux. When this has been done, throw in one ounce of the most perfectly sublimated and refined sulfur for every pound of the metal. It will be burned there, and in the course of that operation, it will attract to itself on the surface the lightest metal, while it will leave the heavier at the bottom. Let them stand in this way until cool. So in the one <term>regulus</term>, two metals will be found—not mixed together as before, but opposed to each other and separated by the sulfur as if by a wall, just as oil separates two bodies of water so that they cannot join and be commingled. In the same way, sulfur acts with these metals. Sulfur, therefore, is an <term>arcanum</term> <note>a profound secret or mystery of nature</note> worthy of the highest esteem.

Volatile and fugitive metals, such as gold and silver, if they are to be separated from their minerals, should be amalgamated, separated, and extracted by means of *Mercurius vivus* <note>living mercury or quicksilver</note>, since they can neither be treated in the fire nor with strong waters. Afterwards, the *Mercurius vivus* must be removed and separated from the <term>calx</term> of the gold or silver by the process of distillation.

In this way, other metals too—such as gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, and substances prepared from these, like <term>red electrum</term>, <term>white magnesia</term>, <term>aurichalcum</term> <note>brass</note>, lead ashes, <term>laton</term> <note>latten, a brass-like alloy</note>, casting brass, part with part, etc., and whatever transmuted metals of this kind there are—must be removed and separated from their extraneous substances by means of *Mercurius vivus*. For this is the nature and quality of *Mercurius vivus*: it is amalgamated with metals and wholly united with them, though more quickly or more slowly with one than with another, according to whether the metal is more or less akin to its nature.

Again, gold and silver leaf, as well as every metal that has been ground or pounded and used for writing with a pen or pencil on cloth, parchment, paper, leather, wood, stone, or other material, can be dissolved with <term>Mercurius vivus</term>, provided that the <term>Mercurius vivus</term> can afterwards be separated and removed from these metals again.

The separation of metals in <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note>, <term>aqua regis</term> <note>nitro-hydrochloric acid</note>, and similar strong corrosives, is performed in the following manner: Let the metal which is mixed and joined to another be taken and reduced into very thin plates or most minute portions. If it is silver and contains gold, all the silver will be dissolved into the liquid, while the gold will be <term>calcined</term> and sink to the bottom in the form of black sand. By this method, the two metals, gold and silver, will be separated. But if you wish to separate the silver alone without distillation, and to drive it to the bottom like black sand—bringing it back to its <term>calx</term> state from its dissolved state—then put into that solution a small copper plate; thereupon the silver will sink in the liquid and occupy the bottom of the glass vessel like snow, while it will begin gradually to consume the copper plate.

The separation of silver and copper by means of common <term>aqua fortis</term> is accomplished in the following way: Reduce the copper which contains silver, or the silver which contains copper, into very thin plates or into grains; put it into a glass vessel, and add as much common <term>aqua fortis</term> as necessary. In this way, the silver will be <term>calcined</term> and will go to the bottom in the form of white <term>lime</term> <note>powder</note>, while the copper will be dissolved and converted into transparent liquid. The separation of hidden gold from any metal is effected by the degree of extraction through <term>aqua regis</term> <note>nitro-hydrochloric acid</note>; for this water does not work to resolve any metal except fine gold alone.

This same <term>aqua regis</term> also separates fine gold from gilded <term>clenodia</term> <note>jewels, ornaments, or precious treasures</note>. If it is smeared over these, it wipes away and sunders the gold.

Moreover, also, two metals mixed together can be separated from each other with a <term>cement</term> <note>a powder used in the dry process of refining metals</note> by the degree of <term>reverberation</term> <note>the process of heating in a furnace where the flame is reflected onto the material</note>, especially if they are not in a similar degree of <term>fixation</term> <note>the state of being non-volatile or resistant to heat</note>, such as iron and copper. A metal which has very little fixation, such as tin and lead, is altogether consumed in the cement by the degree of reverberation. The more fixed any metal is, the less it is affected or consumed by the cement.

It should be known, too, that fine gold is the most fixed and perfect of all metals, and can be consumed by no cement. Next to this is fine silver. But if gold and silver are mixed together in one body, which is generally called "<term>part with part</term>" <note>an alloy of equal parts gold and silver</note>, or if silver contains gold, or gold silver, in itself—if these mixtures, I say, be cemented and reverberated together, then the gold always remains entire and inviolate, while the silver is consumed by the cement, and is extracted from the fine gold; and so is copper from silver or iron, or tin from copper and iron, or lead from tin; and so on in order with the others.

### CONCERNING THE SEPARATION OF MINERALS.

So far we have explained the separation of metals from their earth and matter, and of one metal from another; and have shown how it was to be done, using the greatest brevity consistent with accuracy, and following the alchemical art and practical experience. Now, next in order, it will be necessary also that we treat of those things out of which metals grow and are generated, such as are the three principles, <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Sulphur</term>, and <term>Salt</term>, and other minerals, among which is found the first essence of metals, that is, the spirit of metals, as is evident in <term>marchasites</term>, <term>granites</term>, <term>cachimiæ</term> <note>metallic ores or furnace residues</note>, <term>red talc</term>, <term>lazurium</term> <note>lapis lazuli or azure-colored mineral</note>, and the like. In these the first essence of gold is found by the degree of <term>sublimation</term>. So, too, in <term>white marcasite</term>, <term>white talc</term>, <term>auripigment</term> <note>orpiment, a yellow arsenic sulfide</note>, <term>arsenic</term>, <term>litharge</term>, etc., the first essence of silver is found. In <term>cobalt</term>, <term>zinctum</term> <note>zinc or a zinc-like substance</note>, etc., the first essence of iron. In <term>zinctum</term>, <term>vitriol</term>, <term>atramentum</term> <note>a black vitriol or metallic ink-like substance</note>, <term>verdigris</term>, etc., the first essence of copper. In <term>zinctum</term>, <term>bismuth</term>, etc., the first essence of tin. In <term>antimony</term>, <term>minium</term> <note>red lead</note>, etc., the first essence of lead. In <term>cinnabar</term> is found the first essence of silver.

Concerning this first essence, it should be known that it is a fugitive spirit, still existing in a volatile state, as a child lies hidden in the womb of its mother. It is sometimes likened to a liquid, sometimes to alcohol. Whoever, therefore, is anxious to have the prime essence of any body, and to separate it, needs great experience and knowledge of the <term>Spagyric Art</term> <note>the art of separating and recombining the principles of bodies; alchemy</note>.

### CONCERNING THE SEPARATION OF VEGETABLES.

The separation of those things which grow out of the earth and are combustible—such as fruits, herbs, flowers, leaves, grasses, roots, woods, etc.—is also arranged in many ways. By distillation, first the <term>phlegma</term> <note>the watery or tasteless component of a substance</note> is separated from them, afterwards the Mercury, after this the oil, fourthly their sulphur, and lastly their salt. When all these separations are made according to the Spagyric Art, remarkable and excellent medicines are the result, for both internal and external use.

But since laziness has grown to such an extent among physicians, and all work and every pursuit is turned only toward arrogance, I do not wonder, indeed, that preparations of this kind are everywhere neglected, and that coals stand at so low a price. If blacksmiths could do without coals for forging and fashioning metals as easily as these physicians do without them in preparing their medicines, there is no doubt that all the coal merchants would have been reduced to extreme poverty long ago. In the meantime, I praise and honor, with the credit rightly due to them, the Spagyric physicians. These do not give themselves up to ease and idleness, strutting about with a haughty gait, dressed in silk, with rings ostentatiously displayed on their fingers, or silvered daggers fixed on their waists, and smooth gloves on their hands. But they devote themselves diligently to their labors, sweating whole nights and days over fiery furnaces. These do not kill time with empty talk, but find their delight in their laboratory. They are clad in leather garments and wear a belt to wipe their hands upon. They put their fingers among the coals, the <term>lute</term> <note>a clay or cement used to seal vessels</note>, and the dung, not into gold rings. Like blacksmiths and coal merchants, they are sooty and dirty, and do not look around proudly with smooth faces. In the presence of the sick, they do not chatter and brag about their own medicines. They perceive that the work should glorify the workman, not the workman the work, and that fine words go a very little way toward curing sick folks. Passing by all these vanities, therefore, they rejoice to be occupied at the fire and to learn the stages of alchemical knowledge. Of this class are: Distillation, Resolution, Putrefaction, Extraction, Calcination, Reverberation, Sublimation, Fixation, Separation, Reduction, Coagulation, Tincture, and the like.

The Alchemical Art, using distinct degrees of fire, has been discussed generally before, and it would be pointless to repeat the same thing here. To move on to specifics and briefly explain the practical method, let it be known that not all things can be separated by one and the same process; that is to say, the water, spirit, liquid, oil, and so on, from herbs, flowers, seeds, leaves, roots, trees, fruits, and woods, according to the grade of distillation.

Herbs require one process, flowers another, seeds another, leaves another, roots another, trees, stalks, and stems another, fruits another, and woods another, etc. And in this grade of distillation, the four degrees of fire must be considered. The first degree of fire is the *Balneum Mariæ* <note>a water bath used for gentle, indirect heating</note>. This is the distillation performed in water. The second degree of fire is distillation performed in ashes. The third is in sand, and the fourth is in open fire, just as distillation is generally performed with <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid or other strong corrosive mineral acids</note> and other violent waters. Herbs, flowers, seeds, and the like, require the first degree of fire. Leaves, fruits, etc., need the second. Roots, branches, and trunks of trees, etc., require the third. Timber and the like require the fourth. Each of these substances must be minutely cut up or pounded before being placed into the still. So much has been said regarding the distillation of waters and vegetable substances. Regarding the separation and distillation of oils, the same process must be followed as we have spoken of in the separation of waters, except that, for the most part, they have to be distilled by descent <note>a method where the heat is applied from above and the vapors or liquids are forced downward into a receiver</note>. They cannot, like waters, ascend in the still; therefore, in this case, the process must be changed. Liquids, however, are not separated like waters and oils by distillation, but are squeezed out from their physical substances under a press. And here it should be known that some oils, in the same way as liquids, are squeezed out from their physical substances and separated by means of the press for this reason: they can endure hardly any combustion or heat from the fire without acquiring an unpleasant odor. Of this kind are the oils of almonds, nuts, hard eggs, and the like. This is also to be noted: that all oils, if they are prepared or coagulated according to Spagyric and Alchemical Art, produce varnish, electuary, gum, or a kind of resin, which might also be called a <term>sulphur</term>; and if the remnants left in the still were calcined and reduced to ashes, alkali could be extracted and separated from them with simple warm water alone. The ash which is left is called dead earth, and nothing more can be produced or separated from it.

When this paste has been prepared, extracted, and separated from the human body according to the prescribed method, a most excellent styptic arcanum and specific remedy is produced, with which a wound or ulcer can be quickly healed and the edges brought together, just as two sheets of paper are stuck together with paste, if you only apply two or three drops of that dissolved substance to the wound. This arcanum is also of singular efficacy for burns and the falling off or roughness of the nails if it is spread over them with a feather. In this way, the bare flesh will be covered over with a cuticle.

Many other separations of various things might also be recounted here; but since we have mentioned them in other places, it would be pointless to repeat them now.

Here it is only necessary to write down what we have not mentioned elsewhere.

But finally, at the end of all earthly things, the final separation will be brought about, in the third generation, on that great day when the Son of God shall come in His majesty and glory. Before Him shall be carried not swords, chains, diadems, scepters, and treasures, or other royal jewels with which princes, kings, and Caesars conduct themselves pompously, but His Cross, and crown of thorns, and nails piercing His hands and feet, and the spear with which His side was wounded, and the reed and sponge on which they offered Him what they gave Him to drink, and the rods with which He was scourged and beaten. No crowd of horsemen with far-sounding drums shall accompany Him; instead, the four trumpets shall be blown by the angels toward the four parts of the earth, and at their tremendous sound all who are among the living shall be slain, and these, together with the buried dead, shall immediately rise again.

> For a voice shall be heard, “Rise, you dead, and come to judgment!” At this, the Twelve Apostles shall sit down on thrones prepared from the clouds and shall judge the twelve families of Israel. In that place, the Holy Angels shall separate the bad from the good, the cursed from the blessed, the goats from the sheep. Then the cursed shall be thrown down like stones and like lead, but the blessed shall fly like eagles. Then from the tribunal of God shall issue a voice to those standing on the left hand, “Go away, you cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared from eternity for Satan and the devils. For I was hungry and you did not feed Me; I was thirsty and you gave Me no drink; I was sick, and a prisoner, and naked, but you did not visit Me, did not set Me free, did not clothe Me. In a word, you were not touched with pity for Me. Therefore, here you shall meet with no pity!” On the contrary, to those standing on the right side it shall say: “Come, you blessed and elect, into the Kingdom of My Father, which has from the beginning been prepared for you and for all the angels. For I was hungry and you gave Me food; I was thirsty and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger and you received Me; I was naked and you clothed Me; I was sick and you visited Me; I was in prison and you came to Me. So will I receive you also into My Father’s house, in which are the many mansions of the saints. You pitied Me; and so I will pity you!”

When all these things are finished and done, all the elementary subjects shall return to the first matter of the elements and shall be turned about for eternity, yet never consumed. On the contrary, all sacramental creatures shall return to the primal matter of the sacraments; that is, they shall be glorified, and in eternal joy they shall worship God their Creator, from universe to universe, from eternity to eternity. Amen.

# BOOK THE NINTH.*

## CONCERNING THE SIGNATURE OF NATURAL THINGS.

In this book, our first business, as we are about to philosophize, is with the signature of things—as, for instance, to set forth how they are signed, what signator exists, and how many signs are reckoned. First of all, then, let it be known that there are three types of signs. The first are things signed by man; the second are signed by Archeus; the third are signed by the Stars of the Supernaturals. In this way, then, only three signators exist: Man, Archeus, and the Stars. Moreover, it should be noted that the signs signed by man carry with them perfect knowledge and judgment of occult things, as well as an acquaintance with their powers and hidden faculties.

The signs of the stars provide prophecies and omens. They point out the force of supernatural things and put forth true judgments and disclosures in <term>geomancy</term>, <term>chiromancy</term>, <term>hydromancy</term>, <term>pyromancy</term>, <term>necromancy</term>, <term>astronomy</term>, the <term>Berillistic art</term>,† and other astral sciences.

Now, in order that we may explain all the signs as correctly and as briefly as possible, it is necessary above all else that we put forward those of which man is the signator. When these are understood, you will more rightly attain to the others, whether natural or supernatural. For instance, it is known that

It is universally boasted concerning faith that it can accomplish many things. This is, indeed, not far from the truth, for Christ Himself bears witness to it. Jews wear a yellow sign on their cloaks or on their coats. What is this but a sign by which anyone who meets them may understand that they are Jews? So, too, the lictor is known by his multicolored tunic or armlet. In the same way, every magistracy decorates its ministers with its own proper colors and ornaments.

The craftsman marks his work with his own unique sign, so that everyone may understand who has produced it. For what purpose does the courier carry the insignia of his master or his city on his garment, except to make it clear that he is a messenger, that he serves one person or another, that he comes from one place or another, and thus secures for himself a safe passage?

So, too, the soldier carries a sign or symbol—black, white, green, blue, or red—so that he may be distinguished from the enemy. From this, it is known that one is on the side of Caesar, or of the kings; that one is an Italian, another a Frenchman, etc. These are signs which relate to rank and office; many more of them might be listed. Nevertheless, since we have proposed to describe other signs of natural and supernatural things, we will not overload our book with those signs that are foreign to our purpose.

It is necessary to explain more clearly those signs which man applies, which lead to a knowledge not only of rank, office, or name, but also of discernment, intelligence, age, dignity, and degree. Next in order, regarding money, it should be remembered that every coin carries its proof and sign by which it may be known how much that coin is worth, to what power it belongs, and where it circulates and is accepted. Here the German proverb applies: “Nowhere is money more welcome than where it is minted.”

The same is to be understood of the customary signs which are attached by jurors and those appointed for the purpose, after a proper inspection has previously been made. An instance of this is found in the cloths marked with distinguishing signs by which it may be known that, upon examination, they have been found good and genuine. Why is a seal attached to letters except so that there may be a certain authority which none will dare to violate? The seal is the confirmation of the letter which gives it authority among men and in trials. A receipt without a seal is dead, useless, and empty.

In the same manner, by a few letters, names, or words, many things are designated, just as books which, though labeled on the outside with only one word, signify their contents in that way.

Such, too, is the condition of the vessels and boxes in pharmacies, which are all distinguished by specific names or labels attached to them. If that were not done, who could distinguish one from the other among so many different waters, liquids, syrups, oils, powders, seeds, ointments, and the like? In the same way, too, the alchemist in his laboratory marks with their own proper names and labels all the waters, liquids, spirits, oils, <term>phlegmata</term>, <term>crocuses</term>, <term>alkalis</term>, and powders—and then all the different kinds of these, one by one—so that he can select from among them whatever he wants. Without this safeguard, it is impossible to remember each separately.

### CONCERNING MONSTROUS SIGNS IN MEN.

Many men come into the light deformed with monstrous signs. One man has an extra finger, another a finger too few; and the same may be the case with the toes. Another brings with him from the womb a distorted foot, arm, back, or other limb; another has a weak or a hunched back. So also there are born <term>hermaphrodites</term> and <term>androgyni</term>—men, that is to say, who possess both <term>pudenda</term>, male as well as female, and sometimes lack both. I have noted many monstrous signs like this in both males and females, all of which are to be regarded as monstrous signs of secret sins in the parents. From this has grown the old proverb: "The more distorted, the more wicked"; and again: "lame limbs, lame works." These are signs of vices and rarely denote anything good.

Just as the executioner brands his sons with degrading signs, so also bad parents mark their offspring with harmful supernatural signs, so that people may be more cautious when they see the example of wicked men who carry <term>stigmata</term> on their forehead or cheeks, or in defective ears, fingers, hands, eyes, or tongues.

Each of these signs of infamy designates some particular vice. If there is a brand burnt into the face of a woman, or if there is a cutting off of the ears, it mostly indicates theft. The loss of fingers tells of cheating gamblers. The loss of a hand indicates those who violate the peace. The loss of two fingers points out perjury. The loss of an eye indicates that people engage in sharp and subtle crimes. The cutting off of the tongue designates blasphemers and slanderers. So you can recognize those who are called <term>mamelukes</term>, or deniers of the Christian religion, by a cross burnt into the heel of their feet, because they denied Christ their Redeemer.

But let us dismiss these matters and return to the monstrous signs brought about by wicked parents. It should be known that all monstrous signs are not produced only by the parent, but frequently also from the stars of the human mind, which rise and set at every moment through <term>Phantasy</term>, <term>Estimation</term>, or <term>Imagination</term>, just as they do in the heavens above. Because of fear or fright on the part of those who are pregnant, many monsters are born, or children are marked with signs of monstrosity in the mother's womb. The primary cause of these things is alarm, terror, or intense desire, by which the imagination is aroused. If the pregnant woman begins to imagine, then her womb is moved in its motion just like the upper heavens, with each movement rising or setting. For, as in the case of the greater heavens, the stars of the <term>microcosm</term> also move by imagination.

### CONCERNING THE ASTRAL SIGNS IN THE PHYSIOGNOMY OF MAN.

The signs of physiognomy derive their origin from the higher stars. This science of physiognomy was held in the highest esteem by our ancestors, especially among the heathens, Tartars, Turks, and others whose custom it is to sell men and slaves; nor was it entirely lost among Christians. However, many errors that had not yet been noticed by anyone crept in when every fool and every clown took it upon himself to judge everything offhand. It is remarkable that these mistakes were not discovered through the evil deeds and limited powers of the men themselves.

Now, if anyone at this point argues against us, saying, “The signs of physiognomy come from the stars, but no one has the power to compel or influence the stars,” they do not speak wrongly. Yet, this distinction must be noted at the outset: the stars compel one person and do not compel another. It should be known who can rule and coerce the stars, and also who is governed by the stars. The wise man can dominate the stars and is not subject to them. Indeed, the stars are subject to the wise man and are forced to obey him; he does not obey the stars. The stars compel and coerce the <term>animal man</term> <note>the man governed by his lower, instinctual nature</note>, so that he must follow where they lead, just as a thief follows the gallows, a robber the wheel, a fisherman the fish, a fowler the birds, and a hunter the wild beasts. What other reason is there for this, except that man does not know or value himself or his own powers, nor does he reflect that he is a <term>microcosm</term> <note>a lesser universe</note> and has the whole firmament with its powers hidden within himself? Thus, man is called animalistic, unwise, and the slave of all earthly things, even though he received from God in Paradise the privilege of ruling over and dominating all other creatures, rather than obeying them. This is why God created man last, after all other things had been made before him. This right was afterwards lost by the Fall. Yet, the wisdom of man was not made servile, nor did he lose his freedom. It is right, then, that the stars should follow him and obey him, not he the stars. And although he is the "son of Saturn," and Saturn is his parent, he can still withdraw himself from his influence and

It happens much in the same way to him as to the miner, who for a long time has hired out his labor to the master of the mines, and managed his department honestly at the peril of his life. At length he holds this discourse with himself: 

> "Are you going to spend all your life underground and endanger your body—nay, your very existence—by continuous labors? I will seek release from my master, and follow another where my life shall flow pleasantly on, where I shall have plenty of food and drink, where my garments may shine, where no work and much reward shall be given to me, and where I shall not be oppressed by the mountain overhanging me."

In this way he can make himself a lord where otherwise he would remain all his life a slave and a hired hand, wasting away with hard labor and scanty food.

Moreover, as you have now perceived that man rules the stars, and can free himself from a malignant planet and subject himself to another better one—passing by virtue from slavery to freedom, and rescuing himself from the prison of an evil planet—so also the animal man, who is the son of Sol, Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury, can withdraw himself from that benevolent planet and subject himself to Saturn or to Mars. This man is like one who, fleeing from a religious community and being tired of their soft life, becomes a soldier, or in other respects a man of no reputation, who must afterwards spend all his life in pain and care. Such, too, is the rich man, who, out of mere frivolity, wastes all his goods unjustly—gambling, feasting, keeping evil company—until at last, when all is gone, he comes to want. In a miserable conflict with discreditable poverty, he deservedly rouses laughter and contempt in everyone, so that you even hear from the boys in the streets: 

> "Look at that worthless man, who, when he could have been a master, scorned dominion and preferred to be a slave, a beggar, a servant of servants, so that he cannot now even aspire to his former mastery." 

It is to this that a bad star or a bad parent has led him. Had he not been foolish and wicked, he would not have left to the stars so unquestioned a dominion over himself, but he would have struggled against them. And, although he himself had not known how to fight against his stars, yet he could have turned his mind to the examples of other men, thinking thus within himself: 

> "See how rich this man was; but by foolish and shameful enterprises he involved himself in mere poverty!" 

Again, 

> "This or that man lived splendidly, and without any great bodily labor; but, though having received good food and ample pay, he was not able to bear his fair fortune. Now he has to live frugally and miserably. In place of wine he has to drink water, and while his daily labor increases, his income is diminished." 

How often must such a man address himself this way: 

> "What have I done? How have I thrown myself headlong down by wasting prodigally the wealth I had collected and acquired? Who will restore it to me? If I could only recover what I have lost, quite another mode of life would be begun; and so I would learn wisdom from my own loss, and compensate for my evil deeds."

He who has wasted his substance once will waste it again. He who perishes once, perishes again. He who throws the dice once will throw them again. All this is done by the animal man, who is the servant and slave of the stars; who is swayed backward and forward by the stars like a reed in the waters. This is the reason why he has to spend his life in misery and die in dishonor. Who, then, would bear so disgraceful a slavery and not free himself from such a squalid prison? For by applying his own wisdom, and with the help of his star, anyone can free himself. 

Look at the matter this way: A fowler, relying on his own prudence and by the assistance of his star conquering another star, has no need to pursue birds, for the birds will follow him; and though their nature might rebel, they will fly together to unaccustomed places. In like manner, to the fisherman who is at ease and relying on his wisdom, the fish will swim of their own accord, so that he can catch them with his hands. The hunter, exerting his wisdom by means of his star, collects wild beasts so effectively that he has no need to pursue them; they pursue him, contrary to the guidance and impulse of Nature. And it is the same with other living creatures.

In order to grasp these things, it must be remembered that stars are of two kinds: terrestrial and celestial. The former belong to folly, the latter to wisdom. And as there are two worlds, the lesser and the larger, and the lesser rules the larger, so also the Star of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>The "lesser world," referring to man as a reflection of the universe.</note> governs and subdues the celestial star. God did not create the planets and stars with the intention that they should dominate man, but that they, like other creatures, should obey him and serve him. And although the higher stars do give the inclination and, as it were, sign man and other earthly bodies for the manner of their birth, yet that power and that dominion are nothing, except for a predestined mandate and office, in which there is nothing hidden or abstruse remaining; rather, the inner force and power is put forth through the external signs.

But to return to our proposition concerning the physical signs of men: know that these are twofold, similar indeed in outward form, but dissimilar in power and effect. Some are from the upper stars of heaven; others from the lower stars of the microcosm. Every superior star signs according to birth up to middle age. That signature is predestined and is not without its own peculiar force. It is attested by a man's nature and condition of life. But whatever the lower star of the microcosm signs from birth has its origin from the father and the mother, as often as the mother affects it by her imagination or...

appetite, her fear or dread, [marks] the unborn child in her body with supernatural signs by means of their own close contact. These are called <term>mothers' marks</term>, or <term>uterine marks</term>. We have spoken of these before, so we shall spare ourselves the labor of repetition, since it is our purpose to treat of physiognomical signs alone. Among these, we understand those signs in men the likes of which neither the father nor the mother carried in their bodies. Of this category are black or grey eyes, eyes too small or too large; a long, crooked, or sharp-pointed nose; hollows in the jaws, high cheekbones, a flat or broad nose, small or large ears, a long neck, an oblong face, a mouth large and drawn down; hair thick or fine, abundant or scanty, black, yellow, or red, etc. If one or more of these signs appear in a man, be sure that he will not lack the qualities signified by them. However, you must judge them according to the rules of <term>physiognomy</term> and have experience in the <term>art of signature</term>, by which you can judge a man by outward signs.

Moving, then, to the practical portion of our subject, let us repeat a few of these signs and their meanings.

Black eyes not only denote a healthy constitution, but also, for the most part, a steady mind free from doubt and fear, healthy and hearty, truthful and loving virtue.

Grey eyes are the sign of a crafty man, ambiguous and inconsistent. Weak eyes denote good counsel, clever and profound deliberations, and so on. Bright eyes, which turn up, down, and to both sides, denote a false, clever man who cannot be deceived, faithless, shirking work, desiring ease, and seeking to gain his livelihood in laziness—by gambling, usury, impurity, theft, and the like.

Small eyes, somewhat deeply sunken, indicate weak sight and often impending blindness in old age. At the same time, they denote brave men, warlike, crafty, and skillful, inclined to dissent, capable of enduring misfortune, and whose departure from life is, for the most part, of a tragic character.

Large eyes denote a greedy, gluttonous man, especially if they project far out of the head.

Eyes which are constantly winking indicate weak sight, and a timid and cautious man. Eyes which move quickly here and there, under the glance of men, indicate an amorous heart, one who is forward-looking and of quick invention.

Eyes continually cast down show a reverent and modest man.

Red eyes show a bold, brave man.

Glittering eyes, which do not move readily, point out a hero, a high-minded, brave, quick man, formidable to his enemies.

Large ears indicate good hearing, a retentive memory, attention, diligence, and a healthy brain and head.

Depressed ears are a bad sign. For the most part, they point out a man who is malicious, fraudulent, and unjust. They indicate bad hearing, a treacherous memory, and a man who readily exposes himself to danger.

A long, downward-curved nose is a good sign. It denotes an energetic, far-sighted man, secretive and cruel, yet still just.

A flat nose indicates a malicious man, false, lustful, untruthful, and inconsistent.

A pointed nose indicates a changeable person, prone to mockery.

A long nose shows a man who is slow in business, yet of good reputation.

Hollow cheeks denote a talkative, contemptuous, and argumentative person.

An oblong chin, with a long face, shows an irritable man who is slow at his work.

A cleft chin shows a faithful man, dutiful, with complex and varied speech; a man who says one thing and means another; quick to anger, yet repenting of his passion; clever and inventive.

A large, wide mouth shows a gluttonous man, dull, foolish, shameless, and fearless. A small mouth indicates the contrary.

When the lips are drawn together and the upper is larger than the lower, it shows an irritable, combative, and courageous man; yet for the most part, he is of a dull, unchaste character, like a pig.

Lips that are larger on the bottom show a thick-headed, stupid, and slow person.

Regarding the hair of the head or beard, the signs are not very clear, since experience teaches us that these can vary greatly depending on whether the hair is black, yellow, red, white, grey, or curly. Furthermore, hair can be made soft or hard according to a person's desire. Hence, many people who are otherwise well-skilled in the <term>science of physiognomy</term> are miserably deceived when they hastily judge based on hair, attributing to the stars what should instead be credited to men. Still, it cannot be denied that firmly rooted hair shows good health, both of the head and of the whole body. This is why people who buy horses pull at their tails to judge their health. Similarly, pigs are judged by their bristles, fish by their fins and scales, birds by their feathers, and so on.

If the neck is unusually long, exceeding the limits of Nature, it denotes a careful, prudent, and attentive man.

Broad shoulders and a broad back show a man who is strong for carrying and moving things. Muscular arms also show a man who is strong and robust in hitting, thrusting, throwing, and the like.

Hard hands indicate a hardworking, hired laborer; soft hands indicate the opposite.

A short body and long legs denote a good runner, one who is easily satisfied with food and drink, but generally a man with a somewhat short life.

Large and prominent veins in a man below middle age signify that he is full of blood and bodily fluids; but after middle age, they indicate a sickly man who is, nevertheless, still lively.

Regarding manners and gestures, a man cannot be so easily known or judged by these. Experience teaches us that these can be changed at any moment, so as to deceive the <term>signator</term> and lead him to a mistaken judgment.

### CONCERNING THE ASTRAL SIGNS OF CHIROMANCY.*

Regarding the signs of <term>chiromancy</term>, it should be understood that they arise from the higher stars of the seven planets, and all of them ought to be learned and judged according to the seven planets. Now, chiromancy is a science that does not only inspect the hands of men and make its judgment from their lines and wrinkles; moreover, it also considers all herbs, woods, flints, soils, and rivers—in a word, whatever has lines, veins, and wrinkles. But this science is not free from the errors that astronomers have alleged against it. For they have assigned the fingers of both hands to the planets and the principal stars, even though there are only five fingers on one hand but ten on both hands, while the planets are only seven in number. How can these things be made to agree? Now, if there were seven fingers on each hand, then it might be possible to assign a finger to each of the planets. It often happens, indeed, that a man has only seven fingers on his two hands, the others being lost by some accident. But the stumps still exist, and, furthermore, the persons were not born that way, so this matter has no relevance here. Besides, if it did happen that a man was born with seven fingers either on one hand or on both, that would be a monstrous birth, not according to Nature, and therefore not to be assigned to the stars. So here, again, no comparison can be established. It would have been better, then, for the planets to cast lots and see which two should retire. This, however, could not be done, because the planets had neither dice nor lots up in the firmament; so one wonders who took it upon himself to allot the planets by name, giving the thumb to Venus, the index finger to Jupiter, the middle

Every peculiarity of line, whether in leaves or in human hands, has its special meaning. Then there is no renewal for that herb. The root is dead and no longer contains life. However, how that spirit is taken from the root with the herb, or from the earth with the root—so that its virtue returns either to the root or from the root into the earth—must not be discussed here. The younger and less aged herbs are, the more they excel in their power and their faculties. For just as a person is weakened by old age and fails in their natural powers, so it is with herbs.

But in order to know what the <term>chiromancy</term> is, and what the age is, of herbs and similar bodies, long experience is required, since the number of years is not written upon them but must be divined solely by <term>chiromancy</term>, as we have said. Now <term>chiromancy</term> provides not numbers, not letters, and not characters, but only lines, veins, and wrinkles as a means of calculating age. The older anything is, the larger and more visible are the lines displayed, and the power and operation of the thing are less active. For just as a disease of one month or one year is more easily cured than one of two, three, four, or five months or years, so a herb of one year more quickly cures its disease than one of two or three years. And for this reason, young herbs and those which are fewer years old should be given for old illnesses, but for recent ailments, old herbs and medicines should be administered. For if old is joined to old, the blind lead the blind and both fall into the ditch. This is the reason why many medicines are ineffective. They are in the body and they fill the limbs, but only as mud sticks to shoes. Consequently, the diseases are often doubled.

Now, here is a matter which, up to this time, has never been considered by unskilled sophists, while through their ignorance they have lost more patients than they cured. The very first thing you physicians ought to know is that the medicine must always be younger than the disease, in order that it may overcome it and be stronger in expelling it. If the medicine is more powerful than the disease, the disease will be expelled, just as fire will be extinguished by water. If the disease is more powerful than the medicine, that medicine turns into a poison, and afterward diseases are redoubled and made more severe. Thus, if the disease is like iron, the medicine must be steel. Steel cannot be conquered by iron. The more powerful conquers; the weaker is subdued.

Although, therefore, it was no part of my original plan to write anything about medicine in this place, still, for the sake of true and genuine physicians, I could not pass by these matters in silence.

To pursue our current goal, I will move on to a very brief practical explanation regarding the chiromancy of mines. The deeper and broader the veins are, the older they are known to be. When the paths of the veins stretch for a very long distance and then gap open, it is a bad sign. For as the paths of the veins gap, so do the mines themselves, a fact they indicate by their depth. Although good mines are sometimes found at a very deep level, they mostly disappear more and more, so that they cannot be worked without a great expenditure of labor. But where those veins are increased by other secondary ones, or are frequently cut off in any other way, that is a lucky sign. It indicates that the mines are good not only on the surface, but that they increase in depth and multiply, becoming rich mines that yield a very large treasure.

It is relevant to the subject that many metallurgists praise those mines that run straight down and move from east to west. However, logic and experience within the mines also teach us that veins stretching from west to east, or from south to north, or conversely, from north to south, often contain just as much metal as others. Therefore, no single vein is to be preferred over another, and there is no need for further discussion on this point.

As for those signs concerning the colors of minerals and the inner earth, one may deal with them briefly. When miners come across clayey soil from which a vein of pure and fresh metal flows, that is a very good sign, indicating that the source of the metal is now not far off.

Similarly, if the earth being dug out lacks metal but is rich and of a white, black, clayey, red, green, or blue color, then that is also a favorable sign of hidden metal. In such cases, the work should be carried on briskly, with no pause in the digging. A yellow coruscation reveals golden metals. Add to this that a slight and subtle coruscation is the best sign. It is just as you see in the case of trees: where there are fewer flowers, you get better fruit. So, too, small and subtle coruscations indicate subtle and excellent metals, and *vice versa*. In addition to this, it should be known that as long as these flashes appear—be they great or small, of this color or of that—the metal is not yet perfect and matured in its ore, but still exists in its first essence, like a man’s seed in the womb of a woman.

Now let us explain what this coruscation is. It appears sometimes during the night in mines like sparkling fire, just like gunpowder spread in a long trail that, when lit at one end, shows a drawn-out fire. In the same way, this coruscation, or sparkling, travels along its own track, sometimes from east to west or, conversely, from west to east, from south to north, or *vice versa*. And so, a straight line drawn from any hour or part of the mountain map toward the nearest opposite hour divides the map—which is marked off into twenty-four hours or parts—into two sections.

All these coruscations, whenever they appear, provide the most reliable indications of metallic lodes, so that from them the metals may also be recognized

...as certain gifts of God coming out of the earth. For whatever God has created for the use of humanity, He has placed in man's hands as a possession, so that it should not remain hidden. And although He created it hidden, He also added these specific outward signs to guide our investigation. Here, His marvelous predestination should be recognized. In just the same way, when people bury treasure themselves, they mark the place by adding certain sure signs. They bury them near landmarks, statues, fountains, or other objects so that, if necessary, they can find them again and dig them up. If the ancient Chaldeans and Greeks feared siege or exile during wartime, they buried their treasures and marked the place only by choosing a specific fixed day, hour, and minute of the year. They waited until the sun or the moon cast a shadow there, and in that spot, they hid or buried their treasures. They called this art <term>Sciomancy</term> or the Art of Shadows. From these studies of shadows, many arts arose, and many occult matters were revealed—for example, the methods by which all spirits and celestial bodies might be identified. These are the infallible <term>cabalistic</term> signs and should be watched carefully.

You must take particular care, however, not to let yourselves be deceived by divinations obtained through unreliable arts. These are vain and misleading; foremost among them are the divining rods, which have deceived many miners.<note>Elsewhere Paracelsus says that it is faith which turns and directs the divining rod in the hand.—*On the Origin of Invisible Diseases, Book I.*</note> If they point correctly once, they deceive ten or twenty times. Similarly, no confidence should be placed in other deceptive signs of the devil which appear at night or at inappropriate times, contrary to the way of Nature—such as specters, visions, and the like. Be sure that the devil gives these signs merely through fraud and with the intent to trick you. No temple is ever built where the devil does not also have his chapel; no chapel where he does not have his altar. Good seed is never sown without him sowing weeds along with it. That is the meaning of visions and supernatural apparitions, whether they appear in crystals, mirrors, waters, or similar things. Ceremonial necromancers have foully abused God’s commandment and the light of Nature itself in this way. Visions, however, are not to be rejected entirely. They have their place, but only when produced by a different method.

We no longer live in the first, but in the second generation. As Christians in our regenerate state, we should no longer use ceremonies and conjurations as the ancients did in the Old Testament, for those people lived in the first generation. Those men were foreshadowings for us who were to live under the New Testament. Therefore, whatever the ancients accomplished under the Old Testament or the first generation by means of ceremonies and conjurations, we Christians—who belong to the second generation and live under the New Testament—ought to obtain through prayer. That is, we should seek it in faith by praying, knocking, and asking. In these three primary points consists the whole foundation of magical and cabalistic...
