<note>* Natural sleep is the rest of the body, which restores its wasted energies. Now, the day pertains to bodies and the night to spirits; bodies work during the day, spirits at night. The sleep of the body is the waking time of the spirit, for the two cannot operate together, being opposites and mutually incompatible things. Whatever is done by the body during sleep is actually performed by the spirit. For some speak and give answers in their sleep; some arise and walk during it, but all this is done by the spirit governing the body. This is why it happens that if such a man is called by his name, he wakes up because the spirit within him is terrified by being called by the name of the man; for spirits are no less terrified by the voice of a man than men are by the voice of a spirit. A man in baptism receives a name, but the spirit does not. Therefore, the spirit is terrified when the man is called. 

For this reason, sleep-walkers should by no means be left alone in their rooms, and this is especially the case with those who are afflicted by the <term>Sagæ</term> (that is, divining spirits), because it is of great importance that such persons should be addressed by name; for in this way, all nocturnal divining spirits, all formidable specters, and all waking visions are driven away and dispelled. But it should be noted that not all men, indiscriminately, who talk in their sleep are to be called out to or shouted at in this way, because they may be in communion with a spirit whose voice is not heard. For, although the spirit's voice may be much clearer than that of humanity, it is not commonly audible to humans, for the material ear can be, and is, closed by the power of such an intelligence, as is well known to those who divine by <term>necromancy</term> through the spirits of the air, who are intermediate spirits, neither strictly good nor evil. 

No man holding such a conversation should be disturbed as long as his tone is cheerful; but if he answers with trembling, fear, and consternation, this is a sign of a bad apparition, and such a person ought to be awakened by shouting. Such conversations are not, however, always conducted with the physical vocal organs of the sleeper, but also with those of the spirit, in which case there is no audible sound; this latter kind of speech is not only more frequent but of greater importance. It was deeply investigated by the ancient <term>Magi</term>, who by this means could extract from the spirits of the deceased a knowledge of those secrets which they had concealed from the whole world while they still lived in the body. In this way, they became acquainted with the mysteries of Alchemy, Astronomy, Astrology, Medicine, Theology, etc.—namely, by direct communication of their spirits with the spirits of those who had practiced these sciences on earth. 

In order to acquire the secret method of communication with such intelligences, the first requirement is to pray with faith for the mercy of God in the matter; then we must also, with faith, make an image of that man with whom we desire to communicate. On the body of such an image, the name of the man must be written, and also the question to be asked. Place this image at night under your head and sleep upon it. That man himself will then appear to you spiritually and will answer your questions, teaching you whatever he can. There is, however, a more certain and better way. This does away with the image and relies only on faith and imagination. No danger is attached to this experiment, but it requires great confidence in the validity of the operation. I have several times had practical evidence of its truth. — *On Philosophy*, Tract V.</note>

# Concerning the Nature of Things.

...per has the stars of Venus; iron has the stars of Mars; tin has the stars of Jupiter; lead has the stars of Saturn; quicksilver has the stars of Mercury. As soon, however, as they have reached their perfection and are coagulated into a fixed metallic body, their stars withdraw from every one of them and leave their bodies dead. Therefore, it follows that all these bodies are equally dead and ineffective, and that the unconquered star of the metals subdues all of them, converts them into its own nature, and so makes them all astral. For this reason, our gold and silver, which are colored and prepared with our tincture, are much more noble and more excellent for the composition of medicinal <term>arcana</term> <note>Secret remedies or medicinal mysteries.</note> than the gold itself which Nature generates in mines and afterwards separates from other metals. So also corporal *Mercurius*, made astrally from another metal, is much nobler and more fixed than common mercury. In the same way, you may judge the other metals. I assert, therefore, that every alchemist who possesses the star of gold turns all red metals into gold by tingeing them. So by the star of silver, all white metals are turned into silver; by the star of copper, into copper; by the star of quicksilver, into corporal Mercury; and so with the others. How all these stars are prepared by the <term>Spagyric art</term> <note>The alchemical art of separating and recombining substances to produce pure essences.</note> is no part of our present purpose to declare. That explanation belongs to the book on the *Transmutation of Metals*.

So far as relates to the true signs of these, I would have you know that our red tincture, which contains within itself the stars of gold, is of a substance fixed above all consistency, of most rapid penetration, and deepest redness; its powder recalls the color of saffron, and its entire body that of the ruby. Its tincture can be melted like resin, is clear as crystal, brittle as glass, but very heavy in weight.

The white tincture, which contains the stars of <term>Luna</term> <note>The Moon, signifying silver.</note>, is, in the same way, of a fixed substance, of changeless growth, of consummate whiteness, fluid as resin, clear as crystal, brittle as glass, and in weight like the adamant <note>A diamond or an extremely hard stone.</note>. The star of copper is of a supreme citrine <note>A lemon-yellow or golden-green color.</note> color, like an emerald, can be melted like resin, and is much heavier than its own metal.

The star of tin is white-flowing like resin, somewhat dark, and suffused with a clay-like color. The star of iron is of remarkable redness, clear as <term>granatum</term> <note>A garnet.</note>, can be melted like resin, is brittle as glass, of fixed substance, and much heavier than its own metal. The star of lead is like cobalt, black but transparent, fluid as resin, brittle as glass, equal to gold in weight, and heavier than other lead. The star of quicksilver is of a white, glittering color, like snow in a deep frost, very subtle, penetrating, and of corrosive sharpness, clear like crystal, easily melted as resin, very cold to the touch, but extremely warm within the fire, and moreover, volatile, having a substance which easily flies before the fire.

From this description, you will know the stars of the metals, and you will understand that for the preparation of either tincture, the red or the white, you must at first take not the body of gold or of Luna, but the first essence of gold or of Luna. If a mistake is made at the outset, all the subsequent work and labor will be thrown away.

Moreover, this fact applies to metals: each of them in the fire exhibits some specific sign by which it can be recognized. Among these are sparks, flames, brightness, colors of the fire, smell, taste, etc. For instance, in the <term>reverberation</term> <note>A process of heating a substance in a furnace so that the flame is reflected back onto it.</note> of gold or silver, the genuine sign is a brightness above the vessel or vat. When this appears, it is certain that the lead and other accessory metals have disappeared in the fumes, and so the gold and silver are thoroughly purified. Iron, which is completely fused in the furnace, sends forth clear, bright sparks which rise to a height. As soon as these appear, unless the iron is at once removed from the fire, it will be burnt up like straw.

In the same way, every earthly body exhibits its own specific and distinct signs in the fire, whether it has any <term>Mercury</term>, <term>sulphur</term>, or <term>salt</term>, and which of these three principles it has the most. If it smokes before it bursts into flame, it is a sign that it contains more Mercury than sulphur. If, on the other hand, it burns with a flame and blazes forth without any smoke, it is a sign that a good deal of sulphur, and no Mercury—or very little—lies hidden within it. This you see taking place with fatty substances, such as fat itself, oil, resin, and the like. But if nothing goes out through the fumes and there is no flame, it is a sign that much Mercury and very little sulphur exists within it. This you see taking place with herbs, flowers, and the like; and also with other vegetable substances and volatile bodies, such as minerals and metals still in their first essence and not yet mixed with corporeal sulphur. These send forth only smoke and no flame.

Minerals and metals which in the fire emit neither fumes nor flame—that is, neither smoke nor blaze—show an equal mixture of Mercury and sulphur, and a stability and perfection beyond all consistency.

### CONCERNING CERTAIN PARTICULAR SIGNS OF NATURAL AND SUPERNATURAL THINGS.

We must now, in due course, speak of some specific signs about which nothing has been passed down up to this time. In this treatise, it will be very necessary that you who boast of your skill in the science of <term>signatures</term>, and who also wish to be called <term>signators</term>, should rightly understand what we say. In this place, we are not going to speak theoretically, but practically, and we will put forth our opinion expressed in the fewest possible words for your understanding.

First of all, know that the signatory art teaches how to give true and genuine names to all things. All of these Adam the <term>Protoplast</term> <note>The "first-formed," referring to Adam as the first human.</note> truly and entirely understood. So it was that after the Creation he gave its own proper name to everything: to animals, trees, roots, stones, minerals, metals, waters, and the like, as well as to other fruits of the earth, the water, the air, and the fire. Whatever names he assigned to these were ratified and confirmed by God. Now these names were based upon a true and intimate foundation, not on mere opinion, and were derived from a predestinated knowledge—that is to say, the signatorial art. Adam is the first signator.

Indeed, it cannot be denied that genuine names also flow from the Hebrew language and are bestowed upon each thing according to its nature and condition. The names given in the Hebrew tongue indicate, by their very bestowal, the virtue, power, and property of the very thing to which they belong. So when we say, "This is a pig, a horse, a cow, a bear, a dog, a fox, a sheep, etc.," the name of a pig indicates a foul and impure animal. A horse indicates a strong and patient animal; a cow, a voracious and insatiable one; a bear, a strong, victorious, and untamed animal; a fox, a crafty and cunning animal; a dog, one faithless in its nature; a sheep, one that is placid and useful, hurting no one. Hence it happens that sometimes a man is called a pig on account of his sordid and piggish life; a horse, on account of his endurance, for which he is remarkable beyond all else; a cow, because he is never tired of eating and drinking, and his stomach knows no moderation; a bear, because he is bigger and stronger than other people; a fox, because he is versatile and cunning, accommodating himself to all, and not easily offending anybody; a dog, because he is not faithful to anything beyond his own mouth, and shows himself unaccommodating and faithless to all; or a sheep, because he hurts nobody but himself, and is of more use to anyone else than to himself.

In the same way, many herbs and roots have obtained their names. So the *euphrasia* or *herba ocularis* is thus called because it cures ailing eyes. The sanguinary herb is named thus because it is better than all others at stopping bleeding. The scrophularia (*chelidonium minus*) is so called because it cures hemorrhoids <note>The original text uses "piles," a traditional term for hemorrhoids.</note> better than any other herb. And so it is with many other herbs, of which I could cite a vast number, all of which were named on account of their virtue and faculty, as I have shown more at length in my Herbary.

Then, again, many herbs and roots got their names, not from any one inborn virtue and faculty, but also from their figure, form, and appearance, as the *Morsus Diaboli*, *Pentaphyllum*, *Cynoglossum*, *Ophioglossum*, *Hippuris*, *Hepatica*, *Buglossum*, *Dentaria*, *Calcatrippa* (*consolida regalis*), *Perforata*, *Satyrion* or *Orchis*, *Victorialis*, *Syderica*, *Perfoliata*, *Prunella*, *Heliotrope*, and many others which need not be recounted here, but separately in the Herbary.

The same is true as to the signs of animal matters, because, in like manner, all diseases which lie hidden in men are recognized from the blood and its circulation, and from the urine and its circulation. From the liver of a slaughtered animal all its flesh can be judged as to whether it is fit for food or not. For if the liver is not clear and of a red color, but livid and yellow, rough and perforated, it is inferred that the animal was sick and that, on this account, its flesh is unwholesome. It is no marvel that the liver indicates this by natural signs. The origin of the blood is in the liver, and from there it flows forth through the veins over the whole body, and is coagulated into flesh. For this reason, from a sickly and ill-affected liver no healthy and fresh blood can be produced, just as from morbid blood no wholesome flesh can be coagulated. But, moreover, there are other signs which are worthy of our wonder, when, for example, the <term>Archeus</term> is the <term>signator</term> and marks the umbilical cord of the <term>fœtus</term> by means of knots, from which it can be told how many children the mother has had or will have.

The same <term>signator</term> marks the antlers of the stag with branches by which its age is known. As many branches as the antlers have, that is how many years old the stag is. Since there is an addition of a new branch to the antler every year, the age of the stag can be determined up to twenty or thirty years.

So, too, the <term>signator</term> marks the horns of the cow with circles from which it is known how many calves she has borne. Every circle indicates one calf.

The same <term>signator</term> pushes out the first teeth of the horse so that for the first seven years its age can be certainly known from its teeth. When the horse is first born it has fourteen teeth, of which it sheds two every year, so in seven years all of them fall out. For this reason a horse more than seven years old can only be judged by one who is very skilled and experienced.

The same <term>signator</term> marks the beak and claws of a bird with particular signs, so that every experienced fowler can judge its age from these.

The same <term>signator</term> marks the tongues of pigs with blisters, by which their impurity can be known. If the tongue is foul, so is the whole body.

The same <term>signator</term> marks the clouds with different colors, by which the storms of the sky can be predicted.

So also he marks the circle of the moon with distinct colors, each one of which has its own special interpretation. Redness generally indicates coming wind; greenness or blackness indicates rain. The two mixed indicates wind with rain. At sea this is a sign which generally portends tempests and storms. Brightness and clear whiteness are a good sign, especially on the ocean. For the most part they predict quiet and serene weather.

It is known to all that if a seed is cast into the earth and concealed therein, the latent nature of that seed, at the proper time, manifests it above the earth, and anyone may see clearly what manner of seed has lain in that place. It is the same with the heart (*cor*) and seed of man: out of that seed Nature produces a body so that anyone can see what kind of heart has been there. And, although there is a great difference between herbs or trees and men, yet art in man sufficiently demonstrates and proves those things. We men in this world explore all things which lie hidden in the mountains by means of traces and external signs. For we investigate the properties of all herbs and stones by their signed sign (*signum signatum*). Similarly, nothing can lie hidden in man which is not outwardly marked on him, for, as the physician has his own knowledge, so also the astronomer explores from the signed (*ex signate*). So now there are three things by which the nature of man and of everything that grows is revealed: **Chiromancy**, which concerns the extremities, as, for example, the hands, the feet, the veins, the lines, and the wrinkles; **Physiognomy**, which regards the constitution of the face and the parts belonging to the head; **Proportion**, which considers the condition of the whole body. These three should be combined: according to these three every created thing can be recognized: by the physician, that is to say, the remedy; by the astronomer, that is, the man; and by the metallurgist, that is, the metal. Such is the condition of the mother which manifests that which is latent in anything. Whoever is incapable of understanding these three things can be in no sense a natural philosopher, astronomer, or doctor, or know anything of the <term>arcana</term> and mysteries of Nature. The foundation is in this, that all things have seed, and in seed all things are contained, for Nature first fabricates the form, and afterwards she produces and manifests the essence of the thing. — *Explicatio Totius Astronomiæ*.

To make myself more easily understood, let me add an example. To the planet <term>Sol</term> belong the crown, the scepter, the throne, all royal power and majesty, all dominion, and all the riches, treasures, ornaments, and trappings of this world.

To the planet <term>Luna</term> are subject all agriculture, navigation, traveling, and travelers, and everything concerned with matters of this kind.

To the planet <term>Mars</term> are subject munitions (as they are called), all breastplates, cuirasses, spears, and all arms, along with everything relating to war.

To the planet <term>Mercury</term> are subjected all literary men, all mechanical instruments, and every requirement of art.

To the planet <term>Jupiter</term> are subject all judgments and laws, the entire Levitical order, all ministers of the church, the decorations of temples, ornaments, and whatever else belongs to this class.

To the planet <term>Venus</term> are subject all things relating to music, musical instruments, amorous exercises, loves, debaucheries, etc.

---

The method is as follows: They guide the hand and mark the points until a judgment is made concerning the matter proposed. But the spirits know exactly how many points are required to make a figure that will explain the matter. If their direction is right, the figure is also correct and valid. For example, suppose I ask who is standing at the door, and what kind of tunic is he wearing? Take the seven colors, assign a geomantic sign to each, and consult that figure. Then, whatever sign appears indicates the color. Now, if I knew what color it was, but you did not know, I might guide your hand, forming certain points in a line so that, by erasing or wiping them off, the color red would remain. If the tunic itself was red, then you would reply correctly: "It is a red tunic." But I knew that before and directed your hand to those points. The spirits do the same with all the figures; and since they know all things, it is easy for them to describe the figures and to guide your hand. Every rhombus is described by guiding the hand. In this manner, <term>Geomancy</term> is established. 

Moreover, many superstitions are added to it by men to increase its complexity—for example, that it should be performed when the sky is clear and serene, or in the quiet and silence of night. Also, that you should not operate for your own purposes. Again, that you should say such and such a prayer at the beginning and commence under good auspices, etc. All these are human superstitions; for, not knowing the foundation on which the art depends, they add to it, but it is as much a superstition as an art. <term>Geomancy</term>, as it was called at first, is constituted such that the ascendant is twofold—natural and of spirits. For the natural has its own art, namely, <term>Astronomy</term>. The spirit has its <term>Pyromancy</term>. Accordingly, if a nativity is calculated from the stars, it is astronomically erected. If it is made according to spirits, it is <term>Pyromancy</term>. 

But <term>Pyromancy</term> consists of the spirit being connected with the ascendant, and it leads the infant, for example, into immorality, thefts, and lies. And as the art progresses and succeeds, the spirits suggest to astronomers that if a conjunction of this or that star takes place, then this or that event will occur—not because Nature herself will accomplish such things, but because I myself will see to it, and, being everywhere, will bring about such effects. But as no one can trace my actions, they will be attributed to the stars or the elements. Hence it happens that people pay more attention to the stars than to God. This is a clever trick of the devil. It is the spirits who cause the astronomical and other predictions to be fulfilled so that the reputation of the art may be sustained, and so that men may be involved in error and loss, while, intent on vain fantasies, they forget the true God. Their devices are favored by those they deceive; for in the case of twenty prophecies, if only one is fulfilled, the seekers will never stop inquiring until the other nineteen lies have been fulfilled as well. Meanwhile, they are so deluded by the spirits themselves that they cannot arrive at the true <term>fundamentum</term>. For it is the property of spirits to lie. 

We have finished, then, with the foundation as far as the spirits are concerned. Now one thing is wanting, now another; now the fault lies with the house, now with the exaltation, etc. In this discipline, men have labored for many thousands of years, yet they have not discovered the truth, which, indeed, is impossible to find, as the whole foundation is based on falsehood. We now see for what reason astronomy is called <term>Pyromancy</term> when the operation proceeds pyromantically. The same spirits make their way into the third element, which is water. For <term>Geomancy</term> was named from the earth, as if it arose from the nature of the earth. Nor is this without reason, for the earth also has its own heaven or stars; but the spirits who are pyromantically recognized have devised them. Similarly, in the element of water, there is a star where the pyromantic spirits dwell who instituted <term>Pyromancy</term>, chiefly in the times of the Greeks, who, being easily led into all manner of delusions, promptly subjected themselves to the spirits. <term>Pyromancy</term> is an art consisting of signs and figures harmonizing with the universal figure of the heaven. The process is as follows: Take a basin full of water, set it down, and notice the direction of the wavy movements as the water quiets down. Notice also the tremor, the rest,

To the planet <term>Saturn</term> are subject all those who work in and under the earth, such as metallurgists, miners, sextons, and well-diggers, along with all the tools used by them.

<term>Pyromancy</term> puts forth its signs by the stars of fire; in common fire by sparks, flames, crackling, and so forth; in mines by flashes; in the firmament by stars, comets, thunder and lightning, <term>nostoch</term> <note>a jelly-like substance traditionally thought to be fallen star matter</note>, and the like; among specters by <term>salamanders</term>, ethnic <note>likely "Etneici," or spirits of fire</note>, and other similar spirits which appear in the form of fire.

<term>Hydromancy</term> gives its signs by the stars of water, by waves, floods, droughts, discolorations, <term>lorindi</term> <note>supernatural water phenomena</note>, new floods, and the erosion of territory. In magic and necromancy, it shows signs by <term>nymphs</term>, visions, and supernatural monsters in the waters and the sea.

<term>Chaomancy</term> exhibits its signs by the stars of the air and the wind, by discoloration, and the loss and destruction of all tender and subtle things that the wind opposes, by the shaking off and stripping of flowers, leaves, branches, and stalks. If the stars of chaomancy are excited, the *<term>Necromicæ</term>* fall down from the upper air, and frequently voices and answers are heard. Trees are plucked up from the earth by their roots, and houses are thrown down. <term>Lemurs</term>, <term>Penates</term>, <term>Undines</term>, and <term>Sylvans</term> are seen. So also <term>Tereniobin</term>, <term>Tronosia</term>, and <term>Manna</term> fall upon the trees.

<term>Necromancy</term> puts forth its signs by the stars of death, which we also call <term>Evestra</term>, marking the body of the sick and those about to die with red, bruised, and purple spots, which are certain signs of death on the third day after their appearance. Now, the spirit moves the bubbles, originates the shaking, the rest, or the calm, according to the necessity of the sign, so that a figure may result which indicates what is desired. Those, therefore, who have cooperative spirits, to whom few things are forbidden, make good sorcerers in the art. On the other hand, a bad sorcerer has a silent and lying spirit. Among spirits, one may be more silent and lying than another. When, therefore, one sorcerer is said to be more certain than another, it does not follow that he has greater skill, for he may possess a more reliable spirit. Now, the spirits delight in annoying and deluding men to cause them to hate one another, and this, indeed, is their primary object. If the foundation of this art were more closely investigated by men, it would be seen that it was a hoax of the spirits. Yet, even if men achieved perfection in this art, what solid advantage would it give them but a futile prediction and an excuse for wasting time? Suppose I desire to marry and consult an omen as to the result; even if I get an answer, I shall be uncertain of its truth; it is just as likely to speak falsely as truly. But if the prediction is fulfilled, it may be by the devil's arrangement. In any case, how will it help me? If I escape this evil, it will take shape in another way. Consequently, no faith can be placed in these arts. In addition to the methods which have been already mentioned, there is <term>Necromancy</term>, which is the art of the air. And although others define differently what is meant by *Necro*, this is genuine—that it is the art of shades, for only shades are in the air, and these things are known by the shades. . . . Some people, at night, see figures in the air, just as figures sometimes appear in the heavens which have a certain meaning. This is Necromancy. Men appear walking in the air, the clash of arms is heard, etc. Wondrous shades are likewise occasionally visible in water. The cause of all these things is that the spirits display what they wish according to their own pleasure. A part of their deception is to make men fancy that the spirits must be appeased by prayers, or compelled by force and conjuration to produce miracles. Now, all these things are sheer superstition. It is also thought that man can compel spirits, through God, to do this or that; but it is highly displeasing to God that we should be occupied with such trivialities, and the spirits are rejoicing meanwhile that, in opposition to God, we have become their accomplices. The prayers, conjurations, fasts, and other ceremonies are nothing but a cloak for superstition. The pronunciation of various words is committed to memory, but these are not the real names of the spirits, and they are altogether unimportant. For although each spirit has his own peculiar name, yet they salute one another by different names at different times, and so they make fun of men. Now, concerning the nature of shades, whatever is seen in a figure or image is to be considered such. He who is favored by spirits sees many things, but otherwise, little or nothing. Did God permit it, these beings would be always in our midst, enticing us to desert God and devote our minds to them. But if we carefully regard what they have performed during a given year, we shall see that it has been mere trifling, devoid of use and profit, destructive to body and soul, health and property, praise and honor—in a word, disgraceful allurements, frauds, and devices, sprung from the root of lies itself.

* In certain editions the following dedication is prefixed to the Nine Books containing the *Nature of Things.*—Theophrastus Paracelsus gives greeting to the honorable and prudent gentleman, John Winckelstein of <term>Friburg</term>, his close friend and dearest brother:—It is right, my close friend and dearest brother, that I should satisfy your friendly and persistent prayers and petitions which you have addressed to me in your several letters. Since, in your latest letters of all, you have earnestly and courteously requested that I should at length come to you, if it were consistent with my convenience, it is not appropriate for me to hide from you that this course is, by reason of various hindrances, impossible. But with regard to the second request you have made to me, that I should furnish you with an excellent and clear instruction concerning certain matters, I neither can nor will refuse you, but am compelled to gratify you therein; for I am well acquainted with your disposition; moreover, I know that you hear and behold with delight anything that is fresh or marvelous in this art. I know, also, that you have devoted a great portion of your life to the arts, which have formed the chief element of your curriculum. Since, therefore, you have displayed not only benevolence but brotherly loyalty toward me, I am rightly powerless to forget either your loyalty or your benefits, but am indeed of necessity grateful. In case I should not see you in person again, I must leave a brotherly farewell to you and yours as a memorial of myself. For herein I shall not only answer and clearly explain those points concerning which you have consulted me and asked me in brotherly fashion, but will dedicate to you a special treatise on those points, which treatise I shall name *Concerning the Nature of Things*, and shall divide it into nine books. This work satisfies all your requests, and, indeed, more than you have requested of me, although you will greatly wonder at its matter, and will doubt whether things are just as I have described them. But do not act so, nor think that they are mere theories and speculations, whereas they are of practice and proceed from experience. And, in spite of the fact that I have not personally verified them all, nonetheless, I both possess, have proved, and know these things by experience from and by means of other persons, as also from the light of Nature. But if in certain places you do not rightly understand what I say, and in one or more processes require of me a further explanation, write to me secretly, and I will put the matter more clearly before you, and give you a sufficient instruction and understanding, although I do not believe that there will be any need for this, but that you will easily comprehend without it, since I know how richly you have been endowed by God with the arts and with good sense. Moreover, you know myself and my feelings, why you will easily and quickly take my meaning. But, above all, I hope and am confident that you will look upon the present work, and will fittingly regard it as a treasure, will by no means publish it, but exclusively keep it in great secrecy for you and for yours, exactly as a vast hidden treasure, noble gem, and precious thing, which is not to be cast before swine—that is, before <term>sophists</term> <note>deceptive or superficial scholars who prioritize rhetoric over natural truth</note>, those who despise natural blessings, arts, and secrets, which persons are not worthy to read, much less to have, know, and understand them. And, although this book is very small, containing few and scanty words, yet it is full of many great mysteries, for herein I shall not write from speculation and theory, but practically from the light of Nature and experience itself, nor will I burden you and render it tedious by much speech. Why, dearest friend and most close brother, since I have addressed this book out of love to you alone, and to no one else, I request you to keep the book as a precious and secret thing, and not to part with it until your dying day. After death, in similar fashion, command your children and heirs to preserve it also in secrecy. Furthermore, it is my special request that it should remain only in your family, and at no time become so public as to fall into the hands of <term>sophists</term> and mockers, who despise all things which do not agree with them, and cover them with slander; who also are pleased only with that which is their own, as is the case with all fools; who are pleased only with their own trumpets, but not with that of another; and do hate all wisdom, regarding that as of small account and even as folly which is greater than theirs—that is to say, what is in their own head, because it does them no good, nor do they know the use of it. One workman cannot use the tools of another, and so in the same way a fool can use no better instrument than his own key, nor is any sound sweeter to his ear than the tinkling of his own bells. Why, dearest friend, be faithfully admonished, as I have entreated you; do that which I expect of you, and you shall do well and rightly. Farewell, under the care of God.—Given at <term>Villacus</term> <note>Villach</note>, in the year 1537.

## THE PARACELSIC METHOD OF EXTRACTING MERCURY
### FROM ALL THE METALS.

---

To extract Mercury from metallic bodies is nothing other than to resolve them, or to reduce them into their first matter: that is, running Mercury, exactly as it was in the center of the earth before the generation of the metals—namely, a damp and viscous vapor, containing invisibly within itself natural Mercury and sulfur, the principles of all metals. Such Mercury is of unspeakable power and possesses divine secrets.

The reduction spoken of is made by mercurial water, which was not known to <term>John of Rupescissa</term>, or to others, however they may boast. It must, therefore, be carefully studied and treated with unwearied assiduity. Let the aforesaid mercurial water be prepared thus:

Take three pounds of Mercury sublimated seven times by <term>Vitriol</term>, <term>Salt-Nitre</term>, and <term>Alum</term>; one pound and a half of <term>Sal ammoniac</term>, clear and white, three times sublimated from salt. Grind these well together, alcoholize them, and sublimate in a sublimatory by means of sand for nine hours. When the mass has cooled, remove the sublimate with a feather, and sublimate with the rest as before. Repeat this operation four times, until it will no longer sublimate, and in the bottom there remains a black mass of fluid like wax. Having cooled this, take it out; grind it again, and imbibe it in a glass dish several times with the prepared water of <term>Sal ammoniac</term>. When it is spontaneously coagulated, imbibe it again and dry it, repeating this process nine or ten times, until it will scarcely coagulate any further. Grind it very small on marble in a damp place, and dissolve it into a beautiful oil, which you must rectify from all its dregs and residue by distillation in ashes. Carefully preserve this water, for it is by far the chief of all waters. Take eight ounces of it, and put in it plates of the purest gold or silver carefully cleansed, weighing an ounce and a half. Place this in a closed vessel for digestion over hot ashes during a period of eight hours. Then you will see your body at the bottom of the vessel transmuted into a subtle vapor or Mercury. Having made a solution of the whole mercurial water, separate it, by sublimation in an <term>alembic</term> over a slow fire, from its first matter, and keep it carefully in a glass vessel. You will thus have the true Mercury of the body, the use of which in desperate

# THE SULPHUR OF THE METALS.

---

**T**HE Sulphur of the metals is an oiliness extracted from the metals themselves, endowed with many virtues for human health.\* Another sulphur is drawn from metals before they have undergone the fire, such as from the golden and silver marchasites and others, which take their rank and excellence according to the nobility of the mineral. So also is it drawn from the mineral of marchasite and cobalt, according to the nature and property of each.

The more common mode of extraction is to take <term>Acetum</term> carefully distilled, which has stood for twenty-four hours on a <term>Caput Mortuum</term> made out of distilled Vitriol, Salt, Nitre, and Alum, which also has itself been distilled by means of an alembic. This, I say, you must pour on the pulverized metallic body in a glass vessel so that it shall stand above it by the height of seven fingers. Then place it to digest in horse manure for nine days. Distill the colored <term>Acetum</term> in the ashes until it comes to a superfluous oil, which you will rectify in a bath, or in the sun. You will then have the very truest Sulphur of the metallic body, which you will rightly use at your discretion.

The extraction can also be made by means of a sharp and thoroughly separated <term>lixivium</term>. But other sulphurs are less suitable for internal bodily use on account of the alkali of the ashes, out of which we make a <term>clavellated</term> corrosive substance, and also on account of the lime of which such lixivia are composed. The Sulphur thus extracted can be washed with sweet water and precipitated. The subsequent digestion requires a double space of time. The <term>lixivium</term> also ought to be rectified from all earthy deposit by means of sublimation, so that such sulphurs may not be incorporated with it and become corrosive so as to cause injury to sick persons. It is to prevent this that the separation spoken of should be made. So far concerning the crude materials.

But now, these having been fused and purified, you may draw forth their sulphur. There is no more certain, noble, or better way than by the water of salt or by its oil, prepared in the way I have clearly described in my

# THE CROCUS OF THE METALS, OR THE TINCTURE.

The <term>Crocus</term> <note>In alchemy, a fine powder or oxide, often reddish or yellow.</note> of the Metals is of four kinds: of the <term>Sun</term> <note>Gold</note>, of <term>Venus</term> <note>Copper</note>, of <term>Mars</term> <note>Iron</note>, and of <term>Chalybs</term> <note>Steel</note>. The best is that of Chalybs. It is extracted by reverberation or by calcination, reducing the aforementioned bodies to dust. In like manner, filed iron is consumed by rust. The consumption of the rust is made by the imbibition <note>The process of soaking or absorbing a liquid.</note> of those things which produce rust, and by a decoction extracting the color of rust.

Take old urine poured away from its deposit, several cups of it, in which dissolve three handfuls of ground salt. When you have strained it, boil it and skim it carefully. In this again dissolve a handful of bruised <term>Vitriol</term> <note>A sulfate mineral.</note>, with two or three ounces of bruised <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>Ammonium chloride.</note>, and then carefully skim again. With this liquid imbibe some filings, and boil until it can be pulverized. The dust thus produced reverberate over a powerful fire, continually stirring it with an iron rod, until it changes from its own color to another, and at last into the hues of most brilliant violet. From this you can easily, with spirits of wine or distilled <term>acetum</term> <note>Vinegar</note>, draw off the tincture; and when it is extracted by separation of the elements, you will collect what remains at the bottom of the glass. By means of this, you will be able to produce wondrous effects, both within and without the body.

For making the crocus of Venus, take one or two pounds of copper-rust carefully <term>alcoholized</term> <note>Ground into an extremely fine, impalpable powder.</note>, pour on it plenty of distilled acetum, and stir it well three times every day. Gently pour off the colored acetum, and thoroughly sublimate it in ashes until it is dry. Let this powder be afterwards washed nine times with warm water to remove all acridity, and then dried. You will then have the prepared Crocus of Venus, or Flower of Brass, from which, if you wish, you can easily extract an oil according to the instructions given in the great work on Surgery, where also its use is explained.

The Crocus of the Sun should be extracted by the water of salt, whereby the metallic nature, or malleability, is destroyed. When the residue has been washed with warm water, the Crocus can be extracted with spirits of wine; and, this being again separated, the Crocus will remain at the bottom. This is changed into the liquid, or truest <term>quintessence</term> of the Sun, by means of elevation, and sublimating with five different grades of fire. With this you

# THE PHILOSOPHY OF THEOPHRASTUS CONCERNING THE GENERATIONS OF THE ELEMENTS.*

---

## BOOK THE FIRST.

### CONCERNING THE ELEMENT OF AIR.

### TEXT I.

IN the beginning, the Iliaster, which is nothing, was divided, thereby producing and arranging the four elements.† It was just like the seed from which the stem grows. What the seed gives out, it does not receive back into itself in the same form. However, this Iliaster again attracts the four elements back to itself. Thus, that world is dissolved and becomes what it was before the four elements were produced, provided only one year of the world has passed. The four elements are the growth produced from the Iliaster. And the seed does not provide those exact things from which the infant is produced after this world's year; instead, the four elements are both mothers and daughters. Nothing of this family is found surviving after death; its end is the same as its origin, and so whatever exists within it perishes at the same time. Although another world follows after, which is called the daughter of this one, it is not so in form, essence, or anything similar. For this will not pass away, but will remain like the

---

* The philosophy of Paracelsus regarding the generation of the four elements and the three primary principles—Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt—seems to have been viewed by himself and his editors as an essential part of his alchemical doctrine and practice. Including it in the first section of this translation is certainly relevant to the subject of <term>Hermetic Chemistry</term>. Paracelsus was not the first adept who considered the process of achieving the *Magnum Opus* as providing a strict analogy to the creation of the greater world. All alchemy insists on this connection. Anyone who succeeded in accomplishing the Grand Magisterium—the creation of the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term>—was thereby initiated into the secret of the *Mysterium Magnum*. Conversely, an exact understanding of the true principles involved in universal creation was enough to provide anyone with a complete and practical illumination regarding the <term>arcanum</term> of philosophy. The cosmological philosophy of Paracelsus is the necessary complement to his alchemy; whether or not studying them together sheds light on either, the student must be given the opportunity to compare the two. The treatises selected for this purpose are translated from the second volume of the Geneva folio. The extensive notes added here are derived from similar writings that Paracelsus left unfinished or that have survived in an imperfect state for other reasons.

† When God determined to form the world and deliberated with His Divine Prudence regarding its nature and the manner of its creation, He divided it into four parts or bodies. He intended these to be the mother of all things, yet subject to the one whom God intended to create in His own image—the man Adam. Therefore, when the matter had been deliberated upon and decreed by God, those four bodies were created: namely, heaven, earth, water, and air. For, as the Scripture says, heaven was created first, then earth, and subsequently the other two. Therefore, you must know that these four bodies, mothers, or <term>matrices</term>, exist so that they may produce fruit and provide the necessities for man's nourishment. Thus, for example, the earth brings forth its specific products, but it is man, not the earth, who uses them. Similarly, heaven is a body, independent in itself, from which fruits proceed simply for the use of man. —*Liber Meteorum*, Preface.

### TEXT II.

Now, it is quite certain that the Eternal Father, who is not only the father of His own Son, but also of all things—mortal and immortal, permanent and temporary, blessed and damned alike—created <term>Domor</term>, that is, heaven and earth, the firmament and the water, to which He also gave His own Divine will. We will not further discuss this subject here, as the same things can be read in the <term>Paramira</term>.<note>This is explained more completely and extensively in the treatises and fragments of treatises from which the following notes have been translated.</note> He formed the natural from the non-natural. From that which had never perceived any nature, He produced another nature, and following that nature He willed that yet another nature should be produced, while a year revolves, wherein His majesty Himself carries on the Divine rule, which man now moderates and possesses. Yet these primal natures differ, so that from the earth springs the pear tree, from the sand the thistle, from the water <term>cachimiæ</term>, from the sky chaos, and from the fire snow. But seeing how wonderful these things are, and how unlike they seem to the first source from which they sprang, we ought to make it a matter of knowledge and of philosophy that the element of water is not water only, but a mineral as well; that the element of earth is not earth only, but a grape as well, and so with the rest. For that philosophy is vain which claims that the earth is an element, indeed, but not a nut, or that fire is an element, but not snow. So, too, those who say that the four elements exist in all and everything talk mere nonsense.

### TEXT III.

The earth is an element, and whatever is produced from it is also an element. So is the water and all produced from it. So then, an element is that which produces. And an element is a mother, and there are four of them: air, fire, water, and earth. From these four matrices everything in the whole world is produced. And the speech is thoughtless of those who assert that an element is simply endowed with one complexion—warm, dry, cold, or moist—or a compound of these. All these qualities are in all these four elements. You can understand it thus: the earth is cold and dry, cold and moist, warm and dry, and warm and moist. This is how matters stand. Whatever thing which is warm and dry grows out of the earth, grows out of that which in the earth is warm and dry. Whatever is produced as cold and moist is produced from that in the earth which is of a similar nature. So also from fire, four complexions proceed. Snow, for example, comes from that in the fire which is cold and dry; and lightning from that in the fire which is warm and dry. It is the same with the other two elements. I would have you then, at this point, before all else be advised not to define the elements according to their com-

It remains so whether it is warm, dry, cold, or moist. The water is moist, perceptible, and tangible, but not in a physical or material way. And such is the element, whether it be cold or warm. The fire is a firmament and is the element of fire, even though it may be warm in one place and cold in another. The air is a heaven which contains all things and is moist, warm, cold, or dry, as will be explained hereafter.

### TEXT IV.

Now, in order to progress toward the established principle regarding the elements, understand this: The Iliaster was originally divided into four parts—the air, which is a heaven embracing all things; fire, which is a firmament producing day and night, cold and heat; earth, which provides fruits of all kinds and a solid foundation for our feet; and water, from which all minerals and half of the nutrition for living things are provided.

These nutrients are twofold: one is found in air and fire, the other in earth and water. The first two nourish us spiritually and invisibly, as it were; the latter two nourish us materially and physically. These four elements are divided into two classes. One consists of air and fire; the other of earth and water. The air sustains fire, and the earth sustains water. Air and fire hold water and earth, while these two hold air and fire. Thus, all things were created in proper order, so that one might support, seek, and nourish the other. In this way, the Iliaster was divided into one <term>domor</term>, which consists of two globules—an outer and an inner—each enclosed by two elements.

Beyond this is nothing, so far as we know. Within is what we see and touch, and what the light of nature suggests to us. He who created these things is not among us but dwells outside of us. However, He who was begotten of Him is among us. Still, we must not philosophize further concerning the four elements than what Nature teaches and points out to us.

### TEXT V.

In the beginning, the body of the four elements was established with the same form and reach as the extended heaven; and it was made corruptible or perishable wherever the air surrounds it.<note>But now we must understand the nature of the body of heaven. Earth, water, and air each have their own specific bodies, but indeed, all four bodies of the four elements are made from nothing—that is, they are made only by the Word of God. This "nothing," from which something is produced, turns into substance and body. The bodies of all four elements are divided into three species, so that the creative *fiat* resulted in a triple body. Thus, the earth and the other elements are all threefold. At the same time, there is such a distinction between the elements that the four things are not one single body. The air is one body, the earth is another, and the water is a third. Heaven would be the same if these four had a similar body. But the earth has three bodies, as do water, heaven, and air; yet a piece of wood is one body, a metal another, a stone another, and a sponge another. So also, the four elements of bodies are distinct and separate, as if someone were to take lead and create from it minium, ceruse, glass, and spirit of Saturn. Therefore, these three species are distributed into four elements, with a specific body assigned to each. To pay closer attention to these numbers, God Himself chose three, and constructed all things out of three, and separated all three. For the origin of this number is directly from God, the principle [of...]</note> There was the throne

It should be known, then, at the outset, and before the philosophy itself is unfolded, that God has made the center of His heaven, and even Himself, perishable. Of man, the heart will endure; of the world, the flower will be permanent.

### TEXT VI.

As for the manner in which God created the world, take the following account. He originally reduced it to one body while the elements were developing. This body He made up of three ingredients: <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Sulphur</term>, and <term>Salt</term>, so that these three should constitute one body. Of these three are composed all the things which exist, or are produced, in the four elements. These three have in themselves the force and the power of all perishable things. In them lie hidden the mineral, day, night, heat, cold, the stone, the fruit, and everything else, even while not yet formed. It is just as with wood that is thrown away and is only wood, yet in it are hidden all forms of animals, of plants, and of instruments, which anyone who can carve—from what would otherwise be useless—invents and produces. So the body of the <term>Iliaster</term> was a mere trunk, but in it lay hidden all herbs, waters, gems, minerals, stones, and <term>chaos</term> itself, which things the supreme Creator alone carved and fashioned most

in the Deity being three. Now, the word also was threefold, and the word is the beginning of heaven and earth and of all creatures. All things are synthesized in three, and there is nothing on earth which does not consist of and in three, and is not reduced again into those three. On the one hand, then, it is evident that each creature can be divided into three, each in its place; but, on the other hand, what they dogmatize concerning the four things or elements—to the effect that each thing consists of four elements—is false. Each thing, however, contains in itself one complexion and no more, nor can it have any other element than that which it receives from its mother. For instance, every herb has only one element—that of the earth; every stone has one element—that of the water. But in addition to this, it receives a complexion: cold and humid, cold and dry, warm and humid, or warm and dry. Yet that is not a whole element; rather, the element is the matrix, such as water or earth. For instance, man is taken from the slime of the earth; but the element is not slime, it is <term>quintessence</term>. Yet it again becomes an element; that is, it returns to the element with the distinction that exists between an element and flesh. Hence the elements only recur into three, and these three are the <term>prime matter</term> of the elements. However, the nature of the <term>prime matter</term> of water, earth, air, and heaven is diverse, for the number three constitutes only three species in reality, which make a perfect body, and these same are found by art in all natural bodies. These three are the first matter and have only one name. The first matter is as God; and as in the Deity there are three persons, so here each species is separate by itself as to its function, but the three functions are comprehended under the one name of the first matter. This first matter has been distributed by God among four parts or elements. Whatever resides in the first matter of the earth is being separated or has been separated into earth. The case is the same with the other elements. So, everything has been ordained into its predestined form, earth having been ordained to be earth, with its function, and so of the rest. So all things consist of one body, and yet there are four bodies, and the four elements are all distributed into four bodies and are formed from one matter which is in itself triple, having been originally formed out of the word. The three first things are three parts, namely, fire, salt, and <term>balsam</term>. All bodies consist of these three—all elements and all fruits thereof. Earth is threefold in its body—fire, salt and <term>balsam</term>—while that which grows from it is similarly distributed into three species. The body of a tree is fire, salt, and <term>balsam</term>, and the things which are generated from <term>balsam</term> are

### TEXT VII.

The four fields, therefore, having been set apart and separated in this way, there also remained four storehouses for keeping the four elements: namely, the hot, the cold, the moist, and the dry. Each of these was far from being unimportant. First the air was arranged; afterwards the fire; then the earth; and, lastly, the water, in the following way: From the air proceeded <term>chaos</term>, the throne, the chain, and the foundation. From the fire, night and day, the sun and the moon. From the earth, trees and herbs, grasses and fruits. From the water, minerals and stones. Of these, the succession was so arranged that from the surplus something else was continually produced. For instance, from the <term>Iliaster</term> of the earth, beech wood was extracted and the wood of apples removed. Each was disposed in its own place; nothing was corrupted or intermixed. In water, gold was separated from the rest of the metals, and afterwards the others were also removed in turn. In the fire, the cold withdrew from the heat, and the light from the darkness. In the air, <term>chaos</term> was set in order for preserving all things, and for separating earth from heaven. These four <term>Iliastri</term> having been created and arranged according to elements—that is, according to the <term>matrices</term> of their fruits—the air was prepared before all else; then afterwards the fire. These two were linked together in union. Afterwards the earth, too, and the water, being separated from the first two, were joined into one. These are now conjoined <term>Iliastri</term>. The air is by itself, and the fire is as well. In like manner, also, are the earth and the water.

It is the same with heaven, of which the fruits are the sun, etc. It is likewise with snow and rain. Therefore, the art of Nature does not teach us how to extract anything out of fruits except fire, salt, and balsam, which are also so separated from one another by the force of fire that the fire, salt, and balsam become separate. Now, fire is also called <term>sulphur</term>; salt is called balm; and liquor is called <term>mercury</term>. However, it is necessary that we should have a clear idea of what an element is. Now, man has a large body containing many substances. But that which is the man himself—namely, soul and spirit—is a small thing. The reason why the body is called "man" is because the man remains hidden in the body. So also, the eye is a considerable part of man, but the force which sees is very small in comparison to the eye. In like manner, the earth is called an element, whereas it is a crude body, and its true element is hidden within it invisibly, like the spirit in man. It is the same with the other elements, which are indeed corporeal, but are yet spirits according to their nature and substance. Therefore, as often as you hear that this or that proceeds from an element, understand that it proceeds from the element itself, and not from its body. In man, the tongue speaks and yet does not speak, for the spirit speaks through it; its intimate mixing and union with the body causes it to be thought that the body does everything. . . . The odor of the box tree is the spirit of the box tree; everything else is its body. The soul of musk is in its odor. In corals, the color is the spirit. Thus, all fruits, like their element, have spirit as well as body, and the true fruit is not seen by the eyes. Yet there is a certain difference between the natural and the supernatural spirit, for the first is corporeal and material, subsisting in a corporeal body, but the second is altogether devoid of a body. The body of the natural spirit is clothed by Nature with another body of its own element. But concerning heaven, it is to be noted that God has given it the name of <term>firmament</term>. The <term>firmament</term> is the heaven and its whole substance. The three other elements are included in the <term>firmament</term>, as the egg is in its shell. By the demonstration of the name which He has given to it, God teaches that He has endowed the <term>firmament</term> with power so that it may be like a secure shell, in which all the creatures of Nature are firmly contained. And, just as the yolk remains immovable in its place, whether the egg be positioned up or down, so it is with heaven. Wherever we dwell, we live at a high or low level, and can call ourselves dwellers above or dwellers below. For a circle has neither summit nor base.—*<term>Liber Meteorum</term>, chapter 2.*

Thus it was that God made the material center of His throne, and afterwards divided it into three primal elements, from which everything that is born constantly emerges. Without these three, nothing in the four <term>Iliastri</term> can grow. But while they grow they are elements; and so, moreover, they lose their name of <term>Iliastri</term> and are called elements.

### TEXT VIII.

These four elements were separated into their own places and positions, so that none of them should be mixed. All these were removed, just as a sculptor making a statue throws away what does not suit the intended image. So there are four elements, but only three primary ones: three in the air, three in the fire, three in the earth, and three in the water. Everywhere there is only a single triad of the primaries—that is, one <term>Mercury</term> in all, one <term>Sulphur</term> in all, and one <term>Salt</term> in all. Yet they differ in their properties. Whatever is growing—herb, leaf, grass, or the like—was assigned to the earth. Whatever is mineral withdrew into the water. Whatever is warm, cold, day, or night, moved to the fire. Whatever is air spread itself out over chaos. And all these three are one, each in itself. It is just as when a stone is divided into four parts, and out of one is made a statue, out of another a pitcher, out of a third some other kind of vessel, and out of the fourth a milestone; yet all are stones—indeed, all are one stone, though divided into four portions.

Of these <term>Iliastri</term> there are four, and no more, as these are sufficient. So God disposed the world in a quaternary. He was satisfied with this number, though He could have made eight parts. One portion of nourishment He conferred on the air, a second on the fire, a third on the earth, and a fourth on the water. Nowhere was there any deficiency.

And now it is further necessary that in the course of our philosophizing we should go on to treat of these four under the name of elements, to tell of their possibilities and performances, and to state in what they excel. We will begin with the air and conclude our philosophy with the water, adding such explanations as the nature of inanimate things requires.

### TEXT IX.

The element of the air was appointed for no other purpose than to be the abode of the other three, each to be preserved, as it were, within its enclosure in the following way.* The air encloses in itself every mortal thing,

---

<note>* The elements and all that exists are built upon the element of air, even as a house is built upon its foundations. We should philosophize, however, concerning that which sustains the air. This power is situated in the exterior part of the air in which the Triune God dwells, so ruling and sustaining the air that it does not yield, nor is it broken. For it is impossible that perishable things should fall into the sphere of the imperishable. Moreover, it cannot fall, because all things tend upwards, nothing downwards, nor is there any bottom or depth. For the air is so compacted and confirmed in its circle that it can no more be broken or dissolved than the external kingdom can perish until its time arrives, when it will collapse inward towards the center, the air and stars rushing towards the globe of earth, and then the globe shall by them be so utterly consumed that not a single ash shall remain. For the manner of this destruction shall be such that nothing shall collapse outwardly from the circle, but all inwardly to the center. And this is the highest secret of philosophy—that the circle rushes to the center because there is no depth outside.—*Alius Liber Primus Meteorum, De Elemento Aeris.*</note>

and shuts it off from what is immortal, as a wall divides a city from the fields. It strengthens the world and keeps it together, as a dam does a marsh. And just as there is nothing in an egg to one who looks at it from the outside that matches what is inside, so the sky is a shell dividing heaven and earth, just as the eggshell separates the egg from what is outside it. The air, again, is like a skin in which a body is stored up—namely, the whole world—and in which the earth is contained and preserved. The air, then, is this sky: a skin, or eggshell, or wall, or mound, beyond which nothing can burst through, and within which nothing can break in. Moreover, the air is breath, from which all draw their life. This is truly air itself, and it provides the air which nourishes the four elements and, at the same time, sustains the life of man. Without it, none could live. Without this, no element could advance, no wind could blow, no rain or snow could fall, no sun could shine, no summer could flourish, no water could flow, and no earth could sustain. All this force proceeds from the air and is attracted by the four elements. For just as the lungs inhale air every moment, so does the earth, while the water and the fire each do the very same thing. It is a palpable error to claim that winds are caused by the air. They burst in upon us like poison, not as a means of life. The first element brings air, but fire provides the winds.

### TEXT X.

From this same element, too, flows a power by which fire is joined to the air so that it may not fall down. Thus, it is like a chain which, without materiality or visibility, holds together and binds. This it does by means of its <term>chaos</term>, which it inserts between the <term>pellicle</term> <note>a thin skin or membrane</note> and the earth. There is also a middle space extending from heaven to earth, in which the fire, the earth, and the water are balanced. And as the chicken is sustained in the egg by its <term>albumen</term> without touching the shell, so <term>chaos</term> sustains the globe and prevents it from tottering. This <term>chaos</term> is invisible, though it appears to have a slight green tint. It is an intangible <term>albumen</term>, having the power and property of sustaining so that the earth shall not fall from its position. As the chick is in its <term>albumen</term>, so this globe of earth and water is balanced in the air. As a ship is borne up by the ocean, so is this globe by the air. It is one vast and marvelous <term>albumen</term> which invisibly supports the globe of earth and water. It bears up even the firmament itself, which is placed in it just as the seed of a cucumber is placed in its mucilage. And as every morsel of flesh lies in its own liquid, or the generative seed in the sperm, so the stars lie in this <term>albumen</term> and move within it like a bird in flight. They are supported in no other way than what is clear from the illustrations already mentioned. There is at least only this difference: that <term>chaos</term> is unlike <term>albumen</term> or sperm in that it is impalpable and extremely subtle. Otherwise, in all its powers and energies, it corresponds exactly to those things which have been listed.

### TEXT XI.

While discussing the powers of this element, it should, moreover, be pointed out that the air and its chaos and the sky exist in a round form which is inherent in them. No one can point out or distinguish what is above or what is below. Let us give an example. If it were possible for someone to be shut up within an egg, it would be impossible to know which part looked toward the sky and which toward the earth.<note>Air preserves the elements and all creatures so that they may persist in their course and center. Land and sea are the center of a circle of which the air is the circumference. Earth and water constitute one globe, resting on nothing but free on all sides, encompassed by the element of air. This air is like a vast chaos which conceals what the ignorant call heaven. Within this chaos all creatures are included and involved. Between the circle of the air and the globe of earth and water at the center, a sustaining operation intervenes, which may be compared to the albumen (egg white) placed between the shell and the yolk of an egg.—Ibid.</note> The roundness prevents there being any “up” or “down.” So we are imprisoned within a shell, and do not know which is up and which is down. Walking over the whole world, we look up to the sky, and everywhere there is height, while at the same time everywhere there is depth. The cause lies in the roundness of the globe and of the sky; thus it is natural to every mortal body that all things grow in a threefold line. Not only does man walk this way, but also trees, veins of metal, and springs take this course. As God created the circle of the globe and the sky, so He founded also the semicircle, the diameter, and the meridian—a threefold line—and other similar ones. For in heaven and earth, in fire and water, are found all lines and all circles. Here, too, are the true Geography, Cosmography, and Geometry. By the elementary geography of the air, the structures of the air are preserved—that is, the sun and moon, all the stars, the trees of the earth, and other things, such as the minerals of the water and the rest. Here, too, beyond a doubt, is found the true basis of all geometry, where man stands like the straight line looking up to heaven. Of this geometry God alone is the artificer, the mason, and the geometrician. From this line nothing falls away or emerges, be it water, fire, earth, tree, man, or beast. All things tend toward this aerial geometry, which God made and engraved as a mason does the statues on a tower.

### TEXT XII.

Now, as to the philosophy of the three prime elements, it must be seen how these flourish in the element of air. Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt are so prepared as the element of air that they constitute and make up that element. Originally the sky is nothing but white Sulphur coagulated with the spirit of Salt and clarified by Mercury, and the hardness of this element is in this thin skin and shell thus formed from it. Then, secondly, from the three primal parts it is changed into two—one part being air and the other chaos—in the following way. The Sulphur dissolves itself by the spirit of Salt in the liquor of Mercury, which of itself is a liquid distributed from heaven to earth, and is the albumen of the heaven and the middle space. It is clear, a chaos, subtle, and transparent. All density, dryness, and all its subtle nature, are

### CONCERNING THE ELEMENT OF FIRE.

#### TREATISE I. TEXT I.

WE have spoken thus far concerning the element of air, according to the position in which the elements have been arranged. The air is first in position; next to it is the fire. These two constitute and surround the entire globe.<note>* Fire and air constitute the chaos that encircles the globe of earth and water. The two superior elements send down their impressions upon the two inferior ones. Fire is arranged and transformed by God into the stars. — *Ibid., chapter 7.*</note> We shall next philosophize as to what concerns the element of fire.

First of all, from the <term>Iliaster</term> were separated the air and the fire. Afterward, these two were separated from one another, so that the air occupied the first place, as we pointed out in the previous book. The fire occupied the place next to this. By a process of separation, these two elements, air and fire, were divided. From the air the heavens were produced; from the fire came forth the <term>firmament</term>. As in the air there is only <term>chaos</term> and nothing besides, so, in the element of fire, we find nothing but heat and cold, light and darkness. But, whatever withdraws from the globe and from the air is sustained in the element of fire. It is not, however, called the element of fire because it can only burn, as many have foolishly said. It is not the element of fire that burns, but that which burns and is contrary to it is <term>congelation</term>. The element of fire is not by its constitution warm and dry; the cold and the moist come from the element of fire. They are quite beside the mark, then, who seek the element of fire in the element of earth or of water. Though these probably produce something of a warm nature, still that warmth does not constitute the element of fire. This element is not, therefore, called an element because it is fire, but rather because in it the whole firmament subsists. It is an element from which should proceed day, night, brightness, white or red, rain, tempests, winds, and all impressions. It is also the place and portion of the four parts of creatures. Therefore it is called an element. For as the earth gives heat and cold together, though it is the element of

### TEXT II.

Beyond these there is no element of fire. Whatever virtue they are endowed with beyond this is only trifling. This is more fully shown in the treatise <term>De Naturâ</term>. Here it is sufficient to know that this element, the <term>firmament</term>, namely, is nothing but stars. What these produce and send to the earth—such as snow, rain, wind, hail, cold, heat, night, day, summer, winter, and the like—all these things come from the element of fire, as an infant from its mother, or an apple from its tree.

This element of fire is placed in the element of air. For as the water and the earth are comprised in one globe, so the fire and the air are mingled in one, neither injuring the body of the other. They move freely in the air, not leaning or propped up on any foundation. As birds fly in the air, so the sun moves in the sky, that is, in the air. For just as it is appointed that man walks on the earth, the bird flies in the air, the fish swims in the water, and the <term>gnome</term> lives within the earth, so has it been arranged concerning the elements, that one lies still, another flies, one is in this mode, another in that, not moving from one seat or place. ### [TREATISE THE SECOND.

### CONCERNING THE SUN, LIGHT, DARKNESS, AND NIGHT.*

In the first treatise it was stated that the primal <term>Iliaster</term> was supplied with all the colors, and with brightness and splendor all mingled together. From there, the four <term>elements</term> were separated. In this section, it will be stated in proper sequence what was added or subjected to the element of fire. In the beginning, the first element—that is to say, the air—was extracted from the <term>Iliaster</term>, and afterward the element of fire. From this, a separation was made. First of all, the white brightness was drawn out, and from it a material body was made: the sun. Within it is all the white brightness of the element of fire, and besides this, there is no white brightness at all in the entire element. The red transparency was also extracted and transferred to the stars—that is, to the moon and the other stars—which were distributed into many parts. While the white brightness was gathered into one form, the red brightness was divided into many parts. Hence now follow day and night. For since all the white brightness was concentrated into one globe, it will be day wherever that globe is. Where that globe is absent, there is no white brightness, but it is night and darkness; for the red brightness transfers no light to the white brightness. Moreover, it must also be known that in the element of fire two natures exist: a warm one and a cold one. Heat is universal in the white brightness, and cold is in the red. All fire which is warm is in the sun, and not in any other element. All coldness is in the stars; there is none in the sun. Hence it is clear that summer comes from the sun, and winter and cold from the stars. In the sun is an expulsive heat, and in the stars an expulsive cold—thus: The sun emits heat from himself to the earth by means of his rays. For just as the wind blows from its cave, or as a stalk rises from the ground above the earth, so heat goes forth from the sun over the globe.

Heat is the fruit of the sun on the globe, and it has no other fruit. From this, it follows that the sun has two operations—a greater and a lesser heat—in this way: the sun divides its heat into two modes. Thus, it is permitted for the stars to lose their coldness. The matter stands like this: for us Germans, if the sun is at its highest, its heat is greatest for us. Then the autumn and harvest are at hand. In winter, the cold arrives, not because the sun is low and depressed (for it is the same sun that can shed heat everywhere with its rays), but because its harvest is not then imminent as it is in June. All fruits are then in a state of rest and have been harvested. But below us, in Ethiopia and other places that border the antarctic pole, the sun is warm while it is cold for us, for this reason: because it is its harvest time there, while it is the fallow season for us. This fallow season it makes more or less intense. Everything that must produce fruit needs rest and sleep; and unless the sun were lying fallow, its heat would be just as intense for us in winter as it is in summer.

In the meantime, while the sun is lying fallow, the harvest and autumn of the cold stars take its place, so that during the whole year there will be no sterility, but fruits will be constantly produced. Now the snow falls, and the north wind blows. Then follow the east and the south winds, which are the attendants of the sun. In this way, winter and summer, night and day, and the entire year are produced. Thus, there is a transition from one autumn to another through the year of the sun and the year of the stars.

Moreover, on this subject it must be remarked that dryness and humidity occur in this way: dryness is in heat—that is, in the sun. There is no other dryness in the entire element of fire except for that which the sun has within itself. Moisture is in cold—that is, in the cold stars, which have a red brightness. This is the true state of the case. Humidity cannot coexist with heat. Heat consumes all moisture and brings back dryness. Coldness never coexists with dryness. What is cold is dissolved if heat coagulates. Thus, the element of fire is divided into two. In one is dryness, and this is in the sun; in the other is humidity, and this is in the cold. If coldness sometimes seems to be dry, the dryness is only like when one sweats in the sun, where that moisture is quite foreign. So, too, is that coldness foreign. It is true, indeed, that a humid body on the earth can be dried by the stars, though not because of their dry nature, but because of their cold nature, by which they are able to coagulate a thing so that it seems dried up. Thus, their nature must be understood as frozen water. This is also the sun's method for making things moist: by its heat, it melts wax so that it liquefies, as does tallow. But what does this have to do with the matter? Nothing. These things are only given as illustrations. There is dryness, too, in the stars—for instance, snow, hoar-frost, sleet, hail, lightning, and the like—as well as metals and stones coming from them. But what is the dryness of snow, which does not last? In what respect is a metal dry if it returns to its original matter? And so it is with the sun. Where is its humidity? It does not last.
