It dries wood so that it never afterward grows damp again—that is, as long as it remains ashes. But what does the star do? It wets *Salpalla* <note>A term possibly referring to a specific alchemical salt or mineral substance</note> so that it never again returns to dryness, but always remains moist. The stars moisten the rain, which always remains moist and is never again dried. Wherever it is poured out, wherever it breaks forth, it is always moist, always wet. So, that which is dry remains in heat; what is wet, in cold; dryness never grows wet, and moisture never grows dry. In like manner, lime remains lime; glass, glass; wine, wine, etc.

But in order that the element of fire may be more thoroughly understood, we will, in the first place, describe the sun, the account of which is as follows: All heat is drawn together and rounded out into *Magdalion* <note>A term used here to describe the physical globe or body of the sun</note>. The whole white light is within it. Thus, then, white light and heat make up *Magdalion*, composed of ignited white *Sulphur*, congested into one body of noblest *Mercury*, pre-eminent over all the other elements, and coagulated by the most subtle spirit of salt. Out of these three the sun exists, so dry and so warm that there is no place for any humidity, for it would all be consumed. In this way, both the daily rain and whatever water is poured out by the three other elements is consumed by the force of the sun, lest a too abundant supply of water should cause an inundation. So, then, the sun is the death of watery nature, both of the sea and of the Rhine, Danube, Nile, and Tiber. They are consumed by the heat of the sun so that they do not increase in volume. Death exists in all things for this very purpose: so that they may not increase too much but may keep within their bounds. So man has his own form of death, which is invisible. So dryness has its death, namely, water. So, too, the waters have their death, fire; and it is not true to say that what the fire consumes reappears elsewhere. It perishes entirely in its own form.

But the spirit remains, and this the sun consumes. It is the veritable death, consuming and taking away the other three elements—likewise with man on the earth and with the bear in the cave.

But now to philosophize more about the sun. It regulates its course by Divine providence, which decides when and how all things should exist. By this it is arranged that the sun, going around the globe, rounds out its circle for the sake of this autumn and harvest of the sun. In this course is nothing but day and night, summer and winter, light and darkness; and the darkness which falls upon some lands is intercepted from others in due succession. From this impetus and motion no wind is aroused; but the sun moves and proceeds just as a ball is driven along the surface of the earth without any wind arising, or as a ship in the sea, which does not of itself generate any wind. So neither does the sun produce wind. It does not grow warm by its motion; for, although the globe should roll on for a hundred years, it would not of itself grow warm. If it be warm, it must have been warm before. So the sun going upon its course is a globe, and may be compared to birds in its

But now, in due course, we must speak of the other stars in which coldness and red brightness exist—as, for instance, in the moon, the planets, and the rest. In this red brightness is a different kind of rest from that found in the sun. For the moon has no fallow season, but simply dies and departs. Only the seed is left there, from which the new moon is born. This generation is of such a nature that it gains its power of growth from the sun. Whatever grows does so by the force of the sun's heat, and without that heat, nothing grows at all. Therefore, when the Creator made the moon in such a way that she should wane and wax, He did it for this purpose: so that the moon, like a seed, should be united with the sun and should from that source acquire her power to grow. Thus she increases and reaches fullness, and then afterwards wanes. For whatever increases also decreases. Just as a man wastes away and dies from disease, the decrease of the moon is her sickness, leading even to death, in which she passes away, leaving only her seed behind. The moon is, in fact, the phoenix of the firmament, from which, when it dies, a new one constantly issues forth. 

Similarly, there are other stars, and they are composed of the redness of <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>Salt</term>. There is also a cold form of <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>Salt</term> which originates from the same virtue from which the sun received its own. Thus, the moon has such a strong influence over the earth because of her coldness and her humidity. She is superior to all the other stars in this element of the coldness of fire. The other stars are also composed of these three primal elements, yet they are divided into many parts. For the cold within the element of fire is divided into a thousand essences and natures. Thus, some stars produce winds that circle over the entire globe; in others, snow, rain, and the like originate. In truth, they are so varied that many different natures and virtues flow down from them to the earth; this could not be the case if there were only one <term>Magdalion</term>, like the sun, possessing only a single nature, which is heat. 

Therefore, there are many cold natures in the stars. Cold produces many more forms of outward flow than heat does. A warm man is a healthy man. A cold man is exposed to more misfortunes than twenty warm ones. Because cold has a nature that is contrary and opposed to the sun, the element of fire is divided into many stars, so that each virtue may exist by itself without the interference of another nature. From these come forth warm winds, warm showers, warm tempests, and the rest,

### CONCERNING WINDS.*

Throughout the course of the globe, there are scattered the windy stars which continually bring about their autumn and harvest. They surround <term>Zedoch</term> in a circle and at the same time embrace the globe above and below. Therefore, just as the firmament revolves around the globe in its roundness, and the round globe lies within it, so the stars exist within the circle of <term>Zedoch</term>, and the globes touch <term>Zedoch</term> in the center. Consequently, two winds proceed to the two sides and separate above and below—that is, one part toward the arctic and the other toward the antarctic pole. These stars are the actual stars of the winds, because they blow upon us annually and have their own year, which is the year of the winds. The other stars of the winds blow above and below us, not according to the year, but occasionally; they blow at some times and not others, affecting only a single region, wherever that may be. The true stars of the winds each blow according to their year continually, above and below, across the entire globe, and are without hail, lightning, frost, or flashes.

* Since the meteorological principles have now been fully explained and recognized, the next step is to provide information regarding generated meteoric things, or their origins. However, we will first write of the rise or generation of the winds, proceeding from their predestined circles. There are four parts to the orb and circle of the winds: one faces the east, another the west, a third the south, and a fourth the north. The nature of the circles is as follows: Just as two elements, earth and water, are placed in the center of the firmament, and the element of air stands between the element of heaven and the lower globe—as the earth is placed in the middle and the heaven completely surrounds it—so there proceeds or advances a circle transversely on a level in the middle of heaven, earth, and water, surrounding them in a similar way. . . . In the same way, you will further note that heaven revolves around the world in a certain circle. In this circle stand the mothers of the winds and the places where the predestined winds arise. When these are about to emerge from that circle, they blow upon the globe through the element of air. But as they reach the roundness of the terrestrial globe and strike against it, it is possible for the winds to be either stirred up below the globe and driven toward those who live below us, or driven above the globe to those dwelling higher up; or again, they may be divided and driven in either direction through the heights and depths of the globe. Thus the winds are driven through the air across land and sea, persisting until they are exhausted by the distance, the path, or the violent motion, etc. Each of these four parts has a nature peculiar and proper to itself; for the eastern part is warm and dry, not because of the sun or its position in the east, but because such a nature is derived from the three prime principles. Therefore, in the true southeast wind and its satellites, no nature or operation is perceived other than warm and dry. On the other hand, the west wind, associated with the setting sun, is cold and humid—not because it rises from the west (for the temperament of the east and the west is one and the same), but because the matter of the winds was created cold and humid in the west. From the north blow winds of a cold and dry nature, which they also impart to those regions; it is not that the winds are affected by the regions, but the regions receive that nature from the winds. The south wind is warm and humid, not because much water is accumulated there or because moist and humid places abound, but because such is the unique nature of this wind, which is then imparted to the region it occupies. For it should be observed that the winds acquire no properties from external sources, but are tempered by their own nature and are not affected by the regions they pass through. The generations of the winds, therefore, are circular by their very nature. They are produced from their stars, and the stars are their mothers. Stars of this kind are innumerable across the four quarters. All winds proceed from these. For although winds are also stirred up by the stars of rain or hail, these are not counted within the circle or the four cardinal points. And since we have already spoken of the location and dispersion of the winds—how they flow from the farthest heaven across sea and land—it must now be added that those stars have the power to generate winds and dispose of them according to their nature and quality. Just as a tree puts forth its fruit from its internal nature, which consists of wood and marrow, the same is to be understood of the stars. But the seed of the winds is the first matter of the three principles: <term>salt</term>, <term>sulphur</term>, and <term>liquor</term>. These three are the mothers from which are born those offspring we call winds. In the northern quarters, they are of a cold and dry nature; in the south, warm and humid; in the east, warm and dry; and in the west, cold and humid. For as the nature of the three principles is, so are their fruits. Moreover, you must know that the winds arise from their stars by their mode of motion.

There are very many stars which surround the whole <term>Zedoch</term>, like the Galaxy, and opposite the Galaxy is Deneas. Regarding the elementary nature of these stars, it may be said that they are all humid. Antiquity has given four names to these which we retain, though not with the ancient interpretation. All those stars which are situated in the north throughout the entire <term>Zedoch</term> are called Boreas. Censeturis is dry and cold, yet not altogether dry. It is cold and frozen—that is, its humidity is coagulated—which is why it appears dry. Zephyrus comprises the western stars, all being humid and cold, but not frozen. Thus, by comparison with these, Boreas is accounted dry because of its freezing. The other stars in <term>Zedoch</term>, Eurus and Auster, are entirely cold. As soon, however, as the winds issue forth from their stars, they become warm from the sun whose beams they pass through; thus they are considered warm, although they are not so by their own nature. Eurus is considered dry, but is not. The sun consumes the humidity it possesses until it reaches the moisture contained within it, which the sun cannot remove. Auster is called humid, and it is so because the sun does not take away as much of its humidity as it does with Eurus. That is prevented by the sea, which supplies the sun with sufficient moisture for its consumption. So Auster, with its humidity, bursts forth upon us throughout the lower and upper parts of the globe.

# Concerning the Generations of the Elements.

As for how wind proceeds from the stars, this must be held to be the method. Just as the sun pours its heat upon the world, so in these stars there is no other nature or property except to produce winds, which are decocted from <term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, and <term>Salt</term>, and issue forth according to <term>Adech</term>. Their wind blows daily and hourly, moving gently and peacefully over the whole world. Thus, the respective winds must be learned in the course of our exposition regarding the other windy stars.

### CONCERNING THE TEMPERATE STARS.
-><term>Zedoch</term>.<-

The following is the theory concerning the stars in the firmament.<note>The philosophy concerning the stars in the firmament and, generally, concerning the constitution of heaven, is discussed elsewhere at greater length by Paracelsus, in connection with the four elements, as follows: It has been said that the elements are four. Man has need of these. But they are divided into four complexions, which are by no means as the ancients imagined them—for example, that the earth is cold and dry. This is without foundation; certainly in some places it is cold and dry, but in others it is cold and wet, while in yet others it is warm and dry. Nevertheless, it is an element, which is to say, the mother of fruits. It is called an element because it is the mother of these things, not because of its complexion. The case is the same with water. This is specified to be cold and humid. It ought certainly to be humid, but not equally cold. At the same time, that humidity is often dry and warm, by reason of its virtue. The body itself, in its physical nature, is humid. The earth is dry, so that its fruit can be conceived within it and come forth from it. So, also, the heaven is not of one complexion, but of many complexions. It is not fire, but is understood as fire because it proceeds from it. Its fire is at times water, at others fire, now cold, now warm, etc. We must consider, therefore, that the elements are only matrices, nor are they restricted to one complexion. For, as the offspring is, so is that which generated and produced it. Thus, a <term>flammula</term> proceeds from a <term>flammula</term>, and <term>solatrum</term> from <term>solatrum</term>. Accordingly, listen to these things. It pertains to the earth to bear and sustain man and his dwelling-place, as well as rocks, stones, sands, and all growing things. Hence it is clear that the earth is necessarily compact and solid, so as to be capable of bearing them. Consequently, it is hard and requires cutting and ploughing. In the same way, it is equally necessary for water to be moist, so that fishes may move and swim through it, which can by no means take place on land. It also ought to produce salt and stones. Now, all these things must be humid in their first matter, and must pass from humidity into a coagulate. But that which is born from the earth has seed—that is, a dry body, such as seeds, roots, trees, etc. For all these things are dry and compacted from the first matter. But in the first matter of water there is no compact body, the whole being liquid. Its matrix is from the element of water. In this element grow those ultimate matters, the principle of which is liquid and humid. The third body is the air. This element requires another kind of body, which must not be humid like water, or solid like earth. Whatever things are born out of this element have their entrance into the body of the air, just as fish are in water. Man has been surrounded by an aeriform vehicle so that he may walk in it, just as the fish moves in water. Thus the air also sustains all trees and whatever grows. It is necessary, therefore, that the air should be a <term>chaos</term>; not earth, not water, but something perspicuous, transparent, and impalpable, so that the palpable and the visible may be contained (literally, *tenched*) by it, and may be seen through it as through glass. Furthermore, the heaven is a body of this kind: not humid as water, not transparent as air, nor solid as the earth, but one of another essence. Thus, heaven is not earthy, but is yet compact in its essence, though not with earthly compactness. It is also thin and permeable as water, but still is not water; it is likewise limpid and transparent without being air. It is most comparable to smoke, which is different from other bodies in respect to its physicality and substance—that is, it is not like stone or wood, earth, water, or air, but is a body without mixture or affinity with others. It is the same with heaven, and the bodies which are born from it are at once bodies and not bodies, compact and not compact, permeable like water yet not water, transparent and intangible as air yet not air. Such a body is the sun, such is the moon, and such are the other stars. Heaven is without complexion and is the element of fire, and the matrix out of which fire is generated and grows. For as fire has a certain physicality, so have heaven and the stars, which take their nature and substance from heaven. Consider, therefore, that such physicality is derived from heaven, its peculiar quality, and the very element of fire; and whatever fire is about to do, the same is performed by heaven, from which fire proceeds. But we must make inquiry concerning the color of heaven.</note> Every star has in it a certain amount of coldness. This causes winds. Cold is the parent of all winds. But the nature of cold is that some cold produces winds with rain, some with snow, some with hail and the like. The truth is that all winds, intermittent and temporary, proceed not from <term>Zedoch</term>, but are collected from all quarters out of particular stars. The common nature of all the stars comprised in the sky and the firmament is that, every day, nay, every hour and moment, they exude. For the stars attract to themselves the heat of the sun, just as the fruits of the earth absorb the same. The solar heat causes the stars to be resolved from their

The color of earth tends towards black. Whatever is of another color therein belongs to <term>minera</term>. So water has its own color alike through all things. Its color, however, has no name, for it is neither white, nor grey, nor blue, nor green, and yet it can be called all these. Earth, too, is really neither black nor purple, and yet up to a certain point it corresponds with both. The case is the same with air, which is pure and pellucid in <term>chaos</term>, and yet is neither white, nor blue, nor citrine, etc., while it is still partially assimilated to these. So also heaven has its special color—like blue, like red, like green, and yet none of these colors is present therein otherwise than apparently. For elementary bodies are so formed as to have no perfect color by which they may be named. But the things which are produced from them have their distinct, determinate colors, and to these names can be given. Thus, many colors are produced from the elements, and they are therefore composed of many, even of that number which they produce from themselves. From the earth proceed blue, red, black, etc., while from water all colors come forth, and so also from air and heaven. Accordingly, colors are collected from many into one, heaped together and mixed, and such mixture produces no express, determinate, and definite color. Give heed to an example taken from heaven and its fruits. For you see that everything which grows from the earth has its palpable foot and root, as are trees and herbs, etc. But the stars are the fruits of heaven, yet they do not put forth their roots in heaven, for they stand immovable below the heaven, without any support or attachment. Earth and heaven are opposite in this respect—one yields its fruits with roots, the other without; one tends upwards, the other downwards, and as fishes rest upon nothing, and, without feet, swim about in the water, so in like manner, stars swim about in the heaven, that is, in the body of heaven, preserving that order which God has prescribed them, some moving at a higher, some at a lower, level, at different distances apart, and with a quicker or slower motion. The details of this question must be referred to astronomers, but this, at least, should be remembered, that heaven is a body which, like water, is capable of sustaining a swimming thing, yet it is not water, but dry, while that which floats in it is also dry. It is not strictly swimming, but has analogy therewith; it is not going or running, since it is not effected by hands or feet; it is the miraculous work of God, and an element which contains and includes all the rest, and drives them in a round or a circle. The stars were born from heaven, and stand therein as if they flew like a bird through the air, according to the order and circle, even as God has destined and formed them to motion. Having been once formed, they henceforth remain forever the same. The trees and fruits of the earth fall and are reborn. The stars can perish once only, namely, at the end of the world. Whatever else is formed in the elements is eaten away by mold, moth, and death. It is only the stars of the celestial heaven which remain in immunity, and yet their fruits rise and fall, as rain, snow, etc. But they have a unique and special color, which is fiery. Thus, earth chiefly displays greenness, though it has also other colors. The sun is peculiar in color, and if the same be igneous, it is not after the manner of wood, but of an element. . . . We must repeat concerning fire that it has been enumerated as one of the elements, but with manifest absurdity. The earth, indeed, exhibits itself as an element, water in like manner, and so also air. But consider the fourth element. This cannot be fire, for it confers nothing elemental and no fruits upon man, nor does it possess any affinity with man, or *vice versa*, but it has an altogether fatal power, whereby the soul is separated from the body. It is, therefore, necessary that heaven should be regarded as the fourth element, for this is akin to man, nor can man dispense with it, whereas he can dispense with fire and can live without it. The possibility of his dispensing with fire shows that it is not an element, but such rather is that heaven which brings forth day and night, summer and winter, increasing all fruits, and helping the other elements. The Scripture states that God created the heaven and the earth first. In heaven are the other elements, and even as the jar is made ready before the wine is pressed out, so the element of heaven is in reality the first element, which we have here named for the fourth. — *Liber Meteorum, c. 1.*

### CONCERNING NEBULAE.

A nebula is nothing other than a vapor of this kind, differing from the previous one only in this: while not yet fully matured, it is excreted by certain stars. When it falls to the earth like hoar-frost, it rests on the land and the water, and is like smoke. It cannot be completely resolved into hoar-frost or dew. A certain part of the vapor turns into dew, and the rest into nebula. A nebula is imperfect dew that has not yet fully matured. If it is thin, it falls to the earth and vanishes. But if it is dense, though not yet prepared, it descends to its own higher region, where it is consumed by the sun. If, however, it is mixed with rain-clouds, then rain is produced from it, but of a more subtle kind than other rain. Very often, nebulae of this nature descend and produce a spell of rainy weather. For if the stars are rainy, they cannot be resolved into dew, but only into nebula. But if they sometimes bring clear weather, the cause is that the nebula, being more refined in its preparation, disappears on the surface of the globe.*

This is proved by the fact that its fruits are bodies—such as rain, snow, hail, the thunderbolt, etc.—for a body can only be generated from a body. For this reason, they are separate from the heaven, while at the same time remaining within the heaven. At the same time, they do not leave their own mansions any more than a tree leaves its garden. Now, just as there is a new genus among trees, there is likewise a new genus among stars. The same must be understood of herbs and all things that grow on the earth. There is no star that attracts rain and then pours it down again. The operation of rain proceeds from a nature innate to it. # CONCERNING METALS, MINERALS AND STONES
## FROM THE UPPER REGIONS.

### TEXT I.
#### CONCERNING METALS.*

The metals which come from the upper regions derive their origin from the seven planets. But these planets are varied. There are many suns, many moons, many Marses, Mercuries, Jupiters, and Saturns. They are called "seven" only because they produce seven metals, and one kind of metal is assigned to each planet. These are not the planets that astronomers point out; they are in error when they assign those to the metals, nor are they in agreement among themselves in what they say. From these seven kinds of planets proceed the seven metals, and they are composed of the same three prime principles, just as in the element of water. The only difference is that within the three prime principles, these metals are volatile and not fixed in their species. In this way, the metals found in these regions do not withstand the same tests as the lower metals. Neither, again, do the lower metals withstand the test of the superior ones. There is not one and—

---

—are strengthened by their own heat until they reach the highest degree, when they again gradually fail. Then the winter stars rise in their turn, display their own nature, afterwards die out, and are succeeded by another summer. The varying cold of winter and the varying heat of summer are caused by changes in the power of their respective stars. The moon is the chief among the stars of winter and is accompanied by a significant escort. If the summer stars were to fail, there would be no summer, for the sun, whether high or low, provides a consistent heat. Therefore, unless the summer stars arrived, perpetual winter would prevail. The summer stars, however, derive their growth from the sun. Likewise, we must not assign a different origin to day and night. The day arises from the light of the sun, but the night from the light of the moon. The departure of the sun by no means causes night. It is the specific nature of certain stars to produce darkness, which is so thick that unless the moon intervened with her presence, nothing whatever would be visible. God has imposed such a course upon the stars so that, as they travel around the entire firmament, they maintain their order and continuous progress. To prevent them from stopping or having a general holiday, God has ordained that when some are absent, others are present to fulfill their operations. Thus, the nocturnal stars take the place of the receding sun. The bodies of the <term>three prime principles</term> are the cause of those bodies from which day and night proceed. The sun is a clear and transparent salt, clarified and extracted from these principles, being purified from all darkness. Its brilliance has been extracted from the mass of the first matter of heaven. And whereas a white brilliance has been digested into the sun, a red brilliance has been placed into the moon and stars. The transparency and clarity of the white were extracted into sulphur, salt, and liquor to make the sun from them. Afterwards, the brilliance of the red was put into a body of sulphur. Thus, salt is the body of the sun, sulphur is the body of the moon, while liquor is the body of darkness. — *Ibid.*, c. 3.

* Metallic natures also exist in the element of fire, for just as there are stones in heaven, so also there are metals, but they are different beyond all recognition from those of earth. Fiery thunderbolts, with their flashes of light, are actually metals—harder than any iron or steel, as meltable as copper, mixed with colors, and shaped like a thunderbolt. Their fall is solely due to some miraculous conjunction of elements, which produces them in physical form. Many marvelous things are carried up into heaven and fall down to us. If it were possible for the stars of mercury, salt, and sulphur to be joined in a similar union, several occurrences of this kind would fall every hour. But the arrangement of things is not favorable to this, except in the case of the thunderbolt. — *De Meteoris*, Lib. II.

<summary>This text explains that metals originate from seven types of planets (distinct from those of astronomers) and describes the cyclical nature of summer and winter stars. It also defines the sun and moon as products of the three prime principles—salt, sulphur, and liquor—and identifies thunderbolts as a form of heavenly metal.</summary>

So, again, there is a volatile nature of this kind in the element of fire, which is the metallic operation and nature of all the seven stars; this also falls down from them to the earth at the same time, just like rain and similar outflows. Many such metals lie under their own stars: some in Asia, a few in Africa, and fewer still in Europe. These stars do not reach our earth, so those metals are not found among us. All those grains, however, which are found among the seven metals and are rough in external appearance, come down from the stars and not from the element of water. And all the metals which are solidified without fire, and are rounded in shape like pulses, of whatever kind they are, have come down from the seven stars, whether they lie above them or not; and the earth strikes against them just as rivers do. But where they are found is neither their source nor their root; rather, they come forth just like kidneys <note>This likely refers to kidney-shaped nodules or ore deposits</note>. Their origin is in the stars, and all have come down from there. For there, in the element of fire, is no coarseness or density to mix itself in. It purges itself according to its own stars and solidifies of itself purely and entirely. These metals, just like those in the element of water, exist in a mixture with Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury, except that the fire-based metals do not have a watery fixation, just as the water-based metals do not have a firmamental fixation.

### TEXT II.

When, then, the three primary principles have completed their effect in the metallic star—as when, in the star of the sun, a composition has been formed of the Mercury of the sun with the solar Sulphur and Salt—then they are digested into a perfect metal by <term>Adech</term>, who shapes from them the form of his own gift. Then at length the star throws off its outflow, warm and liquefied, as if from some furnace. This is shaken in falling, is solidified in the cold, and lands upon the globe. In the same way, also, the star of the moon makes a composition of Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt. When these are brought to their effect (just as in the case of the sun), it casts them forth. The same thing takes place with Saturn, Mars, Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter. It must be remarked, however, that out of the seven kinds of the seven stars, each one embraces the three primary principles of one metal; it is not as in the element of water, where the seven are latent within one <term>Ares</term>. The names of the seven metals, therefore, refer to the seven metals not of the earth but of the stars. In the same way, too, many liquids fall down from the stars, not yet being in a state of solidification. If the earth is moistened with these, a brightness rises from there like <term>cachimiæ</term>, talcs, and sometimes <term>marcasites</term>, though it does not fully and perfectly arise from any of these, nor perfectly refer to the same. From this it will be inferred that the superior metals excel those of the lower earth by many degrees in goodness, in purity, and in nature, and so in all respects deserve greater praise.

<summary>This text explains the celestial origin of metals, asserting that they fall from the "seven stars" (planets) to the earth as pure substances formed within the element of fire. It distinguishes these superior, firmamental metals from terrestrial ones formed in water, noting they are both composed of the three primary principles: Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury.</summary>

### TEXT III.

### CONCERNING STONES FROM ABOVE.*

In the same way, there are also other stars that cast forth from themselves gems, garnets, and other forms of stones. For Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury in the element of fire possess a powerful force for generating gems. There are many stars that consist of ruby Sulphur, many of sapphire Salt, and many that are powerful in emerald Mercury. There are also stars that contain the <term>primals</term> of copper, vitriol, salt, or alum. Hence, many of this kind appear rainy. If these are prepared, they manifest themselves. From these stars, sapphires of lazurium are generated. There, Salt is the body, solidly coagulated with pure Sulphur and with the spirit of Mercury. In the emerald, Mercury is the body, having the nature but not the body of copper. It takes its color but not its body from copper. In this way, all the colors of gems that proceed from fire are found in proportion to the nature and condition of the three <term>primals</term> which are found united in the ratio of colors in the metals. For instance, in copper, there is redness. But these three <term>primals</term>, if they do not have a metallic body, become green. So, from silver, if the metallic body is lacking, lazurium is produced; from iron, a red body; from lead, the same; from Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, a clay-colored one mixed with white; from gold, a purple body; from mercury, one that is saffron-colored. In a similar manner, also, if only the Salt predominates, it produces various colors, such as are visible in certain stones—purple or blue, whether lightly or deeply impressed. Likewise, that which comes only from Mercury is marked by many colors: saffron, red, and so on. That which comes from Sulphur has for its prevailing colors white, red, saffron, black, cerulean, and so forth. These stones are very rare, and those that are of a metallic nature are exceedingly precious. Thus, the emerald is a copper stone; the carbuncle or jasper is a golden stone; the ruby and chalcedony are iron stones; the sapphire lazurius is a silver stone; the white sapphire is a stone of Jupiter; the jacinth is a mercurial stone. In this manner, then, stones are generated in their own stars, which closely adjoin the planets, and then they are ejected just as metals are ejected, and so are found in the highest parts of the earth, according to the manner of their generation.

---

<note>
* In the height of the firmament stand the three principles from which impressions arise. These are so high and so lofty that we cannot behold their form, and yet they have a form. We see, however, the green which is their color. From this, it is gathered that in the element of fire, generations of stone also take place. But where stones are generated, they fall. Although this may be considered wonderful, rare, and unheard of, it happens more frequently in the sea than among us. The generations of these stones take place as follows: if the principles of thunderbolts are present, any number of thunderbolts may be generated, for with every peal of thunder, there is a stone. The matter of such stones exists first of all in an aerial condition and is afterward coagulated into an earthy one, so that the air can retain them no longer, and they ultimately fall to the earth. Furthermore, the matter of these stones may collect into one place in the absence of any storm, but it will remain aerial until it comes in contact with a contrary nature, when it will at once begin to coagulate and to fall, just as a cloud is precipitated downward in the form of rain.—*Ibid.*
</note>

# TEXT IV.

## CONCERNING CRYSTALS AND BERYLS.

Regarding crystals and beryls, it should be known that they are generated from snowy stars, which produce snow, in the following manner: In snowy stars, the power of congelation is so strong that they sometimes have a double nature; that is, the same star contains within it both snow and the power of freezing, and so becomes twofold. Now, a star of this nature, which has gained at the same time the power of congealing and also of producing snow, easily generates the crystal, the citrine, and the beryl. For if snow falls and frost accompanies it—especially if a place is given to it on the globe where Boreas <note>The North wind</note> predominates, while the sun or the solar nature does not prevail strongly—then the water which is combined with the snow is coagulated into a stone. Now, if this water is caught by an intense frost midway while the snow is falling, stones are formed from it before they fall to the earth. Thus, large or small granules are found in proportion to how the frost caught the snow as it fell. 

But if this freezing has not been so sudden, the frost collects and drives together all the water contained in the snow (which, however, is not itself snow) into one center toward the bottom of the earth; and when it is massed there, it coagulates it into ice. This ice, however, does not melt again like other frozen bodies, nor is it dissolved, because it is derived from snow-water. Other waters, it is true, which are frozen, are partly snowy, but the snow is dissolved with them. Here, this does not take place; instead, the water is extracted from the snow. The fact that the snow remains happens only through the snowy star, wherein the power of congelation also exists; so that wherever they meet in one place on the earth, the snow does not melt but continues until the intended process or operation is complete. In snows of this kind, stones such as crystals and the like are produced, both pure and dark together, for this reason: because the <term>S.S.</term> <note>Likely an abbreviation for "Sulphur" or "Substance"</note> of Mercury and Salt have clarified and purified themselves. Very often, too, crystals, beryls, and citrines of this sort are found in places which are not snowy. The reason for this is that they have been coagulated in the higher regions and have fallen down in that form. They are nothing but coagulated snow-water. But their shape, species, and angularity are bestowed upon them in proportion to whether the Salt in them exists in a subtle or a dense state.

# THE PHILOSOPHY OF 
# THE GENERATION OF THE ELEMENTS

## BOOK THE THIRD.
## CONCERNING THE ELEMENT OF EARTH.

---

### TEXT I.
### CONCERNING THE EARTH, PER SE.

To philosophize concerning the element of earth, its matter was first created according to the following principle: Its three primals were separated, as if out of the great <term>Iliaster</term>, from the two primal elements into another form and nature, so that in the beginning not only the element of earth, but also the element of water was separated, and these were afterward joined together into one globe, which is the center of the exterior elements. From these two elements, first the earth was completed, and afterward the water. But concerning the earth, it should be known that all the power and nature which lay hidden in the Great <term>Iliaster</term> for nourishing not only humans, but cattle, by means of food and other necessities, were collected into the element of earth, and consisted of all trees, herbs, and other growths. But they were so divided from the other three elements that this virtue exists in the element of earth alone, and not in any other element. Therefore, this <term>Iliaster</term> is unique to the element of earth so as to provide nourishment. For this reason the earth is called, and is, an element, because in it consists all the power and strength of nourishing things which are necessary for living beings.

### TEXT II.

These three—<term>Sulphur</term>, <term>Salt</term>, and <term>Mercury</term>—are the earth, taken out of the great <term>Iliaster</term>, from that nature which is the element of earth. For there this element and the three others were one <term>Iliaster</term>, in which the four elements existed. They were, however, divided from one another, and the <term>Iliaster</term> was divided. Never again, then, can the four elements from this point forward be joined or stand together, but each exists separately by itself in its own place. Those, therefore, labor in vain who endeavor to separate the four elements, or to seek besides these a <term>fifth essence</term>.

<summary>This text describes the creation of the element of earth and water from the primal matter known as Iliaster, establishing earth as the unique source of nourishment for all life. It emphasizes that the four elements are now permanently separated into their own distinct natures and cannot be recombined or reduced to a fifth essence.</summary>

From these three primals, separated from the other elements, the matter of the earth was produced in the form it is now seen. Just as the air became heaven, the fire became the firmament, and the water became the sea, etc., so did separation bring it about that this element should turn into matter and take a spherical form. In it were included all the virtues of trees, herbs, and fungi, so that from it all those types which had been silently sown and lay hidden within it should be produced in the world.

### TEXT III.

In this element of earth was hidden the seed of wood, of roots, of herbs, and of fungi, as well as the force by which the stem rises, and is formed and planted according to the will and pleasure of its cultivator. The seed here proceeds invisibly from the nature of the element, which alone is that seed, acting as the home and seat of the same, in which it is developed and prepared. But originally, that force is separated into its own type, so that the two do not remain joined as one, but each type exists solely and separately: one in wood, a second in the herb, and a third in fungus. Each of these, again, develops separately—this into cedar, that into <term>anthos</term>, this into balsam, and that into <term>botin</term>.* Among herbs, too, one becomes <term>meligia</term>, another a lily with thorns—and so with the rest. But in order that this seed may be rightly understood according to its distribution, it should be noted that in the separation of the great <term>Aniadus</term>, the nature of trees was collected in one place, <term>botin</term> in a second, and ebony in a third. So too with others. Likewise, the great <term>Aniadus</term> arranged the herbs so that grass was cast into one portion of earth, trefoil into a second, and <term>lavendula</term> into a third. For to each land is given its own herb and its own tree. We should pay attention to the distribution made by the <term>Aniadus</term>.

### TEXT IV.

As to why the <term>Aniadus</term> was thus distributed among trees so that one soil produces the orange, a second the plum, a third the fig, and a fourth acorns, the cause may be supposed to be that the fig and the orange require their soil to be of a specific kind favorable to their growth, just as they also require an appropriate climate. ### TEXT V.

But we must proceed with our philosophy of the earth. The fruits proceeding from the element of earth are of two kinds. The earth either produces them of itself or by means of seed. In this way, all growths are produced by the element out of the soil in two ways; that is to say, either from the proper seed of the soil, or from seed entrusted to the earth. The proper seed is when the earth puts forth a herb which springs from itself. Seed that is sown is foreign and not native. Here, the gifts of herbs are twofold. Neither spelt, nor wheat, nor lily, nor pear tree, nor anything of this kind grows spontaneously out of the earth, but all have to be sown. Here, the philosophy of this treatise is deep: to find out from where those seeds come which do not issue from the earth itself. If neither spelt nor wheat is sown, none of these things will be produced. But herbage and grass do grow. Herbage and grass, therefore, are growths of the earth itself, unlike apple trees and cherry trees. So there remains another philosophy by which we learn from where spelt, apple trees, and pear trees are produced. You must know that the seeds of all these growths are propagated from Paradise, sown outside of it, then planted and cultivated far and wide. These fruits of Paradise come to be understood in the same way as we understand that Christ was God and yet a mortal man.

### TEXT VI.

As to the method by which the seed passes into its shoot, it must be known that the seed takes from the earth nothing more than its growth and formative power. The rest is from Paradise, and is taught in the *Paramirum*.* But as to how much of an element is taken from the earth,

An illustration may be taken from trees, which have their bark, their wood, and their roots, which are distinct in themselves, and yet coexist in a single seed.—*Paramirum*, Book II., chapter 1.

For the seed is that which exists of itself, but is not yet manifested. Out of this proceeds first the root; from this, afterward, the stalk. From the root and stalk issue forth the branches. From these three burst out the leaves. After this appear the flowers and fruits. This shoot or growth is formed by the great <term>Aniadus</term> <note>A Paracelsian term for the vital or celestial virtue that directs the growth and properties of plants.</note> and is like a man. It has its skin, which is the bark. It has its head and hair, which are the root. It has its figure, its signs, its mind, and its sense in the stalk, the injury of which is followed by death. Its leaves, flowers, and fruit are for ornament, just as in man there is hearing, vision, and the power of speech. Gums are its excrement, and the parasite is its disease. Its death and passing away are the span of its years. A pear tree will stand for ten or twenty years; after that time, it dies. Thus, a shoot or a tree growing in the earth dies according to the time appointed for its death. Its decay is the element of fire. That is, fire destroys wood, leaves, and grass. Whatever is left in the field decaying and passing into rottenness is consumed by the sun and the movement of the galaxy, so that no more is left on the earth than if it had never grown there, just as happens to wood in a fire. Thus are growing things consumed and eaten away so that no remnant remains, but all are removed like dust. The very remnants are so dispersed by a strong wind that not a fragment survives or remains at the end of a year.

### TEXT VII.

Since, then, trees, herbs, grain, and vegetables are produced out of the earth, the power of this element should be learned before all else. This is because some growing things are food and sustenance, such as vegetables and fruits; others are drink, such as grapes and <term>barberries</term>; others purge the body, like <term>turbith</term>, <term>hellebore</term>, and <term>colocynth</term>; others strengthen it, such as cinnamon, caraway, and mace; others have their virtue in the root, such as parsnip and gentian; others in the leaves, such as pot-herbs and cabbage; others in the flowers, such as ox-tongue; others in the fruits, such as apples, pears, etc.; and others in the seeds, such as pepper, nuts, and the like. Now, it is worthwhile to know how all these things take place. It is the <term>Aniadus</term> of the Earth who thus distributes them. He arranges the nutritional virtues in three parts: the seed, the roots, and the extremities. Thus, the apple is a fruit on the tree because the <term>Aniadus</term> thrusts it forth and shapes the fruit into the form of an apple, or a pear, or a fig, etc. In the core is a species of seed, just as in wine there is a species of drink. So, then, the <term>Aniadus</term>, before man, performs the first preparation, and man directs the second for his own convenience. * *Just as trees from the element of earth turn into wood, so in the same element there is a certain <term>sulfur</term> which can be separated and turns into food. Of this kind are vegetables and cereals. Dry and humid sulfurs are united, being the <term>three principles</term> duplicated according to nature and essence. One of these is for use, the other is not. Thus the <term>avena</term> <note>Oat.</note> is sulfur, but it is not edible. The seed, however, is edible. The <term>non-esile</term> <note>Inedible.</note> sulfur is first of all developed into the stalk, etc., and subsequently the <term>esile</term> <note>Edible.</note> sulfur is collected into the grains of the cereal.*—*On the Element of Earth*, Tract III., Text I.

<summary>Paracelsus describes how the element of earth differentiates into various tastes, scents, and medicinal virtues within plants. He also distinguishes between the edible and inedible parts of plants based on their specific sulfur compositions.</summary>

# THE PHILOSOPHY OF
# THE GENERATION OF THE ELEMENTS.

---

## BOOK THE FOURTH.

### CONCERNING THE ELEMENT OF WATER WITH ITS FRUITS.

### TEXT I.

Regarding the element of water, the first things to consider are: its origin, how it is divided, and what the element is *per se*. The element of water is a seed from <term>Yle</term>, producing stalks and fruits—namely, water and its fruits, such as various kinds of stones and metals. Regarding the seed of the element of water, it must be established that it lies hidden in its workshop, just as a seed lies in the soil. From this workshop emerge the stalk, its branches, and its fruits in this manner: the stalk is produced from this seed, breaking out from the soil into the light, while the seed itself remains lying in the earth. For, just as the element of earth bears its fruit within the body of <term>chaos</term>, the earth is likewise a body that sustains growing things, such as the trees and fruits produced by the tree of the element of water. No element exists that does not require a body by which it may be sustained. <term>Chaos</term> bears impressions. The element of fire sustains the fruits of the earth; the earth supports the fruits of water; and water supports those of the air. Thus, the fruits of each element are sustained by another element. Now, just as the tree of an element emerges from its seed, its tree is a flowing stream distributed throughout the whole earth. All things are one tree, having one origin and one root from a single stalk. The streams of the entire globe are the branches of this one stalk. All the fluid of the entire globe is <term>Abrissach</term>, which falls from the branches of this tree and pervades every pore of the globe through its distillation. For, just as fragments from fir trees fall from above to the ground, so these branches from the water fall into the hollows of the earth. In this way, the generation of the element of water occurs. All water and all its fruits come from the element of water, but they are not the element itself. The element itself is never seen by anyone, yet an element of water nonetheless exists. From it, nothing but water emanates. It is called an element because of the water and its fruits, not because of its own constitution or quality, just as is the case with the other elements.

<vocab>element of water, Yle, chaos, Abrissach, distillation, generation of the elements, per se</vocab>

<summary>Paracelsus describes the element of water as a seed-like force within the earth that produces water, stones, and metals as its fruits. He conceptualizes the world's waterways as a single interconnected tree, where fluid called Abrissach distills through the earth's pores.</summary>
<keywords>element of water, Yle, chaos, Abrissach, distillation, generation of elements, mineralogy, stones, metals</keywords>

--- Page 251 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the element of water, detailing the structure of its metaphorical "tree" and its branches, such as rivers, before transitioning into the nature of decay and consumption.</meta>

### TEXT II.

Regarding its course and goal, as well as its locations and boundaries, the truth is that the tree has its own origin and end; it rises and falls, is produced and perishes. Thus, all water that flows from it is new, not old, and was never seen before. For just as the element of water lies in the middle of the globe, so the branches spread out from the root around its circumference on all sides toward the plains and toward the light. From this root, very many branches are born. One branch is the Rhine, another the Danube, another the Nile, etc. So, there are also smaller branches, all born out of that root which rises from the seed, from which the element of water proceeds. All the stalks belong to one tree, which is born from the root along a triple line in the circle of the outer firmament of the two elements, fire and air. 

Then, the tree is distributed by this triple line over the universal globe, tending toward the light. So the stalk and its branches grow out from the center of the globe until they reach the two external elements where the line ends. It does not go on to its own body, or <term>Yliadum</term>. For, unless the <term>Yliadum</term> were placed in that position, every tree would grow straight up to the sky, extending itself further outside the earth than from above, where it is fixed in the earth. Similarly, the fruits of the element of earth do not grow farther than the prescribed limit of the <term>Yliadum</term>, which is the lower chaos of the earth, not occupying more of the earth than the height to which growing things rise. 

Chaos, therefore, is twofold. That which is above is the chaos in which fire is sustained; and, unless the <term>Yliadum</term> acted as a barrier, the element of earth would extend its fruits to the middle of the heavens. So, too, would the element of water. The course and progress of the stalk of the tree is that it continues to its <term>Yliadum</term> above the plain of the earth, where its height ends. But how far it extends since it lies in its <term>Yliadum</term> must be sought from philosophy, because all the branches reach their <term>Yliadum</term> in the sea, where they all meet. For, as there is one root, it is compelled to reach one summit or canopy, which is the sea. 

The sea itself is not the stalk or the tree, but is, as it were, the canopy of the stalk; it is not born directly from the root but is composed of the branches. Why it is salty is because of its position and because salty waters flow together into it, as will be shown later where we speak about the subject of salts. The cause of its ebb and flow is that all the fruits (or the humors) flow downward by night, but by day they swell to a height, which is <term>clissus</term>. And this <term>clissus</term> in water is the same as in other fruits, increasing and decreasing, going and returning.

### TEXT III.

Now, since it is important to know all these things, their death—that is, their consumption—should also be understood. Nothing is free from this consumption. It should be understood, then, that everything, when it comes to its <term>Yliadum</term>, is subject to putrefaction and is consumed. Decay is a kind of consumption and the passing away of the thing to which it belongs.

<summary>Paracelsus explains the element of water through the metaphor of a great tree whose branches are the world's rivers, terminating in the sea. He also introduces the concept of the Yliadum as a boundary for growth and the inevitability of decay for all things.</summary>
<keywords>element of water, Yliadum, clissus, rivers, the sea, chaos, putrefaction, tides, elemental philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the metaphorical "tree" of the element of water, shifting from its physical distribution to its internal cycle of decay and the "fruits" (minerals and salts) it produces.</meta>

so that it is consumed just as if it had never existed. This is the operation of its nature. As Nature produces things, so does she remove them again. As a thing proceeds from nothing, so it returns to nothingness again. Hence it is clear that the element of water itself is subject to putrefaction or corruption. If it reaches its canopy—that is, the sea—it grows putrid and is consumed by itself; no outside force contributes to this, but it happens through its own nature and design. As fire consumes and extinguishes itself, so, in like manner, does water. This is the way, then, in which the tree of the element of water and its branches are distributed. What fruits lie hidden within it remains to be seen, as well as their nature and the generation of their offshoots. The nature and property of this element are such that it bears some of its fruits within itself, casts others out, and completely discards others. It must also be learned separately how many natural modes and essences its flows and streams arise from. But so that everything born of water may be understood in its death, it should be realized that the branches—but not the fruits—return to their canopies. Concerning the death of fruits, it should be said that they all flow into <term>Drachum</term>. In that moment they are consumed, as should finally be understood and maintained regarding the subject of <term>Drachum</term>.

### TEXT IV.

To simplify any study regarding the origin of fruits, we will consider the following to be the fruits of the element of water:*—salts, minerals, gems, and stones. There are, therefore, four kinds of growths out of the seed of the element of water, in this way: Fresh water is the stalk. Afterward, its nature becomes manifold within the matrix. One matrix is of salt, one of minerals, one of gems, and, lastly, one of stones.† Each of these, again, is divided in a different way. For instance, there are three fruits of salt—salt, vitriol, and alum. And each of these has many genera ranked under it. There are many kinds of salt, many of vitriol, and many of alum.‡ Some are metals, some marcasites, and some <term>cachimiæ</term>. But even these, again, individually, allow for more kinds. There are seven metals, nine marcasites, twelve

But with regard to their division and separation, all such fruits consist of one root, out of which each nature is separately born according to its condition. If, therefore, the distribution proceeds in this way—from <term>Yle</term> into its own stalk, and fruit is produced after its kind—then different things are found proceeding from the element of water: salt on one stalk, a mineral on a second, and something else on a third. As, therefore, in the earth every seed produces its own fruit, so the seed of water is the seed of numberless things springing forth from it. Now, if these are brought to their <term>Yliadum</term>, and await their autumn-tide, then at length the autumn and harvest come for the fruit of every branch, which fruit is in itself of this autumn-tide and this generation.

<note>Regarding metallic affinity, vitriolic salt is of a copper-like nature. Copper, in like manner, is combined with vitriol. Indeed, its generation teaches us that it is entirely vitriol. At the same time, vitriol in itself remains a salt and derives its body from the liquid of the metals. For this reason, it acquires a certain fiery quality and brilliance. Alum (<term>Alumen</term>), on the other hand, by no means has an affinity with metals but is a free salt, consisting solely of acidity (<term>acetosity</term>), and having a body which is devoid of earthy quality—unlike vitriol, which arises solely from a mixture of metallic bodies. Hence it exhibits a similarity to <term>marcasites</term> and <term>cachimiæ</term>, which come forth in the first generation of metals. The medium which unifies and joins copper with vitriol is a <term>phlegma</term>. — *On the Element of Water*, under the section *On the Kinds of Salts*.</note>

# APPENDIX I.

<note>In the Geneva folio of 1658, which is by far the largest and best collected edition of the works of Paracelsus, there are many included treatises that clearly overlap with one another. Furthermore, there are many independent treatises devoted to exactly the same subjects. For example, the *Philosophia Sagax* covers similar ground and at equal length as the *Explicatio Totius Astronomiæ*, and the latter is substantially identical to another astronomical interpretation included in this translation. In much the same way, the *Economy of Minerals* corresponds to the *Liber Mineralium*. However, considering the metallurgical importance that attaches to both these works from the Hermetic standpoint, it was decided to include the following treatise in an appendix.</note>

## A BOOK ABOUT MINERALS.

Since I have carefully considered the matter beforehand and resolved to write about minerals in general—including everything relating to minerals and all things concerning their generation and nature—I want you to know above all else that many people have published on the origin of minerals before me. When I read their works, I found that they were involved in many errors. As far as one can judge from their writings, they have never fully understood what the <term>ultimate matter</term> was. Now, if the <term>ultimate matter</term> is not understood, what, I ask, will happen to the <term>first matter</term>? Whoever can describe the beginning will probably be certain about the end and the ultimate. What is a theologian who is ignorant of the end? What is an astronomer who is full of boasting but has no experience of light? Since these authors are clearly found to be delusional about the end—that is, the <term>ultimate matter</term>—how can they be more worthy of credit regarding the beginning? I reject their writings and their letters; they are not the foundation. But, so that you may have positive proof in a short space of time that I possess much greater skill in writing about this matter than my predecessors had, I will first of all explain the <term>ultimate matter</term> of minerals to you. In this way, you may clearly know the basis on which I treat this subject, and therefore may more rightly understand—

What is the beginning? It is necessary that a physician should first be familiar with the disease with which he has to deal; when he knows this, the method of treatment will spontaneously unfold itself. But to know a disease is the end, not the beginning. The Art resides in the departure, not in the entrance. The entrance is dark and dubious; the outcome is evident. In this, knowledge lies hidden. I point this out, therefore, as the foundation: namely, that every matter must be thoroughly known at its commencement, so that it may also be more exactly understood for what purpose the matter has been framed. 

Now, if man is to lay out the works of God before himself and use them rightly, it is necessary that they should not be hidden from him; otherwise, he will be sure to abuse them. What good is an axe to a person who is ignorant of its purpose? Let him hand it over to one who knows all about it. In the same way, whatever God has created ought to be in the hands of a man who knows how he ought to employ it. Men should know and learn these things, not mere trifles and phantoms conjured up by the devil.

But when I propose to write about the origin of minerals, I shall do this not of my own accord, but from my experience, and by means of him from whom I myself received it. What I said in my first paragraph, I here repeat: namely, that the last must be known before the first, and from the last, the first should be understood. I make this clear from the example of Christ, who was not understood until He sent the Holy Spirit, who, at His coming, revealed all things. Through Him we understand Christ, though He came after Christ. So, from the same ultimate—that is, by the Holy Spirit—we now understand both the Father and the Son.

Now this fits in exactly with the philosophy of minerals, because the <term>ultimate matter</term> is made up of those things which teach the beginning of their mother, or of their birth. From them, this birth must be understood. Already in other philosophical paragraphs I have named these three substances—Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury—as being the principle of all those things which spring from four <term>matrices</term>, that is, the four elements. In the generation of minerals, it is necessary to explain that iron, steel, lead, emerald, sapphire, flint, <term>duelech</term> <note>A Paracelsian term typically referring to a tartarous stone or calculus formed in the body, here used in a broader mineral context.</note>, etc., are nothing else than Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury. 

Everything produced by Nature is frail and corruptible, and it can be ascertained by Art from what it has issued forth. And here is a proof from Nature, since those three substances just spoken of are in the air no less than in other things, such as fire, balsam, mercury, etc. If, by the aid of Art, you resolve steel, gold, pearls, or corals, you will still find Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury. When these are extracted by Art, nothing more of that mineral remains, but all is dissolved. Seeing, then, that the dissolution of substances reveals particularly what they are and what is in them, you can gather that those things are three: namely, Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury. These three are the body, and everywhere there is one body and three substances. Concerning these three substances, I will now begin my teaching, by which you may know that in the <term>ultimate matter</term> there are three substances, neither more nor fewer, and out of these three, all

...minerals have been formed. Furthermore, how God created Nature shall also be stated. On this basis, nothing shall be found lacking.

In the beginning, it pleased God to create one element—water—into which He infused the power of generating minerals, so that they might grow immediately and thus adapt themselves to human needs. Water, I say, He destined for this purpose: that it should be the Matrix of the Metals by means of these three substances already mentioned—namely, Fire, Salt, and Mercury. In this arrangement, so much foresight and discrimination were observed that from the single element of water, metals, gems, stones, and all minerals were produced. And though the fruit is unlike its parent, God willed that each should be produced according to its own nature. One is a bird of the air, another a fish in the water. And just as these differ from one another, so do the natures of other created things. All these depend on the power of God, who willed that His good pleasure should be fulfilled in them.

Now, it should first of all be realized that the element of water is the mother of all minerals, although water itself is utterly unlike them. Similarly, the earth is related to wood, even though earth is not wood. Nevertheless, wood comes from it. In the same way, stone, iron, and so on, come from water. Water becomes that which it is not of itself. It becomes earth, which it is not. In the same way, it is necessary for man also to become what he is not. Whatever is destined to pass into its ultimate matter must necessarily differ from its beginning. The beginning is of no use by itself.

Now, in water is the primal matter—namely, the three first substances: Fire, Salt, and Mercury. These have certain different natures within them, as will be pointed out hereafter. They contain metals, gems, stones, flints, and many things of this kind. One is a metal, another a stone, another a flint. Likewise in the sky, one thing is snow, another thunder, another the rainbow, and another lightning. In the same way on earth, one thing is wood, another a herb, another a flower, and another a fungus. God has shown Himself to be such an artisan, the Master of all things, whose works no one is able to rival. He alone is in all things. He is the primal matter of all; He is the ultimate matter. He *is* all things. Then, when we come in due succession to explain minerals, we will, in the following discourse, speak above all else concerning the properties of the matrix—that is, the element of water. The things I write about were supposed by the ancients to spring from the earth. Their meaning was good, but their position was impossible to prove. In this point they were mistaken, as they also lacked the materials to establish that proof.

The principle, then, was first of all with God—that is, the ultimate matter. He transformed this ultimate matter into primal matter. It is just the same as when fruit, which is to produce other fruit, has seed. The seed is in the primal matter. So in the case of minerals, the ultimate matter is reduced to the primal, as in the case of seed. The seed here is the element of water. God determined that there should be water. From Nature, man takes these things and reduces them to their ultimate matter. That is, where Nature ends, man begins. The ultimate matter of Nature is the primal matter of man. So, then, by an admirable design, God has appointed that the primal matter of Nature should be water, which is soft, gentle, and potable <note>Drinkable</note>. Yet its offspring or fruit is hard, such as metals or stones, than which nothing is harder. The very hardest, therefore, derives its origin from the very softest—fire from water—in a way beyond the capacity of man to grasp. But when the element of water becomes the matrix of minerals, this is not beyond the capacity of Nature. God has produced a wonderful offspring from that mother. You judge a man by his mother. Everyone has his own special feelings and properties, not according to his bodily organization, but according to his nature. Thus, all metals according to their body are water, but according to their special properties they are metals, stones, or marcasites. In no other way can reason grasp that these things are diverse in substance and in body.

Thus, then, God created the element of water so that it might be the element of all metals and stones; and He separated it from the other three elements into a unique body which was not in the air, in the earth, or in the sky, but was something special, different from these. This He placed on the lower globe so that it might be above the earth and occupy the cavity in the earth where it lies. He founded it with such wonderful ingenuity that, together with the earth, it should support men, who might walk and move upon it. And the first thing which moves our wonder in this respect is that it surrounds and encircles the globe and yet does not fall away from its appointed station; so that the part lying under us is turned upwards just as we are, and in the same way hangs suspended downwards. Then our wonder is increased, seeing that the bed or pit of this genuine element, at its center of greatest depth, is quite bottomless, so that the water receives no support from the earth on which it lies; but it stands freely and firmly in itself like an egg, where nothing falls away from the shell; and this is a clear miracle of God.

Moreover, as you see, all fruits grow out of the earth into the air, and none of them remain in the earth, but they go out of it and separate themselves from it; in the same way, growing out of the water, there go forth <term>metals</term>, <term>salts</term>, <term>gems</term>, <term>stones</term>, <term>talcs</term>, <term>marcasites</term> <note>Pyrite or other metallic minerals</note>, <term>sulfurs</term>, etc.—all proceeding from the matrix of this element into another matrix, that is, into the earth, where the water completes its work. But the root of minerals is in the water, just as the root of trees and herbs is in the earth. However, they are brought to perfection above the earth and pass on to their ultimate matter, which is entirely in the air.

In the same way, that which grows in the water is completed on the earth. So, then, when the root is in the water, the growth takes place on the earth; therefore, the doctrine of those writers is clearly erroneous who argue that minerals grow out of the earth, and that all these minerals, however many there may be, recognize the earth as their mother. This idea is worth nothing. Indeed, nothing grows from the earth except leaves, grasses, wood, herbs, and the like. Everything else comes from the water. Otherwise, by the same logic, it might be said of the things growing from the earth that they grow in the air since they live in the air; but this is clearly false. Their roots are found in the earth, and thus we learn that their origin is in the earth, while their perfection is in the air. In the same way, that which originates in the water acquires its perfection in the earth. The growth of minerals follows the same course, convincing us that they are aqueous <note>Water-based</note> and proceed from the water, existing in the water as the <term>primal matter</term> of those same minerals, just as all fruits of the earth are generated in the earth; after the predestined period, they burst forth into harvest or autumn and produce what is within them. When a root of this kind is born, it first rises into its own special tree—that is, its body—from which the particular mineral, metal, or other growth should be produced in the earth. Similarly, the nut or the cherry does not spring directly out of the earth, but first the tree is produced and afterward the fruit; so, also, in the water, <term>Nature</term> first puts forth a tree, which is the aqueous body, and this afterward grows out into the earth—that is, it occupies the pores of the earth just as the tree fills the air. When this tree is extended into the earth, the fruits are immediately born, existing naturally with the tree according to their nature and condition. In one place, the metal grows in its own special kind; in another, some sort of salt is produced; elsewhere, some type of sulfur breaks forth, and in another place, some kind of gem is pushed out. And just as many cherries or pears are found on one tree, so similar fruits of the water are found at the extremities and, as it were, on the shoots of the trees belonging to the element of water. Again, just as some trees put forth many fruits and others only a few, there is a similar property, nature, and condition here as well. Therefore, trees of this kind should be sought first, and their fruits afterward. A man who practices his craft in the soil is taught how he should pursue his husbandry and where fruits must be found.

Careful attention, too, should be given to this method of generation, so that the illustration from the earth may hold true—in this way: There are some trees which bear their fruit, not openly, but under mixed conditions. The chestnut, the nut, and other similar growths have a bark that is thorny in appearance, and another layer inside, while, lastly, a thin skin encloses the kernel. In the same way, there are also metals and minerals lying hidden in flesh and skin, such as the ore of iron, the ore of silver, and so on. These have to be removed so that, after separation, the desired fruit may be extracted. On the other hand, there is another kind which produces its fruits openly, such as cherries, plums, and grapes. From these nothing is thrown away, but all is useful and good. So in the aqueous fountain are found pure and uncovered silver, gold, coral, <term>carabe</term> <note>Amber</note>, and the like. These are all so arranged by Nature that there may be different sorts of trees and barks in which the mineral lies, which also depend upon the variety and division of water, climate, and geographical position. That which lies hidden within has to be extracted from the bark or shell, just as in the case of fruits. And yet further, as you see in the kernel a body and the kernel itself, so be well assured that, similarly, in the element itself there is a body and a spirit, so that the body has first to be sought for, and then the spirit in the body. Now, it is the spirit that makes the body, and so it also makes the mineral (or the nutriment). The mineral has one body, the fruit another. That is the same as saying that, although there may be gold in a body, and the body is worthless because it is impure and must be separated by the goldsmith, gold also has a body which is not impure. There are two bodies. In the second is incorporated the fruit of the mineral, which does not need to be separated from that gold. So then the fruits are first developed out of the element into a tree, afterwards into a body, and within the first shell that which is precious and good. Just as man is a twofold body—a dense body which is worthless, and within this another body which is good—so it is with all growths. Whatever God has created, He perfects its corporality by a similar process. He has made man in one way, a tree in another, and a stone in another. But He made man more carefully, because He willed that man should be created in His own likeness, so that eternity, in which other created things have no share, might reside in man.

The same judgment is to be passed concerning the death of elements, because water has its own death no less than other things. Indeed, water is its own death, eating into, strangling, and consuming its own growth. We have proof of this in the earth. That which grows from it returns to it and perishes, so that no part of it any longer survives. So yesterday perishes and no man will ever see it again, and it is in the same way with the night past. In like manner also pass away all things born of the earth, which return to the earth and are consumed by it; and yet the earth is not heavier by half an ounce than it was yesterday, nor is it heavier today than it was a thousand years ago.
