In the same way, the element of water is its own death, because it consumes and deadens its own fruits. That death is in the great center and boundary of water, the open sea, into which all water flows. Whatever passes into it dies and decays, passing away just as wood is consumed in the fire. And as, year by year, new fruits emerge from the earth while the old ones perish, so every day new minerals are created—whether they be metals, marcasites, gems, stones, salts, or springs. These all come forth surrounded by death, like an infant who brings death along with them, bound up with life. By the same reasoning, metals also bring their own death with their beginning, and they die in the boundary of the water—that is, in the open sea. The Rhine, the Danube, the Elbe, and other rivers are not the element itself; they are its fruits. The element is in the open sea. It is that from which all grow and into which all must necessarily return, and thus they acquire death from where life is assigned to them. This death will be more fully described later in separate paragraphs, when it is pointed out separately how each mineral comes into being and dies.

Now, regarding the tree of the element of water, note this. When Nature is about to put forth any growth into the world—whether it be gold, silver, copper; whether it be a gem, emerald, sapphire, garnet; whether it be a spring, sweet or brackish, warm or cold; whether it be coral or marcasite—she then raises up, from the element of water, a tree on the earth, so that its root is fixed in the center of the sea (or of the matrix). That tree sends forth its seed into the earth and spreads its branches. Know, therefore, that its trunk has the form of a liquid, which is not water, oil, bitumen, or mucilage. It has the appearance of wood produced from the earth, but still it is not wood, nor seed (or trunk), and yet it is of the earth, and each has its own body. That liquid is the trunk, and its branches are that same liquid, just as a tree is wood and its branches are of the same kind. So, then, the mineral tree is formed into a body of this kind and afterwards divided into its branches, so that one branch very often extends from another into a second or third, running out and separately extending itself for a distance of twenty, forty, or sixty miles. One branch turns to the German Alps, another to Lungia, another to the Valley of Joachim <note>St. Joachimsthal</note>, and another to Transylvania. Such is its distribution throughout the whole world. In this way, innumerable trees are interwoven wherever the earth extends. As trees grow in this fashion, one after another on all sides, their ends extend to the furthest parts of the earth. Sometimes they crop up to the surface of plains under the open sky; sometimes they remain in the earth according to the nature and condition which is specific to each tree. From this you may learn that the primal matter of all minerals is assembled in water, and that this primal matter is nothing more or less than Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury, which are made the soul, spirit, and true essence of the element. These three substances contain within them all metals, salts, gems, and the like. And when, at the predestined time, it is about to beget those fruits which it must produce, then each genus and species gives birth to that which is like itself. Thus, if any person had different seeds—as many as the world produces—mixed together in a bag, and if he were to cast these out or sow them in a garden, Nature, being equal to the task, would eventually allot to each its own fruit, bringing every separate seed to its own vigor and perfection without harming the others. It is exactly the same with the element of water, as though it were the bag filled with seeds of all kinds to be sown. Here, too, every genus and species is brought to its own nature and perfection. God, according to His marvelous plan, has gifted the four elements with these miracles of creation. These are the elements from which come the fruits destined for the service of man. Every different kind has been created by God. Through such investigations as these, the mighty works of God are explored and understood.

Surely, therefore, that philosophy is worthy of all praise which focuses only on the works of God for our consideration. Every man is bound to learn all he can about these, so that he may know what and how much his Creator has done for his sake.

True, the enemy has intruded and sown his tares in this philosophy. Such as these are *Aristotle*, *Albertus*, and *Avicenna*, with their accomplices, who are mere tares of the field. That enemy, bursting in, has devastated everything and produced other harmful philosophers whose system is devoid of all knowledge of Nature and lacks any foundation at all. Lacking all light of experience, such philosophy violates the light of Nature in the most disgraceful way. Its professors are busybodies who, involving themselves in all good things, present themselves to the devil as sons of perdition.

Gold is not a single thing but manifold, just as a pear or an apple is not one but manifold. Therefore, there are just as many Sulphurs of gold, Salts of gold, and Mercuries of gold. The same applies to metals and gems. As many sapphires as there are—some more valuable, others more common—there are just as many Sulphurs of sapphire, Salts of sapphire, and Mercuries of sapphire. The same is true of turquoise and all other gems. Nature holds all these things, as if in a single closed hand, from which she brings forth every separate kind—the best and noblest that she possesses. In this way, the <term>three primals</term> are to be understood: they embrace as many created species as grow, and yet they are only composed of one Sulphur, one Salt, and one Mercury. Just as a painter depicts countless figures and forms with a single color, none of which are alike, so Nature is like that painter. In this alone they differ: Nature produces these things with life, while the painter produces only dead ones. Nature's productions are substantial; the painter's are mere shadows.

Then again, the reasoning regarding colors leads to a similar conclusion. On that point, take note of this brief information: all colors proceed from Salt. Salt gives color, balsam, and coagulation. Sulphur gives the body, substance, and structure. Mercury gives virtues, power, and <term>arcana</term>. Therefore, these three ought to be combined; one cannot exist without the other. God gives life to those whom He has predestined to receive it from these substances, as it has seemed good to Him. Now Nature herself extracts colors from Salt, giving each species its suitable color. The body appropriate to each species is taken from Sulphur. Likewise, the necessary virtues are derived from Mercury.

Thus, whoever wishes to learn about the bodies of all things must, above all else, become acquainted with Sulphur. Again, he who desires to know colors must seek his knowledge from Salt. Let him who wishes to learn virtues scrutinize the secrets of Mercury. In this way, he will have laid the foundation for examining the mysteries of every growing thing, just as Nature has infused these mysteries into each separate species. But you should know that Nature has mixed these bodies, colors, and virtues with one another; yet, with a little effort, it is possible for anyone who is willing—and to whom God gives the power—to separate them again, to form, color, and endow them. You see and know how it awakens our wonder when a tree adorned with bright and joyous colors, leaves, fruits, and flowers emerges from a dark black seed. This mystery of Nature, as it exists in flowers, is so sublime and great that no one can fully investigate it. God is to be greatly admired in His works, and one ought not to withdraw from the contemplation of these by night or day, but constantly take delight in studying them. This is, in the truest sense, to walk in the ways of God.

## II.

Regarding the generation of metals, you may be certain that there is a great number and a vast variety of them. A metal is that which fire can conquer and from which the artisan can craft some tool. Included in this class are gold, silver, iron, copper, lead, and tin. Everyone calls these metals. But there are also, besides these, certain metals that are not considered metals—neither in the writings and philosophy of the ancients nor by common people—and yet they are indeed metals. To these belong <term>zinc</term> and <term>cobalt</term> (which are conquered and forged by the force of fire), as well as certain <term>garnets</term> (as they are usually called), of which there are many kinds, which are also metals. But many more are those that are not yet known to me at this time, such as many different types of <term>marcasites</term>, <term>bismuths</term>, and other <term>cachimiæ</term>, which produce metals, but of types not yet known. Only the principal ones are known, which are more available and convenient for use, such as gold, silver, iron, copper, tin, and lead. The rest are almost completely neglected, and nobody cares about their properties—neither the smith nor the ironworker, the tinsmith, the brazier, or the goldsmith. Nevertheless, these metals are intended for other workers who are not yet born. No one is capable of learning except in one way and through a single art. The assertion that <term>quicksilver</term> is a metal has no truth in it. It belongs to another class of minerals; it is not a metal, a stone, a marcasite, or a sapphire, etc. It is a unique growth of Nature, gifted with its own body like the rest, and provided with its pro-

...properties. The custom of assigning seven metals to the seven planets is also passing away. This practice arose because people, lacking full knowledge of metals, counted quicksilver as one of them. According to their comparison of things, gold is Sol, silver is Luna, copper is Venus, lead is Saturn, and tin is Jupiter. But come, organize these things. If you join Venus and copper, you will soon see how they align and agree with one another. Join and compare lead with Saturn, and notice what happens. Compare tin and Jupiter, and see what result will arise. Such philosophy is nothing but rubbish and confusion. Not the slightest trace of any foundation or light appears in it. Such remarks are merely ignorant, and not philosophy at all. 

The assertion that quicksilver is Mercury is of the same kind. Compare the complexion, nature, operation, quality, properties, and various virtues and essences, and see how they align and agree with one another. They are completely incompatible. One has not the slightest resemblance to the other. It is true that the "Philosophy of Plants" has arranged seven herbs according to the seven planets; but these are merely the dreams of physicians, with no stability or power of proof in them. According to them, <term>mercurialis</term> is Mercury, <term>heliotrope</term> is Sol, and <term>lunaria</term> is Luna. 

But do you think—you "Fathers"—that you can fly away to the sky and have the power to compare earth with heaven without any astronomy or philosophy, when you cannot even glimpse what lies hidden in so common a plant as the heliotrope? Therefore, this classification should be accepted by no one, but instead should be relegated to those who do not judge by the light of Nature, but by their own long robes <note>Academic or clerical garments worn by those the author considers pseudo-authorities.</note>. 

The chapter on metals teaches you that those metals are six in number, as far as they are known to me, and I have listed them above. To these are added a few others—some three or four—which are known to me, and their number and species shall be given in due course. I think it very likely that many still remain. For through the testing of metals, many pieces of evidence present themselves that are metallic—that is, they are considered according to the nature of the six metals, though they do not entirely agree with them; so I would predict from this that a great number of metals still remain. Every mineral can be thoroughly known and identified if subjected to a sufficient examination.

With regard to the generation of Gold, the true opinion is that it is Sulphur refined to the highest degree by Nature and purged of all dregs, blackness, and filth whatsoever—so transparent and lustrous (if one may say so) as no other metal can be, having a higher and more exalted body. Sulphur, one of the three primary elements, is the first matter of gold. If alchemists could find and obtain this Sulphur, just as it is at the roots of the gold-bearing tree in the mountains, it would certainly be a cause of great joy for them. This is the "Sulphur of the Philosophers" from which gold is produced, not that other sulphur from which iron, copper, etc., are derived. This is a small part of their universality. Furthermore, Mercury, refined to the highest degree according to its metallic nature and free from all earthly and accidental

admixtures, is changed into a mercurial body with perfect clarity. This is the Mercury of the Philosophers which generates gold, and is the second part of the primal matter. The third part of the primal matter of gold, or of the tree from which gold should grow—just as a rose grows from a rose-seed—is salt, crystallized to the highest degree, and so highly separated and purified from all its acridity, bitterness, acidity, aluminous, and vitriolic character, that it no longer has anything of the kind belonging to it, but is carefully illuminated within itself to the absolute highest point, and advanced to the supreme transparency of the beryl. These three ingredients together are gold, which is decocted in the way we have already mentioned.

Moreover, the genus of gold is not simple, but manifold. Its grade is not only one, but Nature herself gives thirty-two degrees to the finest gold. In our Art, twenty-four degrees are established for the best gold. The cause of this is that gold in its tree is like a cow in the pastures, or like Epicurus in the kitchen. As soon as he has left, all vigor and animation fall and diminish. So it is with gold: because if it is reduced to be the first matter of man, then, as if it had left its kitchen, it immediately loses eight of the thirty-two degrees previously mentioned. But there are diversities in the kitchens, too, some being better and others worse. Depending on whether the gold falls into one or the other, it is either increased or diminished in degrees, from a maximum of twenty-six degrees down to a minimum of ten degrees. The grades below this are too pale and unrecognizable. For it is the nature of gold to be either light or dense. This happens because of some impediment caused by the stars or other elements that assist in the decoction. Just as one man is denser or more subtle than another, gold also does not always reach its full grade, primarily because too much body, or Salt, or Mercury, has been added, from which fault and error are certain to arise. Too much Salt causes too much paleness. Too much Mercury makes the gold too similar to the color of corn. Too much Sulphur gives it an excessive redness. And it must be remembered, too, that sometimes the weights are unequally divided. Nature sometimes errs as well as men. If this happens, the grade is unequal. It reaches a point from twelve to twenty-four. But if the extra weight is removed (as it can be by Art)—for example, by antimony, by <term>quarta</term>, as it is called, by <term>regal cement</term>, or by other means—the irrelevant weights are removed and the twenty-four degrees remain. The alchemist, therefore, should not rashly attempt to graduate gold, which is done in this way. For the excess weight is unfit to take its degree and be reduced to a proper standard. But what is not good of its kind cannot be exalted. Yet it is possible that gold which is too pale in its decoction may be graduated. But a key piece of knowledge regarding this is that it does not lose its body in <term>regale</term>, antimony, or <term>quarta</term>. Indeed, it persistently retains both its color and its weight. This is a property of good gold.

### A Book about Minerals. 251

Gold becomes white by Sulphur in the manner already described. But the other two, Mercury and Salt, are white and of a golden nature. These so tint a sulphurous body that it loses its redness and becomes white. Sulphur takes the tint of other colors. For though the whole may be red, white, or clay-colored, its color is changed by the tincture composed of Mercury and Salt. When, therefore, the body is Sulphur, the tincture of Alchemy can easily change its color. However, in this case, it is necessary that the other tincture—namely, the alchemical one—should tint the Mercury and Salt from whiteness to redness. In this way, gold assumes the color it ought to have. And it should be realized that there are complexions in gold and in other metals, just as there are in man himself.

Another fact that should be accepted is that the white complexion is also changed by physical <note>corporal</note> transmutation. So, too, is redness. These two colors separately belong to <note>inhere in</note> redness. Yellowness belongs to whiteness; and these are subject to the primary colors. This transmutation can be achieved by means of Alchemy, provided that it is directed toward the complexions and that it is first of all tested in man—so that one may be made of a melancholy or a sanguine temperament, just as cattle may be made black or white by a tincture. Indeed, Nature, in her mineral work, acts exactly as she does with man in his generation. In the same way, man also ought to act in the generation of Nature, being superior to Nature in this respect, provided Nature has gifted him with the astral mysteries of the arts. This method of treatment, however, I now relegate to astronomy.

Attention must also be paid to the fact that, at this point, Nature takes the lead in such matters. In Sulphur, there is nothing except a body; in Salt, nothing; only in Mercury. Sulphur and Salt are useful in that one gives the body in which the gold resides, and the other adds strength. Regarding nature, force, and virtue, all of this is due to Mercury. Whatever property exists in Sulphur belongs to all alike. There is nothing in it except the body when Mercury is not present. So it is in Salt. But know that Salt is a balsam and preserves Mercury so that its virtues and properties do not putrefy or decay. Thus, this virtue is incorporated with gold, and if it is separated after coagulation in Salt, it cannot be detected by Art, just as the properties of Sulphur cannot be discovered. But all of these are readily found in Mercury. So, when Art separates them, it leaves the body behind and pays no heed to its medicine. In the same way, it leaves Salt, along with its medicine. And although the body has some influence as a body, and Salt as Salt, these medicines must not be sought there, but only in Mercury, which contains all things. For this is the *rationale* of creation: that in all things growing out of the four elements of Nature, not only are those things present which are seen and understood by themselves, but they also contain within them the magnet which, during decoction and preparation, attracts the essences of the three primals—that is, the <term>Quintessence</term>, as the ancients call it, though they should instead call it the quart-essence. For the mineral

When Nature is thus prepared and <gloss>led</gloss> to such increase, the gold first becomes a tree according to its kind. This spreads itself, and afterwards the branches are generated. The flower follows; then the fruit. The flower in the earth, like that of any other tree, is at the extremity. And as the flower and the nucleus—while still immature—are at the extremity, the same method is observable in the generation of gold and of all metals. When the flower falls, the fruit is born in its place. It is true that this does not always burst forth where the flower stood; rather, it is the nature of the auriferous <note>gold-bearing</note> tree that the fruit sometimes flourishes at a distance of several hundred ells <note>a unit of measurement</note> within the interior of the tree itself, sometimes immediately in the open air, and others midway between the two. There is thus some difference among auriferous trees, as their natures vary from one another. Hence they are found distributed in different ways, just as God has assigned a unique mode of growth to other trees.

Furthermore, regarding gold, this fact also deserves to be well weighed: it is sometimes overloaded with impediments, so that occasionally nothing occurs except the generation of Mercury. If this happens, it leads one astray. If corrosive salts fall on the flowers, they are eaten away, just as actual flowers on trees are eaten by worms. The gold, too, is chilled by Mercury or burnt by Salts. There are many mishaps of this kind. The earth, the firmament, and the air may destroy it. Unless these are fruitful, they bring forth no good. As trees are burnt up by a blazing sun, so here it also takes place in the water. The light of philosophy teaches us all these matters, and they are abundantly established by experience. Therefore, the minerals of gold and others are forced to submit to hindrances of this kind. There is nothing in existence that is not occasionally shaken by its own tempests. But there are other impediments that usually affect the degree. In this class are cachimiæ <note>mineral dross or slag</note>, resins, and other marcasites, which insinuate themselves into the workings and send forth their tinctures. All these are rejected in the Art <note>Alchemy</note>.

### CONCERNING SILVER.

Silver is generated from white Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury; when these are most subtly prepared and rendered transparent, they are restored to a fixed nature. That is, they are fixed by their special nature nearest to gold in a fire of ashes, but not with antimony, regale <note>a purification process</note>, and quarta <note>quartation, a method of separating gold and silver</note>. Here is the difference in fixation between gold and silver: gold is male and possesses masculine virtues, while silver is female and possesses feminine virtues. Herein lies the difference between the fixation of gold and silver. Since gold is male, it can bear more fixation, but silver can bear less. Thus, the matter of silver is comprised of its primals, as is the case with a woman. Gold

### CONCERNING JOVE.

Regarding the generation of Jove <note>Jupiter, or tin</note>, it should be known that it is produced from fixed white Sulphur, fixed Salt, and from Mercury that is not fixed; this is because Jupiter is fixed according to its body, but not in the substance of Mercury. It loses all its fusion and malleability. Afterward, it ceases to be a metal; for the metallic spirit is separated from it by Art <note>alchemy</note>. As soon as this has been done, it is nothing else but white Sulphur, Salt, and dried Mercury.

### CONCERNING SATURN.

Saturn <note>lead</note> is born from a black, sulphurous, and dense body, more so than all other metals. On account of its density, it consists of the thickest Mercury and the most fluid Salt, so that the most fluid body of Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury is received into Saturn. These same materials, moreover, are the three most dense natures of all the metals. If this metal is dissolved and ceases to be lead, it becomes ceruse <note>white lead</note>, spirit of Saturn, lead ochre, and finally glass. It consists of three colors: the lemon color it gets from Sulphur, and the white from Mercury. It gets its spirit from Salt, and from all together its glass-like nature, just as all the metals have.

### CONCERNING IRON AND STEEL.

On the other hand, iron is generated from the least fluid Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury, being the very opposite of tin and lead. It is coagulated into a hard metal and joined within itself. For two metals are joined together in one: iron and steel. Iron is feminine and steel is masculine. This union resembles that of gold and silver—that is to say, the male and female grow together. They can, therefore, be separated in their turn: the female to her sex, and the male to his. The female can be applied to her uses, and the male to his in the same manner.

### CONCERNING VENUS.

Copper <note>Venus</note> is generated from purple Sulphur, red Salt, and yellow Mercury. If these three colors are mixed with one another, copper is produced. Now, copper contains within itself its own female element, that is, its dross <note>scoriae</note>. If these are separated by Art and the body is reduced, it emerges as male. The nature of each constituent is such that the male does not allow itself to be destroyed again, and the female no longer emits dross. They differ from one another in fluidity and malleability, just as iron and steel differ. If that separation is made, and each is assigned to its own nature, two metals are produced, differing altogether in essence, species, and properties.

### NOTE.

Such and so many in number are the metals, as I have listed them: namely, gold, silver, tin, lead, iron, steel, female copper, and male

There are seven well-defined and publicly known metals: gold, silver, tin, lead, iron, steel, and copper. The last is counted as one metal because the male and female are forged together and not separated, as they should be.

### OF MIXED METALS.

You can see, from what has already been said, that the male is not always alone without a partner, but often they coexist. This is the case with gold and silver, and iron and steel, which grow together in one process. From this, each retains its own special nature, yet they are mixed so that one does not hinder the other, nor are they naturally separated from one another. This is also often the case with tin and lead. But where they are joined in this way, no good result comes of it. They do not fit together into one body; rather, it is better that each should be separated into its own body.

### CONCERNING SPURIOUS METALS.

Metals can be adulterated. Only gold and silver mix with the other metals because they are the most subtle. Therefore, only when such a primal matter is present does each grow up by itself. It may easily happen that six or seven different fruits are grafted together on the same tree; there is the same marvelous kind of implantation here in Nature.

### CONCERNING ZINC.

Moreover, there is a certain metal, not commonly known, called zinc. It has a peculiar nature and origin. Many metals are adulterated within it. The metal itself is fluid because it is generated from three fluid primals. It cannot be hammered, but only melted. Its colors are different from other colors, so that it resembles no other metals in its state of growth. Such, I say, is this metal that its ultimate matter is not yet fully known, at least to me. It does not allow for mixing, nor does it allow for the fabrication of other metals. It stands alone by itself.

### CONCERNING COBALT.

Furthermore, another metal is produced from cobalt. It is fluid like zinc, with a peculiar black color darker than lead or iron, possessing no brightness or metallic sparkle. It can be worked and is malleable, but not to such an extent that it is fit for practical use. The ultimate matter of this substance has not yet been discovered, nor has its method of preparation. There is little doubt that the male and female elements are joined in its makeup, as in the case of iron and steel. They cannot be worked, but remain as they are until Art <note>alchemy</note> discovers the process for separating them.

### CONCERNING GRANATES.

Besides these, there is another peculiar metal found in streams and marshes in the form of a seed, like a large or small bean. It is smelted and worked by itself, but not in a way that makes it suitable for making tools. It has no practical use, nor is it known what properties it contains. Unless Alchemy discloses its nature, it is not likely to be made clear at all. It permits many mixtures of silver and gold, which penetrate it just as they do copper or lead. It is produced from citron-colored sulfur.

### NOTE.---CONCERNING GEMS.

There are other transparent granates <note>garnets</note> in the form of crystal, in which both silver and gold are hidden.

### CONCERNING QUICKSILVER.

Furthermore, there is a certain category which is neither hammered nor smelted; it is a mineral water of metals. As water is to other substances, so is this in relation to metals. It should be considered a metal insofar as Alchemy reduces it to a state where it can be hammered and worked. It usually has no solid consistency, but sometimes it does. The correct opinion about it is that it is the primary matter of the alchemists, who know how to extract silver, gold, copper, and so on from it, as the results prove. Possibly, tin, lead, and iron can also be made from it. Its nature is complex and marvelous, and it can only be studied with great labor and constant application. This, at least, is clear: it is the primary matter of the alchemists for generating metals and is, moreover, a remarkable medicine. It is produced from Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, with the remarkable nature of being a fluid that does not wet things, and it runs about even though it has no feet. It is the heaviest of all the metals.

### NOTE.

Thus far, then, all the metals have been described to the extent that they are known to me, according to their substance and origin, following the guide and based upon the foundation supplied by the ultimate matter. By means of this, the first three <note>the Tria Prima: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt</note> are identified—what their species are and where they come from. Indeed, the generation of the others cannot be explained in any way except through experience, which is finally proven by the primary matter in Vulcan <note>the alchemical fire or forge</note>. In this way, no one can err.

### CONCERNING CACHIMLE, THAT IS, THE THREE IMPERFECT BODIES.

Attention should be paid to a certain category of minerals which is indeed of a metallic nature but is not a metal. The things belonging to this category possess peculiar qualities, of which I shall give several examples. For instance, all marcasites—which are varied, both red and white—as well as pyrites, which are also varied, white and red, and of a different category than marcasites. There are, moreover, the types of antimony, which are many, both perfect and imperfect; next are the varieties of arsenicalia <note>arsenical compounds</note>. To these also belong

### GENERAL RECAPITULATION CONCERNING GENERATION.

This chapter and text is entitled "Concerning the Three Imperfect Bodies" for this reason: it is concerned with a metallic growth that bears the same relation to metals as tumorous fleshy growths bear to natural flesh, as a mushroom bears to a plant, or an ape to a human. Of these things, some are in the body of sulfur, such as marcasites, pyrites, and cobalts; others are in the body of mercury, such as antimony, arsenicals, and orpiment; yet others are in salt, such as talc.

### OF THE GENERATION OF MARCASITES.

Marcasite is of two colors, citrine and white, metallic and brilliant. It is generated from imperfect metallic sulfur, which is destined to become marcasite by a natural necessity.

### AUTOGRAPH SCHEDULE BY PARACELSUS.

There are, then, in human beings only seven planets, four of which are bodies *in themselves*, not forming part of anything else. There are also other minerals, namely those of the three primary principles, which come from Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, and are specifically called mineral because they are either minerals themselves or form parts of minerals. There are two minerals, and several parts, which enter partially into their composition. Gold, for instance, carries with it three parts: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury; and all species comprised under minerals are made up of these three parts. Every planet has a perfect <term>Yliadus</term> <note>Paracelsus' term for a vital force or the spiritual aspect of matter</note>. The other parts do not have the same; for instance, <term>sal gemmæ</term> <note>rock salt</note> forms a species, not a part; a marcasite is a species, and <term>cachimiæ</term> is a species. But spirits have species within them, just as the salt of a gem has arsenic, fixed sulfur, and liquid mercury. The <term>Yliadus</term>, however, differs from the former <term>Yliadus</term> because the former has its substance and mineral perfect. Minerals have such species; they do not have a manifest body as planets do. Therefore, the <term>Yliadus</term> is to be understood in a twofold sense: one referring to the body, and one to the spirits. The physical <term>Yliadus</term> shares with the spirits of the <term>Yliadus</term>, but the spiritual does not share with the former.

# APPENDIX II.

---

[The alchemical importance attached to a proper conception of the four so-called elementary substances is explained in a note appended to the *Philosophy of Paracelsus Concerning the Generation of Elements*. The origin, nature, and operation of the three prime principles are, however, of no less importance. Since these principles must clearly be distinguished from salt, sulfur, and mercury of the common kind, it is necessary to emphasize the distinction by contrasting at some length the references to the principles contained in the text of the present volume with the knowledge displayed by Paracelsus on the subject of ordinary salt, sulfur, and mercury. The treatise concerning the first of these substances, which has been selected for translation here, is derived from a collection entitled *De Naturalibus Rebus*, which can be found in the second volume of the Geneva folio.]

### CONCERNING SALT AND SUBSTANCES COMPREHENDED UNDER SALT.

GOD has driven and reduced man to such a state of necessity and want that he is unable in any way to live without salt, but has the most urgent need of it for his food and meals. This is man's need and condition of compulsion. The causes of this compulsion I will briefly explain.

Man consists of three things: sulfur, mercury, and salt. Everything that exists anywhere also consists of these, and of neither more nor fewer constituents. These are the body of every single thing, whether endowed with senses or deprived of them. Now, since man is divided into species, he is therefore subject to decay, nor can he escape it except insofar as God has endowed him with a natural balsam which also itself consists of three ingredients. This is salt, preserving man from decay; where salt is deficient, that part which is without salt decays. For just as the meat of cattle which is salted is made free from decay, so also salt naturally infused into us by God preserves our body from putrefaction. Let that theory stand, then: that man consists of three bodies, and that one of these is salt, as the preservative element which prevents the body born with it from decaying. As, therefore, all created things and all substances consist of these three, it is necessary that

In sulfur is its own sulfur, in mercury its own mercury, and in salt its own salt. Nature contains all these things as one. Thus, from this liquid, which is the nourishment of natural things, natural salt is decocted.

By the same reasoning, it is clear that man himself must also be nourished in the same way: that is to say, that his sulfur must receive nutritional sulfur, his mercury its nutritional mercury, and his innate salt its nutritional salt, so that through these three, man may be sustained and preserved in his species. Whatever burns is sulfur, whatever is humid is mercury, and that which is the balsam of these two is salt. Upon this depends the diversity of human foods. Man needs heat-giving foods for the sustenance of his sulfur; he requires moist foods to maintain his supply of mercury, and he eats salt to nourish his nature of salt. If this order is violated, that species in the body perishes, whichever one is neglected; and when one part perishes, the rest perish with it. This order must be kept in its proper sequence. The Academics know nothing of this philosophy—a fact not to be wondered at, since in other matters they neither know nor can do anything.

Now, all over the world, there are heat-giving foods such as meat, fish, bread, and so on. Likewise, there are humid foods, such as springs, flowing streams, and seas. Similarly, salt is found everywhere. These things are distributed over the whole world, so that everywhere the supply of them is ready at hand.

Now, concerning the nature of man, the following should be accepted: The reason man desires food is because of his sulfur. Why he needs drink—whether it be water or wine—is because of the mercury; and the reason he desires salt is because of the salt within himself. These facts are little known, yet nature nonetheless craves these things. And this is not only the case with men; animals, too, become fatter, stronger, more useful, and healthier with salt than without it. If the proper quantity of salt is not supplied, some defect arises in one of the two species, so that the animal decays and dies. Its nature is no longer supported by those necessary foods which it requires. Man's condition is similar. Without nutrients of this kind, he cannot live. The natural appetite with which he is born requires satisfaction in proportion to his need. It is reported, indeed, that in certain newly discovered islands, men prepare no food cooked with salt, nor do they give such food to their animals; but it is quite certain that their own nature and that of their cattle require the saltwater of the sea, and that they have cooked their food mixed with this. Nature never rests at ease, but constantly reaches for and seeks that which its necessity and use require, and thus compels cattle—not to mention man—to lick salted things.

# Concerning Salt and Substances comprehended under Salt. 259

For ourselves, custom and necessity alike dictate that we eat salt in our food. Such a practice is natural and wise. In this way, three nutrients meet; that is to say, salt and food as one, and with these a third, namely, drink. By these, nature is nourished and sustained.

I have said of salt that it is the natural balsam of the living body. That is, as long as the body lives, the aforementioned salt is its balsam against decay. By this balsam, the whole body of man, as well as that of other creatures, is kept and preserved. But if any decay—or, if I may call it so, any corpselike state—occurs in man, as in the disease called **Persian fire** <note>A historical term for various inflammatory skin conditions, such as anthrax, shingles, or carbuncles</note>, this is the reason. Now, if everything in creation is to be dissolved, it is clear that even the balsam itself contains the elements of dissolution, and once this dissolution begins, its strength and power increase. If the balsam is dissolved or corrupted (and the various ways in which this may take place are given in my *Theory of Medicine*), then corruption and decay begin immediately, according to the way in which the salt has been corrupted. If the salt has not undergone corruption, then neither the external nor the internal body of man decays. 

Hence we must conclude that salt is like a balsam in man, and that the natural salt which man eats is his food and nourishment. I have discussed the subject of salt at some length for the sake of ensuring a fuller understanding of the matter. Putting aside, therefore, the idea of a natural balsam, I would point out, moreover, concerning the salt in food, how it is endowed—with what gifts it is endowed by God—both for preserving the health of men and for warding off many diseases. But since nothing is so good as to not have some evil combined with it, it remains for us to describe the evil there is in salt, so that in this way the good and evil may be joined, and the one separated from the other. The nature and condition of salt are very remarkable. If salt can preserve a dead body or corpse, much more will it preserve live flesh. If by its power and efficacy salt preserves a dead body from worms, it does so much more for the living body, and for this reason: that it is not only a nutrient, but a necessary food and a medicine useful for old and young alike. Salt must be supplied to all.

But there are three kinds of salt. There is **sea salt**, which is salt of itself, not salted by others. Just as wine differs from water, so the sea in its nature differs from other waters. Other waters are sweet; this is salt. Secondly, there are some **springs** which are sweet yet salt at the same time. These have a special nature, insofar as they do not share that nature with the sea, but of themselves contain a different kind of salt. Thirdly, there are also **mineral salts**, with the appearance of a stone, of a different kind from other metals or minerals. The best salt is from springs. Next comes that from minerals. The harder it is, the better. Then there is sea salt. And as salt is divided into many kinds, so also is it separated into many and various properties distinct from one another. As to the way in which salt is prepared, there is no need to discuss that subject here, since it is clear enough. Neither is this the place to describe how it grows. That topic belongs rather to the *Book on*

It should be known at the outset that this is the nature of every kind of salt: it is a corrective for food. When salt is lacking, food is not properly balanced. For example: if the stomach takes food that has no salt, its digestion is sluggish and its assimilation is imperfect. From salt comes an expulsive force for excrement and urine. If these two functions do not proceed regularly, and the expulsions are not genuine, everything is wasted. Moreover, if the food is not properly salted, it is certain that those liquids in man—which absorb nothing unsalted—cannot be nourished. The blood becomes disorganized. Where salt is not incorporated or united with the food, the blood does not attract it. Whatever is sluggishly and faintly attracted causes decay in the blood. Now, in order to avoid this, and for the sake of those specific parts of the body, food should be salted so that they may not be deprived of their proper nourishment. 

Moreover, there is a solvent power in salt. If any obstructions of the pores or other conditions arise, salt removes or clears these so that they pass away in the urine. Urine is the salt of the blood; that is, it is the salt of natural salt. Natural salt is united with nutritional salt, and that combination causes the excrement to be expelled. If, however, salt is not supplied in the proper manner and in sufficient quantity, a natural union cannot be achieved. Now, let every physician know that, since natural salt is usually expelled by means of salt, the use of salt should be all the more frequent. It is a great advantage if the salt called <term>sal gemmæ</term> is used, as it is much more effective than all other salts for expelling natural salt. It is peculiarly the duty of physicians, therefore, not to neglect the three species of salt and the operations of each, but to use them diligently.

Salt is useful in many other cases beyond those we have so far listed regarding external diseases of the body. So many virtues are hidden in the use of salt. In conclusion, it should be noted that over time, the liquid removes and cures baldness and mange.

## CONCERNING SULPHUR.

God created the resin of the earth and endowed it with many indescribable qualities, not only for remedying diseases, but also for alchemical operations. Other virtues also are conspicuous in sulphur, which is a resin of the earth. It will be appropriate, then, not only to discuss the medicinal virtues of sulphur, but also to treat its alchemical and other uses. Much has been written and published on the subject of sulphur, but no one has ever yet reached the source of its true power. Many authors have undertaken to describe everything, but they understood nothing. They piled up heaps of matter, but deduced nothing from the source as a good writer should do. They did not understand the subject themselves; and though ambition led them to keep on compiling books, those books were without spirit or life—in fact, a mere dead letter.

I, as an experienced man, will lay before you what I have learned about sulphur, and what is contained in it regarding medicine, alchemy, and in other respects. Unless God Himself intervenes and prevents it, the operations of sulphur are stupendous, so that the natural light in man cannot admire them enough. If God does not prevent it, any defect lies with the craftsmen, who handle their sulphur so that the result does not correspond to its innate virtue. When every simpleton is made a doctor and every trifler poses as an alchemist, this fact accounts for science not being brought out into the open light. And the foundation is that so many <term>arcana</term> <note>Hidden or secret mysteries and powers</note> and powers of both fields are contained in sulphur, that they cannot be thoroughly investigated by anyone—because, I repeat, such excellent virtues are hidden within it, they are deservedly the subject of universal wonder. After long experience gained in both fields, these powers of sulphur were discovered and understood by me, and I realized that scarcely any exist which are superior to them, or which can even be compared to them in medicine and in Alchemy. Sulphur refutes Aristotle when he says that the species of things cannot be transmuted.

<summary>This page introduces a treatise on sulphur, described as a "resin of the earth" with extraordinary medicinal and alchemical properties. Paracelsus criticizes previous authors for their lack of true understanding and asserts that sulphur's hidden powers can even refute Aristotle's views on the transmutation of species.</summary>

<keywords>Sulphur, Alchemy, Paracelsus, De Naturalibus Rebus, The Economy of Minerals, medicine, arcana, transmutation, Aristotle</keywords>

Sulphur transmutes them; and if Aristotle were alive today, he would be completely put to the blush and made ashamed of himself.

One who practices as a physician or an alchemist does not use Sulphur as it exists *per se*, but rather as it is separated into its arcanum <note>a secret remedy or essential spirit</note>, and so cleansed from its impurity that it becomes in its virtue whiter than snow. This is accomplished by Ysopus <note>a Paracelsian term for the art of separation</note>, that is, the art of separating, which was anciently called the Ysopaic art in Alchemy and in all kinds of sequestration <note>the separation or isolation of substances</note>. Even when crude, it is remarkable for common use and for all external purposes. But, in order to be quite accurate in explaining Sulphur, I will differentiate it first according to its nature. It is not produced from one matrix, but from many. Hence it has diverse modes of operation and comprises many natures, differing one from the other. These I will detail separately, so that no physician may make any mistake, and so that it may be clearly known what its use is in medicine, and also how far it is serviceable for Alchemy. When these points are established, I will go on to specify its daily uses. So, then, once we have explained accurately and in due order its use in medicine, in Alchemy, and in other respects, all its operations will be understood by everybody, so that they will be able to handle it without danger of error.

### CONCERNING THE KINDS OF SULPHUR.

As often as you get new metal, so often you get sulphur; because no metal is without sulphur. Every metallic body consists of three things: sulphur, salt, and mercury. In the perfection or generation of metals, however, the superfluous sulphur is removed. You see a nut generated, not simply *per se*, but with a skin and a shell, and you know that these are superfluous except for the embryonic preservation of the kernel, as is explained in the treatise concerning generation. I provide this illustration to show that there are as many kinds of sulphur as there are metals, each bearing relation to the nature of its own metal. And this is true not only of metals, but of stones. There are as many kinds of sulphur as there are stones. All bodies having their own substance are made up of the three constituents just mentioned. On this account, they have an embryonated nature. Hence arise different names for sulphur—for example, the embryonic sulphur of gold, silver, sapphire, marble, etc. The sulphur is distinguished by the name of the embryo, which arises from the generation of a single product, be it metal or stone. Nor do I speak of metals and stones only, but also of all the different corporalities, such as vitriol, alum, marcasite, bismuth, antimony, etc. Each of these comprises an embryo, which takes its name according to the specialty of its own generation. For instance, the embryonate sulphur of Mars <note>iron</note> is different from the embryonate sulphur of vitriol or of jaspis <note>jasper</note>. The same holds good concerning growing bodies of the earth, such as woods, herbs, and the like, each of which contains in itself a sulphur of this kind.

### CONCERNING EMBRYONATED SULPHUR.

Concerning embryonated sulphur <note>Sulphur in its early, unrefined, or formative state within a mineral host</note> it should be known that it has different virtues according to that from which it is derived, that is, from its generators. Let us use an illustration to explain our meaning. A nut, *by itself*, is simply the kernel. But the kernel contains within itself a covering which corresponds to the nut. As in foods, the kernel differs from its covering; so do their virtues differ. Beyond this, again, a dry shell is produced, which is of a nature altogether different from the nut. As the bodies differ, so do their properties. Over this, finally, grows a green rind or bark, where the same diversity is once more observed. The chestnut, for example, has these two coatings. And as the chestnut differs from the bark when chewed in the mouth, so do the properties differ. I say this in order that you may understand how embryonated sulphur is also a similar impurity from its embryo and differs from its true products by as wide a distance as its form, essence, substance, and physicality differ. The virtue of the nut is not to be looked for in the shell; so neither is it in embryonated sulphur that one must seek the virtue of gold, silver, tin, copper, emerald, or jacinth; instead, another virtue must be selected for medicine. Many virtues are hidden in these sulphurs, each differing from the other. This, also, which we are now going to say should be noted before all else: namely, that with all these sulphurs the spirit of arsenic blends, more subtly in one than in another. They only know the sulphur of the peddlers' shops. They would not even know that if they had not heard it talked about. Yet, all these things ought to be known thoroughly from Nature herself, if we would not lend ourselves to robbery, but would have a good conscience towards God. You Academics think nothing of this, content with one thing—if money flows into your pockets. You care nothing for God, the Creator of yourselves and of all Nature.

Moreover, note this with reference to the embryonated sulphur of the metals. It can be clearly seen how it firmly preserves and restores its own particular organ. ->CONCERNING MINERAL SULPHUR.<-

### CONCERNING THE ALCHEMICAL VIRTUES OF SULPHUR: AND FIRST CONCERNING EMBRYONATED SULPHUR.

The extraction of <term>embryonated sulphur</term> <note>sulphur found within ores or in an early stage of development</note> is achieved by <term>sublimation</term>, and sometimes by <term>descent</term> <note>a method of distillation where the substance is heated and the vapor travels downward</note>, if the sulphur is properly ripened and there is a plentiful supply without the mixture of other bodies. Sometimes, if it is too subtle, it will not allow for sublimation or descent, but must be extracted with <term>strong waters</term> <note>acids, such as nitric acid</note>, so that by means of other bodies it may be reduced to liquid and then coagulated again from that liquid. There are many kinds of these strong waters, which we will not list here, but they should be of such a kind as not to take away or change the power of the sulphur. For if they are extracted by art according to their own concordance, they will not, indeed, be golden, but in alchemy, they will be very useful sulphurs for other preparations. They allow for <term>fixation</term>, and so produce in <term>cements</term> <note>powders used in the process of cementation to refine metals</note> a volatile, subtle gold in metals, in such a way that they withstand separation in strong waters and release their gold. Otherwise, nothing can be hoped for from this sulphur in alchemy unless it is extracted, according to its concordance, from those things in which it is hidden, and afterwards fixed. If, as is often the case, it contains gold, that is discovered by <term>fulmination</term> <note>a process of refining gold or silver using heat</note>. It is likewise fixed so as to retain all volatile gold that cannot otherwise be restrained, nor is it captured in separation because of the thinness of its subtle physicality. Many processes have indeed been tried for making a <term>tincture</term> out of

Unless gold were contained within it, nothing can be sought there; nor should it be attempted to produce gold in other bodies. There is none of a silver character, only golden—and one kind more so than another. As far as it concerns antimony, red talc, gold, marcasite, etc., they are rarely lacking in gold. Whoever wishes to treat this, let him take care to separate the sulphur so subtly that nothing departs from the gold. And unless God opposes—for He does not wish all to be rich, and He Himself knows the reason why goats do not have longer tails—much could be imparted there in few words. But since riches lead the poor man astray and take away his modesty and humility, replacing them with haughtiness and pride, it is therefore better to remain silent and let these people stay poor.

### CONCERNING MINERAL SULPHUR.

Next in order, I will share some marvels with you, though I am aware that this discourse concerning the wonderful use of sulphur in alchemy will be unwelcome to many. It is known to all that the spirit of the sciences does not take a holiday, but works constantly and unremittingly so that it may hunt out and discover those facts in the secrets of Nature which God has hidden. With this spirit, there usually goes another bad and false spirit—not only in this art, but in others too, even those regarding the soul. But concerning this false spirit, I remain silent. The devil indeed involves himself in all matters, but I make no remark on his deceits. For the sake of this mineral sulphur, the alchemical art has made many attempts to form something from it that shall be more than sulphur. Now, this itself is a miracle—to make something more out of a thing than the thing is by itself. This, however, God has allowed to be accomplished by art. Now, since this would be the very potency of art, the great Master of the art Himself has, by superintending the art, experimented with what can be formed from sulphur and how—something which is not in the sulphur itself, but can, however, be obtained from it. The woman by herself cannot beget children, but she begets them with the man. If this conception is to be accomplished, it must be by means of two. Here art is the man and the father who brings all things to perfection. But now, that stage of the operation has been reached where the spirit of transmutation has given its prescription for making the <term>liver</term> <note>likely referring to "liver of sulphur" (potassium polysulfide) or a similar preparation</note> or lung from oil of flax and sulphur. The distillation of this liver or lung is manifold. But it is discovered through operation that this liver produces a "milk" which differs in no respect from common milk, except that it is thick and fat. It also gives a red oil, like blood. This milk and that blood have not confused their color and essence in the process of distillation; instead, they have remained distinct and separate, the white sinking to the bottom and the red ascending to the top. Art, it is true, has urgently sought to form silver out of the white (or the milk) and gold out of the red. But I am certain that this has never been accomplished, either by the ancients or by those of more

He then describes an alchemical process involving sulphur and flax oil that produces distinct white and red substances, though these have not yet been successfully turned into silver or gold.</summary>

But concerning this red oil, which gives the liver-mark: Any crystal or beryl that has been previously well-polished, if it is placed in this oil for some time—namely, for three years—becomes a <term>jacinth</term>. If a <term>ruby</term> that is not highly graduated is placed in it, in the space of nine years it becomes so clear and bright that it shines in the darkness like a burning coal and can be seen everywhere. This has been proved experimentally. Alchemists, indeed, have tried to make a <term>carbuncle</term> of it by placing a <term>jacinth</term> of good quality for some time in the oil. But my experience says that this cannot be done. And this coloring does not take place only in the ways that have been mentioned; the same oil also tints a <term>sapphire</term> a blue color mixed with green. In the same way, it colors other gems. Over glass and similar substances, it has no power. But it so exalts gems that they attain their highest degree of excellence—a higher one, indeed, than that to which they could be raised by Nature. Concerning other gradations and colorings of gems, nothing more has been heard or written than that the red blood of <term>sulphur</term> colors and tints them. And observe here that all silver, if it is placed therein and left for a due time, by and by grows black and deposits a <term>calx of gold</term>, which is not fixed until the proper season but is a volatile and immature substance. If, however, it reaches its proper limit, by its own speed it hastens other things, about which I must not say more here. So, then, note concerning <term>sulphur</term>: that if it is duly graduated, the more subtle, beautiful, high, and quick in operation it is, the higher and greater the result will be. In this way, metals and stones are formed. Let him who is about to make the attempt not merely think, but be sure, that he can do it. For this is the most perilous work of all in <term>alchemy</term>, needing great experience and continual practice for its accomplishment. It should not depend on mere hearsay, but on extensive practice. Of the virtues <note>medicinal or inherent powers</note> themselves and how they are graduated, I cannot say anything. I speak of the colorings only, that they should be exalted to the highest degree. But I do not think it possible for this to take place in colors. This is a <term>tincture</term> not of virtue, but of mere color.

### CONCERNING THE USE OF SULPHUR OF THE METALS IN ALCHEMY.

I have several times in this chapter mentioned <term>sulphur</term> prepared from the decomposed metals, and added something as to their use in medicine. So far as relates to <term>alchemy</term>, I would have you know that many have tried to extract from it a <term>tincture</term> with which they should change things from one tint to another. This has not been successful, for a reason not to be mentioned here. But whoever has the <term>sulphur of gold</term> can by means of it graduate other gold from 24 to 36 grains or more, so that gold cannot mount any higher, while it abides and remains in <term>antimony</term> and <term>quartarium</term>. But the <term>sulphur of silver</term>, too, so exalts silver in its whiteness that if copper and silver are mixed in

In the same way, by the sulphur of copper, the metal copper can be brought to such a state that it is proof against lightning, even though it is not <term>graduated</term>, and it retains its own color. From the sulphur of Mars <note>iron</note> is made the best and most excellent steel. From the sulphur of Jove <note>tin</note>, the best tin is made, which will withstand the lightning. So far, then, you have learned how many kinds there are, and what the nature, properties, and essence of sulphur are. Anyone who wanted to say all that can be said about sulphur would consume a great deal of paper. The subject demands a careful workman, a ready and skilled artist—one who does not shout or trade in trifles, who does not deal with his art by mouth and tongue only, but puts it to the test of the work itself. Miracles will abound for such a person. He who knows nothing about sulphur is a man of no worth, unskilled in both philosophy and medicine, and aware of none of Nature’s secrets.

## THE MERCURIES OF THE METALS.

In the year 1582, an octavo edition of the *Archidoxorum Libri Decem* was published in Latin at Basel and included several other treatises of great importance, some of which are absent from the Geneva folio. Among these, there is one regarding the Mercuries of the Metals, which fills a somewhat curious gap in the writings of Paracelsus, as there is no other surviving work attributed to him that treats Mercury individually; meanwhile, concerning Salt and Sulphur, there is an abundance of material which makes selection quite difficult. It is entirely devoted to experiments, and it will consequently be of more value to practical students of early chemistry.

### A LITTLE BOOK CONCERNING THE MERCURIES OF THE METALS, BY THE GREAT THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS, MOST EXCELLENT PHILOSOPHER AND DOCTOR OF BOTH FACULTIES.

Extract aquafortis out of 4 lbs. of salt nitre, with 3 lbs. of green vitriol, 2 oz. of alum, and 1 oz. of sal ammoniac. After it has settled with a little copper, dissolve in this water 1 oz. of crude sal ammoniac, which has previously been slightly pounded. From this, let aqua regia be produced through V <note>likely referring to a specific vessel or distillation process</note>. In this water, dissolve 2 oz. of gold, which has previously been well and most exactly purified by antimony. After the dissolution has taken place, let the calx settle; effect separation by drawing off the aquafortis; and then reduce the calx by washing it to a sweet <note>neutralized</note> condition. For this purpose, wash it six or seven times with fresh water until no sharpness <note>acidity</note> of the aquafortis remains any longer. Subsequently, dry the calx over a slow fire, weigh it, and you will find that a third part of the weight has been extracted. To that, add an equal proportion of very finely pounded sulphur, a double quantity of vitriol, and white calcined tartar equal to the weight of all the aforementioned things. Pound all of them very finely, place them in a glass vessel, and pour exceedingly strong vinegar upon the top, together with salt water, so that the aqueous matter may float upon the top to the height of about two fingers. Seal the vessel effectively, and place it in a cupel, or alchemist's furnace, for thirty days. The furnace must not be hot enough to burn a finger when placed inside. At the expiration of the specified time, break the glass, and the matter will be in the form of washed silver, or a calx of silver which

### MERCURY OF THE MOON.

Let silver be reduced to thin plates in such a way that it may be easily moved and, at the same time, well purified. Sprinkle one of these plates with strong vinegar and set it aside in a damp place for a short time, until it becomes completely blue. Then dissolve it with <term>aquafortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> separated by the separation of solution. After it settles, and the <term>aquafortis</term> has been poured off but not sweetened by washing, and dried gradually, pour vinegar again upon the <term>calx</term> <note>the powder remaining after a metal is roasted or chemically dissolved</note>, and then separate it until the whole becomes completely blue.

Then take <term>℥ii.</term> <note>two ounces</note> of mountain or mineral <term>cinnabar</term> ground to a very fine powder, and afterwards <term>℥i.</term> <note>one ounce</note> respectively of <term>calx</term> of silver, <term>cinnabar</term>, <term>alumen</term> <note>alum</note>, <term>sulphur</term>, and <term>vitriol</term>. When ground finely, place all these in a jar, including the <term>calx</term> of silver, which should sink to the bottom. Furthermore, cover the surface of the matter, or compound, at the top of the jar with welding sand, such as ironworkers are accustomed to use. Afterwards, place this jar mouth-downward on the top of another jar, which must be filled with pure water and buried in the earth by descent. Kindle a slow fire around the upper jar, and increase it more and more until the whole of the said upper jar becomes white with heat. Let it cool a little, and the Mercury of the Moon will be found in the lower jar. Let the jar remain for two hours, more or less, at a white heat; thus, out of <term>℥ii.</term> of the Moon, <term>℥i.</term> and a half of Mercury is produced, which is entirely like crude mercury. This is again pressed through the <term>corium</term> <note>leather filter</note> so that the pure may be separated from the impure.

### MERCURY OUT OF MARS.

Reduce Mars <note>iron</note> into coarse filings, but avoid <term>chalybs</term> <note>steel</note>; therefore, filings *de calcaribus* <note>of spurs or iron hardware</note> are the best. Afterwards, wash the Mars in such a fashion as to avoid separating the turbidity. At length the water becomes clear, for the turbidity sinks to the bottom in the form of a red viscosity. Separate the water gradually by straining; keep the matter; dry it so that no waste or coarse part may remain. Take ℥v. <note>five ounces</note> of this viscid matter and ℥xxx. <note>thirty ounces</note> of pounded sulphur, and compound them delicately into the form of fine flour. Then let it cool, break it, and a grey powder will be found. Add to this ℥i. <note>one ounce</note> of <term>spume of glass</term> <note>scum or dross from glassmaking</note>, ℥ss. <note>half an ounce</note> of <term>sal ammoniac</term>, and ℥v. <note>five ounces</note> of vitriol. Place it on a smooth stone in a humid spot, and the water will flow out. But leave it for ten days; crush it in your hands, and you will have live Mercury, which is the Mercury of Mars. Out of ten pounds of Mars, one drachm and a half will be obtained. It is black and dull in color.

Moisten the filings again, and dry them again; separate a similar skin a second time, and repeat this process until there is enough of the white <term>calx</term>. ### MERCURY OF SATURN.

Take Villarensian Lead, or any other in which there is no silver; otherwise, it must be purged in the following manner: If it has been calcined <note>reduced to a powder by heat</note>, let the <term>calx</term> boil for two whole hours in a <term>lixivium</term> <note>a solution of alkaline salts, such as lye</note> composed of willow ashes, in which one ounce of alum and eight ounces of salt have first been dissolved. When the material receives the heat, Mercury comes forth; the fire is maintained in good order and intensity until no more of the lead powder remains. Therefore, the Mercury of Saturn which flows into that wooden container should be well washed and purified so that if any raw lead flows down at the same time (as often happens), it may be separated. From ten pounds of Saturn, eight pounds—and often eight and a half pounds—of Mercury are made. ## DE TRANSMUTATIONIBUS METALLORUM.

In the year 1581, a *Congeries Paracelsicæ Chemiæ de Transmutationibus Metallorum* appeared in octavo at Frankfort. In the notes to the *Aurora of the Philosophers, Concerning the Spirits of the Planets*, and elsewhere, some references have already been made to this work, which predates by nearly a century the Geneva edition of the writings of Paracelsus. As its title indicates, it attempted to collect and digest into a single methodical treatise the whole substance of alchemy, as taught and practiced by Paracelsus. While in many respects the digest was passably well done, and affords a tolerably representative notion of the opinions and experiments of Theophrastus, it is perhaps needless to say that, as it was included in the compass of a small volume, it is really very meager. There is, however, one point in which it may be of value to the student. The *Congeries* is, in all probability, an adaptation of autograph manuscripts, and where its readings (which is by no means always the case) can be distinguished from editorial interpolations and extensions, they may be useful in so far as they vary from the readings of the Geneva folio and some other less carefully supervised editions. Perhaps, after all, the value, such as it is, of this point, is likely to be appreciated only by that very small circle of readers who believe that in ancient practical alchemy there are chemical secrets hidden which are unknown to the chemistry of today. For these, the importance of a perfect text of the old alchemical processes, whether in the case of Paracelsus or in that of any other recognized master, is no doubt very high. In the present instance, the difficulty of distinguishing between the text and its editor, in so far as there are substantial variations, makes it needless to tabulate the readings, and the purpose of this appendix is of a far less pretentious character. There are a few paragraphs in the *Congeries* which it has not been found possible to identify in the collected editions of Paracelsus, or at least they offer very conspicuous differences, and these it is desirable to cite. The first has regard to the construction of the philosophical furnace, which *The Aurora of the Philosophers* affirms is difficult to describe, at least as regards its form, while the specific direction contained in the third treatise, *Concerning the Spirits of the Planets*, only partially corresponds to what is stated in the following excerpt, which constitutes the fourth chapter of the *Congeries Paracelsicæ Chemiæ*. ### CONCERNING THE VISIBLE AND LOCAL INSTRUMENTS: AND FIRST OF ALL CONCERNING THE SPAGYRIC UTERUS.

<margin>✓</margin>Before we come to the matter, we must describe in order all the instruments, both actual and local, which are required in this art. We have said that the first actual instrument is the fire. The first local instrument is the furnace, designated by the ancients under the alchemical name of <term>athanor</term>. This takes the place of the uterus in <term>spagyric</term> generation.

Hermes Trismegistus, though he was not the inventor of this art, no less than Paracelsus in <term>spagyric</term> medicine, deserves to be called its restorer.

He asserts that this <term>spagyric</term> work, in which human philosophy reaches its extreme point, originated in the meditative contemplation of the greater world, suggesting that the <term>spagyric</term> <term>athanor</term> ought to be constructed in exact imitation of the heaven and earth. In order to exercise the ingenious, it will not be out of place to examine this comparison, and I think I shall be able thereby to benefit my readers.

No philosopher will deny that the sun generates a sun like itself; but it is not everyone who will acknowledge that this fetus exists in the center—least of all those disciples of the philosophers who have no other knowledge of the <term>Aetnean fire</term> than that which comes from the fleshly eye, just like rustics in this respect. This earthly sun of the lower, or elementary, machinery is kindled by the fire of the higher sun. Just in the same way, the center of our matter is kindled by the center of our world, or <term>athanor</term>, which is a fire, performing in a manner the function of the natural sun.

Who does not see—I ask you, my brothers—that the form of the whole created universe has the likeness of a furnace, or, to speak more respectfully, the form of that which contains the matrix of a womb—the elements, that is to say, in which the seeds of the sun and the moon, cast down by the stars in their different influences, are decayed, concocted, and finally digested for the generation of all things? These things are transparently clear, I will not say only to philosophers, but even to boys; therefore we will not insist upon them further.

Let us come, then, to the construction of our <term>athanor</term>.

First let a furnace be built seven spans in height, and let the rounded interior be the height of one span, the lower part a little broader than the upper part inside, and let it be polished, so that the coals, when put in, may not stick because of the roughness of the surface, but may be able easily to fall down through the grating while they are being burned. To equalize this, let there be two or three holes, with which two or three lateral or uterine furnaces—or, if you like, a single one—shall correspond: the breadth of the mouths should be

What has happened to both of us except what may happen to anyone else—namely, to err? We are all human; and error happens to humans more than it does to irrational beasts, who are moved solely by the promptings of Nature. I confess that I err in very many things, and you err as well. It is your part to confess it, and mine to admonish, not to judge. Let it be your duty, as it is mine, not to enviously disclose those things of your brothers which have not been properly done, before you have admonished him with a certain amount of modesty, according to the discipline of true philosophy. Otherwise, neither you, nor he, nor I—if we act in a contrary manner—are worthy of the name of philosophy. But this philosophic discipline (alas, that it should be so!) is attacked even by the most learned; and the dogma of pagan philosophers has prevailed so much—being very celebrated among these people today—that they do not take a comprehensive view of what is outside and inside; they display nothing beyond a mere ambition for honor and renown. This is the chief goal of their study and labor. Hence it has come about that everyone tries to gain credit for themselves by tripping up or slandering the character of someone else. But these wretched people do not consider that no great evil can be done which will not incur an even greater punishment—at least if we are all foolish together, and nobody even approaches wisdom. Many are wise, a few are very wise, but they still maintain no middle ground. Let us see to it, then, lest what we parade as wisdom may, even in our own day and generation, be turned by the good God into open folly, and that through our own efforts. If, then, we have erred at all, and our own conscience tells us that we have done so—by which error on our part it seems only too likely that we may mislead others—let us retract in the presence of God and men, and do so without reserve. The wisest of men are always ready to acknowledge their common error, but stubborn men and fools are not ready to do this. Every mad course seems like the straight road to them, and *vice versa*.

### A VERY BRIEF PROCESS FOR ATTAINING THE STONE.

I neither am nor wish to be a teacher or a follower of that Stone which is taught in different ways by so many. Leaving, therefore, this process for its attainment, I have proposed to describe in very few words that which has been discovered by me through practice and experience. This, no less than the other, affects the bodies of men, though it is not prepared by the same process. Take, then, <term>mercury</term>, otherwise the element of mercury, and separate the pure from the impure. Afterward, let it be reverberated until it is white, and sublimate this with <term>sal ammoniac</term> until it is resolved. Let it be calcined and dissolved again, and digested in a <term>pelican</term> for one month, being afterward coagulated into a body. This is no longer burned, or in any way consumed, but remains in the same condition. The bodies penetrated by it are permanent in the <term>cineritium</term>, so that they cannot be reduced to nothing or be altered; but it takes away, as we have often said, all superfluous qualities from both sensible and insensible things.

Although I have set down a very brief method and process here, it requires long labor, and one that is involved in many intricate circumstances; it demands, at the same time, an operator who is untiring and in the highest degree diligent and expert.

# APPENDIX VI.

## THE VATICAN MANUSCRIPT OF PARACELSUS.

In the nineteenth chapter of his *Rituel de la Haute Magie*, Eliphas Levi observes that "among the rare and precious books which contain the mysteries of the Great Arcanum, there must be placed in the first rank the *Chemical Pathway*, or *Manual* of Paracelsus, which contains all the mysteries of demonstrative physics and of the most secret cabala. This manuscript work, unique and priceless, exists in the library of the Vatican. A transcription of it was made by Sendivogius, and this was used by Baron Tschoudy for the compilation of the Hermetic Catechism contained in his work entitled *The Burning Star*. This catechism, which we point out to instructed cabalists as a substitute for the incomparable treatise of Paracelsus, contains all the true principles of the great work in such a satisfactory and explicit manner that a person must be absolutely lacking in that quality of intelligence which is required for occultism if <u>they</u> fail to attain the absolute truth when <u>they</u> have studied it." The manuscript to which reference is made in this interesting citation is still an unpublished treasure, although, as will be seen in the next appendix, there has been at least one *Manual* attributed to Paracelsus which has been in print for four centuries. In the absence of the Vatican treatise, the student who desires to make acquaintance with a work of Paracelsus which adepts in the Art of Alchemy seem to prefer before all published writings of the same author, must make do with the Hermetic Catechism, as suggested by Eliphas Levi. He will find it an exceedingly <u>succinct,</u> and simple presentation of the fundamental alchemical theories. Though it may not initiate the reader, whatever the quality of his intelligence, into the mystery of the Great Arcanum, it is, in its way, very lucid and direct. Whether this merit belongs to Paracelsus or his interpreter is a pointless subject of speculation in the absence of the original text, which few persons have had the opportunity or inclination ~~to~~ to consult. The work of Baron Tschoudy was published in two volumes at Hamburg in 1785, and later on there was another edition in Paris. Considering its period, it is a sensible, though somewhat romantic, attempt to trace Free Masonry back to its historical origin; furthermore, it constitutes a valuable handbook of the analogies which exist between that system and Hermetic science, especially alchemy. The catechism itself,
