## A SHORT CATECHISM OF ALCHEMY
### BASED ON THE MANUAL OF PARACELSUS PRESERVED IN THE VATICAN LIBRARY.

Q. What is the primary study of a Philosopher?
A. It is the investigation of the operations of Nature.
Q. What is the end of Nature?
A. God, Who is also its beginning.
Q. From where are all things derived?
A. From one and indivisible Nature.
Q. Into how many regions is Nature separated?
A. Into four principal regions.
Q. Which are they?
A. The dry, the moist, the warm, and the cold, which are the four elementary qualities from which all things originate.
Q. How is Nature divided?
A. Into male and female.
Q. To what may we compare Nature?
A. To Mercury.
Q. Give a concise definition of Nature.
A. It is not visible, though it operates visibly; for it is simply a volatile spirit, fulfilling its office in bodies, and animated by the universal spirit—the divine breath, the central and universal fire, which gives life to all things that exist.
Q. What qualities should be possessed by those who examine Nature?
A. They should be like Nature herself. That is to say, they should be truthful, simple, patient, and persevering.
Q. What matters should next occupy their attention?
A. The philosophers should most carefully determine whether their designs are in harmony with Nature, and of a possible and attainable kind; if they would accomplish by their own power anything that is usually performed by the power of Nature, they must imitate her in every detail.
Q. What method must be followed in order to produce something that shall be developed to a higher degree than Nature herself develops it?<gloss>2</gloss>
A. The manner of its improvement must be studied, and this is always achieved by means of a similar nature. For example, if it is desired to develop the intrinsic virtue of a given metal beyond its natural condition, the chemist must make use of the metallic nature itself, and must be able to distinguish between its male and female distinctions.

Q. Where does the metallic nature store her seeds?
A. In the four elements.
Q. With what materials alone can the philosopher accomplish anything?
A. With the germ of the given matter; this is its elixir or quintessence, which is far more precious and useful to the artist than Nature herself. Before the philosopher has extracted the seed, or germ, Nature will be ready to perform her duty on his behalf.
Q. What is the germ, or seed, of any substance?
A. It is the most subtle and perfect <term>decoction</term> and digestion of the substance itself; or, rather, it is the <term>Balm of Sulphur</term>, which is identical to the <term>Radical Moisture of Metals</term>.
Q. By what is this seed, or germ, engendered?
A. By the four elements, subject to the will of the Supreme Being, and through the direct intervention of the imagination of Nature.
Q. In what way do the four elements operate?
A. By means of an incessant and uniform motion, each one, according to its quality, deposits its seed in the center of the earth, where it is subjected to action and digested, and is subsequently expelled outward by the laws of motion.
Q. What do the philosophers understand by the center of the earth?
A. A certain void place where nothing may rest, and the existence of which is assumed.
Q. Where, then, do the four elements expel and deposit their seeds?
A. In the ex-center, or in the margin and circumference of the center, which, after it has taken a portion, casts out the surplus into the region of waste, <term>scoriæ</term> <note>refuse or slag from metal smelting</note>, fire, and formless chaos.
Q. Illustrate this teaching by an example.
A. Take any level table and place in its center a vase filled with water; surround the vase with several things of various colors, especially salt, taking care that a proper distance exists between them all. Then pour out the water from the vase, and it will flow in streams here and there; one will encounter a substance of a red color and will take on a tinge of red; another will pass over the salt and will acquire a salty flavor; for it is certain that water does not change the places it crosses, but the diverse characteristics of the places change the nature of the water. In the same way, the seed that is deposited by the four elements at the center of the earth is subject to a variety of modifications in the places through which it passes, so that every existing substance is produced in the likeness of its channel. When a seed, upon its arrival at a certain point, encounters pure earth and pure water, a pure substance results, but the opposite occurs in the contrary case.
Q. In what way do the elements produce this seed?
A. In order to completely clarify this point, it must be observed that there are two gross and heavy elements and two that are volatile in character. Likewise, two are dry and two are humid; one out of the four

# A Short Catechism of Alchemy.

one being actually excessively dry, and the other excessively moist. They are also masculine and feminine. Now, each of them has a marked tendency to reproduce its own species within its own sphere. Moreover, they are never at rest, but are perpetually interacting, and each of them separates, of and by itself, its most subtle portion. Their general place of meeting is in the center, even the center of the *Archeus*, that servant of Nature, where, coming together to mix their various seeds, they agitate and finally expel them to the exterior.

Q. What is the true and the first matter of all metals?
A. The first matter, properly so called, is dual in its essence, or is in itself of a twofold nature; one, nevertheless, cannot create a metal without the concurrence of the other. The first and the primary essence is an airy humidity, blended with a warm air, in the form of a fatty water, which adheres to all substances indiscriminately, whether they are pure or impure.

Q. How has this humidity been named by the Philosophers?
A. Mercury.

Q. By what is it governed?
A. By the rays of the Sun and Moon.

Q. What is the second matter?
A. The warmth of the earth—otherwise, that dry heat which is termed Sulphur by the Philosophers.

Q. Can the entire material body be converted into seed?
A. Only its eight-hundredth part—specifically, that which is secreted in the center of the body in question, and may, for example, be seen in a grain of wheat.

Q. Of what use is the bulk of the matter in regard to its seed?
A. It is useful as a safeguard against excessive heat, cold, moisture, or dryness, and, in general, all harmful inclemency, against which it acts as an envelope.

Q. Would those artists who claim to reduce the whole matter of any body into seed derive any advantage from the process, supposing it were possible to perform it?
A. None; on the contrary, their labor would be wholly unproductive, because nothing that is good can be accomplished by a deviation from natural methods.

Q. What, therefore, should be done?
A. The matter must be effectively separated from its impurities, for there is no metal, however pure, which is entirely free from imperfections, though their extent varies. Now all superfluities, <term>cortices</term> <note>outer coverings or husks</note>, and <term>scoriæ</term> <note>refuse or slag from metal smelting</note> must be peeled off and purged out from the matter in order to discover its seed.

Q. What should receive the most careful attention of the Philosopher?
A. Assuredly, the goal of Nature, and this is by no means to be looked for in the <term>vulgar metals</term> <note>common, everyday metals like lead or iron</note>, because, since these have already issued from the hands of the fashioner, it is no longer to be found within them.

# The Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Paracelsus.

Q. For what precise reason?
A. Because common metals, and gold in particular, are absolutely dead, while ours, on the contrary, are absolutely living and possess a soul.
Q. What is the life of metals?
A. It is no substance other than fire, while they are still embedded in the mines.
Q. What is their death?
A. Their life and death are in reality one principle; for they die, as they live, by fire, but their death comes from a fire of fusion.
Q. In what manner are metals conceived in the womb of the earth?
A. When the four elements have developed their power or virtue in the center of the earth and have deposited their seed, the *Archeus* of Nature, during a distillation process, sublimes them toward the surface through the warmth and energy of perpetual movement.
Q. Into what does the wind resolve itself when it is distilled through the pores of the earth?
A. It resolves itself into water, from which all things spring; in this state, it is merely a humid vapor, out of which the principiated principle <note>A principle that has been given a beginning or a specific primary form.</note> of all substances is subsequently evolved; this also serves as the first matter of the Philosophers.
Q. What then is this principiated principle, which is used as the first matter by the Children of Knowledge in the philosophic achievement?
A. It is this very matter which, the moment it is conceived, receives a permanent and unchangeable form.
Q. Are Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, the Sun, the Moon, etc., separately endowed with individual seed?
A. One seed is common to them all; their differences are explained by the location from which they are derived, not to mention the fact that Nature completes her work much more rapidly in the procreation of silver than in that of gold—and so with the other metals, each in its own proportion.
Q. How is gold formed in the bowels of the earth?
A. When this vapor of which we have spoken is sublimed in the center of the earth, and when it has passed through warm and pure places where a certain sulfurous grease adheres to the channels, then this vapor—which the Philosophers have named their Mercury—becomes adapted and joined to this grease, which it sublimes along with itself. From such an amalgamation, a certain unctuousness is produced, which, abandoning its vaporous form, takes on that of grease. It is then sublimed in other places that have been cleansed by the preceding vapor, and where the earth has consequently been made more subtle, pure, and humid. It fills the pores of this earth, joins with it, and gold is produced as a result.
Q. How is Saturn <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for lead.</note> engendered?
A. It occurs when the aforementioned unctuousness, or grease, passes through places that are totally impure and cold.

# A Short Catechism of Alchemy.

Q. How is Venus produced?
A. She is produced in locations where the earth itself is pure but is mixed with impure sulphur.
Q. What power does the vapor, which we have recently mentioned, possess in the center of the earth?
A. Through its continual movement, it has the power to perpetually thin out whatever is crude and impure, and to gradually draw toward itself all that is pure around it.
Q. What is the seed of the first matter of all things?
A. The first matter of things—that is to say, the matter of foundational principles—is created by Nature without the help of any other seed. In other words, Nature receives the matter from the elements and then produces the seed from it.
Q. Strictly speaking, what is the seed of things?
A. The seed in a body is nothing more than condensed air or a humid vapor, which is useless unless it is dissolved by a warm vapor.
Q. How is the generation of seed understood in the metallic kingdom?
A. Through the skill of *Archeus*, the four elements in Nature's initial generation distill a heavy watery vapor into the center of the earth. This is the seed of metals; it is called Mercury, not because of its essence, but because of its fluidity and the ease with which it adheres to everything.
Q. Why is this vapor compared to sulphur?
A. Because of its internal heat.
Q. From what kind of Mercury should we conclude the metals are made?
A. The reference is strictly to the Mercury of the Philosophers and not at all to the common or ordinary substance, which cannot become a seed because, like other metals, it already contains its own seed.
Q. What, then, should actually be accepted as the subject of our matter?
A. The seed alone, also known as the fixed grain, and not the entire body, which is divided into Sulphur (the living male) and Mercury (the living female).
Q. What process must be performed afterward?
A. They must be joined together so they may form a germ, after which they will proceed to produce fruit that matches their nature.
Q. What is the role of the artist in this process?
A. The artist must do nothing except separate what is refined from what is coarse.
Q. To what, then, is the entire philosophic combination reduced?
A. The development of one into two and the reduction of two into one, and nothing more.

**Q.** Where must we turn for the seed and life of metals and minerals?
**A.** The seed of minerals is properly the water which exists in the center and the heart of the minerals.

**Q.** How does Nature work with the help of Art?
**A.** Every seed, whatever its kind, is useless unless by Nature or Art it is placed in a suitable matrix, where it receives its life through the cooking <note>coction</note> of the germ and by the solidification <note>congelation</note> of the pure particle, or fixed grain.

**Q.** How is the seed subsequently nourished and preserved?
**A.** By the warmth of its body.

**Q.** What, therefore, is performed by the artist in the mineral kingdom?
**A.** He finishes what cannot be finished by Nature because of the harshness of the air, which has violently permeated the pores of all bodies, though only on the surface and not in the depths <note>bowels</note> of the earth.

**Q.** What correspondence do the metals have among themselves?
**A.** To properly understand the nature of this correspondence, it is necessary to consider the position of the planets and to pay attention to Saturn, which is the highest of all; it is followed by Jupiter, then by Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and, lastly, by the Moon. It must be observed that the influential powers <note>virtues</note> of the planets do not ascend but descend. Experience teaches us that Mars can be easily converted into Venus, but not Venus into Mars, which belongs to a lower sphere. So, also, Jupiter can be easily transmuted into Mercury, because Jupiter is superior to Mercury—the one being second after the heavens <note>firmament</note>, the other second above the earth—and Saturn is highest of all, while the Moon is lowest. The Sun enters into all things, but it is never improved by those things inferior to it. It is clear that there is a great correspondence between Saturn and the Moon, in the middle of which is the Sun; but in all these changes, the Philosopher should strive to apply <note>administer</note> the Sun.

**Q.** When the Philosophers speak of gold and silver from which they extract their matter, are we to suppose that they refer to common <note>vulgar</note> gold and silver?
**A.** By no means; common silver and gold are dead, while those of the Philosophers are full of life.

**Q.** What is the object of research among the Philosophers?
**A.** Proficiency in the art of perfecting what Nature has left imperfect in the mineral kingdom, and the attainment of the treasure of the Philosophical Stone.

**Q.** What is this Stone?
**A.** The Stone is nothing else than the <term>radical humidity</term> of the elements, perfectly purified and brought forth <note>educed</note> into a supreme stability <note>fixation</note>, which causes it to perform such great things for health, as life resides exclusively in the fundamental moisture <note>humid radical</note>.

**Q.** In what does the secret of accomplishing this admirable work consist?
**A.** It consists in knowing how to bring from potentiality into activity the innate warmth, or the fire of Nature, which is enclosed in the center of the <term>radical humidity</term>.

**Q.** What are the precautions that must be taken to guard against failure in the work?
**A.** Great effort must be made to eliminate waste <note>excrements</note> from the matter, and to preserve nothing but the kernel, which contains all the power <note>virtue</note> of the compound.

**Q.** Why does this medicine heal every species of disease?
**A.** It is not because of a variety of qualities, but simply because it powerfully strengthens the natural warmth, which it gently stimulates, while other medicines <note>physics</note> irritate it with too violent an action.

**Q.** How can you demonstrate to me the truth of the art regarding the tincture?
**A.** First, its truth is based on the fact that the physical powder—being composed of the same substance as the metals, namely, quicksilver <note>mercury</note>—has the ability to combine with them during fusion, as one nature easily embraces another like itself. Second, since the imperfection of the base metals is due to the crudeness of their quicksilver, and to that alone, the physical powder—which is a ripe and refined <note>decocted</note> quicksilver and is in itself a pure fire—can easily share its own maturity with them. It can transmute them into its own nature after it has attracted their crude humidity—that is, their quicksilver, which is the only substance that transmutes them—the rest being nothing but slag <note>scoriæ</note> and waste, which are rejected during projection.

**Q.** What path should the Philosopher follow so that he may attain the knowledge and execution of the physical work?
**A.** Precisely the one followed by the Great Architect of the Universe in the creation of the world, by observing how the chaos was evolved.

**Q.** What was the matter of the chaos?
**A.** It could be nothing other than a humid vapor, because water alone enters into all created substances, which all end in a unique state <note>strange term</note>, this state being a proper subject for the impression of all forms.

**Q.** Give me an example to illustrate what you have just stated.
**A.** An example may be found in the specific productions of composite substances, the seeds of which always begin by dissolving themselves into a certain fluid <note>humour</note>, which is the chaos of that particular matter. From this, by a kind of radiation, the complete form of the plant emerges. It is nothing else but that fixed grain which Nature has infused in the first <term>congelation</term> of mercury—all metals having one origin and a common substance, as will be ultimately revealed to those who become worthy of receiving it through application and diligent study.

**Q.** What follows from this doctrine?
**A.** It follows that, although the seed is more perfect in gold, it may be extracted much more easily from another body than from gold itself; other bodies are more "open"—that is to say, less digested and less restricted in their humidity.

**Q.** Give me an example taken from Nature.
**A.** Common gold may be compared to a fruit which, having reached perfect maturity, has been cut off from its tree. Although it contains a most perfect and well-digested seed, if anyone were to plant it in the ground with the goal of multiplying it, much time, trouble, and attention would be spent in the development of its vegetative capabilities. On the other hand, if a cutting or a root is taken from the same tree and planted in a similar way, it will spring up and produce much fruit in a short time and with no trouble.

**Q.** Is it necessary for a student of this science to understand the formation of metals in the depths of the earth if he wishes to complete his work?
**A.** Such knowledge is so indispensable that should anyone fail, before all other studies, to apply himself to its attainment and to imitate Nature point by point therein, he will never succeed in accomplishing anything but what is worthless.

**Q.** How, then, does Nature deposit metals in the depths of the earth, and of what does she compose them?
**A.** Nature manufactures them all out of <term>sulphur</term> <note>sulfur</note> and <term>mercury</term>, and forms them by their double vapor.

**Q.** What do you mean by this double vapor, and how can metals be formed by it?
**A.** In order to completely understand this question, it must first be stated that mercurial vapor is united to sulfurous vapor in a cavernous place which contains a saline water, which serves as their <term>matrix</term> <note>a place or medium in which something is formed or develops</note>. Thus is formed, first, the Vitriol of Nature; second, by the movement of the elements, a new vapor is developed out of this Vitriol of Nature which is neither mercurial nor sulfurous, yet is allied to both these natures. This vapor, passing through places to which the "grease of sulfur" adheres, is joined with it, and out of their union a glutinous substance is produced—in other words, a formless mass—which is permeated by the vapor that fills these cavernous places. By this vapor, acting through the sulfur it contains, the perfect metals are produced, provided that the vapor and the location are pure. If the location and the vapor are impure, imperfect metals result. The terms perfection and imperfection refer to various degrees of <term>concoction</term> <note>the process of ripening or maturing through natural heat</note>.

**Q.** What is contained in this vapor?
**A.** A spirit of light and a spirit of fire, of the nature of the celestial bodies, which properly should be considered as the form of the universe.

**Q.** What does this vapor represent?
**A.** This vapor, thus impregnated by the <term>universal spirit</term>, represents, in a fairly complete way, the original <term>Chaos</term>, which contained all that was required for the original creation—that is, universal matter and universal form.

**Q.** And can one not, nevertheless, make use of <term>vulgar mercury</term> <note>common mercury</note> in the process?
**A.** No, because <term>vulgar mercury</term>, as already made plain, is devoid of an external agent.

**Q.** How is it that common mercury is without its external agent?
**A.** Because in the exaltation of the double <term>vapor</term>, the commotion has been so great and searching that the spirit, or agent, has evaporated, as occurs very similarly in the fusion of metals. The result is that the unique mercurial part is deprived of its masculine or <term>sulfurous</term> agent, and consequently can never be transmuted into gold by Nature.

**Q.** How many species of gold are distinguished by the Philosophers?
**A.** Three sorts: <term>Astral Gold</term>, <term>Elementary Gold</term>, and <term>Vulgar Gold</term> <note>common gold</note>.

**Q.** What is <term>Astral Gold</term>?
**A.** <term>Astral Gold</term> has its center in the sun, which communicates it by its rays to all inferior beings. It is an igneous substance, which receives a continual emanation of solar corpuscles that penetrate all things—sentient, vegetable, and mineral.

**Q.** What do you refer to under the term <term>Elementary Gold</term>?
**A.** This is the most pure and fixed portion of the elements, and of all that is composed of them. All sublunary beings included in the three kingdoms contain in their inmost center a precious grain of this <term>elementary gold</term>.

**Q.** Give me some description of <term>Vulgar Gold</term>?
**A.** It is the most beautiful metal of our acquaintance, the best that Nature can produce, as perfect as it is unalterable in itself.

**Q.** Of what species of gold is the <term>Stone of the Philosophers</term>?
**A.** It is of the second species, as it is the most pure portion of all the metallic elements after its purification, when it is termed <term>living philosophical gold</term>. A perfect equilibrium and equality of the four elements enter into the <term>Physical Stone</term>, and four things are indispensable for the accomplishment of the work—namely, composition, allocation, mixture, and union. Once performed according to the rules of art, these will beget the lawful Son of the Sun, and the <term>Phoenix</term> which eternally rises out of its own ashes.

**Q.** What is actually the <term>living gold</term> of the Philosophers?
**A.** It is exclusively the <term>fire of Mercury</term>, or that <term>igneous virtue</term> <note>fiery power</note> contained in the <term>radical moisture</term>, to which it has already communicated the fixity and the nature of the <term>sulfur</term> from which it has emanated; the mercurial character of the whole substance of <term>philosophical sulfur</term> permits it to be alternatively termed <term>mercury</term>.

<summary>This page defines the alchemical vapor as the original Chaos and distinguishes between three types of gold: Astral, Elementary, and Vulgar. It explains that the Stone of the Philosophers is crafted from "living philosophical gold," which is the purified essence of the elements.</summary>

**Q.** What other name is also given by the <term>Philosophers</term> to their <term>living gold</term>?
**A.** They also term it their <term>living sulfur</term> and their <term>true fire</term>; they recognize its existence in all bodies, and there is nothing that can exist without it.

**Q.** Where must we look for our <term>living gold</term>, our <term>living sulfur</term>, and our <term>true fire</term>?
**A.** In the house of <term>Mercury</term>.

**Q.** By what is this fire nourished?
**A.** By the air.

**Q.** Give me a comparative illustration of the power of this fire?
**A.** To illustrate the attraction of this interior fire, there is no better comparison than that of the thunderbolt, which is originally simply a dry, earthly exhalation united with a humid vapor. Through exaltation and by assuming a fiery nature, it acts on the humidity inherent to it; it attracts this humidity to itself, transmutes it into its own nature, and then rapidly plunges to the earth, where it is attracted by a fixed nature similar to its own.

**Q.** What should be done by the <term>Philosopher</term> after he has extracted his <term>Mercury</term>?
**A.** He should develop it from potentiality into activity.

**Q.** Cannot Nature perform this herself?
**A.** No; because she stops short after the first <term>sublimation</term>, and the metals are produced out of the matter which is thus disposed.

**Q.** What do the <term>Philosophers</term> understand by their <term>gold</term> and <term>silver</term>?
**A.** The <term>Philosophers</term> apply the name of <term>Gold</term> to their <term>Sulfur</term> and the name of <term>Silver</term> to their <term>Mercury</term>.

**Q.** From where are they derived?
**A.** I have already stated that they are derived from a homogeneous body in which they are found in great abundance; from there, <term>Philosophers</term> also know how to extract both by an admirable and entirely philosophical process.

**Q.** When this operation has been duly performed, to what other point of the practice must they next apply themselves?
**A.** To the preparation of the <term>philosophical amalgam</term>, which must be done with great care, but can only be accomplished after the preparation and <term>sublimation</term> of the <term>Mercury</term>.

**Q.** When should your matter be combined with the <term>living gold</term>?
**A.** Only during the period of <term>amalgamation</term>; that is to say, <term>sulfur</term> is introduced into it by means of <term>amalgamation</term>, and from then on it is a single substance. The process is shortened by adding <term>sulfur</term>, while the <term>tincture</term> is simultaneously increased.

**Q.** What is contained in the center of the <term>radical moisture</term>?
**A.** It contains and conceals <term>sulfur</term>, which is covered with a hard rind.

**Q.** What must be done to apply it to the <term>Great Work</term>?

**A.** It must be drawn out of its bonds with consummate skill, and by the method of <term>putrefaction</term>.

**Q.** Does Nature, in her work in the mines, possess a <term>menstruum</term> which is adapted to the dissolution and liberation of this <term>sulfur</term>?

**A.** No; because there is no local movement. If Nature, unassisted, could dissolve, putrefy, and purify the metallic body, she would herself provide us with the <term>Physical Stone</term>, which is <term>sulfur</term> exalted and increased in virtue.

**Q.** Can you clarify this doctrine with an example?

**A.** By expanding the previous comparison of a fruit, or a seed, which is first placed in the earth for its dissolution, and afterwards for its multiplication. Now, the <term>Philosopher</term>, who is in a position to discern what is good seed, extracts it from its center, consigns it to its proper earth once it has been well cured and prepared, and there he rarefies it in such a manner that its prolific virtue is increased and indefinitely multiplied.

**Q.** In what does the whole secret of the seed consist?

**A.** In the true knowledge of its proper earth.

**Q.** What do you understand by the seed in the work of the <term>Philosophers</term>?

**A.** I understand the interior heat, or the specific spirit, which is enclosed in the <term>humid radical</term>, which, in other words, is the middle substance of <term>living silver</term>, the proper <term>sperm of metals</term>, which contains its own seed.

**Q.** How do you set the <term>sulfur</term> free from its bonds?

**A.** By <term>putrefaction</term>.

**Q.** What is the earth of minerals?

**A.** It is their proper <term>menstruum</term>.

**Q.** What care must be taken by the <term>Philosopher</term> to extract the part which he requires?

**A.** He must take great care to eliminate the fetid vapors and impure <term>sulfurs</term>, after which the seed must be injected.

**Q.** By what sign may the <term>Artist</term> be assured that he is on the right path at the beginning of his work?

**A.** When he finds that the solvent and the thing dissolved are converted into one form and one matter at the time of dissolution.

**Q.** How many solutions do you count in the <term>Philosophic Work</term>?

**A.** There are three. The first solution is that which reduces the crude and metallic body into its elements of <term>sulfur</term> and of <term>living silver</term>; the second is that of the physical body, and the third is the solution of the mineral earth.

**Q.** How is the metallic body reduced by the first solution into <term>mercury</term>, and then into <term>sulfur</term>?

**A.** By the secret artificial fire, which is the <term>Burning Star</term>.

**Q.** How is this operation performed?

**A.** By extracting from the subject, in the first place, the <term>mercury</term> or vapor of the elements, and, after purification, by using it to liberate the <term>sulfur</term> from its bonds through corruption, of which blackness is the sign.

**Q.** How is the second solution performed?

**A.** When the physical body is resolved into the two substances previously mentioned, and has acquired the celestial nature.

**Q.** What is the name which is applied by Philosophers to the Matter during this period?

**A.** It is called their <term>Physical Chaos</term>, and it is, in fact, the true <term>First Matter</term>—a name which can hardly be applied before the conjunction of the male—which is <term>sulfur</term>—with the female—which is silver.

**Q.** To what does the third solution refer?

**A.** It is the moistening <note>humectation</note> of the mineral earth, and it is closely bound up with multiplication.

**Q.** What fire must be used in our work?

**A.** That fire which is used by Nature.

**Q.** What is the power <note>potency</note> of this fire?

**A.** It dissolves everything that is in the world, because it is the principle of all dissolution and corruption.

**Q.** Why is it also called <term>Mercury</term>?

**A.** Because it is aerial in its nature and a most subtle vapor, which partakes at the same time of <term>sulfur</term>, from which it has contracted some contamination.

**Q.** Where is this fire hidden?

**A.** It is hidden in the subject of art.

**Q.** Who is familiar with, and can produce, this fire?

**A.** It is known to the wise, who can both produce it and purify it.

**Q.** What is the essential power and characteristic of this fire?

**A.** It is excessively dry and is continually in motion; it seeks only to disintegrate and to lead <note>educe</note> things from potentiality into actuality; it is that, in a word, which coming upon solid places in mines, circulates in a vaporous form upon the matter and dissolves it.

**Q.** How may this fire be most easily distinguished?

**A.** By the sulfurous <note>sulphureous</note> waste <note>excrements</note> in which it is enveloped, and by the saline environment with which it is clothed.

**Q.** What must be added to this fire so as to emphasize its capacity for incineration in the feminine species?

**A.** On account of its extreme dryness, it requires to be moistened.

**Q.** How many philosophical fires do you list?

**A.** There are three in all—the natural, the unnatural, and the contra-natural.

**Q.** Explain to me these three kinds <note>species</note> of fires.

**A.** The natural fire is the masculine fire, or the chief agent; the unnatural is the feminine, which is the dissolvent of Nature, nourishing a white smoke and assuming that form. This smoke is quickly dissipated unless much care is exercised, and it is almost incombustible, though by philosophical <term>sublimation</term> it becomes corporeal and resplendent. The contra-natural fire is that which disintegrates compounds and has the power to unbind what has been bound very closely by Nature.

<meta>This page continues the "Short Catechism of Alchemy," shifting from the nature of philosophical fire to the identification, extraction, and timing of the work involving the First Matter.</meta>

**Q.** Where is our matter to be found?
**A.** It is found everywhere, but it must specifically be sought in the nature of metals, where it is more easily available than elsewhere.
**Q.** Which kind must be preferred above all others?
**A.** The most mature, the most appropriate, and the easiest; but above all things, care must be taken that the metallic essence is present, not only potentially but in actuality, and that there is, moreover, a metallic splendor.
**Q.** Is everything contained in this subject?
**A.** Yes; but at the same time, Nature must be assisted so that the work may be perfected and hastened; this is done by means familiar to the higher levels of experiment.
**Q.** Is this subject extremely precious?
**A.** It is lowly <note>vile/common</note>, and originally lacks natural elegance. If anyone says it is saleable, they are referring to the species, but fundamentally it is not for sale because it is useful only in our work.
**Q.** What does the Matter contain?
**A.** It contains <term>salt</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, and <term>mercury</term>.
**Q.** What operation is it most important to be able to perform?
**A.** The successive extraction of the <term>salt</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, and <term>mercury</term>.
**Q.** How is that done?
**A.** By unique and perfect <term>sublimation</term>.
**Q.** What is extracted first?
**A.** <term>Mercury</term> in the form of a white smoke.
**Q.** What follows?
**A.** Fiery <note>igneous</note> water, or <term>sulfur</term>.
**Q.** What then?
**A.** Dissolution with purified <term>salt</term>, first volatilizing that which is fixed, and afterward fixing that which is volatile into a precious earth, which is the <term>Vase of the Philosophers</term>, and is completely perfect.
**Q.** When must the philosopher begin his enterprise?
**A.** At the moment of daybreak, for his energy must never flag.
**Q.** When may he take his rest?
**A.** When the work has reached its perfection.
**Q.** At what hour is the work finished?
**A.** High noon; that is to say, the moment when the Sun is at its full power, and the Son of the Day-Star is in its most brilliant splendor.
**Q.** What is the password of <term>Magnesia</term>?
**A.** You know whether I can or should answer: — *I reserve my speech.*
**Q.** Give me the greeting of the philosophers.
**A.** Begin; I will reply to you.
**Q.** Are you an apprentice philosopher?
**A.** My friends and the wise know me.
**Q.** What is the age of a philosopher?
**A.** From the moment of his research to that of his discoveries, the philosopher does not age.

## APPENDIX VII.

---

[The manuscript of Paracelsus which is preserved in the Vatican Library is not the only treatise attributed to him under the title of *Manual*. This octavo volume, which has already supplied the material for the fourth appendix, contains two extensive collections of procedures: one devoted to chemistry and the other to medicine, which are respectively described as the *Primum* and the *Secundum Manuale*. The latter is entirely outside the scope of this translation, but the first, which follows here, would certainly have deserved a position of primary importance in its proper section if there were not serious reasons to doubt its authenticity. The preface has already stated that there are no satisfactory rules for distinguishing between the authentic and forged writings that circulate under the name of Paracelsus. The early date of the Basle octavo might be regarded as favoring its contents; it contains the *Archidoxies*, which are themselves indisputable, and it will be seen that the *Primum Manuale* claims to have been printed directly from an original handwritten manuscript. At the same time, it does not correspond in any traceable manner with what is known of the Vatican treatise, and its “demonstrative physics” would appear to belong more to the most suspicious section of alchemical literature than to serious experimental records. While this, of course, is a personal opinion, it is based upon a fairly broad acquaintance with the great masters of alchemy and on the evidence of other writings contained in the present volume which are less open to question. But whatever its actual value, it would by no means be right to exclude it because it is of doubtful authenticity, or because it is not in correspondence with what is known concerning a manuscript to which few have an opportunity of access. It has, therefore, been reserved for an appendix, where it may be accepted for what it is worth. If it is truly a work of Paracelsus, the veils of the great mystery have been folded very thickly and are not of an inviting texture.]

<summary>This introduction to Appendix VII discusses the Primum Manuale, a chemical treatise attributed to Paracelsus whose authenticity is debated due to its inconsistencies with other known manuscripts. Despite these doubts, the editor includes the text for completeness and historical interest.</summary>

# A MANUAL OF PARACELSUS THE GREAT,

*That most excellent Philosopher and Doctor of both kinds of Medicine;*

->THAT IS,<-

## A THESAURUS OF SPECIAL ALCHEMICAL EXPERIMENTS SIGNED BY THE AUTHOR HIMSELF—PARACELSUS.

---

->THE WORK ON MERCURY FOR LUNA AND SOL, WHICH I HAVE DONE WITH MY OWN HANDS.<-

Take 2 lbs. of calcined tartar and 1 lb. of quicklime. Mix them together. Place them in a well-luted vessel in a potter’s furnace so that they may be calcined and turned white. Dissolve that matter in the following lixivium <note>an alkaline solution or lye</note>. Let it stand until the calx at the bottom becomes tartar turned into water. Then distill it through a filter; afterward, take the lixivium and add 1 lb. of eggshells with 1 lb. of quicklime to it. Boil everything together so that it becomes a stone. Put this to be calcined again as before, and also place it back in the lixivium; dissolve and distill it through the filter. Treat it again with eggshells and quicklime, as described above, and repeat this three or four times; lastly, take the lixivium distilled through the filter and boil it until it congeals. Let that tartar be calcined by itself for 15 or 16 hours; then dissolve it into an oil, and in this way you will have oil of tartar. 

Then take the Mercury and sublimate it with quicklime, eggshells, and calcined sulfur three or four times. Imbibe <note>saturate or soak</note> it nine times with the oil mentioned above, and sublimate it. Preserve what remains at the bottom in a glass vessel. For whatever material ascends, imbibe it another nine times, sublimate it, and preserve what remains. Imbibe it yet again, and continue doing so until nothing ascends. Then take the mercury, grind it well, and imbibe it once more. Then dissolve it into an oil in a cold cellar. When all is dissolved, for every 6 oz. of the liquid, add 1 oz. of silver foil. Place it in horse dung so that it may be dissolved into water; and, once dissolved, coagulate it into Luna <note>silver</note>.

->INTO SOL <note>GOLD</note>.<-

In the place of Luna, take Sol, and during the imbibition of the Mercury add crocus of Mars <note>iron oxide</note> so that it may become red.

### THE LIXIVIUM IS MADE THUS:

| | |
|---|---|
| **℞** | Quicklime |
| | Wood ashes |
| | Eggshells |

of each a sufficient quantity; and boil to the thickness you know to be sufficient.

### THE WORK OF SULFUR, ACCORDING TO OUR OPERATION.

| | |
|---|---|
| **℞** | Sulfur 1 lb. |
| | Crocus of Mars 1 lb. |
| | Colcothar ½ lb. |

Place in a glazed vessel, and boil with the aforesaid lixivium <note>an alkaline solution or lye</note> until it is well reddened. Then distill, calcine the remains, repeat the operation, and do the same twelve times, or even more, until one part of it becomes red and the other remains white. Let that whiteness be distilled by itself as long as it does not burn. Then mix with oil of tartar, and let it fix the mercury. It will congeal it if it is boiled within it, and will be fixed by sublimation and putrefaction, so that one part tinges a hundred parts. Take the red part of that oil, place it on silver foil, and let it stand for a week. Afterward, purify it with ashes, and you will have good and excellent Sol <note>gold</note>. Or boil mercury in the same and a similar result follows. Hamelius first made a lixivium, and says that out of ten pounds there is scarcely one of tartar. Let it be very acid.

### CONCERNING MERCURY.

Take mercury, and pound it with eggshells. Boil it with oil of tartar, and afterward sublimate it. Repeat this fifty times. Then take that mercury, and imbibe <note>soak or saturate</note> it with oil of Luna <note>silver</note>. Having done this, add a little of the oil of tartar and sublimated mercury. Mix all together and put in a flask, well luted <note>sealed with airtight clay</note>, on a gentle fire for 24 hours, and then for four hours on a fierce fire. You will then find a stone which will perform wonders. Dissolve this in water, and the water tinges to Luna. Dissolve in it as much Luna as possible, and afterward coagulate.

### TO REDUCE THE DUST OF METALS INTO ASHES.

Take of the dust of the metal 1 quartal <note>a measure of weight, usually a quarter of a pound or similar unit</note>; borax, tartar, 1 quartal each; imbibe with oil of tartar, and afterward dissolve.

### CONCERNING STELLIONES OR SPOTTED LIZARDS.

If stelliones <note>spotted lizards</note> are distilled by descent, they yield an oil, of which it is said that it should fix mercury and convert it into Sol.

### ANOTHER.

We believe that the ashes of a stellio should convert Luna into Sol, if they are projected <note>thrown or added</note> onto Luna.

### ANOTHER.

If you pour into their stomach, by means of a reed, a quantity of *Mercurius vivus* <note>quicksilver or living mercury</note>, put it into a luted vessel, and burn it, you will find fixed mercury, which is Luna. Take particular notice of these stelliones.

### CONCERNING LIZARDS.

As we have prescribed in the case of stelliones <note>a type of spotted lizard</note>, so do we also write concerning common lizards. The virtues of these animals should be carefully noted.

### TO CUT IRON WITH IRON.

Take a leek, a radish, and some earthworms. Distill the water from them, in which you should steep a small knife for as long as may be necessary.

### AN OPINION ON THE FIXATION OF SPIRITS.

We believe that the fixation <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> of mercury can be achieved in no better way than the following: Take the whites of eggs and purify them with vitriol <note>sulfates</note>, alum, salt of nitre <note>saltpeter</note>, and colcothar <note>iron oxide residue</note>. Distill it repeatedly. Then distill it with calcined tartar and the ashes of eggshells three to six times. Then soak the mercury from the colcothar and calcined tartar with the aforementioned oil until it remains stable on red-hot iron. Place that mercury in a glass vessel and dissolve it in water. That water dissolves Luna <note>silver</note>. When it has been dissolved, put it again to digest until it is altogether turned to water. Coagulate this with water and project <note>add to a metal</note> this stone, whereupon it is dissolved and converted into Luna. It will last forever. But if you desire to turn it to a red color, take gold instead of Luna, and it is colored red with the water of the crocus of Mars <note>iron oxide</note>. Investigate concerning the calx <note>powdered oxide</note> of Luna and fixed arsenic.

### THE PREPARATION OF TUTHIA FOR PERPETUAL REDNESS.

Take some green tuthia <note>zinc oxide</note> and pound it. Mix it with salt, and place it over a fire in a well-luted <note>sealed with airtight clay</note> crucible for a day and a night. Afterward, open the crucible and sweeten <note>wash to remove salts</note> the compound. Repeat this process; then scatter Luna <note>silver</note> upon it, and it will be reddened forever.

### FOR FIXING ALL SPIRITS.

Take 1 lb. each of the salt of tartar, vitriol, and saltpeter; 5 lb. or 6 lb. each of common salt, wood ashes, oak ashes, vine-wood, and aminon <note>likely sal ammoniac</note>, along with 1 lb. of calcined tartar, quicklime, and alum. Pour acetum <note>vinegar</note> over this and let it stand for three days. Constantly shake it, and afterward set it to boil for an hour. Then let it be sealed and leave it to stand for fifteen days, shaking it five times each day. Then distill it by means of a filter and keep it. You can pour fresh acetum upon it until the virtue <note>potency</note> is thoroughly extracted. Then place a spirit in that water, congeal and dissolve it, and it will be congealed.

### THE FIXATION OF SPIRITS.

Take 1 lb. each of prepared common salt, sweet water, prepared salt of alkali, sal ammoniac, oil of urine, and tartar, and 5 lb. of honey. Place these in a glass vessel in horse dung <note>used for gentle, sustained heat</note> for a period of eight days. Afterward, take them out and let them boil gradually in succession. Then you will find a clear white stone. Project <note>add</note> this into acetum <note>vinegar</note>, and it is turned into water. With this water, soak the spirits and the calcined bodies; thus mercury is converted into Luna <note>silver</note>.

The Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Paracelsus.

### THE FIXATION OF SPIRITS.

Soak the spirit with oil of tartar, and then the oil is distilled or extracted from it. Keep doing this until it can withstand a somewhat strong fire. Take the sublimated spirit, etc., and grind it on marble with oil of tartar. Place it in an alembic <note>a distilling apparatus</note> upon the sublimating furnace, and distill the oil from it until it is perfectly dry. Do this until nothing evaporates from the coal. Afterwards, put it in a vial and bury it in dung for ten days, until it is consumed into water. Then place it in a hot furnace with a clear fire until it is congealed.

Note that you can fix the spirit with oil of sulfur, or of sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note>, and with water of white vitriol <note>zinc sulfate</note>. But for conversion into *Sol* <note>gold</note>, it must be treated with water of tartar.

### HOW SPIRITS SHOULD BE DISSOLVED.

Put eggshells, salt of alkali, and sal ammoniac into water. This water is poured on the warm or melted Spirit, and it becomes a powder. Afterwards, dissolve and congeal it. Dissolve it nine times and it will be fixed.

### THE FIXATION OF SALTS AND OF SPIRITS SO THAT THEY WILL REMAIN IN THE FIRE AND MELT LIKE LEAD.

Dissolve salt in acetum <note>vinegar</note> and place in it as much mercury as you like, along with sulfur and arsenic, and they will melt together.

### CONCERNING LIXIVIA.

Make a lixivium <note>a lye or alkaline solution</note> as strong as possible, pour oil on it, and let it stand for two days. Shake it frequently, and it will be converted into milk. Having done this, test whether it will withstand the fire. If it does, well and good; but if not, put it on again until it does withstand it, and it will be fixed. Do this for seven days, soaking and drying it over a slow fire. It will then flow like lead.

### CONCERNING THE VIRTUE OF OIL OF TARTAR.

Distill the oil from crude tartar. It is beneficial in all diseases of the joints and of the spleen, and it also absorbs ulcers.

### THE FIXATION AND TINCTURE OF SPIRITS.

Take one part of calcined tartar and a sufficient amount (*quantum suff.*) of the water of the body. Let it boil, and note that it is well soaked with oil of tartar. Distill until it is dry, and repeat this as long as the ingredients remain in the fire. Afterwards, take the spirit, grind it, and place it within a glass vessel in horse dung. Let it remain for ten days; dry the water produced from it over a fire, and thus it will be fixed. Note that you can fix spirits with oil of sulfur, with water of sal ammoniac, or with water of white vitriol. Mix the water of tartar in the sun with crocus of Mars <note>iron oxide</note>, as described above, etc.

### TO DISSOLVE TARTAR IN ONE HOUR WITHOUT A FURNACE.

Take marble and place some tartar upon it. Let it stand in water as long as possible, but in such a way that the water does not touch the tartar, and it will soon be dissolved.

### TO SEPARATE LUNA FROM VENUS IN MONEY.

### THE COAGULATION OF MERCURY.

Fill an egg-shaped crucible with mercury, fasten the opening with a lute <note>sealing clay</note>, then place it in an open vessel. Pour on lead, and leave it to cool. In this way, you will have it coagulated.

### TO REDDEN SULFUR.

Let it be distilled by descent, and afterward, let water be placed in the lower vessel. The sulfur will adhere and will be colored red.

Then know that this is the water of Luna and Mercurius <note>silver and mercury</note>, and that one ounce of the medicine should be viij <note>8 ounces</note>. And the saffron medicine which falls will be one part on a thousand. For Sol <note>gold</note> it is made thus:—

->Saltpeter ½ lb.<-
->Cinnabar ½ lb.<-

It may be dissolved perhaps in aqua fortis and make this red. Having done this, take 8 oz. of the red water itself and 1 oz. of the aforementioned medicine. What you have placed therein will descend to the bottom in the shape of a crystalline stone. Then draw off the water by means of a filter, as before, and the stones will remain at the bottom. Then take the aforementioned stones, put them in a well-closed glass vessel under warm dung for nine days, and it will be dissolved into a water. This medicine gives one part for every one thousand parts of quick mercury.

### ANOTHER GOOD METHOD.

Make an amalgam of the best mercury, carefully washed, 3 parts, and of good Luna <note>silver</note> 1 part. Then wash very carefully with salt and vinegar, until all blackness disappears. Pound the amalgam on a stone, and dry it. Steep it in urine after wrapping it in a linen rag. Take an alembic <note>a distilling apparatus</note> placed on ashes in a furnace, and make a moderate fire of coals, so that you can touch the top of the urine with your hand. Keep on decocting and pounding in this way until it is thoroughly black, for this is a good sign. Then wash it in the water of common salt, thoroughly pure, until no blackness appears. Then once more pound, decoct, wash, and dry on a linen rag until all blackness has disappeared. Put it then in a glass vessel for sublimation, when it ascends to the sides of the glass, and the Luna with it. Leave it to cool, and again mix all together; pound and decoct twelve times in succession. Then place it in a vesica <note>a flask or bladder-shaped vessel</note> with a long neck, together with sublimated sal ammoniac. Pound it with the said amalgam, and let the sal ammoniac be dissolved in warm water, or, better still, in aqua vitæ <note>spirit of wine or alcohol</note>. Afterwards, let the vesica be luted <note>sealed with airtight clay</note> and dissolve it in warm dung, changing the dung every week so that the matter shall be thoroughly dissolved, and it then becomes an elixir. Afterwards, put it in urine to evaporate, and when the water is evaporated, increase the fire so that all the sal ammoniac may ascend, and the medicine may remain fixed at the bottom. Then remove the sal ammoniac, and congeal the medicine with a slow fire, as if it were Sol <note>gold</note>, for several days, and the thing is done.

If you wish to multiply this elixir, place one part with 100 parts of quick mercury, purified and heated in a crucible. Melt it completely over a slow fire and it becomes brittle Luna <note>silver</note>. If you put one part of this to 100 parts of quick mercury, it will become the purest Sol <note>gold</note>.

### CORPORAL MERCURIES.

Take arsenic and dissolve it in aqua fortis <note>nitric acid</note>. Then take Luna <note>silver</note> and dissolve that. Join them together, and strain them as you know how. Sublimate the arsenic from the body, and it will become a sort of mass. Put it into a damp place, and it will be dissolved into mercury.

### CORPORAL MERCURY.

Take any body <note>metal</note> you will and two parts of arsenic. Pulverize, and then sublimate them. Place in hot water and it will come forth as mercury.

### CORPORAL MERCURY FROM THE METALS.

Take of any metal one part and of purified white arsenic another part. Make thin plates, place them one over the other in layers, and let them be regulated first of all in a slow fire, successively made stronger until it begins to smoke. Then pour quickly into cold water, and you will find mercury.

### MERCURY FROM JUPITER AND SATURN.

Put layer for layer of quicklime and metal <note>tin or lead</note>, and place them in a sublimatory <note>an apparatus for sublimation</note>. Set on the fire, and sublimate as you know how. The mercury ascends, adhering to the alembic <note>distilling vessel</note>, and is quickened <note>revived into liquid form</note>.

### CORPORAL MERCURY FROM SATURN.

Dissolve Saturn <note>lead</note> and put salt upon it. Shake it until it turns to a powder. Then wash it with warm water and dry it. Afterwards put it in a glass vessel and pour upon it the white of eggs and water of sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note>. Lute <note>seal with clay or cement</note> it, put it in horse dung for two days, then take it out, and you will have what you require.

### THE MERCURY OF SATURN ACCORDING TO THE EXPERIMENT OF HAMELIUS.

Take thin plates of Saturn <note>lead</note>, placed layer by layer with common salt in a vessel. Bury it for eight days in the ground. Dilute with common water, and then a part of the mercury will be found at once. Repeat the process with the rest.

### MERCURY OF ALL THE METALS.

Take some sal ammoniac, flos æris <note>verdigris or flowers of copper</note>, vitriol <note>sulfate</note>, and plates of any kind of metal. Put them in layers, and sublimate them. Place the sublimated portion in acetum <note>vinegar</note>, and you will find *Mercurius vivus* <note>quicksilver</note>. Do this until all the plates are turned into mercury.

### MERCURY FROM ALL BODIES.

Take the calx <note>powdered residue or oxide</note> of any metal and place it in acetum <note>vinegar</note>, in which there are two parts of the calx of the body and one part of sal ammoniac. Place these in dung for seven days, and the body becomes mercury. If an amalgam is made from it, together with *Sol* <note>gold</note> and *Luna* <note>silver</note>, by degrees natural mercury is fixed with it.

### CORPORAL MERCURY.

Take Saturn <note>lead</note>, and dissolve it in a tigillum <note>crucible</note>. When it is dissolved, scatter over it sal ammoniac, and stir it with a spatula until it becomes a powder. Afterwards project <note>throw or add</note> the powder into boiling water, and the salt will be dissolved.

### ANOTHER METHOD.

### CORPORAL MERCURY FROM LUNA.

### THIS IS THE FOUNDATION ABOUT WHICH ALL THE PHILOSOPHERS HAVE WRITTEN.

### CORPORAL MERCURY FROM SATURN.

Afterwards let it be divided into minute parts and salted with salt. When this is done let it be again dissolved. Pour warm water over it, and it attracts the water to itself. Then take calx of marble, put it in a closed glass vessel, well luted <note>sealed with clay or cement</note>; set it in horse dung, let it stand for a month, renewing the dung each week, and it is transmuted into mercury.

### TO CONVERT WHITE SOL INTO ALOTH.

Take oil of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note> by descent, calcined oil of tartar, and sal ammoniac in equal parts. Mix them, adding calx of Luna <note>silver</note>, and place in a phial. Set this in horse dung or in a bath of Mary <note>a bain-marie or water bath</note> for four weeks, so that it may putrefy. Open the vessel and put equal weights of pounded sal ammoniac and salt of alkali, with oil of vitriol. Putrefy as before for four weeks, and the body will be entirely converted into Aloth <note>an alchemical term for lead or a specific state of the metal</note>.

### RECEIPT OF THE BISHOP OF STRASBURG.

Take two ounces of Luna <note>silver</note> filings. Dissolve them in aqua fortis. Then distill away two-thirds of the water through the alembic. Dry it using a fustian <note>a type of thick cotton or linen cloth</note> cloth. If it does not become Mercury, sublimate it; you will then have Mercury derived from Luna.

### FREISING.

Take aqua fortis made from two parts vitriol <note>sulfate minerals</note> and one part alum. Dissolve Luna in it, then boil down the calx. Then take two parts of burnt salt of tartar, one part common salt, one part sal alkali, and one part salt of urine.

Grind these salts together with the calx of the moon, and let the amount of the salts be equal to the amount of the moon's calx. Dissolve it all in water; next, add wheat flour and a little brandy. Let it dry until it is as brittle as glass. Then sublimate it. In this way, Luna Mercurius <note>Mercury of Silver</note> is produced.

### NOTE.

Take leaves of Luna beaten extremely thin, the length of a finger and the width of a kreuzer <note>a small coin</note>. Put them into a crucible and heat them in a furnace for nine consecutive days. Purify the silver from the sulfur that emerges, and heat it five or six more times, or until the Luna yields no more sulfur. This occurs when the leaves turn black.

Mix this sulfur into a paste with quintessence of wine <note>concentrated alcohol</note>, and it will become quicksilver <note>mercury</note>. Heat it using wood from an oak or birch tree.

### THE ORIGINAL TEXT STATES.

Dissolve tartar in aqua fortis, then let it evaporate and solidify. Then dissolve the resulting stone into an oil. Pour it upon the sulfur of the moon. Stir it in a vessel with a hard wooden spoon, and you will have Mercury of the Body.

### MERCURY OF THE BODY.

Take one part sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note>, one part sublimated mercury, and one part calx of lime. Pound the sal ammoniac and mercury well together; let them melt gently. Put in the Luna <note>silver</note>, quickly take it out again, place it on a dish with water, and stir it. Then dry it with a towel or leather. You will then have Mercury of the Moon, true and good.

### ANOTHER METHOD.

Take saltpetre which has been well purified. Pound it well and put it into a cucurbit <note>a glass vessel used in distillation</note>. Set it among warm ashes, whereupon the saltpetre will boil like water. Then take the calcined Luna <note>silver</note> and put it into water. Let it stand thus, taking care so the ashes are not too hot. Then mercury of silver will be produced. Strain it through a cloth and collect the mercury.

### CORPORAL MERCURY.

Vitriol also, if it is distilled alone into water and a quantity of filings is placed therein, will in the course of time become Mercury.

### ANOTHER METHOD.

With mercury sublimated seven times, pound the calx or cinder of any metal; add flour and water. It will descend, as it will turn into living mercury. Reduce it to a cinder after solution and repercussion <note>distillation or driving back</note>, cleansing it thoroughly of saltiness and the spirits of aqua fortis <note>nitric acid</note>.

Take filings of Luna <note>silver</note>. Afterwards take mercury, which you must wash with salt and vinegar. Cook the mercury with vinegar and salt. Take three parts of this and one part of the filings of Luna. Make an amalgam and pound it well for two hours on a smooth stone. Then let the mercury evaporate. Afterwards, remove the vinegar and salt with warm water. Calcine that calx of Luna for twenty hours, and a woolly Luna <note>silver in a mossy or fibrous form</note> will be produced. After this calcination, put in the distilled vinegar. Then process the remaining calx, working as described above. Then take the extracted Luna, pound it with some tartar, and it will be live mercury.

### NOTE.

Dissolve filings of Luna <note>silver</note> in aqua fortis <note>nitric acid</note>, draw a third part through the alembic and put it in a cold place, where crystals collect. Take them and weigh them; add the same quantity of sulphur and half that quantity of sal ammoniac, etc., as seen above, in the Bishop's art.

### ANOTHER.

Take the calx of any metal and place it in vinegar, in which there have been distilled two parts of sulphur, one part of sal ammoniac, and one part of sublimated mercury. Let it be placed in dung or in the water bath for eight or ten days, then let it be distilled among the cinders, and Mercury will ascend. With this, make an amalgam of Luna <note>silver</note> or of Sol <note>gold</note>, and you will tinge all bodies. Take of sublimated mercury (as seen above), pound it with steel filings and sal ammoniac, put it into a wet place, and let it be dissolved into oil without water.

### NOTES

Take one part Mercury of the sun <note>mercury derived from gold</note> and one part crude mercury. Put it into a phial and seal it. Subject it to four or five gentle fires at first, increasing the heat gradually until you perceive the red powder. It tinges mercury and all metallic bodies. Treat the white preparation in a similar way. Take two parts Mercury of Luna <note>mercury derived from silver</note> and one part crude mercury. The finishing of the red process should be treated in the same manner.

### XVII.

Take an equal quantity of salt and sulfur and of water of arsenic. Take as much as you like of calx of Luna <note>silver oxide or residue</note>, well sweetened <note>purified by washing</note>. Put it in a cupel, and pour water over it to the height of three fingers. Let it stay for three weeks in dung or in the sun. Let it be well luted <note>sealed with clay</note>. Then place it in sand. ### ANOTHER METHOD.

Let it remain for three or four days in a tepid heat, and it will be changed into mercury.

Then take filings of Mars <note>iron</note>, well washed in sweet water until all the vitriol is removed; after which, pound them heavily in the mortar. Sprinkle the said filings with water of vitriol, then leave them to dissolve for two or three days, whereupon there will result a calx <note>residue or oxide</note> of those filings, but at the bottom of the vessel you will discover mercury.

### AUGMENT.

Take four parts of corporal mercury and one part of fine Sol <note>gold</note> or Luna <note>silver</note>. Make an amalgam in a copper vessel using an ordinary bath. Then leave it to digest for eight days. When it is fixed, augment it with common mercury again, about three times. Afterwards, augment it with crude mercury (though perhaps mercury that has been sublimated and rectified is best). Do this continually, and in eight days it will also be fixed. Or, dissolve mercury in aquafortis <note>nitric acid</note>, then let it distill over, and you will again vivify it with that augment.

### TO MAKE FIXED AUGMENT.

Dissolve Luna <note>silver</note> in aquafortis; allow half of the water to evaporate. If crystals collect, place them in a glass cup in a cellar, and an oil will be produced. Imbibe it with a small amount of augment. Place it for eight days on hot cinders with little heat, keeping the glass open. Afterwards, subject it to a powerful fire and pulverize it well.

### REDUCTION.

->Take of Minium <note>red lead</note> one part,<-
->Ceruse (otherwise litharge) <note>lead oxide</note> one part,<-
->The Fixed Augment one part.<-
Pound these three things well together. Put them into a well-luted <note>sealed with clay</note> crucible and smelt them thoroughly for an hour. Then cool it and clear away the regulus <note>the metallic button at the bottom</note>.

### MERCURY OF THE BODIES.

Take equal quantities of tartar and vinegar. Put them in a long-necked phial into oil of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note>. Inject the calx <note>powdered oxide</note> of any metal. Stir it and leave it to stand for eight days. Next, inject sal alkali and sal ammoniac in the same quantity as in the previous recipes. Place it in dung <note>as a heat source</note> for thirty days, and you will find the calx at the bottom converted into Quicksilver.

### NOTE.

->Take of Mercury sublimate half a pound.<-
->Of Sal ammoniac an equal quantity.<-
Pound them well and put them together in a glass. Let it be well luted. Put it *in carellen* <note>a sand-bath or heating vessel</note>, in warm sand. Kindle a mild fire beneath. In this way, it will become one solid mass. Remove this, pound it small, and put it in a damp compartment to dissolve <note>deliquesce</note>. Afterwards, take one marc <note>a unit of weight</note> of filings of Luna <note>silver</note>. Put it in water. This also becomes water. Coagulate it on soft ashes and reduce it to powder, of which you should inject one part upon ten parts of mercury, of purged Jupiter <note>tin</note>, or of crude mercury.

### MERCURY OF JUPITER.

Liquefy Jupiter <note>tin</note>. Then inject the same quantity of mercury and thus make an amalgam. Next, let them be well pulverized and thoroughly incorporated with water of sal ammoniac, tartar, salt of urine, and the same quantity of common salt. Place these in a flask, well-sealed, and set it in dung for twenty days, after which it will be converted into mercury.

### AUGMENT ON MERCURY OF SATURN.

->Take of Mercury of Saturn 1 ounce.<-
->of Sol <note>gold</note> 1/2 ounce.<-

The amalgam, if kept at a moderate temperature for eight days, changes into a brown powder, which becomes the finest gold. Add to it half-an-ounce of common Mercury. Again let it stand for eight days, when again it becomes a brown or a red powder, and so on with common Mercury. The case is the same for Luna <note>silver</note>, and for Mercury of Jupiter <note>tin</note> with Luna. The whole process must occupy eight days.

->NOTE.<-

Dissolve Luna <note>silver</note> in any quantity of aquafortis <note>nitric acid</note>, and in vinegar dissolve calcined tartar. Then pour the two solutions properly together, in such a manner that none may run over. Afterwards pour it into a phial, which must be well luted <note>sealed with clay</note> at the top. Set it in horse dung to putrefy for fourteen days. Afterwards put it in an earthen pan until it becomes odorless <note>inodorous</note>. Precipitate to the bottom whatever adheres to the upper part of the pan, and let it cook thus until it becomes as thick as a pottage <note>a thick soup or porridge</note>. Then let it become cold, and stir it under the tartar. If mercury collects, remove it. Then take a measure of water and gradually wash off the tartar, whereupon all the mercury will collect.

### CORPORAL MERCURY.

->Take of Luna <note>silver</note> out of sweetened aquafortis 1 ounce.<-
->of Sal ammoniac 1/2 ounce.<-

Mix. Pour over them oil of tartar, which must stand over them to the height of two fingers. Put into a glass well luted, and leave to putrefy for four weeks. Extract the moisture <note>humidity</note> from it. Sublimate the remainder. Whatever ascends is to be put in warm water, vinegar, or oil of tartar, and thus you will have Mercury.

### OIL OF TARTAR IS PRODUCED AS FOLLOWS.

Take of calcined tartar. Pour upon it the quintessence. Allow it to stand for twenty-four hours. Pour out again until at last no more oil remains in the dregs <note>fæces</note>.

### MERCURY OF THE BODY.

Take sal alkali, and pour upon it pure urine of youths, so that it may be dissolved therein. Distill it through the filter, and coagulate. Afterwards take some sal ammoniac and twice that quantity of Mercury sublimate. Grind <note>pound</note> them together, and place them over a glass slab to dissolve. Afterwards take the water thus dissolved, and pour it into a glass. Place the glass in the bath of Mary <note>a water bath</note>, so that the moisture <note>aquosity</note> may be consumed and vanish. You must then test it by means of the blade of a knife, as you know. Afterwards place therein leaves of Sol <note>gold</note>, Luna <note>silver</note>, Venus <note>copper</note>, Jupiter <note>tin</note>, or Saturn <note>lead</note>, for the space of an ordinary day. It will then be converted into Mercury.

### TO CONVERT METALS INTO MERCURY.

Drive it by descent <note>distillation by descent</note>, and the Mercury will descend. And that Mercury being heated devours all metals, until they are reduced to Mercury.

## MERCURY OF THE BODY.

->Take vitriol and<-
->saltpeter in equal quantities;<-
->of calcined alum, half a pound.<-

Make <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note>. Dissolve in it filings of <term>Luna</term> <note>silver</note>, as much as you like. Inject a little salt, and the <term>Luna</term> is precipitated. Dry the <term>calx</term>. Place it in a <term>cucurbite</term> <note>a gourd-shaped glass vessel</note>. Let it stand at the top more than the height of two fingers. Place it in horse dung for four weeks. Afterward, distill it like <term>aqua fortis</term>. Then the vinegar will ascend first, and afterward the <term>Mercury of the Moon</term>. Collect it with a hare's foot, and you will have <term>Mercury</term>. Take as much of this as you wish and put it into the <term>egg of the Philosophers</term> <note>an oval glass vessel</note>. Close it perfectly. Place it in a <term>cupel</term> made of ash wood. Subject it to a slow fire until a black powder emerges. Afterward, increase the fire until a white powder follows. Add to it half the quantity you require of the corporal <term>Mercury</term>, and a third part of reverberated <term>calx of the Sun</term> <note>gold</note>. Digest it until it becomes a red powder. Then you will obtain what you desire.

## EXTRACTION OF MERCURY OF THE MOON.

Take one <term>mark</term> <note>a unit of weight</note> of the <term>calx</term> of <term>Luna</term>; add two drams (or six drams) each of <term>oil of Tartar</term> and <term>sal ammoniac</term>. Mix them in a well-closed glass. Put the glass into cold water. Then the <term>calx</term> of <term>Luna</term> becomes solid like a cheese. Next, let it stand for a day and a night. Then leave it in horse dung for three weeks. Afterward, take it out and place it in the <term>bath of Mary</term> <note>a water bath</note> for fourteen days. Next, set it for three days on cinders so that the water may evaporate and the matter be completely dried. Then take the matter from the glass. Pour fiercely boiling water over it. Pound it for some time. Thus it will become living <term>Mercury</term> <note>quicksilver</note>, and there will be barely four parts out of one <term>mark</term>. Reduce again whatever remains.

## OTHERWISE.

Take <term>Luna</term> dissolved in <term>aqua fortis</term>. Then dissolve <term>tartar</term> into vinegar in the same quantity as the <term>Luna</term>. Pour the two solutions together drop by drop, lest it should crackle. Gently extract the moisture. Then extract from it a strong <term>Mercury of the Moon</term>. Thereupon, a grayish powder attaches itself to it. Take it and rub it with <term>oil of tartar</term> between your fingers, and it becomes living <term>Mercury</term>.

## OTHERWISE.

Take dissolved <term>Luna</term> and dissolve <term>tartar</term> in the <term>quintessence of wine</term>. Let the <term>quintessence</term> be four times as much as the <term>aqua fortis</term>. Unite these solutions, and there is a ready union without any commotion. They combine like an adhesive <term>tincture</term>. Take them out, dry them, and <term>sublimate</term> them. Then the living <term>Mercury</term> comes forth and is produced.

## MERCURY.

Take <term>Mercury</term> seven times <term>sublimated</term> and <term>revivified</term>, as you know how, and place it in a warm stove-bath. Supply the same with leaves of <term>Luna</term> to devour.

### NOTABLE ELIXIR.

### ELIXIR MAKING AN INCREDIBLE QUANTITY OF GOLD.

Take 3 ounces of new lead <note>Saturn</note> and 1 ounce of pure gold <note>Sol</note>. Melt them together. ### TRUE ELIXIR.

### FIXATION OF MERCURY INTO RED.

Take equal quantities of salt of tartar and saltpeter <note>sal nitre</note>. Make a strong <term>lixivium</term>. Inject sublimated mercury. Boil it, and when it has dried up, pour the <term>lixivium</term> in again until it turns red <note>is rubified</note>. Soften it <note>Waxen it</note> with the lime <note>calx</note> of silver <note><term>Luna</term></note>.

### TO PERMANENTLY RECTIFY MERCURY.

Take saltpeter, <term>sal alkali</term>, cinnabar, alum, flower of copper, and sulfur. Let it be soaked <note>imbibed</note> with the water of life <note>aqua vitae</note>. Afterward, let it become <term>aquafortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note>. This water dissolves mercury, and all bodies with mercury will remain in the form of a saffron <note>crocus</note> color; if it has been calcined for half a day, it will be redder than cinnabar; it does not diminish in weight and is dissolved into extremely red water. Afterward, coagulate it and, when coagulated, reduce it with saltpeter; it thus becomes gold <note><term>Sol</term></note>. If further coagulated and dissolved, one part transforms <note>tinges</note> parts <note>number omitted</note> of silver <note><term>Luna</term></note> permanently.

### <term>AQUAFORTIS</term>, IN WHICH LUNA, WHEN PLACED, BECOMES GOLD.

Take Vitriol }
Saltpeter } 1/2 lb. each
Alum 1 oz.

Precipitate the <term>aquafortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note> with crude Mercury <note>quicksilver</note>. It afterwards converts Luna <note>silver</note> into Sol <note>gold</note>.

### ALBATIO BAMBERGENSIS <note>BAMBERG WHITENING</note>.

Take any quantity of Jupiter <note>tin</note>, and the same amount of living Mercury <note>quicksilver</note>. Make an amalgam. Then take sulfur if for the red stage, or arsenic if for the white stage, and <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>, all in equal quantities. Grind them thoroughly. Place them in a well-sealed <note>luted</note> vessel. <term>Sublime</term> <note>vaporize and condense</note> for half a day with a slow fire, afterwards with a fiercer fire for a whole day, and next with an exceedingly strong one for two days. Then take what has been sublimated and set it aside. Let that which has not been sublimated undergo a further process. Then <term>sublime</term> the same from well-prepared salt, twice or thrice, until it becomes as white as snow. Take two parts of these materials and one part of filings of Luna <note>silver</note>. Arrange them in layers in a glass vessel, which must afterwards be sealed with lute. Burn with a fierce fire, so that they may be melted together. Afterwards grind, dissolve, and coagulate at least three times, and it will be an Elixir of which one part tinges eight parts of purified Venus <note>copper</note> into the best Luna <note>silver</note>.

### ARSENIC SUBLIMED BECOMES AS LUNA <note>SILVER</note>.

<term>Sublime</term> it from the <term>calx</term> <note>powdered residue</note> of eggshells, and it becomes just like silver.

### NOTE.

<term>Sublime</term> Mercury <note>quicksilver</note> that has been sublimated from Saturn <note>lead</note>; it makes lead like Luna <note>silver</note>.

### FIXATION OF LUNA <note>SILVER</note>.

Soak <term>cinnabar</term> <note>mercury sulfide</note> with oil of tartar, afterwards cement the Luna <note>silver</note>, melt it with borax, and immediately *in coloritio* <note>in the coloring process</note>. [This process seems to be unfinished.]

### SUBLIMATION OF MERCURY.

Take <term>aquafortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note>, in which you should dissolve as much Mercury <note>quicksilver</note> as you please. Then add the same quantity of common salt. Draw off the <term>aquafortis</term> through the <term>alembic</term> <note>distilling apparatus</note>. Then increase the fire, so that the Mercury may be sublimated; an exceedingly fierce fire must then be employed. Arrange in layers with that Mercury and plates of Jupiter <note>tin</note> in a damp place, and the Mercury will turn into water.
